s-hertogenbosch: 's-Hertogenbosch lies directly south of the Maas, on forested dunes in the middle of a marsh. Its name is a contraction of the archaic Dutch des Hertogen bosch, the forest of the duke. The duke was Henry I, Duke of Brabant, whose family had owned a large estate at nearby Orthen for at least four centuries. The surrounding marshes made a conventional siege impossible.

Henry I is said to have granted city rights and trade privileges in 1185, the traditional date given by later chroniclers; the first mention in contemporary sources is 1196, and the charter is lost. He founded the town to protect his interests against Gelre and Holland, and from the start he conceived of it as a fortress. Gelre and Holland destroyed it in 1203, but it was soon rebuilt.

In the Eighty Years' War the city sided with the Catholic Habsburg authorities. Prince Maurice of Orange besieged it, and it held in 1601 and 1603. Its fortifications were expanded in the years of truce, and the fortress, deemed impregnable, was nicknamed moerasdraak, the Swamp Dragon. In 1629 Frederik Hendrik of Orange diverted the rivers Dommel and Aa, built a forty-kilometre dyke to make a polder and pumped out the water with mills. After three months the city surrendered, a heavy blow to Habsburg strategy in the Thirty Years' War.

The city held against Louis XIV's army in 1672, but fell to French revolutionary troops under Charles Pichegru in 1794 after a short siege. It was part of the First French Empire from 1810 and became the capital of North Brabant in 1815. From January 1943 to September 1944 the concentration camp complex Herzogenbusch operated at Vught, a few kilometres south, holding about 30,000 inmates, some 12,000 of them Jews.

It is the capital of North Brabant. St John's Cathedral, begun about 1220, is known for its Brabantine Gothic design and the many sculptures of craftsmen on its outside. Almost continuous ramparts of the fifteenth to seventeenth centuries still surround the centre. The painter Hieronymus Bosch lived and worked here, and the house where he painted can be visited on the market square.
saad-ibn-abi-waqqas: Saad ibn Abi Waqqas was born in Mecca into the Banu Zuhrah clan of the Quraysh, to which Muhammad's mother Aminah also belonged. He was the seventh free adult man to embrace Islam, at the age of seventeen according to most reports, though Ibn Abd al-Barr gives nineteen. His mother opposed the conversion and threatened a hunger strike until he left Islam; he did not yield, and she finally gave way. Ibn Ishaq deems a wound that Saad gave a Meccan polytheist with a camel bone the first blood shed in Islam. He migrated to Medina and took part in nearly all the military operations against the Quraysh until the Expedition of Tabuk, including Badr, Uhud and the Conquest of Mecca.

In 636 the caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab sent Saad to Iraq to assist the Muslim conquest of Persia, after Abu Ubayd al-Thaqafi had been killed at the Battle of the Bridge. Saad gathered about 30,000 soldiers from the forces already in Iraq. He led the army at the Battle of al-Qadisiyyah against Rostam Farrokhzad. Muslim scholars regard the victory as the beginning of the caliphate's permanent hold on Iraq. He then marched on the Sasanian capital Ctesiphon, which the Rashidun army took, and later sent most of the spoils to Medina.

Saad founded the garrison city of Kufa, adjacent to al-Hirah, and governed it under Umar. He had a canal and a congregational mosque built there. After complaints about his conduct, Umar dismissed him, saying that he still trusted him but needed to prevent further scandals. During the First Fitna, Saad led a neutral faction that included Ibn Abbas, Abdullah ibn Umar and Anas ibn Malik, and refused appeals from the warring parties; some resented its inactivity, and his son Umar ibn Sa'd criticised it.

Saad outlived all the other nine of the ten to whom Paradise was promised, and died at about the age of eighty, around 674. Sunni Muslims honour him as one of the ten and as a companion who fought at Badr. Fifteen hadiths attributed to him are in Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim. A tradition in which he asks Muhammad how much of his wealth to leave to charity underlies the rule limiting bequests to one third of an estate.

Chinese Hui Muslim tradition credits Saad with bringing Islam to China. Scholars dispute this: Donald Leslie calls it highly unlikely that envoys went to China in Muhammad's lifetime, and many Arab historians reject it for lack of records. Tombs and mosques attributed to him remain part of Chinese Muslims' cultural heritage.
saale: The Saale is also known as the Saxon Saale or the Thuringian Saale, which distinguishes it from the smaller Franconian Saale, a right-bank tributary of the Main, and from the Saale in Lower Saxony, a tributary of the Leine. Its name comes from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning marsh, and it may also be related to a root for salt. The Slavic name Solawa, still found in Sorbian texts, comes from Old High German words for salt and water.

The river rises on the slope of the Großer Waldstein mountain near Zell in the Fichtel Mountains in Upper Franconia, at an elevation of 728 metres. It pursues a winding course northward, passes the manufacturing town of Hof and enters Thuringia, where it runs among the wooded low mountains of the Thuringian Forest until it reaches the valley of Saalfeld. At Rudolstadt it receives the Schwarza, in whose valley lies the ruined castle of Schwarzburg, the ancestral seat of the formerly ruling House of Schwarzburg.

Below Saalfeld the Saale crosses the limestone hill region north of the Thuringian Forest and passes the university town of Jena. In Saxony-Anhalt it flows past the spa of Bad Kösen, receives the navigable Unstrut at Naumburg, and continues past Weißenfels, Merseburg, Halle, Bernburg and Calbe. It joins the Elbe just above Barby after 413 kilometres, a course shortened by 14 kilometres by a bypass from a natural length of 427 kilometres.

The river is navigable from Naumburg, and an unfinished canal was planned to connect it from Leuna with the White Elster near Leipzig. The soil of the lower valley is exceptionally fertile and produces large quantities of sugar beet. The valley down to Merseburg has many castles on the enclosing heights. Among its tributaries are the White Elster, the Ilm, the Unstrut, the Salza, the Wipper and the Bode.
saalfeld: Saalfeld is the capital of the Saalfeld-Rudolstadt district of Thuringia. It lies in the valley of the Saale River north of the Thuringian Highland, 48 km south of Weimar, and the local mountain is the Kulm at 481.9 metres. Together with Rudolstadt and Bad Blankenburg it forms a tri-city area of about 70,000 people. It is a popular base for hikers on the Rennsteig, a ridge trail of 168 km, and was traditionally known for its silver mines.

Saalfeld was possibly founded by the 7th century around a fortress now called Hoher Schwarm or Sorbenburg, and it is first mentioned in a deed of 899. In 1012 Henry II ceded the former Carolingian Kaiserpfalz to Count Palatine Ezzo of Lotharingia, whose daughter Richeza left it to the Archbishops of Cologne. Archbishop Anno II founded a Benedictine abbey there in 1071, which was destroyed in the German Peasants' War of 1526. The citizens received town privileges in 1208 from the Counts of Schwarzburg, and in 1389 the town passed to Landgrave Balthasar of Thuringia of the House of Wettin. Mines, transport on the Saale and fishing, shown by the barbels in the coat of arms, made it prosper.

In 1675 Duke Albert V of Saxe-Coburg chose Saalfeld as his residence, and from 1677 Saalfeld Castle was built on the site of the destroyed abbey. His brother John Ernest IV called himself Duke of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld, and the castle was home to four generations of that line. Duke Francis's daughter Victoria became the mother of Queen Victoria, and his son Ernest III was the father of Prince Albert. Another son, Leopold, became in 1831 the ancestor of the royal House of Belgium. On 10 October 1806 a Prussian and Saxon force met a corps of the French army under Marshal Jean Lannes at the Battle of Saalfeld, where Prince Louis Ferdinand of Prussia was killed.

After the First World War Saalfeld became part of the new Free State of Thuringia. As a railway junction it was strongly affected by bombing in World War II, and in the German Democratic Republic its steam locomotive shed made it a destination for railway enthusiasts. The renovated castle is now the town administrative building. The Thüringer Symphoniker Saalfeld-Rudolstadt, an orchestra formed in 1992 by a merger, gives concerts in both Saalfeld and Rudolstadt, and the town has about 28,000 inhabitants.
saar-river: The Saar, in French the Sarre, is a right tributary of the Moselle. It has two headstreams, the Sarre Rouge and the Sarre Blanche, which both start near Mont Donon, the highest peak of the northern Vosges, and join at Lorquin. After 246 kilometres, of which 129 are in France and on the French–German border and 117 in Germany, the river flows into the Moselle at Konz, a town in Rhineland-Palatinate between Trier and the border with Luxembourg. Its catchment area is 7,431 square kilometres.

On its way the Saar passes Sarrebourg and Sarreguemines in France, then in Saarland Saarbrücken, Völklingen, Saarlouis and Merzig, and in Rhineland-Palatinate Saarburg. Among its tributaries are the Blies, the Prims and the Rossel. At Mettlach it makes the well-known Saar loop. The name comes from Saravus, the Latin name used by the Romans, which derives from a Celtic word that ultimately goes back to an Indo-European stem meaning 'to flow'.

In its middle section the Saar was made navigable in 1866 and was used to carry coal upstream and iron ore downstream. In the same year the 64-kilometre Canal de la Sarre was opened at Sarreguemines, linking the river with the Marne–Rhine Canal at Gondrexange. In 2001 the lowest 87.2 kilometres, from the confluence at Konz up to Saarbrücken, were upgraded for large Class Vb vessels, so that goods can be carried northwards, for instance to the seaport of Rotterdam. Vines were once far more widely grown on the river's banks, and before the early twentieth century the wine-growing region reached further up the river towards Saarbrücken.

The lower Saar in Rhineland-Palatinate is a wine-growing region of some importance, producing mostly Riesling. On its banks stands the Völklingen Ironworks, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Some farmers in Saarland have begun to experiment with growing wine again.
saarbrucken: Saarbrücken lies on the Saar, a tributary of the Moselle, and directly borders the French department of Moselle. Two origins are proposed for the second part of its name: the Celtic brigā, meaning hill or rock, since the castle of Sarabrucca stood on a large rock above the river, or the Old High German brucca, meaning bridge or corduroy road, since a ford lay beside the castle. The modern city was formed in 1909 by the merger of Saarbrücken, now called Alt-Saarbrücken, St Johann and Malstatt-Burbach.

The Mediomatrici settled the area in the last centuries BCE, and Julius Caesar's conquest of Gaul brought it into the Roman Empire. The Alemanni destroyed the Gallo-Roman settlement of vicus Saravus toward the end of the fourth century. The oldest document naming the town is a deed of 999 by which Emperor Otto III gave the castellum Sarabrucca to the Bishops of Metz, who granted the area to the Counts of Saargau as a fief. In 1321 or 1322 Count Johann I of Saarbrücken-Commercy gave town status to Saarbrücken and the fishing village of St Johann. From 1381 to 1793 the counts of Nassau-Saarbrücken were the main local rulers.

The Thirty Years' War cut the population from 4,500 in 1628 to 70 by 1637, and in 1677 Louis XIV's troops burned the town, leaving eight houses standing. Under Prince William Henry (1741–1768) the coal mines were nationalised, and the architect Friedrich Joachim Stengel built the Friedenskirche, the Old City Hall and, in 1775, the Ludwigskirche. After 1815 the town belonged to the Prussian Rhine Province, and coal and iron were developed, with the Burbach ironworks opening in 1856.

Saarbrücken was the capital of the Territory of the Saar Basin from 1920, when the Treaty of Versailles gave France the Saar's coal mines for fifteen years; in 1935 more than 90 per cent voted to rejoin Germany. Bombing in the Second World War killed 1,234 people and left 75 per cent of the city in ruins. France later made the Saar a protectorate with Saarbrücken as its capital, and in a referendum in 1955 over two thirds rejected an independent Saar state. The territory rejoined West Germany in 1957.

Saarbrücken is the capital and largest city of Saarland, with about 180,000 inhabitants. Its landmarks include the stone bridge of the 16th century, the Gothic church of St Arnual and the 18th-century castle. It is the seat of Saarland University and of the administration of the Franco-German University.
saarland: Saarland is a landlocked state in the south-west of Germany, with an area of 2,570 km2, about the same as neighbouring Luxembourg. It is bordered by the French department of Moselle to the south and west, by Rhineland-Palatinate to the north and east, and by a short stretch of Luxembourg. It is named after the river Saar, a tributary of the Moselle. A third of the land is forest, and the state is generally hilly. Most inhabitants live in a city agglomeration on the French border around the capital, Saarbrücken.

The region was settled by the Celtic Treveri and Mediomatrici, whose most impressive relic is the fortress of refuge at Otzenhausen. Roman rule ended in the 5th century when the Franks conquered the territory, and for the next 1,300 years the region shared the history of the Kingdom of the Franks, the Carolingian Empire and the Holy Roman Empire, divided into small territories. French kings invaded in 1635, 1676, 1679 and 1734 and founded Saarlouis in 1680. The armies of the French Revolution ended the territories' independence after 1792, and in 1815 most of the region went to the Prussian Rhine Province. Coal and heavy industry gave it importance in the 19th century.

It became a distinct political entity in 1920 as the Territory of the Saar Basin, governed by France under a League of Nations mandate. In the plebiscite of 13 January 1935, 90.8 percent of those voting favoured rejoining Germany. After the Second World War it became the Saar Protectorate under French occupation on 17 December 1947. A plebiscite on 23 October 1955 rejected the Saar Statute, which would have made it independent, and it joined West Germany on 1 January 1957. The Saar franc remained its currency until 7 July 1959.

Saarland has about one million inhabitants and is the smallest German state in area apart from the city-states of Berlin, Bremen and Hamburg. Saarbrücken is its capital and largest city. Coal mining, for 250 years a mainstay of its economy, ended with the closure of the last mine in 2012, and the Völklingen Ironworks is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its people speak Rhine Franconian and Moselle Franconian dialects, and French has a special standing in its schools.
sabac: Šabac is the administrative centre of the Mačva District in western Serbia and the traditional centre of the fertile Mačva region, on the right bank of the Sava. The name is first mentioned in Ragusan documents of 1454, and its origin is uncertain; it may come from the name of the river. The city has been known as Zaslon in medieval Serbian, Szabács in Hungarian, Böğürdelen in Turkish and Schabatz in German.

There is evidence of permanent settlement from the Neolithic. In the Middle Ages a Slavic settlement named Zaslon stood on the site, part of the Serbian Despotate until the Ottomans took it in 1459. The Ottomans built a fortress called Beyerdelen, meaning side-striker. The Hungarian king Matthias Corvinus captured it in 1476, and it stayed under the Kingdom of Hungary until the Ottomans retook it in 1521. Under Ottoman rule it was a typical oriental town with tiny streets, small shops and several mosques, with Muslims and Serbs and smaller numbers of Hungarians and Croats.

Control passed several times between the Ottomans and the Habsburg monarchy. Habsburg rule began in 1718 and ended after the Treaty of Belgrade in 1739; a second period began in 1789, when the storming of the city was one of the early experiences of Józef Poniatowski. In 1806, in the First Serbian Uprising, Karađorđe led the insurgents to one of their first victories over the Ottoman army near the village of Mišar. After the Second Serbian Uprising in 1815 Šabac joined the autonomous Principality of Serbia under the Obrenović dynasty, and from 1820 to 1850 Jevrem Obrenović, the brother of Prince Miloš, helped found a hospital, a pharmacy, a gymnasium, a theatre and a musical society. The Ottoman army evacuated the fort in 1867.

In the First World War the Austro-Hungarian army occupied and devastated Šabac, halving its population from about 14,000 to 7,000 on the orders of Kasimir von Lütgendorf. During the German occupation of 1941 to 1944 its 1,200 Jews were arrested and sent on the Kladovo transport, and reprisals after an attack on the German garrison left 1,130 civilians executed. The Yugoslav Partisans liberated the city in 1944.

Šabac grew after the war into an industrial city around the Zorka chemical plant, which had opened in 1938. A new bridge was built over the Sava and the swamp of Benska Bara was drained and turned into a residential neighbourhood. The city's administrative area had 105,432 inhabitants at the 2022 census, and agriculture, food production and raspberry growing are important in the area.
sabah: Sabah lies in northern Borneo, in the region of East Malaysia. It has land borders with Sarawak to the south-west and with Indonesia's North Kalimantan province to the south, and the island of Labuan lies off its west coast. Its total land area is nearly 73,904 square kilometres, and it is surrounded by the South China Sea, the Sulu Sea and the Celebes Sea. The west is mountainous, with the Crocker Range, and Mount Kinabalu, about 4,095 metres high, is the highest point of both Sabah and Malaysia. The Kinabatangan River is the second longest in Malaysia.

The earliest known human settlement lies along Darvel Bay, at the Madai-Baturong caves near the Tingkayu River, where stone tools and food remains show habitation 20,000 to 30,000 years ago. The site at Skull Hill (Bukit Tengkorak) in Semporna District was the largest pottery-making site in Neolithic Southeast Asia. The state has traded with China since the fourteenth century, and it came under the influence of Brunei in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. Kublai Khan is said to have sent an expedition to northern Borneo in 1292, and many of his followers and other Chinese traders are believed to have settled at the Kinabatangan River.

In 1761 Alexander Dalrymple of the British East India Company agreed with the Sultan of Sulu to set up a trading post in northern Borneo. By 1765 he had obtained Balambangan Island, where a small British factory was founded in 1773, but the British abandoned it two years later when Sulu pirates attacked. The territory was subsequently acquired by the British North Borneo Chartered Company in the nineteenth century.

Japanese forces landed on Labuan on 3 January 1942 and occupied North Borneo until 1945. The Chinese resisted, forming the Kinabalu Guerillas under Albert Kwok, and Kwok and many sympathisers were executed after the Jesselton Revolt. North Borneo became a British Crown colony on 15 July 1946. It attained self-governance on 31 August 1963, and on 16 September 1963, as Sabah, it joined Malaya, Sarawak and Singapore to form Malaysia, after the Cobbold Commission had found the union generally favoured.

Kota Kinabalu is the state capital. Sabah is a state of Malaysia, with a governor as head of state and a chief minister heading the government, in a system modelled on the Westminster parliament. Malay is the official language of the state and Islam its state religion. The state has an estimated 42 ethnic groups, of which the largest indigenous ones are the Kadazan-Dusun, the Bajau and the Murut. Its exports include oil, gas, timber and palm oil.
sabratha: Sabratha lies on the Mediterranean coast of Libya, in the Zawiya District, about 70 kilometres west of modern Tripoli. It was the westernmost of the three cities of Roman Tripolis, alongside Oea and Leptis Magna. Greek writers called it Sabrata, Sabaratha, Sabratha and also Abrotonon. The Phoenician name Tsabratan seems to be a Berber one, which suggests a native settlement existed before the trading post.

The port was established, perhaps about 500 BCE, as the Phoenician trading post of Tsabratan, an outlet for the products of the African hinterland. After the decline of Phoenicia it fell within the sphere of Carthage. Following the Punic Wars it became part of the short-lived Numidian kingdom of Massinissa, which was annexed to the Roman Republic as the province of Africa Nova in the 1st century BCE. The city was romanised and rebuilt in the 2nd and 3rd centuries CE, and reached its monumental peak under the Severan dynasty, founded by Septimius Severus, who was born at nearby Leptis Magna, expanding to nearly twice its former size.

Earthquakes badly damaged it in the 4th century, particularly that of 365, and under the Vandal kingdom in the 5th century large parts of the city were abandoned. It enjoyed a small revival under Byzantine rule, when churches and a defensive wall enclosing only a small part of the city were built, and it was the seat of a bishopric. Within a hundred years of the Muslim invasion of the Maghreb trade had shifted to other ports and Sabratha dwindled to a village.

The theatre keeps its three-storey architectural backdrop, and the site has temples of Liber Pater, Serapis and Isis, a Christian basilica of the time of Justinian, and mosaic floors, best preserved in the seaward baths and the black and white floors of the theatre baths. In 186 CE the emperor Commodus dedicated a temple to Hercules and to his own father, Marcus Aurelius; a wall painting in it showed Commodus carried to heaven on an eagle.

Italian archaeologists have excavated the site since 1921, and a British team directed by Kathleen Kenyon and John Ward-Perkins worked there between 1948 and 1951. The site was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982. Its coast is eroding, and its building stone, calcarenite, weathers easily, so that the baths, the olive press and the harbour have suffered most.
sacred-heart: The Sacred Heart is often depicted as a flaming heart shining with divine light, pierced by the lance wound, encircled by the crown of thorns, surmounted by a cross and bleeding. The devotion grew out of devotion to Christ's humanity and, in particular, to the Holy Wounds and the wound in his side. In the first ten centuries of Christianity nothing indicates that the wounded heart was worshipped. The first indications appear in the eleventh and twelfth centuries in Benedictine and Cistercian monasteries, and Gertrude the Great is named among medieval mystics who anticipated it.

The source of the modern devotion was Margaret Mary Alacoque (1647–1690), a nun of the Order of the Visitation, who said that she received revelations from Jesus between 1673 and 1675 at Paray-le-Monial. In the first, on 27 December 1673, she was allowed to rest her head upon his heart, and she then saw it with a crown of thorns, surrounded by flames and surmounted by a cross, the image that became popular. In 1353 Pope Innocent VI had instituted a Mass honouring the mystery of the Sacred Heart. In 1697 the Holy See gave the feast to the Visitandines but refused a feast common to all.

The devotion spread, especially in religious communities. The plague at Marseille in 1720 furnished perhaps the first occasion for a solemn consecration and public worship outside them. Since about 1850 groups, congregations and countries have consecrated themselves to the Sacred Heart. By a law of 24 July 1873 the National Assembly declared the Basilica of the Sacred Heart at Montmartre of public utility; its first stone was laid on 16 June 1875. Pope Leo XIII wrote an Act of Consecration of the Human Race to the Sacred Heart in the encyclical Annum sacrum on 25 May 1899, influenced by Mary of the Divine Heart, a nun in Porto.

The Feast of the Sacred Heart is a solemnity of the Latin Church, held on the third Friday after Pentecost, and June is traditionally devoted to the devotion. Practices include the First Fridays on nine consecutive months, the Holy Hour on Thursday nights, the enthronement of an image in the home, begun by Mateo Crawley-Boevey in 1907. It is closely linked to devotion to the Immaculate Heart of Mary, popularised in the seventeenth century by John Eudes. Peter Coudrin founded the Congregation of the Sacred Hearts of Jesus and Mary on 24 December 1800, and many schools, hospitals and parishes bear the name.
sadashivrao-bhau: Sadashivrao Bhau was born on 4 August 1730 at Satara into a Marathi Chitpavan Brahmin family, the son of Chimaji Appa, younger brother of Peshwa Baji Rao I, and Rakhmabai of the Pethe family. His mother died when he was about a month old and his father when he was ten, and he was raised by his grandmother Radhabai and his aunt Kashibai. He served as a finance minister during the reign of the Maratha ruler Rajaram II.

His first campaign was in Karnataka in 1746. He won his first battle at Ajra, south of Kolhapur, and took thirty-six parganas. In a later Carnatic campaign he conquered territory from the Nawab of Savanur and put down the revolt of Yamaji Shivdev.

Having seen the effect of artillery and light guns in British hands, he built similar units for the Maratha army. In 1760 he engaged Ibrahim Khan Gardi, a former officer of the Nizam of Hyderabad, who brought 2,500 trained soldiers and fifteen cannons. Within two years the infantry and artillery division had grown to 10,000 men and 56 guns.

Appointed to lead the army to Delhi against Ahmad Shah Abdali, he set out from Patdur on 14 March 1760 with about 55,000 men and roughly 200,000 non-combatants, including families and pilgrims. Unlike Malharrao Holkar and Raghunathrao he did not know the politics of the north. He disregarded the advice of Suraj Mal, the Jat ruler of Bharatpur, to leave the civilians at Agra. The army took Delhi on 2 August 1760 and then stormed the fort of Kunjpura, killing its entire garrison.

Abdali crossed the swollen Yamuna at Baghpat between 23 and 25 October 1760, surprised the Marathas and cut their supply lines. A two-month blockade near Panipat brought famine to the camp, where many civilians and animals died. On 14 January 1761 the Marathas tried to break out. After his nephew Vishwasrao, the Peshwa's heir, was killed around 2 p.m., Sadashivrao reportedly left his elephant and charged on horseback; the empty howdah led some troops to think him dead. He died fighting, and the remaining civilians were massacred. Some records say his headless body was recovered three days later, others that it was never found.

His widow Parvatibai, who had accompanied the campaign, refused the conventional life of widowhood. Around 1770 a man appeared in Pune claiming to be Sadashivrao; he was exposed and became known as Totayaa, the impostor. The Sadashiv Peth quarter of Pune is named after him.
saddam-hussein: Saddam Hussein al-Majid was born on 28 April 1937 in the village of al-Awja, near Tikrit, to a peasant Sunni Arab family. He joined the Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party in 1957. In October 1959 he took part in the attempt to assassinate Prime Minister Abdul-Karim Qasim in Baghdad; he began shooting too early, which disorganised the ambush, and Qasim survived. In July 1968 he took part in the bloodless coup led by Ahmed Hassan al-Bakr, who became president with Saddam as his deputy. As vice president he nationalised the Iraq Petroleum Company and was involved in the Second Iraqi-Kurdish War of 1974 to 1975, in which the Kurds were defeated and hundreds of thousands of Kurdish civilians were forcibly relocated.

On 16 July 1979 Saddam forced the ailing al-Bakr to resign and took the presidency, having long been the de facto leader. Days later he convened a Ba'ath assembly, claimed to have found a fifth column within the party and had 68 alleged conspirators named and arrested; 22 were sentenced to execution. In 1980 he ordered the invasion of Iran, fearing the spread of the Iranian revolution among Iraq's Shia majority. The war ended after nearly eight years in a stalemate, with somewhere around a million lives lost.

When Kuwait refused to waive Iraq's war debt, Saddam accused it of slant-drilling Iraqi oil and occupied it, beginning the Gulf War of 1990 to 1991. A coalition led by the United States defeated Iraq, and the United Nations imposed sanctions. Uprisings of Shia Muslims and Kurds that followed were repressed, and the dead are estimated at 100,000 to 180,000, mostly civilians.

The United States and its allies invaded Iraq on 20 March 2003, accusing Saddam of developing weapons of mass destruction and of ties with al-Qaeda, claims that proved false. Baghdad fell on 9 April, and he was captured on 13 December 2003. He was tried by the Iraqi High Tribunal for the killing of 148 people at Dujail in 1982, convicted on 5 November 2006 of crimes against humanity and sentenced to death by hanging. He was executed on 30 December 2006. Many Arabs praise him as a leader who stood up to Western intervention, while many Iraqis, especially Shias and Kurds, remember a dictator responsible for repression.
sadducees: The Hebrew name, Ṣəḏūqīm, means Zadokites, and the name Zadok is related to a root meaning to be right or just. According to Abraham Geiger, the sect took its name from Zadok, the first High Priest to serve in Solomon's Temple. A rabbinic work, the Avot of Rabbi Natan, tells instead of two disciples of Antigonus of Sokho, Zadok and Boethus, who took his teaching on serving without thought of wages to mean that there is no afterlife or resurrection and so founded the Sadducee and Boethusian sects.

No record of the Sadducees survives from the early period. Many scholars presume that the later sects began to form in the Maccabean era, after the Hasmonean family established an independent kingdom around 142 BCE, and it is often speculated that the Sadducees grew out of the Judean religious elite under rulers such as John Hyrcanus.

Josephus associates the sect with the upper echelons of Judean society. The Sadducees maintained the Temple in Jerusalem, and the priests presided over the sacrifices, including those at the three pilgrimage festivals. Yet not every priest or aristocrat was a Sadducee, and Cohen writes that many were Pharisees and many belonged to no group at all. Members also administered the state, took part in the Sanhedrin, collected taxes, led the army and regulated relations with the Roman Empire.

Not a line of their own writing survives, and what is known comes largely from hostile sources: Josephus, Christian records and the rabbinic tradition. The Sadducees saw the Written Torah as the sole source of divine authority and rejected the Oral Torah of the Pharisees. According to Josephus they held that man has free will and that the soul is not immortal, with no rewards or penalties after death. They denied the resurrection of the dead, a point Paul of Tarsus used to divide them from the Pharisees in the Acts of the Apostles. Many of their disputes with the Pharisees concerned ritual purity.

After the destruction of the Temple in 70 CE the Sadducees appear only in a few references in the Talmud and some Christian texts, and the group became extinct sometime afterwards. In the early days of Karaite Judaism the followers of Anan ben David were called Sadducees and claimed historical continuity with them. The gospels name them mainly among the opponents of Jesus, and the Mishnah, the Dead Sea Scrolls and later rabbinic literature all treat them with hostility.
safavid-empire: The realm's common and official name was the Guarded Domains of Iran, which remained the country's official title under later rulers until 1924. Safavid history begins with the Zahediyeh Sufi order, founded in Gilan by Zahed Gilani. Having no male heir, he married his daughter to his favourite disciple, Safi al-Din Ardabili, who succeeded him in 1301 and made the order a great influence in the city of Ardabil. The order gradually became known as the Safaviyya after him.

From their base in Ardabil the Safavids established control over parts of Greater Iran. The Qizilbash, Turkoman tribes whose name means red-heads, made up the bulk of the army, while ethnic Iranians held the posts in the bureaucracy and in cultural affairs. Ismail I took the title King of Iran, with the idea of an Iranian state stretching from Khorasan to the Euphrates.

The state rested on a division between the Turkic-speaking military and the Persian-speaking administrative elite. Shah Tahmasp began in 1540 to build a third force of ethnic Circassians, Georgians and Armenians, a process widened under Abbas I, in order to restrict the power of the Qizilbash. The shah held total power, legitimised by his descent as a sayyid. Every office had a deputy or superintendent who kept records and reported to him. Local governors were mostly Qizilbash generals, and Abbas I brought some provinces under direct royal control as Crown Provinces. The empire's population is estimated at eight to ten million in 1650.

The Safavids were not the first Shi'i rulers in Iran, but they played a crucial role in forcing Shi'a Islam on the whole country as the official religion. The Silk Road through northern Iran was revived in the 16th century, and Abbas I supported direct trade with Europe, particularly England and the Netherlands, which sought carpets, silk and textiles. In 1602 he drove the Portuguese out of Bahrain, and with help from the English East India Company he later expelled them from the Strait of Hormuz.

Abbas I recognised the commercial value of the arts, and tile making, pottery, textiles, miniature painting, bookbinding and calligraphy advanced in his time. In the 16th century carpet weaving grew from a nomadic and peasant craft into an industry centred on Tabriz, and the carpets of Ardabil were commissioned to commemorate the dynasty. Islamic philosophy flourished in the School of Isfahan, founded by Mir Damad and reaching its height with Mulla Sadra.

The Safavids made Iran the spiritual bastion of Shi'ism and the repository of Persian cultural traditions and of a sense of Iranian identity, acting as a bridge to modern Iran. They also spread Shia Islam in parts of Central Asia, the Caucasus, Anatolia, the Persian Gulf and Mesopotamia.
safed: Safed stands at an elevation of up to 937 metres, making it the highest city in the Galilee and in Israel, 40 km east of Acre and 20 km north of Tiberias. It lies above the Dead Sea Transform, which makes it one of the Israeli cities most at risk from earthquakes. It has been identified with Sepph, a fortified town of the Upper Galilee mentioned by the historian Josephus, and the Jerusalem Talmud names it as one of five elevated places where fires were lit to announce the new moon and festivals in the Second Temple period. Legend holds that a son of Noah founded it.

Little is known of Safed before the Crusaders took the area in 1101-1102, though a Cairo Geniza document shows Jews living beside Muslims there in the 11th century. The Crusaders built a large fortress in 1168. Saladin conquered it 20 years later, and his grandnephew al-Mu'azzam Isa demolished it in 1219. After a treaty with the Crusaders in 1240 a larger fortress was built. The Mamluk sultan Baybars captured it in July 1266 after a six-week siege and had nearly the whole garrison killed. He spared the fortress, unlike the coastal ones, repaired and enlarged it in 1268 and made Safed the capital of a new province spanning the Galilee. By the end of his reign it was a prosperous town.

The Ottomans conquered Mamluk Syria in 1516-1517, and Safed became the capital of the Safed Sanjak. The stability that followed brought nearly a century of growth, in which Jewish immigrants from across Europe made the city a centre of wool and textile production and of the mystical Kabbalah movement; it became known as one of the Four Holy Cities of Judaism. It declined in the 17th and 18th centuries. Druze and Muslim locals raided the Jewish community in 1834 and 1838, and many Jews died in the earthquake of 1837; Moses Montefiore's philanthropy helped rebuild synagogues and homes. Towards the end of the 19th century the population reached 24,000, divided roughly equally between Jews and Muslims, with a small Christian community.

Safed became part of the State of Israel in 1948 and now has an almost entirely Jewish population of 38,687 in 2024, including a large Haredi community. It remains a centre of Jewish religious studies. Its old Jewish quarter holds 32 synagogues, among them those named for Abuhav, Alsheich, Karo and Isaac Luria. The ruins of the Crusader and Mamluk castle still stand on Citadel Hill, and Mamluk buildings include the Red Mosque, completed in 1275. In the 1950s and 1960s the city was known as Israel's art capital, and its Artists' Quarter still holds galleries. Its mild summers and scenic views make it a holiday resort.
saffarid-dynasty: The Saffarid dynasty was a culturally Persianate dynasty of eastern Iranian origin that ruled parts of Persia, Khorasan and eastern Makran from 861 to 1002, and was one of the first indigenous Persian dynasties to emerge after the Islamic conquest. Its founder, Ya'qub ibn al-Layth al-Saffar, was born in 840 at Karnin, east of Zaranj and west of Bost, in what is now Afghanistan. A native of Sistan and a local ayyar, he worked as a coppersmith before becoming a warlord. He moved to Zaranj, left his trade and gained the power to act as an independent ruler.

From his capital Zaranj, Ya'qub moved east into Arachosia, Zamindawar and Kabul; by 865 he had vanquished the Zunbils and forced the Hindu Shahis to move to Udabhanda. He then invaded Bamyan, Balkh, Badghis and Ghor, territories ruled mostly by Buddhist tribal chiefs, taking vast plunder and slaves. The Tahirid city of Herat fell in 870, and the Saffarids annexed Khorasan in 873. They turned west to Khuzestan, Kerman and Fars, and in 876 came within a few days' march of Baghdad before the Abbasid army turned them back. Silver mines in the Panjshir Valley let them mint silver coins. The Abbasids recognised Ya'qub as governor of Sistan, Fars and Kerman, but he had no concept of centralised government.

Ya'qub's brother and successor Amr ibn al-Layth was defeated at Balkh by Ismail Samani and lost Khorasan, leaving the Saffarids Fars, Kerman and Sistan. Under Tahir ibn Muhammad (901–908) they fought the Abbasids for Fars, but a civil war broke out in 908 and the governor of Fars defected to the Abbasids. In 912 the Samanids expelled them from Sistan, which they later regained under Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn Muhammad, though only as a minor power. In 1002 Mahmud of Ghazni invaded Sistan and dethroned Khalaf ibn Ahmad, ending the dynasty.

The Saffarids patronised Persian in court poetry and gave impetus to a renaissance of New Persian literature. After Ya'qub's conquest of Herat, when some poets praised the victory in Arabic, he asked his secretary Muhammad ibn Wasif al-Sistani to compose the verses in Persian.

The religion of Ya'qub is debated, since most sources are hostile and contradict one another: Ibn Khallikan calls him a Kharijite, Nizam al-Mulk an Isma'ili, and the Abbasid caliph's propaganda even claimed he was a Christian. The only contemporary source, al-Ya'qubi, called him a righteous holy warrior fighting on the caliph's command. D. G. Tor argues that Ya'qub was a pious Sunni holy warrior in the tradition of the volunteer frontier fighters, supported by leading hadith scholars, an argument A. C. S. Peacock has called convincing.
saga-prefecture: Saga Prefecture occupies the north-western corner of Kyushu, an isthmus-like area between the Genkai Sea and the Tsushima Strait to the north and the Ariake Sea to the south. It borders Fukuoka Prefecture to the northeast and Nagasaki Prefecture to the southwest and covers about 2,439 square kilometres. Its nearness to mainland Asia made it an important gateway for the transmission of culture and trade throughout Japanese history. Outside the cities of Saga and Karatsu it is largely rural, and agricultural and forested land makes up over 68 per cent of its area.

In ancient times the area of Saga and Nagasaki prefectures was called Hizen Province, and the present name dates from the Meiji Restoration. Rice farming has flourished here since ancient times, and its traces survive at the ruins of Nabatake in Karatsu and at the Yoshinogari site, where villages flourished in the middle of the Yayoi period. The Mongol invasions of Japan began here with the Battle of Bun'ei in 1274 and the Battle of Kōan in 1281, and in 1591 Nagoya Castle was built for the Japanese invasions of Korea.

In the Sengoku period the Ryūzōji clan extended its control over all of Hizen and Chikugo and parts of Higo and Chikuzen. After the death of Ryūzōji Takanobu, Nabeshima Naoshige took control, and by 1607 the whole Ryūzōji domain was in Nabeshima hands. In the Edo period the Saga Domain, with its three sub-domains, remained under the Nabeshima and was politically stable, though the cost of defending Nagasaki and disasters such as the Kyōhō famine and the Siebold Typhoon of 1828 strained its finances. Land reclaimed from the Ariake Sea roughly doubled its yield in koku over two centuries.

Nabeshima Naomasa reformed the domain's finances in the middle of the 19th century and encouraged Arita porcelain, green tea and coal. Technologies such as the reverberatory furnace and models of steam locomotives arrived through the nearby port of Nagasaki. Many people from the domain assisted the Meiji Restoration. After the han system was abolished in 1871 the area was merged into Imari Prefecture, renamed Saga Prefecture in 1872, absorbed into Nagasaki Prefecture in 1876 and set up again as a separate prefecture in 1883. The Saga Rebellion took place in February 1874.

The prefecture has a population of roughly 780,000. Saga is its capital and largest city, and other major cities include Karatsu, Tosu and Imari. Its western region is known for ceramics and porcelain, particularly in Karatsu, Imari and Arita. All of its coal mines closed in 1972 with the closing of the Nishiki mine, and the Yoshinogari History Park opened to the public in 1992.
sagunto: Sagunto lies about 30 km north of the centre of Valencia, on the Costa de Valencia on the Mediterranean, in the fertile comarca of Camp de Morvedre. The municipality has three urban nuclei: the old town, Ciutat Vella, Grau Vell and Puerto de Sagunto, and over half its population lives in the coastal settlement of Puerto de Sagunto. The old town climbs the hill that carries the castle, above the plain.

In the 5th century BCE the Iberians built a walled settlement on the hill, known as Arse; a stretch of cyclopean limestone slabs from the former Temple of Diana survives near the church of Santa Maria. The city traded with coastal colonies such as Carthage and minted its own coins. By 219 BCE Saguntum was a large, prosperous town that sided with Rome against Carthage, and Hannibal besieged it first; after eight months of stiff resistance it fell, and the siege triggered the Second Punic War.

The Romans retook it seven years later, and in 214 BCE it became a municipium. They built a great circus and a theatre seating 8,000, and texts suggest an amphitheatre and about 50,000 inhabitants. Its Catholic patron saint was Bishop Sacerdos, who died about 560.

After the Arab conquest in the early 8th century the town was called Morvedre, from the Latin muri veteres, "ancient walls". El Cid conquered it in 1098, but the Muslims soon recovered it, and James I of Aragon took it in 1238. During the Peninsular War a Spanish attempt to relieve the French siege of the castle failed at the Battle of Saguntum on 25 October 1811, and much of the Roman theatre was dismantled for stone to restore the walls.

A Jewish community lived in the town under Muslim rule; after the massacre of 1391 it was the only surviving community in Valencia, and about 500 Jews left at the expulsion of 1492. A steel industry grew up in the late 19th century, and the last steel oven closed in April 1984.

The remains of Sagunto Castle, with ramparts of Roman and Moorish origin, crown the hill. The Roman theatre on its northern slope, partly restored in the late 20th century, was the first official National Monument declared in Spain, in 1896. The town also has the Gothic church of Santa Maria, the neoclassical Palau Municipal, one of the best-preserved Jewish quarters in Spain and a history museum in the Jewish quarter, whose largest collection is from the Ibero-Roman period.
sahara: The Sahara covers about 9,200,000 square kilometres, 31 per cent of the African continent, and is the largest hot desert in the world. It stretches from the Red Sea in the east and the Mediterranean in the north to the Atlantic, and excludes the fertile Mediterranean coast, the Atlas Mountains of the Maghreb and the Nile Valley. To the south it is bounded by the Sahel, a belt of semi-arid tropical savanna. The name comes from the Arabic ṣaḥrāʾ, meaning desert.

Its landscape includes hamada, or rocky plateaus, ergs, or sand seas whose dunes often rise over 180 metres, gravel plains, dry valleys called wadis, and salt flats. Mountain massifs rise from it, among them the Ahaggar, the Tibesti and the Aïr, and Emi Koussi in the Tibesti is its highest peak. The central Sahara is hyperarid and may go years without rain, and the Libyan Desert is among the driest and sunniest places on Earth. Trees and taller shrubs grow in the wadis and oases, and the vegetation at the margins is sparse grassland and desert shrub.

For several hundred thousand years the Sahara has alternated between desert and savanna grassland in a cycle of about 20,000 years, caused by the precession of Earth's axis, which shifts the North African monsoon. Scientists have identified more than 230 humid periods in North Africa over the past eight million years. The Green Sahara of the most recent humid period was home to Epipaleolithic, Mesolithic and pastoral peoples, whose rock art survives. The remains of a child at Uan Muhuggiag and of another at Tin Hanakaten have been examined in modern laboratories.

From around 7,500 years ago, populations associated with European Neolithic farmers moved into north-western Africa from the Iberian Peninsula, and pastoralists from the Levant also reached the region. The proto-Berber tribes evolved from these prehistoric communities during the late Bronze and early Iron Ages. Archaeological evidence shows that Nilo-Saharan speaking groups lived in the central and southern Sahara before Berber and Arabic speakers, who now largely populate it, arrived around 1,500 years ago.

The Sahara covers large parts of Algeria, Chad, Egypt, Libya, Mali, Mauritania, Niger, Western Sahara and Sudan, and parts of southern Morocco and Tunisia. Its peoples include the Amazigh, among them the Tuareg, the Hassaniya-speaking Sahrawis, the Toubou, Nubians, Zaghawa, Kanuri, Hausa, Songhai, Beja and Fulani. The Haratins are believed to descend largely from ancient black populations of the desert. Arabic dialects are the most widely spoken languages, followed by Berber languages and Beja, all of the Afro-Asiatic family. The Richat Structure in Mauritania is among its unusual landforms.
sahel: The Sahel is a biogeographical region of Africa, the transition zone between the more humid Sudanian savannas to the south and the drier Sahara to the north. It spans 5,900 kilometres from the Atlantic Ocean to the Red Sea, in a belt several hundred to a thousand kilometres wide, and has a hot semi-arid climate. The name comes from the Arabic word sāḥil, coast or shore, explained as a figurative reference to the southern edge of the Sahara. Rainfall varies from around 100 to 200 millimetres a year in the north to 700 to 1,000 in the south.

Around 4000 BCE the climate of the Sahara and the Sahel began to dry at great speed. Lakes and rivers shrank and the land became more desert, and farming communities migrated to the more humid climate of West Africa. For hundreds of years the region has had frequent droughts; one megadrought lasted 250 years, from 1450 to 1700. The larger Sahelian kingdoms emerged from 750 CE and founded several large cities in the Niger valley, among them Timbuktu, Gao and Djenné.

In the eastern Sahel the Christian Nubian kingdom of Alodia was first mentioned in 569 and reached its zenith from the 9th to the 12th century; its capital Soba, near present-day Khartoum, was described as a city of extensive dwellings and churches.

With the forest-savanna mosaic to their south, the Sahelian states could not expand into the forest, because mounted warriors were ineffective there and horses and camels were susceptible to the humidity and diseases of the tropics. The western Sahel fell to France in the late 19th century as part of French West Africa, and Chad was added in 1900 as part of French Equatorial Africa. The French territories were decolonised in 1960. The eastern Sahel was conquered by Muhammad Ali of Egypt in the 1820s, came under British rule by 1899 and was granted independence in 1956.

Traditionally most people of the Sahel have been semi-nomads who farm and raise livestock in a system of transhumance, grazing herds in the drier north during the wet season and trekking hundreds of kilometres south in the dry period. Its peoples include the Fulani, Tuareg, Hausa, Dogon, Songhai, Mande, Kanuri and Arabs. Trans-Saharan trade routes and the spread of Islam created strong historical connections between many Sahelian peoples and Arab communities, which influenced language, religion and social customs.
saigo-takamori: Saigō Takamori was born in Kagoshima, the castle town of Satsuma Domain, on 23 January 1828, into a low-ranking samurai family that faced financial hardship. His father was a division chief in the domain's exchequer. At sixteen he began work in a county office, inspecting farm villages and collecting taxes, which made him aware of the peasants' hardships. In 1854 he became an attendant of the daimyō Shimazu Nariakira, a progressive leader keen on Western learning, and relayed his secret messages as his Edo gardener. Nariakira's sudden death in July 1858 left him exposed.

Facing arrest in the Ansei Purge, Saigō attempted suicide in November 1858 by throwing himself into Kagoshima Bay with the monk Gesshō, who drowned. Satsuma declared him dead and exiled him to Amami Ōshima, and after a quarrel with Shimazu Hisamitsu in 1862 he was sent to the harsher island of Okinoerabujima. Recalled in 1864, he was persuaded by Katsu Kaishū that the shogunate was doomed and worked towards the Satchō Alliance of 1866, brokered by Sakamoto Ryōma.

The Boshin War began in January 1868 at Toba–Fushimi. Saigō commanded the imperial forces and in April negotiated with Katsu Kaishū the bloodless surrender of Edo Castle. In the new government he helped create the Imperial Guard, which backed the abolition of the han system in July 1871. In 1873 he proposed to go to Korea as envoy, expecting his uncompromising stance, or his killing, to give Japan a cause for war. Ōkubo Toshimichi and Iwakura Tomomi opposed it; when the plan was rejected in October 1873 he resigned and went home to Kagoshima.

In Kagoshima Saigō founded private schools in 1874 that became centres of anti-government feeling. In January 1877 the government tried to remove munitions from the arsenal, and students of the schools seized it. Saigō reluctantly led them and set out on 15 February 1877. The siege of Kumamoto Castle lasted 54 days, and the rebels were defeated at Tabaruzaka. On 24 September 1877, wounded at Shiroyama, he was beheaded by his associate Beppu Shinsuke; the usual account says by his own request after seppuku, though an autopsy found no abdominal wound.
His death made him a tragic hero. On 22 February 1889 he was posthumously pardoned and his court rank restored, and a bronze statue of him with his dog was unveiled in Ueno Park, Tokyo, in 1898.
sail: A sail provides propulsive force through a combination of lift and drag, depending on its angle with respect to the apparent wind, the air velocity felt on the moving craft. A sail may be attached to a mast, boom or other spar and is typically raised by a line called a halyard, while its angle to the wind is controlled by a line called a sheet. Sailing craft use two types of rig: the square rig, with the main sails on horizontal yards set square to the keel, and the fore-and-aft rig, with sails set along the line of the keel.

The invention of the sail has been judged by some to be as important as the wheel, or as the Neolithic way of life, but it is not known when or where it took place. Early water transport is believed to have developed in two nursery areas, Island Southeast Asia and the Mediterranean, where warm waters and intervisible islands encouraged travel. The Nile, which flows north against a prevailing wind, offered a way to drift in one direction and sail in the other. Many do not consider sails to have been used before the 5th millennium BCE, while others place their invention much earlier.

Sails from ancient Egypt are depicted around 3200 BCE, and the Sumerians used square-rigged boats at about the same time and are believed to have established sea trading routes as far as the Indus valley. Greeks and Phoenicians began trading by ship by around 1200 BCE.

Lateen sails emerged in the Mediterranean by around the 2nd century CE and became common in the 5th century, probably as a cost-saving simplification of the square rig. Maritime historians have often wrongly presumed that the lateen sailed far better; analysis of voyages and replica vessels shows the two performed very similarly. The popularity of the caravel in Northern European waters from about 1440 made lateen sails familiar there, and they were used as mizzens on early three-masted ships as balancing sails.

The Austronesian peoples developed catamarans, outriggers and the bi-sparred triangular crab claw sail, which let them cross open ocean. From Taiwan they settled the islands of Maritime Southeast Asia and later Micronesia, Island Melanesia, Polynesia and Madagascar. Their sails were woven from salt-resistant leaves, usually pandan, and the proto-Austronesian word for sail dates to about 3000 BCE. In western Island Southeast Asia the tanja and junk rigs later evolved from the crab claw sail.
saint-barthelemy: Saint Barthélemy lies about 30 kilometres southeast of Saint Martin, northeast of Saba and Sint Eustatius and north of Saint Kitts and Nevis. It is a volcanic island, encircled by shallow reefs, with an area of 25 square kilometres. Its highest peak is Morne de Vitet, at 286 metres. The climate is essentially arid, and the hills have poor soil that supports mostly cacti and succulent plants. Its capital and main harbour is Gustavia, built in a U-shaped cove on the west coast.

Before European contact the island was possibly visited by Taíno and Arawak people, but it was probably not permanently inhabited because it lacked fresh water. Christopher Columbus was the first European to encounter it, in 1493, and named it in honour of his younger brother Bartholomew Columbus and Bartholomew the Apostle. By 1648 French settlers had arrived, encouraged by Phillippe de Longvilliers de Poincy of the French West India Company, and they began cultivating cacao. Caribs attacked the settlement in 1656 and it was briefly abandoned.

The island proved economically unsuccessful and was troubled by pirates. British forces captured it in 1744 and it returned to French control in 1764. In 1784 King Louis XVI, deeming it of little worth, traded it to Sweden in return for trading privileges in Gothenburg. The Swedes declared Gustavia, named after Gustav III, a free port, which brought prosperity from trade, and built three forts. British forces occupied the island in March 1801, and the outnumbered Swedes surrendered without resistance. It remained a Swedish colony for nearly a century and returned to French rule after a referendum.

On 19 March 1946 the people of the island became French citizens with full rights. For many years it was a commune forming part of Guadeloupe, and in 2003 its voters chose to separate. It became a separate overseas collectivity of France in February 2007. The Three Crowns of the Swedish arms appear in its coat of arms. The language, cuisine and culture are French Caribbean, the euro is the currency, and the economy rests on tourism and duty-free retail.
saint-basils-cathedral: The site was a busy marketplace between the gate of the Moscow Kremlin and the outlying settlement. Its centre was marked by the Trinity Church, built of white stone. Ivan IV marked each victory of the Russo-Kazan War by building a wooden memorial church beside Trinity Church, and by the end of his Astrakhan campaign it was surrounded by seven wooden churches. In the autumn of 1554, according to Nikon's Chronicle, he ordered a wooden Church of the Intercession on the moat, and a year later a new stone cathedral on the site of Trinity Church to commemorate his campaigns. Dedicating a church to a military victory was a major innovation in Muscovy.

The building was consecrated on 12 July 1561 as Trinity Church, after its easternmost sanctuary. Its popular name Jerusalem arose in the late 16th century, and the name of Vasily the Blessed, who died during construction and was buried on the site, was attached to it at the beginning of the 17th century.

Ivan's architects chose a symmetrical plan with eight side churches around a central core. The core and the four larger churches on the compass points are octagonal, and the four smaller churches between them are cuboid. The central Church of the Intercession is 46 metres tall inside but has a floor area of only 64 square metres. The foundations are of white stone and the churches of red brick, then a relatively new material, and restorers in 1954–1955 found that the brick walls conceal a wooden frame, built as a life-size model of the cathedral and gradually enclosed in masonry.

The building has no analogue in earlier or later Muscovite architecture, and the sources that inspired its builders Barma and Postnik are disputed. Nineteenth-century Russian writers, starting with Ivan Zabelin, stressed the vernacular wooden churches of the Russian North, while a modern hypothesis sees it as a recreation of the Qolşärif Mosque at Kazan. A chapel over the grave of Vasily was added in 1588, and in 1680–1683 arcades and galleries joined the nine churches into one monolithic building.

In the 16th and 17th centuries the church was perceived as the earthly symbol of the Heavenly City, and it served as an allegory of the Jerusalem Temple in the Palm Sunday parade, in which the tsar led the patriarch of Moscow on a donkey. Under the Soviet Union's antireligious campaigns it was confiscated from the Russian Orthodox community and has been part of the State Historical Museum since 1928. It became part of the Moscow Kremlin and Red Square UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1990, and weekly liturgical celebrations have been restored since 1997. The Russian historian Dmitry Shvidkovsky wrote that it is like no other Russian building.
saint-boniface: The earliest life of Boniface does not give his place of birth. It says that as a boy he attended a monastery ruled by Abbot Wulfhard in a place called escancastre, which seems to denote Exeter. Later tradition places his birth at Crediton, but the earliest mention of Crediton in this connection dates from the early fourteenth century. His English name is recorded as Winfrid or Winfred. Before leaving for the continent he wrote a grammatical treatise, the Ars Bonifacii, and a collection of twenty acrostic riddles, the Enigmata.

Boniface first left for the continent in 716 and went to Utrecht, where Willibrord had worked among the Frisians since the 690s. Their preaching was frustrated by the war between Charles Martel and Radbod, King of the Frisians, and he returned to Nursling. The next year he went straight to Rome, where Pope Gregory II renamed him Boniface after a fourth-century martyr and appointed him missionary bishop for Germania, a bishop without a diocese in a region that lacked any church organisation. He never returned to England but kept up a correspondence with his countrymen and kinsfolk.

The support of the Frankish mayors of the palace and later the Carolingians was essential; he was under the protection of Charles Martel from 723. The Frankish leaders wished to defeat the pagan Saxons and incorporate their lands, and his destruction of pagan sites may have helped them. Pope Gregory III made him Archbishop of Mainz. Through his efforts to reorganise and regulate the Frankish church he helped shape the Latin Church in Europe, and many of the dioceses he proposed remain.

According to the vitae, Boniface never gave up hope of converting the Frisians, and in 754 he set out for Frisia with a retinue. He baptised many and summoned a meeting for confirmation near Dokkum, but armed robbers appeared instead and killed the aged archbishop along with 52 others. His remains were returned to Fulda, where veneration began at once; a decorative tomb followed about ten years after his burial, and in 819 his relics were moved to a new apse of the rebuilt abbey church. His feast day is 5 June.

His life became widely known through several vitae, notably the near-contemporary life by Willibald, and through about 150 letters of the Bonifatian correspondence, assembled by order of his successor at Mainz, Lullus. Anniversaries have been marked in Germany since 1805, and Pope John Paul II prayed at his grave in 1980. Tradition credits him with inventing the Christmas tree.
saint-catherines-monastery: The oldest record of monastic life at Mount Sinai is the Itinerarium Egeriae, the travel journal of a Christian pilgrim named Egeria, written about 381/2 to 386. The monastery itself was built between 548 and 565 by order of Justinian I, around a Chapel of the Burning Bush attributed to Empress Helena, mother of Constantine I, at the place where Moses is said to have seen the burning bush. It also encloses the Well of Moses, where Moses is said to have met his future wife Zipporah.

Centuries later the body of Catherine of Alexandria was said to have been found in a cave nearby; her relics made it a pilgrimage site, and it was renamed after her. Its king post truss is the oldest known surviving roof truss in the world.

In the seventh century the isolated anchorites of Sinai were eliminated and only the fortified monastery remained. Until the twentieth century access was through a door high in its walls. During the Fatimid Caliphate a chapel was converted into a mosque, and a Fatimid mosque of 1106 is preserved. In the Middle Ages the community was multiethnic, with Arab, Greek, Syrian, Slavonic and Georgian monks; in the Ottoman period it became almost entirely Greek Orthodox.

During the Crusades both Byzantine emperors and the rulers of the Kingdom of Jerusalem patronised it. From the 1480s Wallachian princes sent alms. In the mid-14th century there were several hundred monks, and a century later only several dozen, as Bedouins harassed the community.

The monastery and its dependencies form the Church of Sinai, headed by an archbishop who is also abbot. Its administrative status is ambiguous: the church itself regards it as autocephalous, others as autonomous under the Greek Orthodox Patriarchate of Jerusalem.

The library, founded between 527 and 565, holds manuscripts in Greek, Syriac, Georgian, Arabic, Armenian, Church Slavonic and other languages. Constantin von Tischendorf found the Codex Sinaiticus there in 1844 and 1859. It left for Russia, was sold by Stalin to the British Museum in 1933, and is now in the British Library. In 1892 Agnes Smith Lewis found the Syriac Sinaiticus, which remains at the monastery.

Since 2011 the Sinai Palimpsests Project has imaged the palimpsests, among them those found in 1975, recovering over 6,800 pages by June 2018. The icon collection begins with a few from the 5th and 6th centuries and holds over 120 icons in the hybrid style of Crusader art. UNESCO made the monastery a World Heritage Site in 2002.
saint-cloud: Saint-Cloud lies in the western suburbs of Paris, about 10 kilometres from the centre, on the Seine. According to the account of its name, Clodoald, a grandson of Clovis, sought refuge in a hamlet on the river then called Novigentum, one of many newly founded mercantile settlements outside the traditional towns. After Clodoald was canonised, the village where his tomb stood took the name Sanctus Clodoaldus.

The Château de Saint-Cloud was built in 1572. It was the residence of several French rulers and served as the main country residence of the cadet Orléans line until the French Revolution. Henri III of France was assassinated at Saint-Cloud in 1589, and Henrietta of England lived and died in the château in 1670. Philippe d'Orléans lived there from 1658 until his death in 1701. The palace was also the site of the coup d'état led by Napoleon Bonaparte that overthrew the French Directory in 1799, and Napoleon lived there as ruler. The château was destroyed by fire in 1870 during the Franco-Prussian War.

The town was also known for Saint-Cloud porcelain, produced there from 1693 to 1766. Its Hôtel de Ville was completed in 1874. The headquarters of the International Criminal Police Organization (Interpol) stood at 22 Rue Armengaud from 1966 until 1989, when it moved to Lyon.

The main landmarks are the park of the demolished château and the Pavillon de Breteuil, which houses the International Bureau of Weights and Measures. The Saint-Cloud Racecourse was built by Edmond Blanc in 1901 and hosts the annual Grand Prix de Saint-Cloud. On the Avenue de Longchamp a bronze statue of Icarus, inaugurated on 19 October 1913, honours the Brazilian aviation pioneer Alberto Santos-Dumont, who made his experiments near the old Aerostation of Saint-Cloud and built the world's first hangar. The original hangar was destroyed for its bronze during the German occupation, and a replica has stood on its site since 1952.
saint-dominic: Dominic was born in Caleruega in Old Castile and named after Dominic of Silos, whose Benedictine abbey lies a few miles to the north. At fourteen he was sent to the Premonstratensian monastery of Santa María de La Vid and then to the schools of Palencia, where he spent six years on the arts and four on theology. In 1191, in a famine, he is reported to have sold his clothes, furniture and manuscripts to feed the hungry. Ordained at twenty-four, he joined the canonry of the Cathedral of Osma, and in 1198 Bishop Martin de Bazan made him subprior of the chapter.

Around 1203 or 1204 he accompanied Bishop Diego de Acebo on a diplomatic mission for Alfonso VIII of Castile to Denmark. On the way home they met Cistercian monks sent by Pope Innocent III to preach against the Cathars, and concluded that the monks failed because their pomp contrasted with Cathar asceticism. Dominic and Diego adopted a more ascetic life and began preaching in the south of France. In late 1206 they settled at Prouille, where Dominic gave the Rule of St. Augustine to a house partly meant for women who had lived in Cathar religious houses. After Diego died in December 1207, Dominic continued alone. Dominican tradition says that in 1208 he saw a vision of Mary at Prouille who gave him a rosary.

In 1215 Dominic and six followers moved into a house given by Peter Seila of Toulouse, and Bishop Foulques gave them authority to preach. Honorius III granted written approval for the Order of Preachers in December 1216. In 1218 Dominic reached Bologna, where the order held its first two General Chapters, and in 1220 the friars took up residence at Santa Sabina in Rome.

Dominic died on 6 August 1221 at Bologna, aged fifty-one, and was canonized in 1234 under Gregory IX. His remains were moved in 1233 and in 1267 to a shrine by Nicola Pisano and his workshop. He is commonly but wrongly associated with the Inquisition: sources of his own time say nothing of it, and it was established only in 1231 in Lombardy and 1234 in Languedoc, though his order later became closely associated with it. The legend grew through a painting for the Spanish Inquisition and Protestant polemic. Dominic is the patron saint of astronomers and natural scientists, and the Dominican Republic and Santo Domingo are named after him.
saint-helena: Saint Helena is a volcanic tropical island in the South Atlantic Ocean, measuring about 16 by 8 kilometres. It lies some 1,860 kilometres west of Angola and 3,280 kilometres east of Brazil, which makes it one of the most remote major islands in the world. Its climate is mild, tempered by the Benguela Current and almost continuous trade winds. The island is named after Helena of Constantinople.

By long tradition the island was sighted on 21 May 1502 by the four ships of the 3rd Portuguese Armada under João da Nova. A paper of 2022 observed that the only primary sources are Portuguese chronicles written at least fifty years later, none of which gives a precise date. The Portuguese found it uninhabited, with many trees and fresh water, brought livestock and fruit trees, and built a chapel, but formed no permanent settlement. It became a source of food for ships on the Cape Route from Asia to Europe, and sick mariners were left there to recover.

The East India Company received a charter from Oliver Cromwell to govern the island and decided to fortify it and settle it with planters. In 1815 the British government chose Saint Helena as the place of exile for Napoleon Bonaparte after Waterloo. He arrived in October 1815, lived at the Briars pavilion until Longwood House was ready in December, and died at Longwood on 5 May 1821. The Company then resumed control until the India Act of 1833 made the island a crown colony. Dinuzulu, the Zulu king, was exiled there from 1890 to 1897.

Royal Navy ships also brought liberated Africans to the island after rescuing them from slave ships. The remains of some 325 of them, disinterred during airport construction, were stored in Jamestown awaiting reburial.

Saint Helena is one of the three parts of the British overseas territory of Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha, with 4,439 inhabitants at the 2021 census. The island is known for its many endemic birds and plants, over 500 endemic species in all, most of them in the highland cloud forest.
saint-helier: St Helier is the most populous of the twelve parishes of Jersey, and the town, the island's only town, lies on the south coast at the eastern end of St Aubin's Bay. The land on which it stands was once a low-lying basin of marsh and sand dunes, with dunes to the west and low hills on the other sides. There is very little evidence of prehistoric settlement in the basin; the one archaeological site was an Iron Age dolmen that stood on Mont de la Ville, the present site of Fort Regent, and was moved to a former Governor's house at Henley-on-Thames in the 1780s. The site is thought to have been settled in the time of Roman control of Gaul.

The town takes its name from Helier, a 6th-century ascetic hermit from Belgium. Tradition dates his martyrdom to 555, and the parish arms of two crossed gold axes on blue refer to his death at the hands of Saxon pirates. His feast day, 16 July, is marked by an annual municipal and ecumenical pilgrimage to the Hermitage. Medieval accounts of his life suggest a small fishing village on the dunes between the marshy land behind and the high-water mark. Evidence of settlement exists from the 13th century, and the town's growth since has been described as spasmodic, reflecting waves of migration to the island.

In 1700 the cattle market moved from Broad Street to a site on the beach, and around 1800 the market was moved to a new building at its present site. Military roads linking coastal defences with St Helier harbour let farmers use fast sailing ships and then steamships to reach the markets of London and Paris first, which began Jersey's agricultural prosperity in the 19th century. By the turn of the century the open spaces around the town were mostly built over. After the First World War ribbon development spread along the coast and into neighbouring parishes, and in the 1930s the States built Jersey's first public housing estate, at Wellington Park.

St Helier is the de facto capital of Jersey. The States Assembly meets in the States Chamber next to the Royal Court, both in the Royal Square. The Town Church, the oldest building in the town, predates the Battle of Hastings; after the Reformation it became a Huguenot temple, and eight successive Rectors were French Huguenot ministers. Elizabeth Castle, a 16th-century castle on a tidal island, was built to supplement the defence provided by Mont Orgeuil. Fort Regent was built as a barracks at the end of the Napoleonic Wars, and the Central Market opened in 1882.
saint-jean-pied-de-port: The name means foot of the pass in Pyrenean French; in Basque the town is Donibane Garazi. It lies on the river Nive in the Pyrénées-Atlantiques department of south-western France, 8 km from the Spanish border and about 75 kilometres by road from Pamplona, the capital of Upper Navarre. The region around it is called the Pays de Cize, or Garazi in Basque. The town's layout is essentially one main street, encircled by sandstone walls.

The original town at nearby Saint-Jean-le-Vieux was razed in 1177 by the troops of Richard the Lionheart after a siege. The Kings of Navarre refounded the town on its present site shortly afterwards. It then belonged to the Kingdom of Navarre and was the seat of the sheriff of the district of Lower Navarre, the merindad of Ultrapuertos or Deça-Ports.

It remained the seat until the period of the Spanish conquest (1512-1528), when King Henry II of Navarre transferred the seat of the royal institutions to Saint Palais (Donapaleu) on safety grounds. The citadel above the town was remodelled by Vauban in the 17th century, and the Porte St-Jacques, the city gate, was added to the UNESCO World Heritage Sites in 1998 as part of the sites along the Routes of Santiago de Compostela in France.

The town stands at the base of the Roncevaux Pass, and the routes from Paris, Vézelay and Le Puy-en-Velay meet there. It was the pilgrims' last stop before the mountain crossing and is the second most popular starting point of the French Way of the pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela.

The cobbled rue de la Citadelle runs from the fifteenth century Porte St-Jacques to the Porte d'Espagne by the bridge, past old houses of pink and grey schist. Nearby stands the 14th-century red schist Gothic church of Notre-Dame-du-Bout-du-Pont, the original of which was built by Sancho the Strong of Navarre to commemorate the 1212 Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa. The town is a member of the association of the Most Beautiful Villages of France. Its notable people include Bernard Etxepare, writer of the first printed book in Basque, and the physician Juan Huarte de San Juan (c. 1530-1592).
saint-kitts: Saint Kitts lies in the Leeward Islands of the Lesser Antilles, with its west side on the Caribbean Sea and its east coast facing the Atlantic. It is about 168 square kilometres in area and 29 kilometres long. Nevis lies 3 kilometres to the south across a shallow channel called The Narrows. The island is named for Saint Christopher, Kit being a formerly common short form of Christopher.

It has three groups of volcanic peaks, and the highest point is the dormant volcano Mount Liamuiga, formerly Mount Misery, at about 1,156 metres. The interior is too steep for habitation, and a ring road runs round the coast.

During the last ice age Saint Kitts, Nevis, Saba and Sint Eustatius were one island. The first settlers were Archaic people who came south from Florida. Around 100 BCE the farming Saladoid people arrived from the Orinoco, and around 800 CE the Arawakan-speaking Igneri replaced them. About 1300 CE the Kalinago dispersed the Igneri and named the island Liamuiga, fertile island. Columbus claimed it for Spain in 1493.

The first English colony was founded in 1623, followed by a French one in 1625. The colonists united to forestall a Kalinago ambush, massacred the Kalinago, and then partitioned the island, the English taking the middle and the French each end. A Spanish force seized the island in 1629, and the English settlement was rebuilt after the peace of 1630. Through the 17th and 18th centuries the island passed repeatedly between English, later British, and French control.

Tobacco was the first crop, but farmers switched to sugarcane in 1640, and the labour-intensive cultivation led to large-scale importation of enslaved Africans. Parliament outlawed the purchase of enslaved people in 1807 and abolished slavery with effect from 1 August 1834, followed by four years of apprenticeship, against which the nominally freed people revolted until martial law was declared. Saint Kitts and Nevis became independent on 19 September 1983.

Saint Kitts and Nevis form one country, the Federation of Saint Kitts and Nevis, whose capital and largest port is Basseterre on Saint Kitts. English is the main language. Brimstone Hill Fortress National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is the largest fortress ever built in the Eastern Caribbean.
saint-louis-senegal: The heart of the old colonial city stands on a narrow island in the Senegal River, a little more than 2 km long and about 400 m wide, 25 km north of the river's mouth. A sand spit 300 m wide, the Langue de Barbarie, separates it from the Atlantic; the seaside neighbourhoods of Ndar Toute and Guet Ndar lie on it, and the older settlement of Sor stands on the east bank. The city lies in the Sahel and is nearly surrounded by tidal marshes, 320 km north of Dakar.

A Wolof settlement at Guet Ndar dates from around 1450 and was a meeting and departure point for Muslim pilgrims travelling to Mecca. Portuguese, Dutch and English traders visited over the next two centuries. The French built a fort on Bocos Island in 1638 and, because of repeated flooding, moved it in 1659 to the island the Wolof called Ndar. It was uninhabited, supposedly because local people thought spirits haunted it. The Diagne of Sor, the local leader, allowed the French to settle there for annual payments of cloth, iron bars and eau de vie.

The trading post exported slaves, gold, hides, beeswax, ambergris and later gum arabic. British forces took Senegal in 1758 and the French recaptured Saint-Louis in February 1779. Between 1659 and 1779 nine chartered companies in turn administered it.

A Franco-African Creole merchant community, the Métis, grew up in the 17th and 18th centuries, known for its signares, women entrepreneurs; it controlled most of the river trade and financed the main Catholic institutions.
