After the Atlantic slave trade declined from 1790, gum arabic became the main trade. Britain held the city again in the Napoleonic Wars and returned it in 1817.

Louis Faidherbe, governor from 1854, built bridges, supplied fresh water and began a telegraph line to Dakar. Saint-Louis was capital of the federation of French West Africa from 1895 until 1902, when Dakar took the role. The railway from Dakar, completed in 1885, let up-country trade bypass its port. From 1920 to 1957 it was also capital of Mauritania. Its population was 10,000 in 1826, 23,000 in 1914 and 39,000 in 1955.

The island was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000 for its colonial architecture, regular town plan and quays. The city had 254,171 inhabitants in 2023 and is the capital of Senegal's Saint-Louis Region. After independence, when Dakar became the sole capital, it declined economically. Its economy now rests on tourism, fishing, sugar production and trade. Gaston Berger University was created there in 1990, and the Saint-Louis Jazz Festival has been held since 1993. Fanals, night processions of giant paper lanterns, take place at Christmas.
saint-malo: The walled city stands on the English Channel coast. It was originally a rocky granite island joined to the mainland only by a narrow sand spit and tidal mudflats called le Sillon. Stonework and a basic road were first laid along this sandbar in 1509, and over the centuries, particularly in the 19th century, the structure was widened and raised to form the modern dyke, La Digue du Sillon, which permanently connects the old town to the coast.

The site was founded by Gauls in the 1st century BCE and was known in Roman times as Reginca or Aletum. By the late 4th century CE a Saxon Shore fort in the Saint-Servan district protected the Rance estuary from seaborne raiders. In the 5th and 6th centuries Armorica received many Celtic Britons fleeing instability across the Channel, and the modern city traces its origins to a monastic settlement founded early in the sixth century.

The city asserted its autonomy in dealings with both the French and the local Breton authorities. From 1590 to 1594 it declared itself an independent republic and functioned as a de facto city-state, which gave it the motto "Ni Français, ni Breton, Malouin suis". It became notorious as the home of corsairs, French privateers and sometimes pirates, who forced English ships passing up the Channel to pay tribute and brought wealth from further afield. Jacques Cartier lived in and sailed from Saint-Malo to the Saint Lawrence River. The explorer Louis-Antoine de Bougainville named the Falkland Islands the Îles Malouines in 1764 after the people of Saint-Malo, his point of departure. The writer François-René de Chateaubriand was born in the city in 1768.

In August 1944 American shelling and bombing almost totally destroyed the walled city during the fight against a German garrison of more than twelve thousand troops in the area. The German commander, Colonel Andreas von Aulock, refused to surrender. The last holdout in the citadel gave up on 17 August, and the island of Cézembre surrendered on 2 September. More than ten thousand prisoners were taken.

Saint-Malo was rebuilt over twelve years, from 1948 to 1960, and in 1967 it merged with Saint-Servan and Paramé, more than doubling its population. It is a subprefecture of Ille-et-Vilaine and has a ferry terminal serving Jersey, Guernsey, Portsmouth and Poole. Its inhabitants are called Malouins. The Route du Rhum, a single-handed transatlantic yacht race to Pointe-à-Pitre in Guadeloupe, starts here every four years.
saint-martin-island: Saint Martin is an island in the Leeward Islands of the Lesser Antilles, in the north-eastern Caribbean, about 300 km east of Puerto Rico. Its area is 87 square kilometres, divided between France in the north and the Kingdom of the Netherlands in the south. It is the only land border shared by France and the Netherlands. The main towns are Marigot on the French side and Philipsburg on the Dutch side, and the highest hill is Pic Paradis, at 424 metres, in the French part. There are no rivers, only dry gullies, and dry forest covers the hilltops and slopes. The island's pre-colonial names include Oualichi, an Arawakan name meaning the island of women, and Soualiga, a Kalinago name meaning the island of salt.

It is commonly believed that Christopher Columbus named the island in honour of Saint Martin of Tours on his second voyage. In fact he applied the name to the island now called Nevis when he anchored offshore on 11 November 1493, the feast day of Saint Martin. Because the small islands of the Leeward group were poorly charted, the name was accidentally transferred to the island now called Saint-Martin or Sint Maarten.

After jointly reclaiming the island, the Kingdom of France and the Dutch Republic agreed on 23 March 1648 to divide it between them, and the Treaty of Concordia created a formal border. The treaty was signed on the hill on the border between Marigot and Philipsburg, known as Mount Concordia. Later conflicts brought 16 border changes over the years, but the border has been stable since 1816. The treaty is one of the oldest still in effect, and it allows freedom of movement between the two parts of the island. A Unity Flag, representing the people of both halves, was adopted on 31 August 1990 at a conference in Philipsburg.

The northern French part is the Collectivity of Saint Martin, an overseas collectivity of France, and the southern Dutch part is Sint Maarten, which since 2010 has been one of four constituent countries of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. Official languages are French in the French part, and Dutch and English in the Dutch part; an English-based creole is the main local vernacular. The island's population comes from more than 70 countries, and tourism is its main industry. Princess Juliana International Airport on the Dutch side is its main airport. Hurricane Irma struck on 6 September 2017 and caused widespread damage.
saint-nicholas: Little is known about the historical Nicholas. The earliest accounts of his life were written centuries after his death and probably contain elaborations, and no contemporary chronicler mentions him. Tradition says he was born at the Anatolian seaport of Patara, in Lycia, to wealthy Greek Christian parents. Shortly after a pilgrimage to the Holy Land he is said to have become bishop of Myra, chosen because he was the first priest to enter the church one morning.

He is said to have been imprisoned in Diocletian's persecution and released on Constantine's orders, but this is not attested in the earliest sources and is unlikely to be historical. A list of attendees at the First Council of Nicaea in 325 includes him, yet neither Athanasius of Alexandria nor Eusebius, who were there, mentions him.

His best-known story, first attested in Michael the Archimandrite's Life of Saint Nicholas, tells of a once-wealthy man who could not afford dowries for his three daughters. Nicholas, too modest to help in public, threw bags of gold coins through the window of the house at night. His secret gift-giving gave rise to the folklore of Santa Claus through Sinterklaas. Other stories tell of him calming a storm at sea and saving three innocent soldiers from execution.

He is patron of sailors, merchants, children, students and many others. In Greek folklore he was the Lord of the Sea, and he is patron saint of Greece and the Hellenic Navy. The Eastern Orthodox Church commemorates his death on 6 December, and icons show him as an elderly bishop with a short white beard holding a Gospel Book.

Less than 200 years after his death the Emperor Theodosius II ordered a church built at Myra over the site where Nicholas had served, and his remains were moved to a sarcophagus there. In 1087, after the Battle of Manzikert had put Myra under Seljuk rule, sailors from Bari seized the main bones over the objections of the Greek Orthodox monks and took them to Bari, where they are enshrined in the Basilica di San Nicola. According to one chronicle, a Venetian fleet took the remaining fragments in 1100. Small bones soon spread across western Europe.

In the late 1950s, when the crypt in Bari was restored, the anatomist Luigi Martino examined the bones. He concluded that the man died at over seventy and had severe arthritis of the spine and pelvis. Two investigations found the relics in Bari and Venice anatomically compatible and possibly from one person.
saint-patricks-day: Saint Patrick (c. 385 – c. 461) was a 5th-century Christian missionary and bishop in Ireland. Much of what is known of him comes from the Declaration, which was allegedly written by Patrick himself. It says that at sixteen he was kidnapped by Irish raiders and taken as a slave to Ireland, where he worked six years as a shepherd. Tradition holds that he died on 17 March and was buried at Downpatrick, and many legends grew up around him over the following centuries.

His feast day was already observed by the Irish in Europe in the ninth and tenth centuries as a kind of national day. It was placed on the liturgical calendar of the Catholic Church in the early 1600s, through the influence of the Waterford-born Franciscan scholar Luke Wadding. In the Irish calendar it was seen as the middle day of spring: weather was expected to improve and farmers began to plant potatoes.

Observances generally involve parades and festivals, Irish traditional music sessions and the wearing of green clothing or shamrocks. Saint Patrick is said to have used the shamrock to explain the Holy Trinity to the pagan Irish, a story that first appears in writing in 1726, though it may be older; Patricia Monaghan says there is no evidence the shamrock was sacred to the pagan Irish. The first link between green and Ireland comes from a legend in the 11th-century Lebor Gabála Érenn about Goídel Glas, ancestor of the Gaels.

Parades began in North America in the 18th century but did not reach Ireland until the 20th, and until the late 20th century the day was often a bigger celebration among the diaspora than in Ireland. Irish soldiers in the Montreal Garrison observed it as early as 1759, and Montreal's parade has been held yearly since 1824.

In 1903 the day became an official public holiday in Ireland under the Bank Holiday (Ireland) Act 1903, introduced by the MP James O'Mara. The first parade in Ireland was held in Waterford that year. On the day in 1916 the Irish Volunteers held parades throughout Ireland, and the authorities recorded 38 of them with 6,000 marchers; the Easter Rising began the following month. The day is also a public holiday in Northern Ireland, in Newfoundland and Labrador for provincial government employees, and in Montserrat. Its celebrations have been criticised as commercialised, as linked to heavy drinking and as encouraging stereotypes of the Irish.
saint-petersburg: Saint Petersburg lies in the middle taiga lowlands along the shores of the Neva Bay of the Gulf of Finland, at the head of the Baltic Sea, and on the islands of the Neva delta. The largest of these are Vasilyevsky Island and Petrogradsky Island. In the south the city crosses the Baltic-Ladoga Klint and meets the Izhora Plateau. Before the 17th century the area was inhabited by the Finnic Izhorians and Votians, and Ingrian Finns moved there from Karelia and Savonia under Swedish rule.

Swedish colonists built the fortress of Nyenskans at the mouth of the Neva in 1611, and the small town of Nyen grew up around it. At the end of the 17th century Peter the Great wanted a seaport to trade with the rest of Europe, since the main one, Arkhangelsk on the White Sea, was closed to shipping in winter. On 12 May 1703 (1 May, old style), during the Great Northern War, he captured Nyenskans. On 27 May 1703 (16 May, old style), he laid down the Peter and Paul Fortress on Zayachy Island, the first brick and stone building of the new city. It was named after the apostle Saint Peter.

The city served as the capital of the Tsardom of Russia and of the Russian Empire from 1712 to 1918, except around 1728 to 1730, when Moscow replaced it. After the October Revolution in 1917 the Bolsheviks moved their government to Moscow. The city was renamed Petrograd and then Leningrad after Lenin's death in 1924. It was the site of the siege of Leningrad in World War II, the most lethal siege in history. In June 1991 voters supported restoring the original name, which took effect on 1 October 1991.

The first Russian railway was built there in 1837. The Kunstkamera, whose collection Peter the Great established in 1714 to gather curiosities from around the world, is sometimes considered the first museum in Russia. In 1914 an international chess tournament, partly funded by Tsar Nicholas II, was the first at which the title Grandmaster was formally conferred, on Lasker, Capablanca, Alekhine, Tarrasch and Marshall.

Saint Petersburg is the second-largest city in Russia, with 5,601,911 residents in the 2021 census, and is governed as a federal city. Its historic centre, mostly Baroque and Neoclassical buildings of the 18th and 19th centuries, has been largely preserved. The Historic Centre of Saint Petersburg and Related Groups of Monuments have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1991. The city has more than two hundred museums, the largest being the Hermitage, which occupies the former imperial residence.
saint-pol-de-leon: Saint-Pol-de-Léon, in Breton Kastell-Paol, is a commune in the Finistère department of Brittany, on the coast of north-western France. It lies on a stretch of about 13 kilometres of coastline, with beaches and creeks, and is linked to the Sainte-Anne islet by a strand of sediment called the Groue, which forms the bay of Pempoul with its harbour. Its inhabitants are called Saintpolitains. The Latin name of the region is Léon, in French Pays Léonard.

A well-preserved double stone alley is the last remnant of prehistoric occupation on the site, and several vestiges show a Roman military presence in the 3rd century. From the 6th century the monastery site became an episcopate, called Kastell Paol, and the city grew beyond its walls. It was long the seat of a bishop and became a sort of religious capital. In the 15th century it was a noted spiritual and cultural centre, the Pempoul harbour was rising, and fortified gates protected its 2,000 inhabitants until the 18th century.

A battle of the Breton War of Succession was fought there in the 14th century, in which the Montfortists and their English allies defeated an army led by Charles of Blois. In the 18th century the bishops of Léon strongly influenced the city's architecture: a new episcopal house was built in 1706 and extended in 1750, the seminary dates from 1708 and the Catholic college from 1788.

The French Revolution took away the episcopate, a rich chapter, a college and many religious houses, and a hundred years of economic decline began; Flaubert judged in 1847 that the town was a dead city. The railway of 1883 expanded agricultural production, and in 1890 the town became the main commercial centre in France for the export of vegetables.

The former cathedral, of the 13th century, stands on the site of the original founded by Paul Aurelian in the 6th century and shows the influence of Norman art on Breton architecture. The Kreisker chapel, of the 14th and 15th centuries, has the highest steeple in Brittany at 80 metres. The old episcopal palace is now the town hall, with a monumental staircase, and the town keeps a 16th-century prebendal house in Breton Renaissance style and the Kéroulas manor, built for a noble canon around 1520. The region remains a strong centre of horticultural production.
saint-sophia-cathedral-kyiv: Saint Sophia was built as the metropolitan cathedral of Kyiv during the reign of Yaroslav the Wise, and an earlier wooden church of the same name may have existed. It was designed as a burial place for Yaroslav and his descendants, and he was interred in a marble sarcophagus that now stands in the northern inner gallery. The metropolitan bishops of Kyiv were probably buried there too, the earliest known case being Cyril II in the 1280s.

The architects faced a task not previously met, a huge church with spacious choirs, and they departed from the standard Byzantine model. To reduce costs they used local materials: brick cross-shaped pillars instead of marble columns, and slabs of pink Ovruch pyrophyllite slate and ceramic tiles instead of marble. It is one of the largest churches built in Europe in the 11th century.

The interior walls keep early 11th-century mosaics and frescoes. The mosaics cover 260 square metres and the frescoes 3,000. Among the masterpieces are the Pantocrator, the Communion of the Apostles, the Deisis, the Annunciation and the Virgin Orans, which is 6 metres high and dominates the vault of the central apse. Eight craftsmen probably worked on the mosaics, each of which carries an explanatory inscription in Medieval Greek.

Priests and visitors also scratched graffiti into the walls. More than 7,000 drawings and texts from the 11th to the 18th century have been found, some in Glagolitic script. They include a record of the death of Yaroslav the Wise, the autograph of Grand Prince Volodymyr Monomakh and a record of a peace treaty between princes at the end of the 11th century.

From 1497 until 1577 the cathedral stood abandoned, until Bogusz Gulkevych-Glibovsky renovated it at his own expense. After the Union of Brest in 1596 it passed to the Ruthenian Uniate Church, and in the 17th century Mohyla regained it for the Orthodox Metropolis and founded a monastery. The mosaics and frescoes had been whitewashed by 1701, and the art historian Adrian Prakhov rediscovered the mosaics in 1884.

In the 1920s the Soviet government called for the cathedral to be demolished and the grounds made into a park, but it was saved. The National Reserve Sophia of Kyiv was established in 1934, services were banned that year, and the reserve opened to visitors in 1935. Reconstruction work won the European Gold Medal for the Protection of Historic Monuments in 1987, and in 1990 the cathedral was included on the World Heritage List.
saipan: Saipan lies about 190 kilometres north of Guam and 9.3 kilometres north-east of Tinian, from which the Saipan Channel separates it. It is about 19 kilometres long and 9 kilometres wide, with a land area of 115.38 square kilometres. The western side is lined with sandy beaches and an offshore coral reef that creates a large lagoon, while the eastern shore is mostly rugged rocky cliffs. Archaeologists have found traces of human settlement over 4,000 years old, including petroglyphs and latte stones. Saipan is one of the main homes of the Chamorro and the Carolinians, the indigenous people of the Mariana Islands.

Spanish rule began in the 17th century, and the island was possibly first sighted by Europeans during Ferdinand Magellan's expedition, which landed in the southern Marianas on 6 March 1521. After the Spanish–American War of 1898 the United States occupied Saipan, but Spain sold it to the German Empire under the German–Spanish Treaty of 1899. Germany administered it as part of German New Guinea and made no attempt to develop or settle it.

Japan captured the island in 1914 and was awarded formal control in 1919 by the League of Nations as part of the South Seas Mandate. From the 1920s settlers from Japan, Korea, Taiwan and Okinawa developed large sugar plantations, and the South Seas Development Company built refineries, ports, roads and schools. By October 1943 there were 29,348 Japanese settlers and 3,926 Chamorro and Carolinian islanders.

Japan treated Saipan as part of the last line of defence of the homeland and garrisoned it heavily, with nearly 30,000 troops by mid-1944. The Battle of Saipan lasted from 15 June to 9 July 1944; American forces landed on the south-western beaches and took the island after more than three weeks of heavy fighting, at a cost of 3,426 killed and 10,364 wounded. After the war Saipan became part of the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands, administered by the United States. The Northern Mariana islanders voted to join the United States in 1975, and the island became a municipality of the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands in 1978. Islanders became United States citizens on 4 November 1986.

About 90 per cent of the population of the Northern Mariana Islands lives on Saipan, and since the whole island is one municipality most publications call it the Commonwealth's capital. The legislative and executive branches of government are in the village of Capitol Hill and the judicial branch in Susupe. Most of the native Chamorro and Carolinian population is Roman Catholic. Sites from the past include latte stones, the Last Command Post of the Battle of Saipan and a Japanese lighthouse built in 1934.
sakarya-river: The Sakarya runs through the region known in ancient times as Phrygia. The source of the river is the Bayat Plateau, north-east of Afyon. It is joined by the Porsuk Creek close to the town of Polatlı and runs through the Adapazarı Plains before it reaches the Black Sea. Four dams stand on it, which from downstream to upstream are Akçay, Yenice, Gökçekaya and Sarıyar.

In Greek classical antiquity the river was considered one of the principal rivers of Asia Minor and is mentioned in the Iliad and in Theogony. Its name appears as Sagraphos, Sangaris or Sagaris. Strabo wrote that it had its sources on Mount Adoreus, near the town of Sangia in Phrygia, not far from the border with Galatia, and flowed in a very tortuous course: east, then north, then north-west and finally north through Bithynia into the Euxine, the Black Sea. Part of its course formed the boundary between Phrygia and Bithynia. Its Bithynian part was navigable and noted for the abundance of fish. Its principal tributaries were the Alander, the Bathys, the Thymbres and the Gallus.

Pseudo-Plutarch told that a man named Sagaris, who often derided the priests of the Mother of the Gods, was struck with madness by her and threw himself into the river Xerobates, which from then on was called Sagaris. The Sangarius Bridge was built by the Eastern Roman Emperor Justinian I, who reigned from 527 to 565. In the 13th century the valley formed part of the border between the Eastern Roman Empire and the home of the Söğüt tribe. By 1280 Emperor Michael VIII Palaiologos had built a series of fortifications along the river, but a flood in 1302 changed its course and made them useless. The Söğüt tribe migrated across the river and later established the Ottoman Empire.
sakhalin: Sakhalin is 948 km long and 25 to 170 km wide, with an area of 72,492 square kilometres, and separates the Sea of Okhotsk from the Sea of Japan. Its north coast lies 6.5 km from the Russian mainland across the narrow Strait of Tartary, and its southern tip lies 40 km north of Hokkaido across the La Pérouse Strait. Nearly two thirds of the island is mountainous. The name comes from the Manchu Sahaliyan, meaning black, which is also the Manchu name of the Amur River.

Humans lived on Sakhalin in the Neolithic. The Ainu live in the southern half, the Oroks in the centre and the Nivkhs in the north. The Ainu later paid tribute to the Yuan, Ming and Qing dynasties, which called the island Kuyedao, the island of the Ainu; control from China was mostly loose and there was no fixed border. Japan proclaimed sovereignty over the whole island in 1845, holding it to be an extension of Hokkaido, against competing Russian claims, and Russian settlers began to establish coal mines, schools and churches.

The Treaty of Shimoda of 1855 allowed nationals of both countries to live on the island, Russians in the north and Japanese in the south, with no clear boundary. Japan surrendered its claims in the Treaty of Saint Petersburg of 1875 in exchange for the northern Kuril Islands. Under the Treaty of Portsmouth of 1905 Japan received the part south of the 50th parallel, which it governed as Karafuto Prefecture, with its capital at Toyohara, now Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk. The Soviet Union invaded southern Sakhalin on 11 August 1945 and completed the conquest on 25 August.

Sakhalin is the largest island of Russia and is administered as part of Sakhalin Oblast. Its population is roughly 500,000, most of them Russians, and the indigenous Ainu, Oroks and Nivkhs are present in very small numbers. Most Ainu on Sakhalin moved to Hokkaido in 1949, when Japanese civilians were displaced from the island.
sakhalin-oblast: Sakhalin Oblast, in the Russian Far East, has an area of 87,100 square kilometres. It borders by sea Khabarovsk Krai to the west and Kamchatka Krai to the north, and Hokkaido in Japan to the south. The name Sakhalin goes back to the Manchu hydronym Sahaliyan Ula, meaning Black River, the Amur. The indigenous peoples of Sakhalin are the Nivkh, Orok and Ainu, the Ainu historically living in the southern part of the island and the Nivkh mainly in the north.

Mamiya Rinzō, who explored and mapped the island in 1809, showed that it is not attached to the Asian continent, and the Russian navigator Gennady Nevelskoy recorded this definitively in 1849. Japan proclaimed sovereignty over the whole island in 1845, but Russian settlers ignored the claim and from the 1850s set up coal mines, prisons and churches. In 1875 the Treaty of Saint Petersburg gave all of it to Russia in exchange for the Kuril Islands, and in 1905 the Treaty of Portsmouth passed the part below 50° N to Japan, which administered it as Karafuto.

In August 1945 the Soviet Union took over the whole of Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands, and by 2 January 1947 the present boundaries of the oblast were set. Most Japanese residents were repatriated, but at least a third of the Koreans who had arrived in the late 1930s and early 1940s were refused permission to leave, and they and their descendants became known as the Sakhalin Koreans. Japan does not count the southern Kuril Islands, which it calls the Northern Territories, as included in its renunciation under the Treaty of San Francisco of 1952.

The administrative centre and largest city is Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk. The population was 466,609 at the 2021 census, and most inhabitants descend from Russian and other Slavic settlers. Oil and natural gas are drilled on and around the island, and coal and some manganese have been mined there since the 1920s. The 1995 Neftegorsk earthquake killed 1,989 people, and the settlement was not rebuilt.
saladin: Saladin was born about 1137 in Tikrit, in present-day Iraq. His personal name was Yusuf; Salah ad-Din is an honorific meaning Righteousness of the Faith. His parents were of Kurdish Rawadiya ancestry, a tribe originally of Arab descent that had become Kurdicized, and his father Najm al-Din Ayyub was a Kurdish mercenary. His military career began under his paternal uncle Shirkuh, a commander in the service of Nur al-Din. In 1164, aged 26, Saladin went with Shirkuh to Egypt to help restore the vizier Shawar, though his role in that expedition was minor.

Shirkuh and Saladin returned in 1169, when Amalric I of Jerusalem besieged Cairo; Shirkuh became vizier and died the same year, and the Fatimid caliph al-Adid appointed Saladin. In 1171, after al-Adid's death, the Abbasid khutba was pronounced in Cairo, ending the Isma'ili Fatimid Caliphate and returning Egypt to the Sunni Abbasid caliph. After Nur al-Din died in 1174, Saladin peacefully entered Damascus, took Hama and Homs, defeated the Zengids at the Battle of the Horns of Hama in 1175 and was proclaimed Sultan of Egypt and Syria by the Abbasid caliph. By 1182 he had taken Aleppo, though he failed to take Mosul, and he escaped two attempts on his life by the Order of Assassins.

On 25 November, at Montgisard near Ramla, a small Templar force surprised his army and he fled to Egypt. His army defeated the Crusaders at the Battle of Hattin in 1187, and Jerusalem capitulated on 2 October 1187. Balian of Ibelin threatened to kill the Muslim hostages and destroy the Dome of the Rock if quarter were refused, and Saladin accepted terms allowing ransom. About 18,000 poorer citizens were ransomed through a collection, while another 15,000 were enslaved.

Hattin and the fall of Jerusalem prompted the Third Crusade (1189 to 1192), partly financed by a special Saladin tithe in 1188. Saladin died of a fever at Damascus on 4 March 1193, having given away most of his wealth; he was buried in a mausoleum beside the Umayyad Mosque. Medieval Europeans held him up as a model of kingship, and Dante placed him among the virtuous non-Christians in limbo. His reputation had been largely forgotten in the Muslim world, eclipsed by figures such as Baybars, until the 19th century, when Walter Scott's romantic portrayal and Wilhelm II's visit to his tomb in 1898 helped to make him a hero of the struggle against the West in the Arab world.
salamanca: Salamanca lies on the northern half of the Meseta Central, in the west-central part of the Iberian Peninsula, straddling the Tormes river, in the comarca of Campo Charro. It is the capital of the Province of Salamanca and stands 64 kilometres from Zamora, 121 kilometres from Valladolid and 123 kilometres from Portugal. The three small hills on which settlements grew, formed by the erosion of two streams, and the nearness of the river suited the early functions of defence and control of the surrounding land.

The Iron Age hilltop site of Cerro de San Vicente, on the right bank of the Tormes, is the first stable settlement, dating to the 7th century BCE. By the 3rd century BCE a settlement at the Teso de las Catedrales had consolidated under the influence of the Vaccaei and Vettones, Celtic tribes. After Roman conquest it became the civitas of Salmantica. After the Roman period the Alans, then the Visigoths, held it, and in 589 it was an episcopal seat that sent bishops to the councils of Toledo. Christian resettlement under the Kingdom of León, led by Raymond of Burgundy, took hold in the 11th century.

Salamanca joined the revolt of the Communities of Castile in 1520 against the taxes of Charles V, and afterwards the king had the upper parts of the towers of the rebels' palaces removed. During the Peninsular War the city was occupied by the troops of Marshal Soult in 1809 and stayed in French hands until the Battle of Arapiles in 1812, when an Anglo-Portuguese army under Wellington defeated Marmont's French army. The French destroyed much of the city for building materials, including the university's colegios mayores.

The University of Salamanca received its royal charter as an Estudio General from Alfonso IX of León in 1218. It was the first institution to receive the title of university, in 1254, and under Alfonso X its schools of canon and civil law drew students even from Paris and Bologna. Antonio de Nebrija's grammar of Spanish appeared here in 1492, and Hernán Cortés studied here briefly before leaving in 1501.

The Old City was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1988. It holds the Baroque Plaza Mayor, designed by Alberto and Nicolás Churriguera, the Casa de las Conchas, whose facade carries about 350 scallop shells, and two cathedrals, the Romanesque Old Cathedral of the 12th century and the much larger Gothic New Cathedral, begun in the 16th century and completed in the 18th. The city had 144,458 inhabitants in 2024 and its Holy Week processions are of international tourist interest.
salamis-island: Salamis lies about two kilometres from the coast of Piraeus, Athens' port, and about 16 km west of the centre of Athens. It has an area of 93 square kilometres, and a significant part of it is rocky and mountainous; the highest point is Mavrovouni at 404 metres. The chief city, Salamina, stands on Salamis Bay, and the main port, Paloukia, on the eastern side connects the island with Perama by ferry.

The traditional etymology derives the name from the nymph Salamis, mother of Cychreus, the first king of the island in tradition. A more modern theory connects it with a root meaning salt and a suffix meaning middle, so that Salamis would be the place amid salt water. From at least the 13th century until the 19th the island was called Koulouri, after its round shape, and the ancient name was then revived.

Salamis was probably first colonised by Aegina and later occupied by Megara, and it became an Athenian possession after a war between Athens and Megara. According to Homer's Iliad it sent twelve ships to the Trojan War under Ajax, who is said to have been born on the island, as was the playwright Euripides, whose birth is popularly placed on the day of the battle. In 480 BCE the allied Greek fleet led by Athens and by Themistocles won its decisive naval victory over the Persian Empire off the island. In the north of the Kynosoura peninsula lie the remains of an ancient tumulus thought to be the burial site of Greek warriors of that battle.

The ancient capital lay in the south according to Strabo, in classical times on the Kamatero Peninsula overlooking the strait, and in modern times lies in the west. The oldest known counting board, of marble and about 150 by 75 centimetres, was found on the island in 1899 and is thought to have been used by Babylonians about 300 BCE. Arvanites were recorded among the inhabitants in 1688. On 23 April 1941, during the German invasion of Greece, the Luftwaffe bombed the harbour and sank the Greek battleships Kilkis and Lemnos.

Since the local government reform of 2011 the island has been administered as one municipality in the Islands regional unit of Attica. About 31,000 people live there permanently, many working in fishing, ferries and shipyards or commuting to Athens, and the number rises sharply in the holiday season. Salamis Naval Base, a major base of the Hellenic Navy, stands beside Paloukia. A festival called Salaminia commemorates the naval battle each year, and the island has a Museum of Folklore Art and History.
sale: Salé lies in northwestern Morocco on the right bank of the Bou Regreg river, opposite the national capital Rabat, which it serves as a commuter town. Rabat and Salé together form a single metropolitan area. The Phoenicians established a settlement called Sala on the south side of the estuary, later the site of a Roman colony, Sala Colonia. The town of Salé proper was probably founded in the 11th century by families from al-Andalus, most importantly the Banu 'Ashara, who included learned jurists and judges and became the city's de facto rulers.

The Banu 'Ashara reportedly hosted Ibn Tumart, the founder of the Almohad movement, in 1121. They resisted his successor 'Abd al-Mu'min, who destroyed the city walls, eliminated the family and seized their palace. In the 12th century the Almohad caliph Yaqub al-Mansur founded Ribat al-Fath, present-day Rabat, across the river, and Salé remained important as a residence of the Almohad caliphs.

He ordered the Great Mosque built in 1196. In September 1260 warriors sent by Alfonso X of Castile raided and occupied Salé, and the Marinid sultan Abu Yusuf Yaqub reconquered it and helped rebuild the walls, including the gate of Bab el-Mrisa. The Marinids also built a protected harbour and the Madrasa of Abu al-Hasan.

In the 17th century Salé became a haven for Barbary pirates, among them Moriscos expelled from Spain after Philip III's decree of 1609. About 2,000 refugees from Hornachos settled around Salé and occupied the kasbah, and thousands more joined them. Rabat and Salé united to form the Republic of Bou Regreg in 1627.

The corsairs captured ships and sold their crews and sometimes passengers into slavery, although their ships were based across the river in Rabat. Spain bombarded Salé in May 1628, and the French admiral Isaac de Razilly did so on 20 July 1629, destroying three corsair ships. Salé was later incorporated into Alawi Morocco.

Salé's historic medina occupies a large area near the mouth of the Bou Regreg and is enclosed by walls, of which Bab el-Mrisa, dating to the 1270s, is the most notable gate. The Great Mosque is the religious centre, beside the Madrasa of Abu al-Hasan, dating to 1342. The Sufi Ibn 'Ashir, who moved to Salé in the 14th century, became the city's patron saint, and his mausoleum dominates the seaside cemetery. Salé was a stronghold of the Moroccan national movement before independence, and many of its activists signed the Manifesto of Independence of Morocco on 11 January 1944.
salem-massachusetts: Salem lies on Massachusetts Bay, between Salem Harbor, which divides it from Marblehead, and Beverly Harbor. Between the two harbors lie Salem Neck and Winter Island. The city has a total area of 18.1 square miles, of which 8.1 square miles is land and the rest water. The peninsula was known as Naumkeag to the Native people who lived there in the early 1600s, the Naumkeag people, whose settlement controlled territory from the Merrimack to the Mystic rivers.

Colonists settled in Naumkeag in 1626, when a company of fishermen from Cape Ann arrived under Roger Conant. The Massachusetts Bay Company replaced him with John Endecott, and Conant received 200 acres in compensation. To mark this peaceful change of government the settlement was renamed Salem, a form of Shalem, the royal city of Melchizedek, which is identified with Jerusalem. Early musters of militia on Salem Common laid a foundation for what became the Army National Guard. On 26 February 1775 patriots raised the drawbridge at the North River and stopped Colonel Alexander Leslie and 300 troops of the 64th Regiment of Foot from seizing stores hidden in North Salem; an agreement ended the standoff without bloodshed.

The Salem witch trials began in 1692 after girls including Abigail Williams and Betty Parris played with an egg and a glass to learn their future husbands' trades. Nineteen people were hanged, and Giles Corey was pressed to death for refusing to plead. After the American Revolution, Salem's owners of large privateers turned to distant trade. In 1795 Captain Jonathan Carnes brought home a bulk cargo of pepper from Sumatra, the first imported into the country, sold at a profit of seven hundred per cent. Elias Hasket Derby owned the Grand Turk, the first New England vessel to trade with China.

Salem is a residential and tourist city of 44,480 people at the 2020 census. It was one of two county seats of Essex County until county governments in Massachusetts were dissolved in 1999. The Salem Maritime National Historic Site, the House of the Seven Gables (1668), the Peabody Essex Museum and the Chestnut Street District preserve its maritime and colonial past. The site of the 1692 executions was identified in 2016 as Proctor's Ledge, now a memorial. Salem State University, founded in 1854 as the Salem Normal School, is in the city.
salem-witch-trials: Witch trials were fading across much of Europe by the middle of the seventeenth century but continued on its fringes and in the American colonies. Witchcraft had been a capital offence in the Massachusetts Body of Liberties since 1641, although the provision was repealed in 1684. The Puritans who settled New England would have been familiar with witch trials in England. The 1629 royal charter of the Massachusetts Bay Colony was vacated in 1684, and the colony passed through constitutional turmoil. Salem Village, now Danvers, was known for a fractious population that quarrelled over property lines, grazing rights and church privileges.

In February 1692 Betty Parris, aged nine, and her cousin Abigail Williams, aged eleven, the daughter and niece of the Reverend Samuel Parris, began to have fits. Local women were accused of causing the girls harm by witchcraft, and when Sarah Cloyce and Elizabeth Proctor were arrested in April they were examined by the magistrates John Hathorne and Jonathan Corwin. A Court of Oyer and Terminer convened in Salem Town on 2 June 1692 under William Stoughton, and Bridget Bishop was the first case brought to the grand jury.

Much of the evidence was spectral evidence, the testimony of the afflicted that they saw the apparition of the accused. The court held that the Devil could not use a person's shape without that person's permission, so such testimony was taken as proof of complicity. On 19 September 1692 Giles Corey refused to plead and was killed by peine forte et dure, a form of torture in which the subject is pressed beneath stones. A new Superior Court of Judicature convened in January 1693 and did not allow spectral evidence; of the cases it heard, three people were found guilty, one of them Elizabeth Johnson Jr.

In 1702 the General Court of Massachusetts declared the trials unlawful, and in 1711 the colonial legislature annulled the convictions. Several accusers, mostly teenage girls, later admitted that they had fabricated their charges. The historian George Lincoln Burr wrote that the Salem witchcraft was the rock on which the New England theocracy shattered.

Acts of 1957 and 2001 absolved victims. The executions took place at Proctor's Ledge, at the foot of Gallows Hill. Researchers have proposed medical explanations for the fits, among them convulsive ergotism from infected rye, while some historians prefer motives such as jealousy and a need for attention.
salento: Salento is a cultural, historical and geographic region at the southern end of Apulia, a sub-peninsula of the Italian Peninsula. It encompasses the entire Province of Lecce, most of the Province of Brindisi and the south-eastern part of the Province of Taranto, though not Taranto itself. The peninsula is composed of limestone and divides the Gulf of Taranto in the west from the Strait of Otranto in the east, with the Adriatic Sea to the north and the Ionian Sea to the south. A depression called the Messapic threshold, running along the Taranto-Ostuni line, separates it from the Murge. The climate is Mediterranean, suited to olives, citrus fruits and palm trees.

In ancient times the peninsula was called Sallentina or Messapia, and the Iapygians are said to have migrated to it from the Illyrian coast in the eleventh century BCE. The Romans took control in 272 BCE. Under Roman rule it was known as Calabria and had a flourishing agricultural economy of wheat and olive oil. The name Calabria later moved to the region now called by it: from 580 the Calabrian province was gradually expanded westward, and by the 10th century the term had shifted.

Justinian I's reconquest of Italy, the Gothic War of 535 to 554, brought Byzantine rule, which strengthened Greek influence, shown in the use of the Greek language and the Byzantine rite. The Lombards tried to conquer the region from 569 and were pushed back.

The Saracens occupied Taranto and other places in 847 and destroyed Ugento in 870, deporting its inhabitants to Africa. The Normans arrived in southern Italy in 1016, and Robert Guiscard governed Apulia from 1059, beginning a period of prosperity. In 1480 the Ottomans under Gedik Ahmed Pasha besieged and sacked Otranto; they killed hundreds of men who refused to convert to Islam, and neighbouring towns were fortified. The Venetians briefly controlled Salento between 1482 and 1484, and in 1534 Charles V restored several castles, among them that of Lecce. The coastal towers, mostly of the 15th and 16th centuries, were watchtowers against maritime attack by the Saracens.

The Salentino dialect of Extreme Southern Italian is predominantly spoken, although an old Hellenic dialect, Griko, is also spoken in a few inland towns. Typical dishes include orecchiette, parmigiana di melanzane, pitta di patate and fried honey cookies called purciaddruzzi. The nearest international airports are those of Brindisi and Bari, and the main railway line ends at Lecce. Its sagre, communal food festivals, show off local cooking traditions.
salic-law: The original edition was commissioned by Clovis I, the first king of all the Franks, and published sometime between 507 and 511. He appointed four commissioners to research customary law that had until then been kept only in the minds of designated elders, who met in council when their knowledge was needed. The code therefore reflects ancient usages, and a written text let monarchs and their administrations govern more effectively. It is written in Late Latin and contains some of the earliest known instances of Old Dutch.

For about 300 years the code was copied by hand and amended, and each of the several dozen surviving manuscripts has its own errors, corrections and organisation. The edition called the Lex Salica Emendata dates from about 798, late in the reign of Charlemagne. It added laws taken from the codes of the Ripuarian Franks, the Alamanni and the Suebi, so that all the Franks of Francia lived under one code.

The criminal law set damages and fines for injuries to persons, damage to goods, theft and unprovoked insults, and one third of each fine paid the court costs. A person who belonged to no family was legally unprotected, and land was divided equally among all living male heirs rather than passing by primogeniture. Another title required the unanimous consent of a village for any newcomer to settle there, and a migrant's tenure became secure only if no one objected within twelve months.

On inheritance the code said that of Salic land no portion would come to a woman, but all would come to the male sex. This applied only to ancestral Salic land, not to other property, and about 570, under Chilperic I, the law was amended to allow a daughter to inherit land if a man had no surviving sons.

In France, when Louis X died in 1316 without a son, his brother became Philip V, and the Estates-General of 1317 declared that women do not succeed in the kingdom of France; the Salic law was not yet invoked. In 1328 the claim of Edward III of England through his mother Isabella of France was rejected with the argument that women cannot transmit a right they do not possess. The monk Richard Lescot invoked the Salic law in 1358 against Charles II of Navarre, and jurists later echoed him in defence of the Valois dynasty.

The principle of agnatic succession spread beyond France. The Carlist Wars in Spain arose over whether the heir should be female or male, and the thrones of Britain and Hanover separated in 1837 and those of the Netherlands and Luxembourg in 1890. Shakespeare uses the Salic law as a plot device in Henry V.
sallust: Sallust was probably born at Amiternum in the country of the Sabines, though Eduard Schwartz held that he was born in Rome. His family, the Sallustii, were provincial nobles of Sabine origin who belonged to the equestrian order and had full Roman citizenship, but not to Rome's ruling class. During the Social War his parents hid in Rome, so he may have been raised there, and he received a very good education. After an ill-spent youth he entered public life as a novus homo, serving as a military tribune in the 60s BCE.

His earliest certain office is plebeian tribune in 52 BCE, the year in which Milo's followers killed Clodius. He supported the prosecution of Milo and organised street demonstrations to pressure Cicero, who defended Milo. In 50 BCE the censor Appius Claudius Pulcher expelled him from the senate on grounds of immorality, probably a pretext for his opposition to Milo, and he joined Julius Caesar. In the civil war he commanded at least one legion in Illyricum in 49 BCE, an unsuccessful campaign. In late summer 47 BCE he was sent with other senators to persuade mutinous soldiers near Rome, but the rebels killed two senators and he narrowly escaped.

In 46 BCE he was praetor and accompanied Caesar to Africa, where he organised supplies through the Kerkennah Islands before the victory at Thapsus. He was then appointed governor of Africa Nova. As governor he made a fortune and was so corrupt that only Caesar's influence saved him from conviction for extortion. He bought and laid out the Gardens of Sallust on the Quirinal, later inherited by the emperors. Without prospects of advancement, he turned to writing history.

Sallust is the earliest known Latin historian with surviving works. His Conspiracy of Catiline, probably written about 42 BCE, tells of Lucius Sergius Catilina's attempt to overthrow the Republic in 63 BCE. The Jugurthine War, written about 41–40 BCE, covers the war in Numidia from 112 to 106 BCE and introduces the rivalry of Marius and Sulla. His Histories began in 78 BCE; only fragments survive. Two letters to Caesar and an attack on Cicero attributed to him are thought by modern scholars to be by a later rhetorician.

His theme is moral and political decline, which he traced to the wealth that flowed in after the destruction of Carthage in 146 BCE. He was influenced by Thucydides, and his style is brief and abrupt, with archaic words, unlike the flowing periods of Cicero. Historians since the 19th century have noted his bias and some errors of geography and dating, and many reject moral failure as the cause of the Republic's collapse.
salo: Salò is a town in the Province of Brescia, in Lombardy, on the banks of Lake Garda, on which it has the longest promenade. Its Latin name was Salodium. The area around the lake is a seismic zone: a meteorological observatory was established in the town in 1877 and a seismic station in 1889, which became an important research centre after the earthquake of 1901.

Legend gives Salò Etruscan origins, but recorded history begins with the Roman colony of Pagus Salodium, whose ruins include the Lugone necropolis. Its autonomy from Brescia dates to about the end of the 13th century, and from 1334 until 1797 it belonged to a federation of town councils along the western shore of the lake, later called the Riviera di Salò. After a short protectorate under Venice, from 1336 to 1349, Salò became a stronghold of the Milanese Visconti, and in 1377 Beatrice della Scala, wife of Bernabò Visconti, had it made capital of the area, with walls and a castle.

On 13 May 1426 the towns of the western shore joined the Venetian Republic, where they remained for three centuries. Venice gave the area great autonomy, and it was styled the Magnifica Patria. Its general council stayed at Salò, though Venice sent a governor with the title of Provveditore, and the linen industry developed. The end of the Venetian republic in 1797 ended Salò's position as capital of the riviera; it joined the Cisalpine Republic and then the Napoleonic Kingdom of Italy, and from 1815 to 1859 it was part of the Austrian Kingdom of Lombardy-Venetia. Garibaldi entered the town on 18 June 1859, and in 1866 it was headquarters of the Italian navy during the war with Austria.

From 1943 to 1945 it was the de facto capital of Benito Mussolini's Nazi-backed Italian Social Republic. Villa Castagna housed the police headquarters, Villa Amedei the Ministry of Popular Culture and Villa Simonini the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

The cathedral of Santa Maria Annunziata, rebuilt in late Gothic style in the 15th century, has a Renaissance portal. The 16th-century Palazzo della Magnifica Patria houses a historical museum with documents on Renaissance history, Italy's colonial wars, the Spanish Civil War and the Resistance, and the Communal Palace holds the Civic Archaeological Museum with finds from ancient Salodium. A column with the Lion of St Mark, symbol of Venice, still stands in the main square.
salt-march: The Indian National Congress issued the Declaration of Sovereignty and Self-rule, or Purna Swaraj, on 26 January 1930, and the declaration included readiness to withhold taxes. Gandhi chose as his target the Salt Act of 1882, which gave the British a monopoly on the manufacture and collection of salt and levied a tax on it. Violating the act was a criminal offence, although salt was freely available to people on the coast by evaporating sea water.

His choice was at first met with incredulity by the Congress Working Committee. Lord Irwin, the Viceroy, wrote that a salt campaign did not keep him awake at night. 2 percent of the Raj's revenue and hurt the poorest most, and that next to air and water salt was among the necessities of life.

Gandhi set out on 12 March 1930 from Sabarmati Ashram with 78 volunteers who came from almost every region, caste and religion of India, and walked to the coastal village of Dandi in Navsari district. In the villages volunteers collected donations and registered new satyagrahis, and village officials resigned. Gandhi called the salt tax inhuman and the campaign a poor man's struggle. At 8:30 in the morning of 6 April 1930 he broke the salt law at Dandi.

Millions then broke the salt laws by making salt or buying illegal salt, and the British arrested over sixty thousand people by the end of the month. The campaign grew into a boycott of British cloth and goods and the defiance of forest laws. In Peshawar a crowd of Khudai Khidmatgar led by Ghaffar Khan was fired on at the Qissa Kahani Bazaar on 23 April, and an estimated 200 to 250 people were killed. Gandhi was arrested on the night of 4 and 5 May, just days before the planned action at the Dharasana Salt Works.

The Salt Satyagraha did not produce immediate concessions or self-rule, and Congress ended satyagraha as official policy in 1934. It drew worldwide attention to the Indian independence movement through newspaper and newsreel coverage and showed the effect of civil disobedience, and the Civil Disobedience Movement it began continued until 1934 in Gujarat. Nehru considered it the high-water mark of his association with Gandhi. Its methods influenced American activists in the civil rights movement of the 1960s, among them Martin Luther King Jr. The National Salt Satyagraha Memorial in Dandi opened on 30 January 2019.
salta: In early 1536 the large expedition of Diego de Almagro, on its way to Chile, passed through the plains of Chicoana west of the present city and fought skirmishes with local tribesmen while foraging. Hernando de Lerma founded Salta on 16 April 1582, intending the settlement to be an outpost between Lima in Peru and Buenos Aires. The origin of the name is a matter of conjecture, and several theories have been advanced.

During the war of independence the city was a commercial and military strategic point between Peru and the Argentine cities. From 1816 to 1821 it was led by the local military leader General Martín Miguel de Güemes, who under the command of General José de San Martín defended the city and the surrounding area from Spanish forces coming from the north. Salta emerged from the war politically in disarray and financially bankrupt, a condition that lasted through much of the 19th century. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries Italian, Spanish, British and Arab immigrants, particularly Syrians and Lebanese, revived trade and agriculture in the area and added to the city's multicultural character.

Salta is the capital and largest city of Salta Province and the cultural and economic centre of the Valle de Lerma Metropolitan Area. It stands at an altitude of 1,200 metres and has a subtropical highland climate, with over 80 per cent of its rainfall between December and March. Around the Ninth of July Square stand the neoclassical Cathedral Shrine, the Cabildo, once the town hall and now a historical museum, a museum of contemporary art and the Museum of High Altitude Archaeology, which houses artefacts from the Inca civilisation, among them the mummies of three Inca children. San Bernardo Hill rises in the east. The local culture blends Spanish and gaucho traditions, and the April Culture Festival lasts the whole month.
salvador-allende: Salvador Guillermo Allende Gossens was born on 26 June 1908 in Santiago. His family belonged to the Chilean upper middle class and had a long tradition of involvement in progressive and liberal causes. His grandfather was a prominent physician and social reformer who founded one of the first secular schools in Chile. Allende was of Basque and Belgian descent. In 1938 he directed the campaign of the Popular Front headed by Pedro Aguirre Cerda, and as Minister of Health in the following government he passed safety laws for factory workers, higher pensions for widows, maternity care and free lunches for schoolchildren.

Allende was a committed member of the Socialist Party, which he helped found, and over nearly forty years was a senator, a deputy and a cabinet minister. He ran unsuccessfully for the presidency in 1952, 1958 and 1964. In 1970 he won a close three-way race as the Popular Unity candidate and was confirmed in a run-off by Congress. As president he pursued what he called the Chilean Path to Socialism, representing the more moderate faction of his party, while its left wing under Carlos Altamirano sought a more radical course.

In the first year his economy minister Pedro Vuskovic's policy brought 12% industrial growth, but by 1972 inflation of the escudo reached 140%. His government returned land to the Mapuche and in 1971 re-established relations with Cuba. A 24-day strike began in October 1972, and on 29 June 1973 Colonel Roberto Souper's tank regiment surrounded La Moneda in a failed coup known as the Tanquetazo. On 22 August 1973 the Chamber of Deputies voted 81 to 47 to accuse the government of breaching the Constitution.

In early September 1973 Allende considered resolving the crisis with a plebiscite, to be announced on 11 September. That day the military under Augusto Pinochet staged the coup. As troops surrounded La Moneda he spoke to Chileans on live radio, refused an offer of safe passage and died in his office, by suicide, though the exact circumstances are disputed. The junta that followed dissolved Congress, and at least 3,095 civilians disappeared or were killed. Allende is buried in the general cemetery of Santiago, and many socialists revere him as a hero and martyr.
salween: The Salween is about 3,289 kilometres long. It rises in the Tanggula Mountains of the central Tibetan Plateau, passes through Cona Lake, and flows through Tibet and Yunnan, where it is called the Nu Jiang, then through Shan, Karenni, Karen and Mon states of Myanmar, where it is the Thanlwin. A short section forms the Myanmar–Thailand border. Its basin is long and narrow, between the Irrawaddy and Brahmaputra systems on the west and the Mekong on the east, and about 89 per cent of the annual flow comes in the monsoon season. Only the last 90 kilometres, at the estuary and delta at Mawlamyine, are navigable. The spelling Salween is an anglicisation of the Burmese name from 19th-century maps.

Human presence along the upper river dates to at least 31,000 to 39,000 years ago. The Mon migrated south from China around 3000 BCE, the ancestors of the Karen from about 1000 BCE, and Tai peoples, ancestors of the Shan, entered the Shan Hills from Yunnan from about 1000 CE. Martaban was a major port on the Maritime Silk Road as early as 200 BCE, and from 738 to 902 CE the Salween formed the south-western boundary of Nanzhao with the Pyu city-states.

In the 1060s Anawrahta of Pagan conquered Thaton and the Mon kingdoms of the delta, and in the late 1100s Narapatisithu brought most of the Shan States under Burmese rule. For almost 500 years the lower Salween defined the frontier between Burma and Ayutthaya.

After the First Anglo-Burmese War of 1824 the Konbaung dynasty ceded the Tenasserim coast south of the river to the British Empire, and Mawlamyine was capital of British Burma from 1826 until 1852. Teak logs were floated down the Salween to the port. In 1935–36 the British geographer Ronald Kaulback walked the length of the river and produced some of the first comprehensive maps of its course.

The Salween is one of the least fragmented large river systems in Asia, with only a few small dams on its headwaters and tributaries. Along with the Lancang and Jinsha rivers it flows through the Three Parallel Rivers World Heritage Site in Yunnan. Its delta is a major rice-growing area and its estuary a rich fishery. The basin is home to many minority peoples, including the Karen, Shan, Mon and Nu.
salzburg: Salzburg stands on both banks of the River Salzach at the northern edge of the Alps. The mountains lie to the south and rolling plains to the north; the nearest alpine peak, the Untersberg at 1,972 metres, is less than 16 kilometres from the centre. The old town is flanked by two smaller hills, the Mönchsberg and the Kapuzinerberg, and dominated by the Hohensalzburg Fortress. The city lies about 150 kilometres east of Munich and 300 kilometres west of Vienna.

The area has been inhabited continuously since the Neolithic. In the La Tène period it was an administrative centre of the Celtic Taurisci in the Kingdom of Noricum. After the Roman invasion of 15 BCE the settlements on the surrounding hills were abandoned for a Roman city, which received the status of a municipium in 45 CE and became one of the most important cities of the province of Noricum.

When Noricum collapsed in 488, part of the Romano-Celtic population remained, and in the sixth century it came under the Baiuvarii. The Life of Saint Rupert credits Rupert with the city's rebirth: Duke Theodo II of Bavaria gave him the remains of the Roman town and an upper castle on the Nonnberg Terrace, and in return he was to evangelise the east and south-east of Bavaria.

Independence from Bavaria was secured in the late fourteenth century, and the archbishopric became a prince-bishopric of the Holy Roman Empire. During the German Peasants' War the archbishop fled to the fortress, which was besieged for three months in 1525. On 31 October 1731 Archbishop Count Leopold Anton von Firmian signed an Edict of Expulsion ordering all Protestant citizens to recant; 21,475 citizens refused and were expelled, and most of them accepted an offer from King Friedrich Wilhelm I of Prussia to settle in East Prussia. Napoleon secularised the archbishopric in 1803. Salzburg passed to Austria in 1805, to Bavaria in 1809 and finally back to Austria under the Treaty of Munich of 1816.

Salzburg's historic centre was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996 and is one of the best-preserved city centres north of the Alps. Prince-Archbishop Wolf Dietrich von Raitenau began to rebuild the medieval town on late Renaissance lines, and Santino Solari's cathedral was the first early Baroque church in the city. The Franziskanerkirche dates from 1208, and the Großes Festspielhaus, opened in 1960, was built for the annual Salzburg Festival. The city has three universities, among them the Mozarteum University for music and drama.
salzwedel: Salzwedel lies on the river Jeetzel in the north-western part of the Altmark, between Hamburg and Magdeburg, and is the capital of the district of Altmarkkreis Salzwedel. It stands on the German Timber-Frame Road. Test drillings in 1968 revealed a significant reservoir of natural gas near the town.

The castle of Salzwedel was first documented in 1112. As part of the Margraviate of Brandenburg the settlement was first mentioned as a town in 1233, and a new town began to develop to the north-east of the old town in 1247. Salzwedel belonged to the Hanseatic League from 1263 to 1518, and in religious matters to the Diocese of Verden until 1648. It became part of the Kingdom of Prussia in 1701, the old and new towns were united in 1713, it joined the Prussian Province of Saxony in 1815 after the Napoleonic Wars, and it received a railway connection in 1870.

Under Nazi rule the town's Jewish residents were systematically deprived of their rights and then expelled. A forced labour camp for some 1,000 women was converted in mid-1944 into a subcamp of the Neuengamme concentration camp, which held over 1,500 female prisoners, mostly Jewish. When the US Army liberated it on 14 April 1945, it found more than ninety women dead of typhus, dysentery and malaria. Five air raids between 1942 and 1945 killed more than 300 people.

The US Army handed the town to the Soviet Red Army, and it became part of the German Democratic Republic. The border crossing near Salzwedel opened on 9 November 1989, and in 1990 the town received its first democratically elected government. Its official name became Hansestadt Salzwedel on 1 April 2008, recalling its Hanseatic past.

The medieval part of the town remains its commercial and administrative centre. It is enclosed by the historic city wall and town gates, among them the Neuperver Gate, built 1460–1470, the Stonegate of around 1530, the Hungerturm tower and the Kluhs, a storehouse of 1490 built on the wall. The brick Gothic churches of St Marien, St Katharina and St Lorenz stand in the old town, and the birth house of Jenny von Westphalen, later the wife of Karl Marx, is also preserved. Local specialities include Baumkuchen, the layered tree cake, Salzwedel wedding soup and Tiegelbraten, a mutton dish.
sam-houston: Samuel Houston was born on 2 March 1793 in Rockbridge County, Virginia, into a slave-owning family, and he owned enslaved people throughout his life. After his father died in 1807 he ran away at 16 to live with a Cherokee group led by Chief John Jolly on Hiwassee Island, learned the Cherokee language and customs, and was known as Raven. He enlisted in the army on 24 March 1813 for the War of 1812, served under General Andrew Jackson and was badly wounded at the Battle of Horseshoe Bend.

After studying law he became district attorney for Nashville in 1819. With Jackson's support he was elected to the House of Representatives in 1823 and governor of Tennessee in 1827. His marriage to Eliza Allen in January 1829 lasted eleven weeks, and he resigned and went to live again with the Cherokee.

Houston crossed into Mexican Texas in December 1832. The Texas Revolution began in October 1835 with the Battle of Gonzales, and Houston led the Texian Army to victory at San Jacinto in 1836. He won the 1836 presidential election and took office on 22 October 1836 after the interim president, David G. Burnet, resigned. He sought normal relations with Mexico, arranged the release of Santa Anna, and urged an end to the importation of enslaved people. Term limits ended his presidency in 1838, and he won another term in 1841.

After annexation in 1845 the Texas legislature elected him one of its first two senators in February 1846. He voted for the Compromise of 1850 but against the Kansas–Nebraska Act of 1854, which he believed would raise tensions over slavery, and he left the Democratic Party over it. He was elected governor in 1859 and campaigned against secession. He was the only Southern governor to refuse an oath of allegiance to the Confederacy and was forced out of office in 1861.

Houston died at Huntsville, Texas, on 26 July 1863, aged 70, of what is believed to have been pneumonia. His record on slavery was complicated: he held enslaved people and governed Texas as a slave state, yet voted several times against extending slavery into the West and put the Union above dividing it over slavery. The city of Houston was founded in his name in 1836, and Sam Houston State University and Fort Sam Houston also commemorate him.
sam-nujoma: Samuel Shafiishuna Daniel Nujoma was born on 12 May 1929 at Etunda, a village in Ongandjera, near Okahao, Ovamboland, in South West Africa. He was the eldest of eleven children, and his mother, Helvi Mpingana Kondombolo, was a Uukwambi princess by descent. He tended the family's cattle, attended a Finnish missionary school at Okahao from the age of ten and completed Standard Six, the highest level open to black pupils at the time.

In 1946 he moved to Walvis Bay, where he worked in a general store and later at a whaling station. In 1949 he went to Windhoek, working as a cleaner for South African Railways while attending night school. He became involved in politics in the early 1950s through trade unions, shaped by his experience of the contract labour system, and was dismissed from the railways in 1957.

In 1959 Nujoma co-founded the Ovamboland People's Organization and was elected its first president. After the Old Location Massacre in December 1959 he was arrested for organising the resistance, and in February 1960 he went into exile to lobby the United Nations. The organisation was reconstituted as the South West Africa People's Organisation (SWAPO) in New York on 19 April 1960, with Nujoma elected president in absentia. He built its headquarters in Dar es Salaam with the help of Julius Nyerere, and in 1962 SWAPO founded an armed wing, later the People's Liberation Army of Namibia.

The first armed clash with South African forces took place on 26 August 1966 at Omugulugwombashe and began the Namibian War of Independence. Nujoma's role in the army has been questioned following allegations of torture and imprisonment of fighters in the Lubango dungeons in Angola, where about 1,000 SWAPO members were held for over nine years. He led SWAPO's negotiators over the proposals that became United Nations Security Council Resolution 435 in 1978, and a ceasefire with South Africa was signed on 19 March 1989. After 29 years in exile he returned in September 1989.

The Constituent Assembly elected in November 1989 chose Nujoma as Namibia's first president, and he was sworn in on 21 March 1990. He proclaimed a policy of national reconciliation to improve relations among the country's racial and ethnic groups, and began a land reform programme in 1990. He was re-elected in 1994, and the constitution was changed so that he could stand for a third term in 1999. His successor, Hifikepunye Pohamba, took office on 21 March 2005, and Pohamba also succeeded him as SWAPO president in 2007. Parliament conferred on him the title Founding Father of the Namibian Nation in December 2005. He published his autobiography, Where Others Wavered, in 2001, and died in Windhoek on 8 February 2025, aged 95.
samaria: Samaria is a historical and biblical name for the central region of the Land of Israel, bordered by Judea to the south, Galilee to the north, the Jordan River to the east and the Mediterranean Sea to the west. Its hills lie between the Jezreel Valley, the Jordan Rift Valley, the Sharon plain and the Jerusalem mountains, and include Mount Carmel, Mount Gilboa, Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim. Mount Ebal, at 935 metres, is the highest peak.

The Hebrew name Shomron is linked in the Hebrew Bible to Shemer, from whom King Omri bought the hill on which he built his capital. Assyrian inscriptions first call the place Bet Ḥumri, the house of Omri, and later Samirin. The name for the whole region is first documented after the Neo-Assyrian conquest, when the land became the province of Samerina.

Settlement grew in the Iron Age II, from about 950 BCE: archaeologists estimate 400 sites, up from 300 in the Iron Age I. After the Assyrian conquest, Sargon II claimed to have deported 27,280 people, mainly to Guzana and to the cities of the Medes, while people from other parts of the empire were settled in Samerina. This resettlement is the basis of the narrative of the Ten Lost Tribes.

The region then passed to the Neo-Babylonian and Achaemenid Persian empires. Many scholars hold that a Samaritan temple was built on Mount Gerizim in the first half of the 5th century BCE. After Alexander the Great's conquest in 332 BCE, Samaria was ruled by the Ptolemies and the Seleucids; around 110 BCE the Hasmonean ruler John Hyrcanus destroyed the cities of Samaria and Shechem and the temple on Mount Gerizim. In 6 CE it became part of the Roman province of Iudaea.

Samaritan revolts against the Byzantine Empire, mostly in 525 and 555 CE, were suppressed with death, displacement and conversion to Christianity, and the Samaritan population fell sharply. Muslim rule followed from the 7th century, then the Crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem, the Ayyubids, the Mamluks and, from 1516 to 1917, the Ottomans.

The ancient site of Samaria-Sebaste covers a hillside above the village of Sebastia and holds Canaanite, Israelite, Hellenistic, Roman and Byzantine remains. Roman-era finds include a colonnaded street, a temple-lined acropolis and a lower city, where John the Baptist is believed to have been buried. The Harvard excavation, begun in 1908 under George Andrew Reisner, was followed in 1931–35 by a joint British-American-Hebrew University dig under John Winter Crowfoot. Their finds include inscriptions, coins and a large collection of ivory carvings from the early first millennium BCE.
samaritans: The Samaritans identify as descendants of the Israelite tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh and of the priestly tribe of Levi, and hold that they preserve the most authentic form of the Mosaic covenant. Their own tradition, recorded in the Kitab al-Ta'rikh compiled by Abu'l-Fath in 1355, traces the split from the southern Israelites to the priest Eli, who is said to have usurped the high priesthood and set up a rival shrine at Shiloh.

In contemporary scholarship the community is generally understood to have emerged in Samaria from populations of the former northern Kingdom of Israel together with people of Mesopotamian origin, its distinctive identity taking shape in the Persian and Hellenistic periods. Josephus, a key source, is considered a prejudiced witness hostile to them.

In 331 BCE the Samaritans rose against Macedonian rule and killed the prefect Andromachus, and the army carried out a brutal reprisal. A Samaritan diaspora is documented in the Hellenistic period, including inscriptions on Delos. Under the Roman Empire Samaria became part of the province of Judaea, and Samaritans appear in the Christian gospels, notably in the account of the Samaritan woman at the well and the parable of the Good Samaritan.

Their numbers were drastically reduced by failed revolts and severe Byzantine repression in the 5th and 6th centuries CE. According to Samaritan sources the emperor Zeno persecuted them, appropriated Mount Gerizim and built a tomb for his son there, and by 484 they revolted, burning five churches in Neapolis and electing a king, Justa, who was killed by the Byzantine commander.

Christianisation under the Byzantines and gradual conversion to Islam after the Muslim conquest reduced them further. In the 12th century Benjamin of Tudela estimated about 1,900 remained in Palestine and Syria. Ottoman censuses of 1525-1526 recorded 25 Samaritan families in Gaza and 29 in Nablus, and the community reached a low of around 100 in 1786. Their situation improved under the British Mandate.

Samaritans recognise only the Samaritan Pentateuch as scripture, which they believe to be the original version of the Torah given to Moses, and it differs from the Masoretic text in some 6,000 places. They hold that Mount Gerizim, not Jerusalem, is God's chosen sanctuary, and that Abraham was commanded there to offer Isaac. Their religion centres on a hereditary high priesthood, strict observance of biblical law and festivals, and the Passover sacrifice on Gerizim.

Many believe that at the end of days the dead will be resurrected by the Taheb, a restorer. They use Samaritan Hebrew and Samaritan Aramaic for liturgy, written in the Samaritan script. The community comprises four families or houses, Cohen, Tsedakah, Danafi and Marhiv, and lives mainly at Kiryat Luza on Mount Gerizim near Nablus and in Holon.
samarkand: Samarkand is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Central Asia and prospered from its place on the trade route between China, Persia and Europe. There is no direct evidence of when it was founded; researchers at the Institute of Archaeology of Samarkand date it to around 700 BCE. It was the central city of the Sogdian civilisation. It was known as Marakanda when Alexander the Great conquered it in 329 BCE. According to some sources the present name comes from the Sogdian samar, stone, and kand, fort or town, though this cannot be proven.

The Persian Sasanians conquered Samarkand around 260 CE, and under their rule the region became an essential site for Manichaeism. Nomadic Xionites took it between 350 and 375, and the Hephthalites controlled it until the Göktürks, allied with the Sasanians, won it around 560. The armies of the Umayyad Caliphate under Qutayba ibn Muslim captured the city around 712. It was the capital of the Samanid Empire in the 9th century, when New Persian gradually replaced Sogdian, and from 1040 to 1212 it was the capital of the Western Qarakhanid Khaganate.

The Mongols under Genghis Khan conquered the city in 1220. According to the historian Juvayni, Genghis killed all who had taken refuge in the citadel and the mosque, pillaged the city completely and conscripted 30,000 young men and 30,000 craftsmen. Samarkand remained in the Chagatai Khanate until 1370. Timur ruled from 1370 to 1405 and made it the capital of the Timurid Empire. Between 1417 and 1420 his grandson Ulugh Beg built a madrasah that became the first building of the Registan ensemble, and in 1428 he built an observatory whose chief instrument was a wall quadrant with a radius of 40 metres.

Muhammad Shaybani of the Uzbek Shaybanid dynasty took the city in 1501, and it became the capital of the new Bukhara Khanate. Russian forces under General Konstantin Petrovich von Kaufman took the citadel in 1868, and the Russian section of the city was built to the west of the old city. Samarkand was the first capital of the Uzbek Soviet Socialist Republic, from 1925 to 1930.

Samarkand is the second-largest city of Uzbekistan and capital of the Samarkand Region. The Timurid and Uzbek Khanate periods gave it the Registan Square, the Gur-i Amir Mausoleum, the Bibi-Khanym Mosque and the Shah-i-Zinda Necropolis, known for their tilework in cobalt and turquoise. UNESCO added the city to its World Heritage List in 2001 as Samarkand, Crossroads of Cultures.
samarra: Samarra stands on the east bank of the Tigris in the Saladin Governorate, 125 kilometres north of Baghdad. Its earliest remains were first excavated between 1911 and 1914 by the German archaeologists Ernst Herzfeld and Friedrich Sarre, and Samarra became the type site of the Samarra culture, which flourished alongside the Ubaid period as one of the first town states in the Near East. A Neo-Assyrian city, Sur-marrati, refounded by Sennacherib in 690 BCE, is insecurely identified with a fortified site opposite the modern city.

In 836 CE the caliph al-Mu'tasim founded a new capital on the Tigris. He built extensive palace complexes surrounded by garrison settlements for his guards, drawn mostly from Central Asia and Iran, chiefly the Turks, or from North Africa. Although often called Mamluk slave soldiers, their status was quite elevated, and some of their commanders bore Sogdian titles of nobility. Earlier, Harun al-Rashid had dug a canal here and laid out the octagonal city of al-Mubarak, abandoned unfinished in 796.

Caliph al-Mutawakkil sponsored lavish palaces, such as al-Mutawakkiliyya, and the Great Mosque of Samarra with its spiral minaret, the Malwiya, built in 847. The Nestorian patriarch Sargis moved the seat of the Church of the East from Baghdad to Samarra to be close to the seat of power. Samarra remained the caliph's residence until 892, when al-Mu'tadid returned the capital to Baghdad. The city was looted around this time, and its population probably fell, though it remained an important market centre. Later the river's course shifted to the east, the main road from Baghdad to Mosul moved to the west bank, and Samarra lost its importance as a trading town.

From the tenth century the city became a pilgrimage site.
