In the 1730–1735 Ottoman–Persian War the Battle of Samarra cost over 50,000 Ottoman and Persian casualties and decided the fate of Ottoman Iraq, which stayed under Istanbul's suzerainty until the First World War. In the 1950s the Samarra Barrage created Lake Tharthar to prevent the flooding of Baghdad.

Samarra is a holy site in Shia Islam because of the al-Askari Shrine, which holds the tombs of the tenth and eleventh Imams, Ali al-Hadi and Hasan al-Askari, and of Hakimah and Narjis, female relatives of the Prophet and the Imams. The archaeological site preserves much of the historic city's plan, architecture and artistic relics, and UNESCO designated it a World Heritage Site in 2007. A story of an appointment with Death at Samarra, from the Babylonian Talmud, was retold by W. Somerset Maugham and gave John O'Hara's novel its title.
samaveda: The Samaveda, from the Sanskrit saman, "song", and veda, "knowledge", is the Veda of melodies and chants. It is a liturgical text of 1,875 verses, all but 75 of them taken from the Rigveda. Its earliest parts are believed to date from as early as the Rigvedic period, but the existing samhita belongs to the post-Rigvedic Mantra period. Michael Witzel, who notes that there is no absolute dating for the Vedic texts, estimates it at 1200 to 1000 BCE, roughly contemporary with the Atharvaveda and the Yajurveda.

The text has several layers: the Samhita, the oldest, then Brahmana texts and finally the Upanishads, likely composed around the 6th century BCE. Three recensions survive. The Kauthuma is current in Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Odisha and West Bengal, the Ranayaniya in Maharashtra and Karnataka among other regions, and the Jaiminiya in Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Kerala. The Jaiminiya preserves the oldest surviving tradition of Samavedic chanting.

The Samaveda has two major parts: four collections of melodies and three books of verses. The Gramageya melodies were for public recitation, and the Aranyageya for personal meditative use, as in the solitude of a forest. The verse books divide into the Purvarcika, with 585 single-stanza verses arranged by deity, and the Uttararcika, arranged by ritual. In all there are 1,549 unique verses. The purpose of the text was liturgical, and it was the repertoire of the udgatar, or singer, priests.

The text is not meant to be read: like a musical score, it must be heard. It contains notated melodies, probably the oldest that survive anywhere. Frits Staal argued that the melodies likely existed before the verses, since some early words fit them well and later ones do not, and that stobha, embellishing syllables, were used to fit words to the music. The Chandogya Upanishad and the Kena Upanishad are embedded in the Samaveda; the Chandogya was cited 810 times by Adi Shankara in his commentary on the Vedanta Sutra.

Theodor Benfey published a German edition in 1848, Satyavrata Samashrami a Sanskrit one in 1873, Filipp Fortunatov a Russian translation in 1875 and Ralph Griffith an English translation in 1893. The Samaveda has received less attention than the Rigveda, since all but 75 of its verses derive from it. In the Bhagavad Gita Krishna says, "Among the Vedas I am the Samaveda." Guy Beck holds that Indian classical music and dance are rooted in its sonic and musical dimensions, and musicologists widely acknowledge its chant theory as a root of Indian music.
sambre: The Sambre is a river in northern France and in Wallonia, Belgium, and a left-bank tributary of the Meuse, which it joins at Namur, the Walloon capital. Its source lies near Le Nouvion-en-Thiérache, in the Aisne department. In France it passes Landrecies, Aulnoye-Aymeries, Hautmont and Maubeuge in the Nord department, and in Belgium Thuin, Montigny-le-Tilleul, Charleroi, Floreffe and Namur.
Its main tributaries include the Helpe Mineure, the Helpe Majeure, the Eau d'Heure, which gives its name to the Eau d'Heure lakes, the Piéton, which joins in Charleroi, and the Orneau.

The river runs through the Franco-Belgian coal basin, formerly an important industrial district. It lies at the western end of the sillon industriel, which remains the backbone of Wallonia's industry even though all coal mining has ceased and the steel industry has declined.

Navigation begins at Landrecies, where the Canal de la Sambre à l'Oise joins the river and links it with the central French waterway network, until navigation was interrupted in 2006 following structural failures. The French stretch runs 54 km with nine locks down to the border at Jeumont. Beyond the border the river is canalised in two sections over 88 km with 17 locks. The Haute-Sambre is 39 km long, with ten locks, down to Charleroi, and the rest of the Belgian river was upgraded to European Class IV dimensions, for barges of 1,350 tonnes, in the years after World War II.

Fleurus, a suburb of Charleroi on the north bank, saw three important battles: the Thirty Years' War Battle of Fleurus in 1622, the Nine Years' War Battle of Fleurus in 1690 and, on 26 June 1794, the Battle of Fleurus, the most significant battle of the Flanders Campaign in the French Revolutionary Wars. The last was fought on both banks of the river after a campaign of many crossings and re-crossings. Heavy fighting also occurred along the river in World War I, at the siege of Namur in 1914, during the Battle of Charleroi, and in the Battle of the Sambre in 1918.
sami-people: The Sámi are the traditionally Sámi-speaking indigenous people of Sápmi, formerly called Lapland. In English they were long known as Lapps, a term some Sámi regard as offensive. Their languages form a branch of the Uralic family. The groups that reached the Finnish Lakeland between 1600 and 1500 BCE later became the Sámi, who arrived in Sápmi during the Bronze Age or early Iron Age.

The first probable mention is by Tacitus, about 98 CE, who called them Fenni. Norse speakers used Finn for the Sámi, as in the Icelandic Eddas and sagas of the eleventh to fourteenth centuries. The word Lapp appears in Saxo Grammaticus's twelfth-century Gesta Danorum, and Johannes Schefferus's Lapponia of 1673 made it standard.

For centuries the Sámi and the Scandinavians had little contact. The Sámi lived mainly in the inland north, while Scandinavians gradually settled the Norwegian coast. Until the bubonic plague reached northern Norway in 1349 the two peoples occupied separate economic niches, the Sámi herding reindeer or fishing along the fjords. How far south the Sámi settled has long been debated: Yngvar Nielsen, commissioned by the Norwegian government in 1889, concluded they had lived no farther south than Lierne until about 1500, but later archaeological finds suggest a presence in southern Norway in the Middle Ages.

From the eighteenth and especially the nineteenth century the governments of Norway and Sweden asserted sovereignty more aggressively in the north and pursued forced assimilation. Generations of Sámi children were taken to missionary or state-run boarding schools, and laws denied the Sámi rights to their beliefs, language, land and livelihoods. In the 1970s the idea of Sápmi as a Sámi nation gained acceptance, and a flag, an anthem and a national day followed in the 1980s and 1990s.

Traditional livelihoods include coastal fishing, fur trapping and sheep herding, and the best known is semi-nomadic reindeer herding. Herders traditionally lived in groups of several families called siidat. About 10 percent of Sámi are connected to herding, which in some regions of the Nordic countries is legally reserved for them.

There are ten distinct Sámi languages, closely related but not mutually intelligible. Many Sámi kept their ancestral religion until the eighteenth century, and most now belong to the Lutheran churches of Norway, Sweden and Finland. The joik, a song-chant sung a cappella, is characteristic of the music, and the craft duodji makes useful objects from wood, bone, antler and leather. The Laponian Area in Swedish Lappland became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996.
samnite-wars: The Samnites were a confederation of four tribes living in the mountains east of Campania. Rome and the Samnites made a treaty in 354 BCE whose terms are not recorded; modern historians have proposed that it made the River Liris the boundary between their spheres. Livy, the only continuous source for the first war, says it began when the Samnites attacked the Sidicini and then the Campanians, and Capua surrendered itself to Rome. Modern historians doubt his three Roman victories of 343 BCE. The war ended in 341 BCE in a negotiated peace: Rome accepted that the Sidicini lay in the Samnite sphere but kept its alliance with the Campanians.

The second war grew out of Roman moves in Campania: a colony founded at Fregellae in 328 BCE and the taking of Naples in 326 BCE. In 321 BCE the consuls Titus Veturius Calvinus and Spurius Postumius Albinus were trapped by the Samnite commander Gaius Pontius in the Caudine Forks and surrendered; their soldiers passed unarmed under the yoke and six hundred equites were given as hostages. Livy says Rome rejected the agreement and avenged it, a claim some modern scholars doubt. Fighting resumed in 316 BCE, and in 304 BCE, after the fall of Bovianum, the Samnites sought peace; Livy says the old treaty was restored.

The third war began in 298 BCE, when the Lucanians asked for Roman protection against Samnite invasion. In 295 BCE Rome faced a coalition of Samnites, Etruscans, Umbrians and Senone Gauls. At Sentinum the consul Publius Decius Mus devoted himself, charging into the enemy line to his death, and Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus won the battle; Livy gives 8,700 Roman dead and 20,000 of the enemy. Livy's surviving narrative ends in 293 BCE, and the last campaigns to 290 BCE are known only in outline.

The Samnites were forced to become allies of Rome, on terms that must have been unequal, and a colony was planted at Venusia in south-eastern Samnia. Gaius Pontius was captured, paraded in a triumph and beheaded. Around Samnia Rome had already bound the Marsi, Marrucini, Paeligni and Frentani by alliance in 304 BCE and the Vestini in 302 BCE, and it annexed the Hernici and the Sabines by giving them citizenship without the vote. The allies supplied soldiers at their own expense and shared the spoils, which greatly enlarged the manpower Rome could call on.
samoan-islands: The archipelago covers 3,030 km2 in the central South Pacific and has 18 islands spread from west to east. It lies between 13° and 14° south latitude, about 800 km from Fiji, 530 km from Tonga, 2,900 km from New Zealand and 4,000 km from Hawaii. The larger islands are volcanic, mountainous and covered in tropical moist forest, while some of the smaller ones are coral atolls with black sand beaches.

In the west, Upolu (1,718 km2) is the most populous island and Savaiʻi (1,125 km2) the largest and highest, with Mt Silisili at 1,858 m. The small islands of Manono, Apolima and Nuʻulopa lie in the Apolima Strait between them, and the four Aleipata Islands lie off the east of Upolu. In the east, Tutuila is the largest island of American Samoa, and the Manuʻa group comprises Ofu, Olosega and Taʻū. The islands may have been formed by the Samoa hotspot, though some evidence long seemed inconsistent with that theory until submarine samples gathered in 2005 gave older ages.

The oldest known evidence of human activity dates to around 1050 BCE, from a Lapita site at Mulifanua wharf on Upolu. The inhabitants share the Samoan language, a culture called faʻa Samoa and an indigenous form of governance called faʻamatai. In 1768 the French explorer Bougainville visited the eastern islands and named them the Navigator Islands, a name that missionaries used until about 1845 and official European dispatches until about 1870.

In the late 19th century the United States, Germany and the United Kingdom competed for control of the islands. In 1892 the ruler Malietoa Laupepa proclaimed that Monday 4 July would occur twice, moving the islands to the eastern side of the International Date Line, probably because of increasing trade with Americans. The Tripartite Convention of December 1899 partitioned the archipelago into German Samoa in the west and American Samoa in the east. New Zealand began occupying the western islands in World War I and governed them under a League of Nations Class C Mandate from 1920 to 1946 and as a United Nations Trust Territory from 1946 to 1962. The Mau movement, popular across the area, led to independence in 1962.

The archipelago comprises all of the Independent State of Samoa, whose capital is Apia, and most of American Samoa, an unincorporated territory of the United States whose capital is Pago Pago. The two jurisdictions are separated by 64 km of ocean at their closest points. Together they have approximately 250,000 inhabitants, and Samoans are one of the largest Polynesian populations in the world. Independent Samoa was known as Western Samoa until 1997. It moved back to the western side of the date line by skipping Friday 30 December 2011.
samogitia: Samogitia, in Lithuanian Žemaitija, is one of the five cultural regions of Lithuania and was formerly one of the two core administrative divisions of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, alongside Lithuania proper. Its capital is Telšiai and its largest city is Šiauliai. The Lithuanian name comes from žemas, low, and žemė, land, and means lowlands. Its people speak Samogitian, a variety of Lithuanian with a broken intonation similar to that of Latvian. The region is predominantly Roman Catholic, with Lutheran minorities in the south.

The territory of ancient Samogitia was much larger than the present region and embraced central and western Lithuania. The original Samogitian culture, known from flat burial grounds in the central lowlands, formed as early as the 5th and 6th centuries. The western part, inhabited before the 12th and 13th centuries by southern Semigallians and southern Curonians, became ethnically Lithuanian between the 13th and 16th centuries.

From the 13th to the 16th centuries the Teutonic Order and the Livonian Order bordered Samogitia, and the land was offered to them or exchanged in peace treaties several times, Lithuania regaining it in later conflicts. Invasions began in 1229, and battles included Saule in 1236, Skuodas in 1259, Durbe in 1260 and Lielvārde in 1262. Between 1345 and 1382 the Teutonic Knights attacked from Prussia some 70 times and the Livonian Knights about 30. Fortresses were attacked, farms and crops burned, women and children enslaved and men killed.

The Samogitians held their lands until the Battle of Grunwald in 1410, where united Polish-Lithuanian forces defeated the Order. In the 15th century Samogitia was the last region of core Europe to be converted to Christianity, and until the 18th century it was the Duchy or Eldership of Samogitia, an autonomous unit of the Grand Duchy. After the partitions of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth it passed to the Russian Empire, and in the 19th century it was the main source of the Lithuanian cultural revival and a focal point for smuggling Lithuanian books, which were banned. After the First World War it became part of the re-established Lithuanian state.

Samogitia corresponds to no present administrative division of Lithuania. Its landmarks include the Hill of Crosses, Tauragė Castle and Plungė Manor, and Palanga and Žemaičių Kalvarija are visited by tourists and pilgrims. Its coat of arms shows a black bear with silver claws on a red shield, and the Lithuanian government recognised it and the region's flag on 21 July 1994.
samora-machel: Samora Moisés Machel was born on 29 September 1933 in the village of Madragoa, now Chilembene, in Gaza Province, to a family of farmers. Under Portuguese rule his father was classified as an "indígena", a native, and had to accept lower prices than white farmers, grow labour-intensive cotton and refrain from branding his cattle; even so he owned four ploughs and 400 head of cattle by 1940. Machel attended mission schools run by Catholic missionaries, finishing the fourth grade, and trained as a nurse.

He began his political activity at the Miguel Bombarda hospital in Lourenço Marques, protesting that black nurses were paid less than white ones. Warned that the Portuguese political police were watching him, he left the country and made his way to Dar es Salaam to join FRELIMO, travelling through Swaziland, South Africa and Botswana.

He was one of the second group of FRELIMO guerrillas sent for training in Algeria and then ran the movement's camp at Kongwa. When FRELIMO began the war of independence on 25 September 1964 he became a key commander, notably in Niassa, and became head of its army after the death of Filipe Samuel Magaia in October 1966.

After the change of government in Lisbon, Machel rejected General António de Spínola's plan for a referendum on independence, saying that one does not ask a slave if he wants to be free. Talks in Lusaka in June 1974 produced nothing, and FRELIMO turned to the military movement then holding power in Portugal. Machel became the first President of independent Mozambique in 1975.

He supported nationalist movements in Rhodesia, whose guerrillas operated from FRELIMO-held areas in Tete province, and sent Mozambican units to fight alongside ZANU guerrillas. In 1977 RENAMO, backed first by Rhodesia and later by South Africa, began a rebellion that plunged the country into civil war. On 30 June 1981 South African commandos attacked houses in Matola, killing 12 members of the African National Congress.

On 19 October 1986 Machel attended a summit at Mbala in Zambia. Although invited to stay overnight, he insisted on returning to Maputo, and his plane crashed that night into a hillside at Mbuzini, just inside South Africa. Machel and 33 others died; nine passengers at the back survived. The Margo Commission concluded that pilot error caused the crash, but the Mozambican and Soviet governments rejected its report, and the Soviet minority report suggested the aircraft was lured off course by a decoy beacon. Speculation continues.

His state funeral was held in Maputo on 28 October 1986, and he was buried in a star-shaped crypt at Mozambican Heroes' Square. Streets in many countries bear his name, and a memorial at the crash site was inaugurated on 19 January 1999 by Nelson Mandela.
samos: The island covers 477.395 square kilometres and is 43 kilometres long and 13 kilometres wide. It is largely mountainous, with several relatively large and fertile plains. Two mountains dominate its relief: the Ampelos massif in the centre, rising to 1,095 metres, and Mount Kerkis, smaller in area but taller, whose summit at 1,434 metres is the island's highest point. Both are a continuation of the Mycale range on the Anatolian mainland. A great part of the island is covered with vineyards from which Muscat wine is made, and the capital is Vathy, in the north-east.

In antiquity Samos was a centre of Ionian culture and one of the twelve members of the Ionian League. By the 7th century BCE it was one of the leading commercial centres of Greece, trading with the Black Sea, Egypt, Cyrene, Corinth and Chalcis, and it founded colonies, mostly in the 6th century BCE. Its rivalry with Miletus broke into open war in the Lelantine War. About 535 BCE the tyrant Polycrates overturned the oligarchy, and Samos reached the height of its prosperity, with a navy that ruled the Aegean. After his death the Persian Empire conquered and partly depopulated the island.
In 440 BCE Samos seceded from the Delian League and, after a long siege, was forced to surrender to an Athenian fleet led by Pericles, and was ordered to pay 1,300 talents in instalments.

The Romans transferred the island in 189 BCE to the kingdom of Pergamon. Under the Byzantine Empire it became part of the Samos theme, and from 1346 to 1566 it was the property of the Genoese Giustiniani family. It came under Ottoman rule in 1475 or about 1479–80, when it was practically abandoned because of piracy and plague. In 1572/3 it was granted to the Ottoman admiral Kilic Ali Pasha, who attracted settlers with tax exemptions and considerable local autonomy. On 18 April 1821, under Lykourgos Logothetis, Samos joined the Greek War of Independence and repulsed three Ottoman attempts to retake it. Great Power pressure made it an autonomous, tributary principality under the Sultan. Greek troops landed in March 1913, and the Ottoman garrison withdrew.

Samos is a separate regional unit of the North Aegean region. Its economy rests mainly on agriculture and tourism, with grapes, honey, olives, olive oil and figs among its products. The town of Tigani was renamed Pythagoreio in 1955 in honour of Pythagoras.
samothrace: Samothrace is 17 km long and 178 square kilometres in size. It is one of the most rugged Greek islands, with Mount Saos and its highest peak, Fengari, rising to 1,611 metres. It never became a state of political significance in ancient Greece, since it lacks natural harbours and most of it is too mountainous for cultivation. The ancient city, whose ruins are called Palaeopolis, stood on the north coast, and considerable remains survive of its walls, built in massive Cyclopean style.

The Sanctuary of the Great Gods was the site of important Hellenic and pre-Hellenic religious ceremonies, the Samothracian Mysteries, which like the Eleusinian Mysteries were open to slaves and free people. Visitors initiated there included Lysander of Sparta, Philip II of Macedon and Lucius Calpurnius Piso Caesoninus, father-in-law of Julius Caesar. The traditional account is that the island was first inhabited by Pelasgians and Carians and later by Thracians, while the archaeological evidence points to Greek settlement in the 6th century BCE.

Samothrace came under Persian occupation in 508 BCE, followed by a period of Athenian control, and it joined the Delian League in the 5th century BCE. It was under Macedonian suzerainty from Philip II until 168 BCE, was then independent, and was absorbed into the Roman Empire by Vespasian in 70 CE. In the imperial period pilgrims flocked to the sanctuary from all over the Roman world. The Byzantines ruled until 1204, when Venetians took their place, and a Genoese family, the Gattilusi, dislodged them in 1355. The Ottoman Empire conquered the island in 1457. It came under Greek rule after the Balkan Wars and was occupied by Bulgaria from 1941 to 1944.

The best-known find from the sanctuary is the 2.5-metre marble statue of Nike, now known as the Winged Victory of Samothrace, which dates from about 190 BCE. The French archaeologist Charles Champoiseau found it in pieces on the island in 1863, and it is now displayed, headless, at the Louvre in Paris. It appears on the island's municipal seal, and the Archaeological Museum of Samothrace stands by the sanctuary. The island's population was 2,596 at the 2021 census, and its main industries are fishing and tourism. The port town of Kamariotissa provides ferry links to northern Greece.
samson: Samson is described in the Book of Judges, chapters 13 to 16, as the last of the judges of the Israelites and one of the last leaders who judged the twelve tribes before the monarchy. According to the account, he lived at a time of repeated conflict between Israel and Philistia, when God was disciplining the Israelites by giving them into the hand of the Philistines.

His father Manoah, a Danite from Zorah, and his wife had no child until the Angel of the Lord told the wife that she would bear a son who would begin to deliver Israel from the Philistines. The boy was to be a Nazirite from birth, never shaving or cutting his hair, and his mother was to abstain from alcohol and unclean foods.

As a young man Samson fell in love with a Philistine woman from Timnah and decided to marry her despite his parents' objections; the account presents the marriage as part of God's plan to strike at the Philistines. Seized repeatedly by the Spirit of the Lord, he was given immense strength. On the way to ask for her hand he tore apart a lion with his bare hands, and he later killed a Philistine army with a donkey's jawbone. At Gaza he tore the city gate from its frame and carried it to the hill in front of Hebron.

He then fell in love with Delilah in the valley of Sorek, and Philistine leaders offered her 1,100 pieces of silver to learn the secret of his strength. He misled her three times, saying fresh bowstrings, new ropes or weaving his hair into a loom would bind him, and each time he broke free. According to the account she finally learned that cutting his hair would end his strength, had it cut while he slept and handed him to the Philistines, who gouged out his eyes and made him mill grain at Gaza.

The Philistine rulers gathered in the temple of Dagon, about 3,000 people in all, to celebrate Samson's capture. Samson's hair had begun to grow again in prison. He asked to lean against the pillars, prayed, recovered his strength and broke them, so that the temple collapsed and killed him and the people inside. Rabbinic literature identifies him with Bedan, a judge named in 1 Samuel 12:11, and Caesarius of Arles read his death as prefiguring the crucifixion. John Milton wrote the closet drama Samson Agonistes about him, and his emblem in Lungau, Austria, is carried in parades first documented in 1635.
samsung: According to its founder, the name Samsung means three stars: the three stands for something big, numerous and powerful, and the stars for something everlasting. In 1938, in the Japanese era, Lee Byung-chul, a member of a large landowning family, moved to nearby Taikyu and founded the Mitsuboshi Trading Company, in Korean Samsung Sanghoe. It began as a small trading company of forty employees, dealing in dried fish, locally grown groceries and noodles. It prospered, and Lee moved its head office to Seoul in 1947. When the Korean War broke out he was forced to leave Seoul and started a sugar refinery in Pusan named Cheil Jedang.

In 1954 Lee founded the textiles company Cheil Mojik and built its first plant in Taegu, the largest woollen mill in the country at the time. Over the next decades the group diversified into food processing, textiles, insurance, securities and retail. It entered the electronics industry in the late 1960s, and the construction and shipbuilding sectors in the mid-1970s. In 1980 it acquired Hanguk Jeonja Tongsin, based in Kumi, and entered telecommunications hardware, with switchboards as its early products; in the 1980s the company grouped its electronics under Samsung Electronics. After Lee died in 1987 the group was divided into five business groups: Samsung Group, Shinsegae Group, CJ Group, Hansol Group and JoongAng Group.

Samsung Group is a South Korean conglomerate headquartered in Samsung Town in Seoul. It is a chaebol, a family-controlled conglomerate, and comprises around 80 companies in fields such as construction, consumer electronics, financial services, shipbuilding and medical services. Key affiliates include Samsung Electronics, Samsung Heavy Industries, Samsung Engineering, Samsung C&T Corporation and Samsung Life Insurance. The group has had a powerful influence on South Korea's economic development, politics, media and culture, and has been a major driving force behind the Miracle on the Han River. Its logo is blue, said to symbolise stability, reliability and corporate social responsibility. The smartphone platform was launched with the Samsung Solstice line in 2008, later developed into the Galaxy line.
samudragupta: Samudragupta was a son of the Gupta emperor Chandragupta I and Queen Kumaradevi, who came from the Licchavi clan. His fragmentary Eran stone inscription says that his father chose him as successor for his devotion, righteous conduct and valour. The Allahabad Pillar inscription adds that when Chandragupta I appointed him, the faces of other people of equal birth bore a melancholy look. One interpretation takes these people to be neighbouring kings, so that the succession was uncontested; another takes them to be Gupta princes with a rival claim.

The Allahabad Pillar inscription, a eulogy composed by his minister and military officer Harishena, gives the most detailed account of his conquests, in geographical and partly chronological order. It says that he fought a hundred battles and earned the title Prakrama, the valorous. It records that he forcibly uprooted eight kings of Aryavarta, northern India, whose territories seem to have been annexed to his empire.

In the south the inscription lists twelve kings of Dakshinapatha, among them Vishnugopa of Kanchi and Hastivarman of Vengi, whom he captured and then released and favoured. Most scholars take this to mean that he restored them as tributaries. Rulers of frontier kingdoms such as Samatata, Kamarupa and Nepala, and tribes such as the Malavas and Yaudheyas, paid tribute. Since the inscription is a royal eulogy, its claims are to be treated with caution.

Samudragupta performed the Ashvamedha sacrifice to prove imperial sovereignty and issued gold coins to mark it. The Eran inscription records the installation of a Vishnu image in a temple, and two disputed inscriptions call him a devotee of Vishnu. He was also tolerant of Buddhism and allowed the king Meghavarna of Anuradhapura to build a monastery at Bodh Gaya.

His coinage was derived from that of the Kushan Empire, from which the Guptas took the name dinara and the weight standard; his standard type shows a sacrificial scene over an altar, and an archer type shows him with a bow. The inscription calls him king of poets and says that his music put Tumburu and Narada to shame, and coins show him playing the veena. Vincent Smith called him the Indian Napoleon. Chandragupta II, his son by Dattadevi, succeeded him.
samuel-de-champlain: Champlain's exact birth date and place are debated. He was the son of Antoine Champlain and Marguerite Le Roy, probably born in Brouage or La Rochelle in Aunis, into a family of mariners. His education was practical, in navigation, cartography and drafting, and did not include Greek or Latin. He served in Henry IV's army in Brittany from 1594 or 1595 to 1598 and by 1597 commanded a company near Quimper. He then sailed on a two-year voyage with his uncle-in-law François Gravé Du Pont, a navigator, and wrote an illustrated secret report on the Spanish holdings he saw from the Caribbean to Mexico City, for which King Henry gave him a pension.

Champlain began exploring North America in 1603 under Du Pont and took part from 1604 to 1607 in establishing Port Royal in Acadia, the first permanent European settlement north of Florida. In spring 1608 Dugua sent him with three ships from Honfleur to found a colony and fur trading centre on the St. Lawrence. He reached Quebec on 3 July 1608 and chose the point of Quebec, covered with nut-trees, for the settlement. In 1609 he allied with the Wendat, Algonquin, Montagnais and Etchemin against the Haudenosaunee, and on an expedition along the Richelieu River became the first European to map Lake Champlain.

On 29 July 1609 he killed two Haudenosaunee chiefs with a single arquebus shot. In 1615 he joined a campaign by the Wendat and their allies against the Haudenosaunee that failed after the attack began prematurely; he was wounded twice in the leg by arrows. In 1613 he travelled up the Ottawa River, writing its first description. Louis XIII ordered him in 1620 to focus on administration. He built Fort Saint-Louis on Cape Diamond and was one of the 100 investors in Richelieu's Compagnie des Cent-Associés, formed in 1627.

Champlain returned to Quebec on 22 May 1633 after four years away, with a commission from Richelieu as Lieutenant General of New France, not governor. Many colonists nonetheless called him their governor. He suffered a severe stroke in October 1635 and died on 25 December, leaving no immediate heirs. His exact burial site is unknown despite research since about 1850, but it is thought to lie near Notre-Dame de Québec Cathedral. His maps of the eastern coast and the Great Lakes combined his own observation with information from Indigenous peoples, and his published works include Des Sauvages (1604) and Voyages de la Nouvelle-France (1632). Lake Champlain bears his name.
samuel-johnson: Samuel Johnson was born on 18 September 1709 in Lichfield, Staffordshire, above the bookshop of his father Michael Johnson. His mother Sarah was 40, an unusually late age for a first birth, and the infant did not cry, so the family feared for his life and had him baptised at once. He attended Pembroke College, Oxford, until lack of money forced him to leave. His father fell deeply into debt and died in December 1731, when Johnson was twenty-two. Johnson was turned down for a post as usher at Stourbridge Grammar School because he had no degree. After working as a teacher he moved to London and began writing for The Gentleman's Magazine.

His early works include the poem London (1738), the Life of Mr Richard Savage (1744) and the poem The Vanity of Human Wishes (1749). In 1746 a group of publishers approached him to make an authoritative dictionary, and a contract with William Strahan and associates, worth 1,500 guineas, was signed on 18 June. Johnson said the work would take three years, remarking that the Académie Française had used forty scholars for forty years. A Dictionary of the English Language appeared in 1755. Critics included Thomas Babington Macaulay, who called Johnson a wretched etymologist, while the biographer Walter Jackson Bate called it one of the most notable single achievements of scholarship.

Johnson then wrote the novella The History of Rasselas, Prince of Abissinia (1759) and edited The Plays of William Shakespeare (1765). In 1763 he befriended James Boswell, and in August 1773 the two set out on a journey to Scotland, which Johnson described in A Journey to the Western Islands of Scotland (1775). There he entered the dispute over James Macpherson's Ossian poems, arguing that they could not be translations of ancient Gaelic writing because nothing had been written in that language in those times. Near the end of his life he wrote Lives of the Most Eminent English Poets (1779–1781), biographies and critical appraisals of 52 poets.

Johnson suffered from scrofula, gout, deafness in one ear and blindness in one eye, and from long periods of depression. His tics and gestures, closely recorded by Boswell, have led to a posthumous diagnosis of Tourette syndrome. He died on the evening of 13 December 1784, aged 75, and is buried in Westminster Abbey. In his criticism he preferred contemporary language and was suspicious of Milton's blank verse and obscure allusions. His Dictionary was pre-eminent until the Oxford English Dictionary appeared some 150 years later, and he changed the course of biography; Boswell's Life of Samuel Johnson (1791) is described by Bate as the best-known single work of biographical art in the whole of literature.
samuel-pepys: Samuel Pepys was born in Salisbury Court, Fleet Street, London, on 23 February 1633, the son of John Pepys, a tailor, and Margaret Pepys. He was the fifth of 11 children and was soon the eldest survivor. He attended Huntingdon Grammar School and then St Paul's School, and in 1649 he watched the execution of Charles I. In 1650 he went to Magdalene College, Cambridge, as a sizar, and took his Bachelor of Arts degree in 1654.

He suffered from bladder stones from a young age. On 26 March 1658 the surgeon Thomas Hollier removed the stone in a bedroom of the house of Pepys's cousin Jane Turner, an operation known to be painful and hazardous. Pepys marked the anniversary for several years. He then worked as a teller in the Exchequer under George Downing.

In 1660, through his cousin Sir Edward Montagu, Pepys became Clerk of the Acts to the Navy Board. He had no maritime experience, learned arithmetic from a tutor and used models of ships, but proved more able and efficient than colleagues in higher positions. He joined the Tangier committee in 1662 and became its treasurer in 1665. When the Second Anglo-Dutch War began in 1665 he proposed a centralised approach to supplying the fleet and was made surveyor-general of victualling in October 1665.

In 1673 he became Secretary of the Admiralty Commission and was elected Member of Parliament for Castle Rising; he later sat for Harwich. He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1665 and was its President from 1 December 1684 to 30 November 1686, and the imprimatur of Isaac Newton's Principia is signed by him in that role. He was imprisoned on suspicion of Jacobitism from May to July 1689 and again in June 1690, without any charge succeeding, and then retired from public life. He moved to Clapham in 1701 and died on 26 May 1703.

On 1 January 1660 Pepys began a diary, which he kept for almost ten years. It runs to one and a quarter million words and names over 3,000 people. He wrote of the court and theatre, his household, his finances and what he ate, and gave eyewitness accounts of the Second Anglo-Dutch War, the Great Plague of 1665 and the Great Fire of London in 1666. It was written in the shorthand called tachygraphy, devised by Thomas Shelton. Fear for his eyesight made him end it on 31 May 1669.

He had the diary bound into six volumes and kept it in his large library of more than 3,000 volumes, which survives as one of the most important private libraries of the 17th century. John Smith transcribed the diary between 1819 and 1822, and the first edition, by Lord Braybrooke, appeared in 1825.
samuel-richardson: Samuel Richardson was baptised on 19 August 1689 and was probably born in Mackworth, Derbyshire, one of nine children. He always concealed the exact location of his birth. His father was a joiner who, by Richardson's own account, had come to the notice of James Scott, 1st Duke of Monmouth, and was forced to give up his London business after the failure of the Monmouth Rebellion. The family later returned to London, and Richardson was probably educated at Christ's Hospital, although accounts of his schooling conflict.

His father could not afford to train him as a clergyman, so he chose printing. In 1706, at the age of 17, he was bound in a seven-year apprenticeship to the printer John Wilde in Aldersgate Street, a master said to grudge every hour that did not serve his profit. Richardson later married Wilde's daughter Martha. All six of their children died in infancy or childbirth, and Martha died in childbirth in 1731. In 1733 he married Elizabeth Leake, the daughter of the printer John Leake, and four of their six children, all daughters, reached adulthood.

Richardson's printing business prospered. He printed the Daily Journal between 1736 and 1737 and the Daily Gazetteer in 1738, and in all printed almost 500 works, working periodically with the bookseller Andrew Millar. In 1739 the booksellers Charles Rivington and John Osborn asked him for a volume of model letters for country readers who could not write for themselves. While writing it he was inspired to attempt a story, and on 6 November 1740 he published Pamela; or, Virtue Rewarded, his first novel, at the age of 51. It was sometimes regarded as the first novel in English.

Pamela was followed by sequels, and then by Clarissa; or, The History of a Young Lady, which was not complete to his satisfaction until October 1746. Readers whom he asked to help shorten it wanted it kept entire. His third and last novel, The History of Sir Charles Grandison, appeared in 1753. Richardson became Master of the Stationers' Company and counted Samuel Johnson, Sarah Fielding, the physician George Cheyne and the theologian William Law among his acquaintances.

All three novels are epistolary, told in letters. Richardson was a tireless letter writer and had faith that letters could portray character accurately. The form let him give distinct characters a voice directly to the reader and offered multiple perspectives. He hoped, however, to lead readers to interpret the text in the ways he chose, towards moral regeneration, and Susan Whyman writes that his goal was to reform reading practices and lives as well. His one major later work was a collection of the moral sentiments of his three novels. He died in July 1761 after an attack of apoplexy.
samurai: Until the late 8th century Japan had a national conscript army, which the imperial court dismantled, ending it by 792. Conscripts were seen as unreliable, and in the war against the Emishi, who relied on mounted warriors, professional mounted archers from wealthy families decided most battles. The government recruited men who already had those skills, acquired through private training funded by their families. The word samurai is thought to come from saburau, to serve, and so means a retainer or vassal; the proper term for a professional warrior is bushi, and the daimyo and the shogun were bushi but were not called samurai.

The Minamoto and Taira clans, both with court positions, became rivals. Taira no Kiyomori became the first bushi given a senior court rank, as chief minister in 1167. After the Genpei War of 1180 to 1185 Minamoto no Yoritomo ruled through a military government in Kamakura and was appointed shogun, and in 1192 he created the gokenin class of warrior vassals, who owed the shogun military service in exchange for privileges. The Ōnin War, which began in 1467, brought down the Ashikaga shogunate and led to the Sengoku period, in which daimyo fought each other.

After the Battle of Sekigahara Tokugawa Ieyasu was declared shogun in 1603, and after the siege of Osaka in 1615 there was a period of peace for 250 years. Under the Tokugawa the samurai first became a truly hereditary class, a process begun by Hideyoshi with the Sword Hunt of 1588 and the Separation Edict of 1591. With no warfare they gradually lost their military function; many served as officials, police, teachers or domain administrators, while keeping stipends and the right to bear arms.

After the Meiji Restoration the abolition of the domains, conscription, the ending of hereditary stipends and the removal of privileges such as wearing swords dismantled the basis of samurai status. Former feudal lords became kazoku, nobility, and most former warriors became shizoku, classes that remained legally recognised until 1947.

The samurai class was highly stratified, by the rank of one's lord and the size of one's stipend. Below the daimyo came the hatamoto, who had the right of audience with the shogun, and then the gokenin. Samurai trained from a young age in swordsmanship, archery and horsemanship. Confucianism, Buddhism and, to a lesser extent, Shinto influenced their culture, and the works Hagakure and Gorin no Sho, written in the Edo period, contributed to the development of bushidō.
san-antonio: San Antonio lies in the southern part of Texas, on the Balcones Escarpment at about 202 m above sea level, with the Texas Hill Country reaching into its far north. It is roughly 75 miles south-west of Austin and 150 miles north of the Mexican border. Its gently rolling terrain is dotted with oak trees, mesquite and cacti, and its climate is humid subtropical, with long, hot summers and mild winters. It is the county seat of Bexar County.

When the Spanish arrived, the Payaya people lived near the San Antonio River valley in the San Pedro Springs area and called it Yanaguana, meaning refreshing waters. On 13 June 1691, the feast day of Saint Anthony of Padua, Spanish explorers and missionaries came upon the river and the Payaya settlement and named the place and the river San Antonio in his honour. A Spanish mission and colonial outpost was founded there in 1718, and in 1731 San Antonio became the first chartered civil settlement in present-day Texas.

The city belonged to the Spanish Empire until 1821, to the Mexican Republic from 1821 to 1836, and to the Republic of Texas from 1836 until annexation by the United States, of which it was part from 1846. It was in the Confederate States from 1861 to 1865. The Roman Catholic Archdiocese of San Antonio traces its origin to 27 August 1784 and was raised to an archdiocese in 1926. The San Antonio Express-News has served the area since 1865. The city is a key military centre, with Fort Sam Houston and nearby Lackland and Randolph Air Force Bases.

San Antonio had 1,434,625 residents at the 2020 census and is the second most populous city in Texas after Houston. Five 18th-century Spanish frontier missions, among them the Alamo and those in San Antonio Missions National Historical Park, were designated UNESCO World Heritage sites in 2015. Because of the Alamo Mission the city is often called Alamo City. About 64% of its residents identify as Hispanic, and Roman Catholicism is the largest religious group, a legacy in part of its Spanish and Mexican heritage.
san-diego: San Diego is a city on the Pacific coast of Southern California, next to the Mexican border. Its bay is the surface expression of a north-south nested graben, and the Rose Canyon and Point Loma fault zones are part of the San Andreas Fault system. About 40 miles east of the bay are the Laguna Mountains. The city is known for a mild Mediterranean climate, beaches and parks, and its long association with the United States Navy.

The area is historically home to the Kumeyaay people, whose town on the site was called Kosa'aay, "drying out place". The San Dieguito complex was established in the area at least 9,000 years ago, and the Kumeyaay may have developed from it or arrived around 1000 CE, a question on which scholars differ. The first European to visit was Juan Rodríguez Cabrillo, who claimed the bay for the Spanish Empire in 1542 and named it San Miguel. In November 1602 Sebastián Vizcaíno surveyed the harbour, Mission Bay and Point Loma, and named the area San Diego de Alcalá after Saint Didacus.
The Presidio and Mission San Diego de Alcalá, founded in 1769, formed the first European settlement in what is now California, and the city has been called the Birthplace of California.

In 1821 Mexico won its independence from Spain, and San Diego became part of the Mexican territory of Alta California. The fort on Presidio Hill was gradually abandoned and the town grew on the level land below it. The Mexican government secularized the mission in 1834 and granted most of its lands to former soldiers. The 432 residents of the town petitioned to form a pueblo, and Juan María Osuna was elected its first alcalde.

California was ceded to the United States in 1848 after the Mexican-American War and admitted as a state in 1850. That year San Diego was made the seat of the new County of San Diego and incorporated as a city, with Joshua H. Bean, the last alcalde, as first mayor. Two years later it was bankrupt, and the legislature revoked its charter and placed it under a board of trustees until 1889.

San Diego is the seat of San Diego County and the second most populous city in California, with over 1.4 million residents. Its economy rests largely on military and defence activities, tourism, international trade, research and manufacturing. The San Ysidro Port of Entry connects it with Tijuana, and the city's present charter was adopted in 1931.
san-francisco: San Francisco lies on the West Coast of the United States, at the north end of the San Francisco Peninsula, and its boundaries take in stretches of the Pacific Ocean and San Francisco Bay. Alcatraz, Treasure Island and the adjacent Yerba Buena Island belong to the city, as do the uninhabited Farallon Islands, 43 kilometres offshore. The mainland within the city limits forms roughly what residents call the seven-by-seven-mile square, and the total area, including water, is nearly 600 square kilometres.

The name, Spanish for 'Saint Francis', comes from Mission San Francisco de Asís, founded in 1776 under Padre Francisco Palóu and named for Francis of Assisi. The first civilian pueblo was called Yerba Buena, 'good herb', and the city has officially been San Francisco since 1847, when its alcalde, Washington Allon Bartlett, renamed it.

The earliest evidence of human habitation dates to 3000 BCE. The Ohlone name for the place was Ahwaste, 'place at the bay', and the Yelamu group of the Ramaytush people lived in small villages there. The Portolá expedition, led by Gaspar de Portolá and Juan Crespí, reached the bay on 2 November 1769, the first documented European visit, and noted the strategic value of its large natural harbour. Settlers from New Spain founded the Presidio of San Francisco at the Golden Gate and the Mission San Francisco de Asís on 29 June 1776. The Mission system marked the beginning of the assimilation of the Ramaytush and the decline of their language and culture.

The California gold rush of 1849 brought rapid growth and made San Francisco the largest city on the West Coast. In 1856 it became a consolidated city-county. The earthquake and fire of 1906 destroyed three-quarters of the city, which was quickly rebuilt and hosted the Panama–Pacific International Exposition nine years later. In the Second World War it was a major port of embarkation for naval personnel bound for the Pacific. After the war returning servicemen, immigration, liberalizing attitudes, the beatnik and hippie countercultures and opposition to the Vietnam War led to the Summer of Love and the gay rights movement, which made the city a centre of liberal activism.

San Francisco is a city on the Pacific coast of California whose boundaries are the same as those of its county; the 2020 census counted 873,965 people. It is known for its steep hills, Chinatown and the Mission District, and for landmarks including the Golden Gate Bridge, cable cars and Alcatraz. The Presidio, the former Spanish military base, is now one of the city's largest parks and the site of museums and institutions.
san-jose-california: San Jose lies in the Santa Clara Valley, in the southern part of the San Francisco Bay Area, and is the county seat of Santa Clara County. Its northernmost part touches San Francisco Bay at Alviso. The Guadalupe River runs north from the Santa Cruz Mountains through the city. The climate is Mediterranean, with warm, dry summers and cool, wet winters. The city takes its name from the Pueblo de San José de Guadalupe, its predecessor.

The Tamien nation of the Ohlone people has lived in San Jose and most of the Santa Clara Valley since around 4,000 BCE. California was claimed for the Spanish Empire in 1542, but for nearly 200 years it remained a distant frontier largely controlled by the Native nations. British gains after the Treaty of Paris of 1763 and Russian colonisation in the north-west led the Spanish authorities to sponsor the Portolá Expedition of 1769. San Jose was founded on 29 November 1777 as the Pueblo de San José de Guadalupe, the first city founded in the Californias.

It became part of the First Mexican Empire in 1821, and in 1833 Mexico secularised the California missions. The United States completed its conquest of California by the end of 1847, and the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo of 1848 formally ceded it. On 15 December 1849 San Jose became capital of the territory of California, and on California's admission to the Union on 9 September 1850 it became the state's first capital.

After the Second World War the city grew rapidly: under the City Manager Dutch Hamann, in office from 1950 to 1969, it annexed property 1,389 times and grew from 17 to 149 square miles. The nickname Silicon Valley was coined in 1971, and in 1988 Mayor Tom McEnery adopted the motto Capital of Silicon Valley. The 1990 census showed that San Jose had surpassed San Francisco in population.

San Jose is the most populous city in the San Francisco Bay Area and in Northern California, with 1,013,240 residents at the 2020 census. San José State University, founded in 1862 as the California State Normal School, has been in downtown San Jose since 1870. The city has historic ethnic districts such as Japantown and Little Portugal, a large Vietnamese population and the largest Sikh gurdwara outside India. Alum Rock Park, established in 1872, is the oldest municipal park in California.
san-jose-costa-rica: San José stands in the middle of Costa Rica, in the mid-west of the Central Valley. It is the seat of national government, the focus of political and economic activity and the country's chief transport hub. Together with the neighbouring cantons of Alajuela, Heredia and Cartago it forms the Greater Metropolitan Area. The city is named in honour of Joseph of Nazareth. Its climate is tropical wet and dry, with average temperatures that vary little through the year.

San José was founded in 1736 by order of the Cabildo de León, to gather the scattered inhabitants of the Aserrí Valley. A chapel was completed a year later with help from the church of Cartago, and St Joseph was chosen as parish patron, which gave the town its name. Unlike Cartago, it was not founded by formal decree and so lacked a city government until the Constitution of Cádiz was enacted in 1812. On 18 October 1813 the presbyter Florencio del Castillo defined it as a city, but the title was lost in 1814 when Ferdinand VII annulled the proceedings of the courts. It was restored in 1820, and in 1823 San José became the capital of Costa Rica.

The installation of the Tobacco Factory in 1782 spurred growth, and capital from tobacco plantations let the city surpass neighbouring provinces economically. In the late 19th century the French coffee entrepreneur Monsieur Amon created the first modern urban neighbourhood, Barrio Amon, in Belle Époque style; it and the National Theater remain symbols of the Costa Rican coffee golden age. The University of Santo Tomas, the country's first university, was established in San José in 1843 and closed in 1888.

San José is the capital and largest city of Costa Rica, with an estimated 352,381 people in its canton in 2022. It holds the National Museum of Costa Rica and the National Theater, considered the finest historic building in the capital; El Teatro Variedades, built in 1892, is its oldest theatre. The Museum of Pre-Columbian Gold and the Museum of Jade are also in the city. The University for Peace, established by the United Nations General Assembly in 1980, is located in San José.
san-juan-province-argentina: San Juan lies in the western part of Argentina and borders Chile to the west, with La Rioja, San Luis and Mendoza as its neighbours. It covers 89,651 square kilometres of mountainous country with scarce vegetation, fertile oases and turbulent rivers. It belongs to the semi-desert Cuyo region: arid plains in the east rise through a few low hills to peaks of 6,000 metres in the west, and both areas are subject to the Zonda, a dry hot foehn wind. The Jáchal and San Juan rivers feed the fertile valleys that are the centre of the province's economy.

Before the Spanish conquest the area was inhabited by the Huarpes, Diaguitas, Capazanes, Olongastas and Yacampis, who were strongly influenced by the Inca Empire. The city of San Juan de la Frontera was founded by Juan Jufré y Montesa in 1562 and moved 2 kilometres south in 1593 because the San Juan River flooded so often.

In 1776 it was annexed to the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata as one of the cities of the Province of Cuyo, and in the same year the first recorded earthquake caused massive damage. José de San Martín was appointed Governor of the Province of Cuyo in 1814 and began from there his crossing of the Andes; San Juan, then a small town, supplied the expedition with gold, men and mules. In 1820 it was granted autonomy from Cuyo, and the rest of Cuyo became Mendoza Province.

After the more liberal government of 1853, exiled intellectuals returned to San Juan, among them the military officer and novelist Domingo Sarmiento. Elected governor in 1862, he made public investments and passed Argentina's first law for compulsory education, at a time when about 80 per cent of adults lacked any education; when he became president in 1868 the policy became national law. In 1944 an earthquake near the capital destroyed most of the city and killed 10,000 people. A stronger earthquake in 1977 did little damage because of the new building codes, though the Cathedral of San Juan was destroyed and a modernist church was opened in its place in 1979.

Agriculture is a leading activity, especially wine and olive oil, with fruit and vegetables grown in valleys irrigated by artificial channels. The Ullum Dam and Reservoir, inaugurated in 1980, expanded irrigated crops such as olives, figs and above all wine grapes. The National University of San Juan opened in 1973. The province also has mining and oil production and a number of paleontological sites.
san-juan-puerto-rico: San Juan lies on the north-eastern coast of Puerto Rico in the Northern Plains region, facing the Atlantic Ocean. The municipality covers 199.2 square kilometres, of which about a third is water. Its main bodies of water are San Juan Bay and two natural lagoons, the Condado and San José. The old city stands on the Islet of San Juan, and all the city's beaches face the Atlantic.

The Taíno were the original inhabitants before Europeans reached the island in 1493. The site of San Juan marked the boundary between two Taíno territories, Guaynabo and Haimanio, led by the chiefs Mabo and Yuisa. In 1508 Juan Ponce de León founded the settlement of Caparra, named for a Roman town in the Spanish province of Cáceres, the birthplace of Nicolás de Ovando, then governor of Spain's Caribbean territories. The settlement was later moved to a site then called Puerto Rico, Spanish for rich port.

San Juan was the first stopover in the Americas for ships sailing from Spain. A network of fortifications was built to protect the transports of gold and silver from the New World to Europe, and the rich cargoes made the port a target of foreign powers. The Puerta de San Juan, built in 1635, is the main preserved gate of the colonial walls.

On 8 May 1898 United States Navy ships under Rear Admiral William T. Sampson arrived at San Juan Bay during the Spanish–American War. On 10 May Captain Ángel Rivero Méndez, commanding the Spanish forces in the fortress of San Cristóbal, ordered his men to fire on USS Yale, the first attack against the Americans on the island.

San Juan is the capital and most populous municipality of Puerto Rico, an unincorporated territory of the United States. It is the second oldest European-established capital in the Americas, after Santo Domingo. The historic district of Old San Juan, with the former defensive walls, Fort San Felipe del Morro, Fort San Cristóbal and La Fortaleza, the oldest executive mansion in continuous use in the Americas, was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983.
san-luis-potosi: San Luis Potosí, officially the Free and Sovereign State of San Luis Potosí, is one of the 32 federal entities of Mexico and takes its name from its capital. It lies in eastern and central Mexico and is divided into 59 municipalities. It borders Nuevo León, Tamaulipas, Veracruz, Hidalgo, Querétaro, Guanajuato and Zacatecas. The state lies mostly on the Mexican Plateau, at a mean elevation of about 1,800 metres, while the Sierra Madre Oriental separates the plateau from the Gulf Coastal Plain to the east. The eastern quarter is the Huasteca potosina, part of a region along the Gulf of Mexico historically associated with the Huastec people.

In pre-Columbian times the territory contained parts of the cultural areas of Mesoamerica and Aridoamerica. The Otomi and Chichimeca, nomadic hunter-gatherers, lived in the north and the west-central parts. Many indigenous people died during Spanish colonisation, but Huasteco groups still live in the state, together with Pame and Nahua peoples.

The discovery of gold and silver in 1592 led to the founding of the first town, known as San Luis de Mezquitique, at the site of the present capital, and Juan de Oñate was appointed first mayor. The name San Luis honours Louis IX of France, and Potosí compares the wealth of the place with the rich silver mines of Potosí in Bolivia, a rivalry the settlers hoped for but never fully achieved. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries Franciscans, Augustinians and Jesuits built churches and other buildings, many still standing.

In mid-1821, after Mexican independence, General José Antonio Echávarri pressed the mayor and city council to surrender the city to the Army of the Three Guarantees, and independence was proclaimed in San Luis Potosí. The first state constitution was written on 16 October 1826 and remained in effect until 1835, when Congress proclaimed a centralist system. The state's part in the Mexican–American War of 1846–1847 earned it the name San Luis de la Patria. During the French Intervention in 1863 President Benito Juárez made the city of San Luis Potosí the capital of the country. In 1866 a telegraph line opened between San Luis Potosí and Mexico City, which helped begin the industrialisation of the state.

Besides the capital, major cities include Ciudad Valles, Matehuala, Rioverde and Tamazunchale. The area around Real de Catorce has some of the richest silver mines in the country, and Guadalcázar's ores yield gold, copper, zinc and bismuth as well as silver. Nahuatl is the most widely spoken indigenous language, followed by Huasteco. The state's coat of arms shows Louis IX of France on a hill at Cerro de San Pedro, where the metals were found.
san-miguel-de-tucuman: San Miguel de Tucumán lies in northern Argentina, 1,311 kilometres from Buenos Aires, on the slopes of the Aconquija mountains, the easternmost range before the large Chaco-Pampean flats. It is the commercial centre of an irrigated area producing sugarcane, rice, tobacco and fruit, which gave the province its nickname, the Garden of the Republic. The climate is humid subtropical, with most of the year's rain falling in the summer months.

Diego de Villarroel founded the city on 31 May 1565, as San Miguel de Tucumán y Nueva Tierra de Promisión, in the Campos de Ibatín, about 60 kilometres south-west of its present site, during an expedition from present-day Peru. In 1685 it moved to La Toma, where the old town stands, because of the poor quality of the water at Ibatín. On 24 September 1812 the Battle of Tucumán was fought near the city. Manuel Belgrano, who had been ordered to fall back to Córdoba but was called on by the inhabitants to resist, attacked the Spanish army from behind with tired troops and local gauchos and defeated it. Belgrano then built a circular fortress, La Ciudadela.

Because the city had patriot barracks and lay between the Río de la Plata and Upper Peru, it was chosen as the seat of the Congress of Independence. On 9 July 1816 the congress declared the independence of Argentina, not only from Spain but from any other foreign domination, and signed the act at the Casa de Tucumán. After the national government broke down in 1820 the town was capital of the short-lived Republic of Tucumán. The first railway arrived around 1870, and immigrants, mostly Spanish, Arab, Jewish and Italian, changed the colonial architecture towards neoclassical and eclectic styles. By 1930 the population had doubled.

The city is the capital of Tucumán Province. The Casa de Tucumán, where independence was declared, was acquired by the national government in 1874, demolished almost completely in 1903 except for the room of the declaration, and rebuilt in 1942 from the original plans and an 1869 photograph by Angel Paganelli. It is a national monument. Other landmarks include the cathedral, the Basílica de San Francisco and the Government House, built in Art Nouveau style at the end of the 19th century. The National University of Tucumán was founded in 1914.
san-pedro-sula: San Pedro Sula lies in the northwest corner of Honduras, in the Sula Valley, about 50 km south of Puerto Cortés on the Caribbean Sea, and is the capital of Cortés Department. Like most cities built in the Spanish colonial period it is divided into quadrants: First Street and First Avenue mark the centre, avenues run north to south and streets east to west. The climate is tropical, with a dry season from January to May and a wet season for the remaining months, and the city is prone to hurricanes and tropical storms.

Before the Spanish arrived the Sula Valley was home to about 50,000 native inhabitants, and the site served as a local trade hub. The Spanish conquest brought a demographic collapse from which the native population never recovered. On 27 June 1536 Pedro de Alvarado founded a Spanish town beside the Indian settlement of Choloma, calling it Villa de Señor San Pedro de Puerto Caballos. It had 35 Spanish citizens, and Alvarado allocated 200 of his slaves to build the town and work the fields. He cancelled the encomienda rights granted under Andres de Cerezeda and reassigned the villages to the town's citizens.

The settlement barely survived the colonial period. In 1601 the Spanish government made Santo Tomás the official port for the Central American colonies, which diverted exports from Puerto Cortés and began an economic decline that lasted through the 17th century, while pirates and French, Dutch and English mercenaries raided the town. After the Spanish built the Fortaleza de San Fernando at Omoa in the mid-18th century, trade increased and the population rose from 70 in 1714 to 357 in 1789. After independence it remained an impoverished village, living from trade between Omoa and the interior; in 1875 an American consul reported 1,200 inhabitants.

The city grew with the banana trade of the 1870s and 1880s, with the Interoceanic Railroad built between 1869 and 1874 to connect it to the coast at Puerto Cortés, and through close ties between local elites and Samuel Zemurray's Cuyamel Fruit Company. The central urban area had 701,200 inhabitants in 2023 and the metropolitan area 1,445,598. It is the main industrial centre of Honduras and its second city after Tegucigalpa, with a large apparel manufacturing industry, the maquila.
san-people: The San are the members of the indigenous hunter-gatherer cultures of southern Africa, which are the oldest surviving cultures of the region. They speak, or their ancestors spoke, languages of the Khoe, Tuu and Kxʼa families. Their recent ancestral territories span Botswana, Namibia, Angola, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Lesotho and South Africa.

Some 10,000 years ago their ancestors were spread from Tanzania, Zambia and Angola down to Cape Agulhas. A set of tools almost identical to those of the modern San, dated to 42,000 BCE, was found at Border Cave in KwaZulu-Natal in 2012. Some interpretations of genetic analysis suggest a divergence from other humans as early as 100,000 to 200,000 years ago.

During the Bantu expansion the San met herder groups, who later became the Khoekhoe, and herder-farmers. They were partly driven off their lands or incorporated by Bantu speaking groups. Other societies often turned to San shamans for rainmaking, as at Mapungubwe, and one writer claims they were involved in the early foundations of the Kingdom of Mapungubwe and of later states such as Great Zimbabwe.

After the Dutch settled at the Cape under Jan van Riebeeck in 1652, the Cape San population was estimated at 30 000 to 50 000. From about 1714 the Dutch East India Company's loan farm system gave stock farmers grazing rights in the dry interior, and Trekboers occupied waterholes, shot the game on which the San lived and overgrazed the land.

The San resisted by raiding stock, and the Trekboers answered with militia units called commandos. From the 1770s to the late 1790s this violence became general along the frontier of the Dutch Cape Colony. Two scholars write that tens of thousands of Khoekhoe and San lost their lives to genocide, murder, mistreatment and disease, and that some commandos hunted San.

Traditionally the San lived in small mobile foraging bands. Women gather fruit, berries, tubers and bush onions and sometimes hunt, and may lead family groups, make decisions and claim ownership of waterholes and foraging areas. Ostrich eggshells serve as water containers, and insects provide perhaps 10 percent of animal protein.

Early spring is the hardest season, and meat matters most in the dry months. Leisure is important at every age, with much time given to conversation, music and sacred dances. In kinship, the older of two people decides what to call the younger, and each child is named after a grandparent or other relative, never a parent.

From the 1950s to the 1990s government modernisation programmes pushed San communities towards farming. San and Bushmen are both exonyms; San comes from a Khoekhoe word for foragers without cattle, and in 2003 San representatives said they preferred to be called by their respective nations.
san-salvador: San Salvador lies in the Salvadoran highlands at an average height of 658 metres, surrounded by volcanoes. The Boquerón Volcano rises to 1,893 metres above the metropolitan area. The city has a tropical wet and dry climate, with a dry season from November to April and a rainy season from May to October, when thunderstorms come almost daily.

The conquistador Gonzalo de Alvarado founded a mission he named San Salvador in 1525. The name probably refers to the feast of the Transfiguration, called Divino Salvador in Spanish, held on 6 August, the day on which in 1456 Pope Callixtus III commemorated the Christian victory at the Siege of Belgrade. Names such as San Salvador became a popular choice for churches and places, and Christopher Columbus had given it to the island of Guanahani in 1492. The city was part of the Kingdom of Spain until 1821, and then of the Mexican Empire in 1822 and 1823 and of Central America until 1841.

The city has suffered from many severe earthquakes, of which the most disastrous came in 1854. When the San Salvador volcano erupted in 1917, three major earthquakes damaged the city so badly that the government temporarily moved the capital to Santa Tecla. On 10 October 1986 another earthquake killed between 1,000 and 1,500 people and left 200,000 homeless. Colonial buildings, cathedrals above all, have been destroyed over time, and the few notable buildings of the historic downtown that survive date from the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

San Salvador is the capital and largest city of El Salvador, with 525,990 inhabitants in the municipality. It is the seat of the Legislative Assembly and the Supreme Court. The National Theatre, built in 1917, is the oldest theatre in Central America, and the National Palace dates from 1905.
san-salvador-de-jujuy: Jujuy lies near the southern end of the Humahuaca Canyon, where wooded hills meet the lowlands, at the junction of the Xibi Xibi River and the Río Grande de Jujuy, 1,238 metres above sea level. National Route 9 passes through it, linking La Quiaca and Salta, and it is 1,525 km from Buenos Aires. It is the capital and largest city of Jujuy Province and the seat of the Doctor Manuel Belgrano Department, and the provincial administrative offices that serve petroleum, sugar, tobacco, steel and fruit production are located there.

In late 1535 a party from Diego de Almagro's expedition to Chile clashed with local indigenous men at Jujuy, and Almagro sent a punitive force of 80 men that dislodged them from a fortified pucará. After attempts in 1565 and 1592, the present city was founded as San Salvador de Velazco en el Valle de Jujuy on 19 April 1593 by Francisco de Argañarás y Murguía. It developed as a strategic site on the mule trade route between San Miguel de Tucumán and the silver mines of Potosí.

The city reached its peak importance in the colonial period and declined to a remote provincial capital after the Argentine Declaration of Independence in 1816. It became the capital of Jujuy Province when the province separated from Salta in 1834, and the earthquake of 1863 levelled the town. Growth began again with the arrival of the Northern Central Railway in 1900, and the National University of Jujuy was created in 1973 from the Economic Sciences Institute of 1959.

The colonial city centre includes the Cabildo, the cathedral and the colourful Andean carnivals. The 2001 census counted 237,751 inhabitants, rising to around 300,000 with the suburbs. Winters are dry and cold and summers humid, and temperatures vary widely between day and night. The city is the provincial government, financial and cultural centre.
sanaa: Sanaa stands at about 2,300 metres above sea level, on a plain of the same name, the Haql Sanaa, between the mountains of Jabal An-Nabi Shu'ayb and Jabal Tiyal. The plain is roughly 50 to 60 km long from north to south and about 25 km wide, bordered by cliffs and mountains from which wadis descend. The Old City is known for its tower houses of stone and fired brick, which can rise to eight storeys. Their ground floors were traditionally used for grain and animals, and the top room, the mafraj, serves as a second reception room.

The city was a secondary capital of the Kingdom of Saba, whose main capital was the oasis of Marib. Its name is probably derived from a Sabaic root meaning well-fortified. From the time of Muhammad, around 622 CE, Sanaa was the governing seat of Yemen until independent sub-states appeared, and all of Yemen's states competed to control it.

The Ottoman Empire entered Yemen in 1538, under Suleiman, and conquered Sanaa in 1547 under Özdemir Pasha. In 1602 the local Zaydi imams, led by Imam al-Mu'ayyad, reasserted their control, and Ottoman troops were forced out in 1629. In 1904, as Ottoman influence waned, Imam Yahya took power in Sanaa and followed a policy of isolation that left the city with little new infrastructure. Before the revolution of 1962 society was divided into five ranked groups, headed by the sayyids and the qadis. The Jewish community, present in Yemen since the 5th century BCE, was expelled in 1679 and returned in 1680 to a quarter outside the walls. After 1948 about 49,000 of an estimated 51,000 Yemenite Jews were airlifted to Israel.

Sanaa is the capital and largest city of Yemen, with a population of about 3,300,000 in 2023. It grew rapidly from the 1960s, when it became the capital of the republic and a new city spread beyond the old one. The Old City, enclosed by clay walls 9 to 14 metres high and holding more than 100 mosques, 12 hammams and 6,500 houses, was made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986. The Great Mosque is more than 1,400 years old. The sung tradition al-Ghina al-San'ani, which dates to the 14th century, was designated UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2003.
sanandaj: The name Sinna first appears in records from the 14th century CE. Before that the main city of the region was Sisar, also called Sisar of Sadkhaniya, or Sisar of the hundred springs, whose exact location is unknown; it has been proposed that Sinna is a contracted form of Sadkhaniya.

The name Sisar disappears in the 14th century, and Sinna replaces it in the works of Hamdallah Mustawfi, who refers to a mountain and a pass of that name. The Kurdish historian Sharaf al-Din Bitlisi mentions that in 1580 an Ardalan ruler named Timur Khan held a land grant that included Sinna and the earlier Ardalan capital of Hasanabad.

The local historian Ali-Akbar Munshi Waqayi-Nigar wrote in 1892/3 that Sinna was founded by the Ardalan ruler Soleyman Khan on the site of an earlier settlement, giving a chronogram that corresponds to 1046 AH, or 1636-7 CE. The town grew greatly under Aman Allah the Great, who reigned from 1797 to 1825. In the 19th century it was a lively commercial centre, exporting oak galls, tragacanth, furs and carpets.

Sanandaj is the capital of Kurdistan province in western Iran, and of its county and district. It lies between the Qishlaq river, a tributary of the Diyala, and Mount Awidar, which separates it from Hasanabad. Its people are mainly Kurdish, most follow the Shafi'i branch of Sunni Islam, and Central Kurdish is the vernacular of daily life while Persian is the language of education and government. It is regarded as a historic centre of Kurdish cultural and intellectual life, with traditions of music, poetry and carpet weaving. Carpet making is the biggest industry.

In the 19th century its population was mostly Kurdish, with a significant Jewish minority and smaller numbers of Armenian and Assyrian Christians, mostly Chaldean Catholic. Until 1979 the city had a small Aramaic-speaking Jewish community of about 4,000 people, and its Assyrian community spoke a dialect of Aramaic called Senaya.
sandinista-national-liberation-front: The Sandinistas took their name from Augusto César Sandino (1895-1934), who led Nicaragua's nationalist rebellion against the United States occupation of the country in the early 20th century. Sandino was assassinated on 21 February 1934 by the National Guard, the US-equipped force of Anastasio Somoza García, whose family ruled the country from 1936 until the Sandinistas overthrew it in 1979.

The movement grew out of opposition and student groups of the late 1950s and early 1960s, with the universities of Léon and the National Autonomous University in Managua as principal centres. Inspired by the Cuban Revolution and the FLN in Algeria, it was founded in 1961 by Carlos Fonseca, Silvio Mayorga, Tomás Borge, Casimiro Sotelo and others as the National Liberation Front. Only Borge lived to see the victory of 1979.

After a defeat at Pancasán in 1967 the Front adopted the doctrine of the Prolonged Popular War. The earthquake of 23 December 1972 destroyed much of Managua, and Anastasio Somoza Debayle's National Guard embezzled much of the aid. The killing of the newspaper editor Pedro Joaquín Chamorro on 10 January 1978 set off riots and a general strike. By mid-April 1979 five guerrilla fronts operated under the Front's joint command, and the Somoza regime fell in the Nicaraguan Revolution of that year.

The Sandinistas inherited a debt of US$1.6 billion, an estimated 30,000 to 50,000 war dead and 600,000 homeless. They first governed through a five-member Junta of National Reconstruction, and took exclusive power in March 1981. The United States, under President Ronald Reagan, authorised the CIA to finance, arm and train the Contras, mostly remnants of Somoza's National Guard, and imposed a trade embargo in May 1985. Elections were held in 1984, and the war continued until 1989. After the Esquipulas II treaty of 1987, the Sandinistas lost the election of 26 February 1990 to Violeta Barrios de Chamorro and passed power peacefully.

In government the Front carried out a literacy campaign, with Cuban teachers, that lowered illiteracy from 50% to 12%, a land reform affecting half of the country's arable land and a Ministry of Culture led by the poet and priest Ernesto Cardenal. Cuba also sent advisers, who numbered over 2,500. Critics reported detentions, censorship of the newspaper La Prensa and abuses against the Miskito people, while supporters and church delegations disputed some allegations as political. Its flag, red above black with the letters F S L N, is a modified version of Sandino's. Daniel Ortega was elected president in 2006, and held the office from 1985 to 1990 and again from 2007.
sandro-botticelli: Alessandro di Mariano di Vanni Filipepi, known as Botticelli, was born in Florence in a house on the Borgo Ognissanti and lived in the same area all his life. He was the youngest of the four surviving children of the tanner Mariano di Vanni d'Amedeo Filipepi and his wife Smeralda.
