His birth date is unknown, but his father's tax returns, which give his age as two in 1447 and thirteen in 1458, show that he was born between 1444 and 1446. Giorgio Vasari reported that Botticelli was first trained as a goldsmith. From about 1461 or 1462 he was apprenticed to Fra Filippo Lippi, from whom he learned intimate compositions with melancholic figures drawn in clear contours.

Botticelli was an independent master throughout the 1470s, and his reputation rose. His only significant time away from Florence was spent painting in Pisa in 1474 and, in 1481 to 1482, in the Sistine Chapel in Rome, where Pope Sixtus IV summoned him and other Florentine and Umbrian painters to fresco the walls. He received patronage from members of the Medici family, including Lorenzo de' Medici and his circle.

The 1480s were his most successful decade. Primavera of about 1482 and The Birth of Venus of about 1485, both now in the Uffizi, depicted classical mythology on a very large scale, which was virtually unprecedented in Western art since antiquity. In the same decade he painted many Madonnas and altarpieces, among them the Bardi Altarpiece, finished by February 1485, and the San Marco Altarpiece, his largest. By the 1490s his style became more personal and to some extent mannered, and his last works moved in a direction opposite to that of Leonardo da Vinci and the painters of the High Renaissance, towards a style many have called more Gothic or archaic.
He painted dozens of Madonnas, many of them in the round tondo shape, as well as portraits, although fewer than have been attributed to him. He had a lifelong interest in Dante.

According to Vasari, Botticelli became a follower of the Dominican preacher Girolamo Savonarola, who preached in Florence from 1490 until his execution in 1498, gave up painting and fell into poverty. Botticelli died on 17 May 1510 and was buried in the church of Ognissanti. His reputation was then eclipsed longer than that of any other major European artist, until the Pre-Raphaelites rediscovered him in the late 19th century.
sandzak: Sandžak covers around 8,500 square kilometres between the south-eastern border of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the borders with Kosovo and Albania. Six of its municipalities are in Serbia (Novi Pazar, Sjenica, Tutin, Prijepolje, Nova Varoš and Priboj) and seven in Montenegro (Pljevlja, Bijelo Polje, Berane, Petnjica, Rožaje, Gusinje and Plav). The name is the Serbo-Croatian form of the Ottoman Turkish sancak, a province; Serbs have historically known the region as Raška, of which it was part in the 12th century.

The Ottoman Empire invaded the Serbian Despotate in 1455. The spread of Islam in Sandžak had several causes: Muslims did not pay the jizya tax or the child levy and were privileged over Christians in administration and the courts; after the Great Turkish War (1683–1699) part of the Orthodox population was driven north and the land was settled by people who were or became Muslim; and the region was a centre of trade. Until 1790 it belonged to the Sanjak of Bosnia, which is why its Muslims identify with the Slavic Muslims of Bosnia.

When Serbian and Montenegrin troops seized the region in October 1912, many Slavic Muslims and Albanians left for Ottoman Turkey. In 1919 an Albanian revolt in the Rožaje, Gusinje and Plav districts against inclusion in the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes was put down; seven hundred Albanians were killed in Rožaje and about 450 civilians in Plav and Gusinje.

In 1941 the region was partitioned between Italian-held Montenegro, the Italian protectorate of Albania and German-occupied Serbia, and Muslim militias, Chetniks and Partisans fought there. On 2 March 1942 the Jews of Novi Pazar were rounded up and killed in camps. In May 1943 Chetnik forces under Pavle Đurišić massacred an estimated 5,400 Albanian men, women and children in Bihor, and an estimated 9,000 Muslims in all were killed by Chetniks and affiliated groups during the war. A Partisan council for Sandžak, founded at Pljevlja on 20 November 1943, accepted on 29 March 1945 the division of the region along the line of 1912.

The municipalities of Sandžak have around 361,656 inhabitants. Bosniaks form 54.8 per cent, Serbs 30 per cent, Montenegrins 5 per cent, people who declare themselves Muslims by ethnicity 3.4 per cent and Albanians 1 per cent. Novi Pazar is the economic and cultural centre. A referendum on autonomy organised by the Muslim National Council of Sandžak between 25 and 27 October 1991 was declared illegal by Serbia. The region remains underdeveloped, and census data show emigration by all its peoples.
sangha: In Buddhism the term refers to the monastic communities of bhikkhu (monks) and bhikkhuni (nuns), traditionally called the bhikkhu-sangha and the bhikkhuni-sangha. As a separate category, Buddhists who have attained any of the four stages of enlightenment, whether or not they belong to the monastic community, are called the āryasaṅgha, the noble Sangha. A glossary by Richard Robinson and others gives two levels of meaning: an ideal level, covering all the Buddha's followers, lay or ordained, who have reached at least the level of srotāpanna, and a conventional level, covering the orders of monks and nuns. The two overlap but are not identical, since some members of the ideal Sangha are not ordained.

Usage differs between schools. Mahayana practitioners may use the word for all Buddhists, whereas the Pāli Canon uses parisā, the assembly, for the larger community of monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen who have taken the Three Refuges. The Sangha is the third of those refuges, and in the Theravada tradition its qualities are chanted daily or on Uposatha days.

The Sangha was established by Gautama Buddha in the fifth century BCE for those who wished to practise full-time, free from the responsibilities of household life. It has also preserved the Buddha's teachings, given spiritual support to the lay community, and taken responsibility for the integrity of the doctrine and for its translation and propagation. Its key feature is adherence to the vinaya, which contains 227 main rules of conduct, known as the Patimokkha in Pāli, including complete chastity and eating only before noon. Transgressions carry penalties from confession to permanent expulsion.

The words bhikkhu and bhikkhuni mean one who lives by alms, and early monastics went on daily alms rounds. The vinaya did not allow the sangha to farm, but in East Asia monastic communities came to engage in agriculture, an emphasis attributed to the Chan master Baizhang Huaihai. In Japan Saichō, the founder of Tendai, reduced the rules to about 60, based on the Bodhisattva Precepts.

In its political sense the word denoted a governing assembly in a republic or a kingdom, and some Buddhists have called the sangha humanity's oldest surviving democratic institution. Nichiren Shōshū holds that the sangha is the priesthood of its head temple Taisekiji, while the Soka Gakkai, expelled from it in December 1991, understands the sangha to include all who practise Buddhism in its way, lay or clerical.
sanliurfa: Urfa, officially Şanlıurfa, lies on a plain about 80 km east of the Euphrates, at the border between the foothills of the Taurus Mountains and the Mesopotamian plain. The earliest name recorded for the city is Admaʾ, found in Assyrian cuneiform of the Old Assyrian period. About 12 km to the north-east is the Neolithic site of Göbekli Tepe, founded in the tenth millennium BCE, and the area was part of a network of the first settlements where agriculture arose. Because of its place in Jewish, Christian and Islamic history, and a legend that it was Abraham's hometown, Urfa is nicknamed the City of Prophets.

The Seleucid king Seleucus I Nicator founded the city as Edessa in 302 or 303 BCE, naming it after the ancient capital of Macedonia. It surrendered to the Rashidun general Iyad ibn Ghanm in 639 without resistance, and the terms guaranteed that the city's Christians would keep their cathedral. The Numayrid emir Waththab ibn Sabiq annexed it after declaring independence in 990.

Urfa was the capital of the crusader County of Edessa for about half a century from 1098, ruling subjects who were a mix of Armenians and Syrians, among whom the Armenians were dominant in the city itself. Nur ad-Din's nephew Sayf al-Din Ghazi II captured it after Nur ad-Din's death in 1174. The city submitted to the troops of Hulagu in 1260 and its inhabitants were spared, though it was left desolate.

The Mamluks gained control in the early fourteenth century and renovated the ruined citadel, but the city attracted few inhabitants because merchant traffic took another route. It was likely incorporated into the Ottoman Empire under Selim I around 1517, and an Ottoman tax register of 1518 documented 1,082 families, 700 of them Muslim and 382 Christian.

During the First World War Urfa was a site of the Armenian and Assyrian genocides from 1915. Armenians were deported and killed; about 400 were taken to the edge of town and killed in four days from 15 to 19 August, and another massacre on 23 September killed 300.

Urfa is the capital of Şanlıurfa Province. The citadel stands on rocky heights south of the old centre, and its first known fortification dates from the early sixth century under the emperor Justinian. The old city walls date from an Abbasid rebuilding in 812. According to legend, the pool of Balıklıgöl was formed when Abraham was thrown into a fire by Nimrod and the flames turned to water. The Şanlıurfa Museum houses some 10,000 artefacts from the Paleolithic through Islamic times, including finds from Göbekli Tepe, and the Haleplibahçe Mosaic Museum displays the oldest known mosaic depicting the Amazons.
sansepolcro: According to tradition the town arose from two 9th-century pilgrims to the Holy Land, Arcanus and Giles. They returned, built a chapel dedicated to Saint Leonard and began a monastic life there. They had brought a stone from the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, which was installed in the monastery and gave the place its name, Santo Sepolcro.

It became a popular pilgrimage site, and the church was raised to the rank of Benedictine abbey, the Badia, and declared an abbey nullius. The first historical mentions date to 1012 and refer to the building of the monastery, around which a commune began to develop. The Emperor Conrad II declared the settlement a market town, and in the following century the abbey affiliated with the Camaldolese Order.

During the conflicts of Guelfs and Ghibellines the town's factions were led by local families, among them the Pichi, Bercordati, Graziani and Bacci. In the 13th century, because of its position on local trade routes, control of the town passed between Uguccione della Faggiola, Lord of Pisa, Guido Tarlati, Bishop of Arezzo, and his brother Pier Saccone Tarlati di Pietramala.

In 1367 Pope Urban V gave it to the Malatesta family, whose heirs ruled it until the Republic of Florence took control in the 15th century with the approval of Pope Eugene IV. Pope Leo X raised it to the rank of a city a century later.

Sansepolcro stands on the upper Tiber in the province of Arezzo, in eastern Tuscany. Its Cathedral of St. John the Evangelist, in Gothic-Romanesque style, was built in 1012-49. It was the birthplace of the painters Piero della Francesca, Raffaellino del Colle, Matteo di Giovanni, Santi di Tito and Angiolo Tricca, and of the mathematician Luca Pacioli. In the World War II the town was saved from destruction when a British officer, Tony Clarke, halted an Allied artillery attack to protect Piero della Francesca's fresco of the Resurrection. That painting is now in the Museo Civico.
sanskrit: Sanskrit is a classical language of the Indo-Aryan branch of the Indo-European family. It arose in South Asia after its predecessor languages had spread there from the northwest in the late Bronze Age, and it is one of the three earliest documented languages descended from Proto-Indo-European. Its closest ancient relatives are the Nuristani languages of the Hindu Kush and the Iranian languages Avestan and Old Persian.

The oldest form is Vedic Sanskrit, found in the Rigveda, a collection of 1,028 hymns composed between 1500 and 1200 BCE by Indo-Aryan tribes moving east into northwestern India. The Dravidian languages influenced its sounds and syntax. Classical Sanskrit, refined and standardised from the mid-first millennium BCE, was codified in Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī. The epics, the Mahābhārata and the Rāmāyaṇa, were composed in Epic Sanskrit, used in northern India between 400 BCE and 300 CE.

The word saṃskṛta means well prepared, perfected or polished. The Rigveda was passed on orally by methods of memorisation of exceptional rigour, as a single text with no variant readings, which makes its archaic forms important for reconstructing Proto-Indo-European. Sanskrit has no native script: from around the turn of the first millennium CE it has been written in various Brahmic scripts, most commonly today in Devanagari. The earliest known inscriptions date from the first century BCE.

For nearly 2,000 years Sanskrit was the language of a cultural order that reached across South Asia, Inner Asia and Southeast Asia, and to some extent East Asia. Inscriptions and manuscripts have been found from Nepal and Tibet to Cambodia, Indonesia, Mongolia, Korea and Japan. Classical Sanskrit covers epics, drama, law, grammar, medicine, astronomy and mathematics; the dramatist Kālidāsa wrote in it, and the foundations of modern arithmetic were first described in it. Its surviving manuscripts number over 30 million.

Sanskrit later stopped being learned as a first language and ceased developing as a living one. It remains the sacred language of Hindu, Buddhist and Jain traditions and is used in worship. It is one of the languages of the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution of India, and the oldest Sanskrit college, the Benares Sanskrit College, was founded in 1791 under East India Company rule.
sant-julia-de-loria: Sant Julià de Lòria lies in the Eastern Pyrenees on the banks of the Gran Valira, the largest river in Andorra. The parish covers an area of 60 square kilometres and is bordered by the capital Andorra la Vella to the north, by Escaldes-Engordany to the northeast and by the Spanish region of Catalonia on the other sides. The town of the same name is the seat of the parish and is headed by a mayor.

The parish has five quarts and eleven villages: Bixessarri, Aixàs, Aixovall, Certers, Llumeneres, Nagol, Aixirivall, Auvinyà, Juberri, Fontaneda and Canòlic. The Naturlandia park occupies about 100 hectares of hill slopes at altitudes between 1,600 and 2,000 metres.

The University of Andorra, the only university in the country, stands in the parish. In the 20th century the region was a major centre of tobacco processing, and the Tobacco Museum occupies the old tobacco factory, which functioned until 1957. Large shopping malls stand close to the Spanish border. The Sant Serni de Nagol Church was built in the 11th century.

Roads connect the parish with the rest of Andorra and with Spain, and buses run to Barcelona, Vic, Tarragona, Lleida, Girona and Toulouse. Andorra has no airport of its own; the Andorra–La Seu d'Urgell Airport in Catalonia lies about 12 km away. The region has more than 20 km of alpine skiing trails, and Naturlandia has a 5,300 metre alpine toboggan course. The parish counts among its notable people Carme Travesset (1925–2022), the first woman to hold political office in Andorra, and Òscar Ribas Reig (1936–2020), the country's first prime minister in 1982.
santa-fe-argentina: Santa Fe de la Vera Cruz, meaning Holy Faith of the True Cross, stands in north-eastern Argentina near the junction of the Paraná and Salado rivers. It lies 170 kilometres north of Rosario and about 340 kilometres east of Córdoba, and is linked by the Hernandarias Subfluvial Tunnel to the city of Paraná. A canal connects it with the port of Colastiné on the Paraná. Its climate is humid subtropical, with hot and humid summers and mild winters.

The conquistador Juan de Garay founded the city in 1573 at the nearby site of Cayastá, during an expedition from Asunción to the Paraná River. Constant flooding of the Cayastá River led to the move to the present site in 1653. Cayastá now has a historical park containing the grave of Hernandarias, the first American-born governor in South America. Santa Fe became the provincial capital in 1814, when the province of Santa Fe was separated from the province of Buenos Aires. In 1853 the National Constituent Assembly met in the city. This history of the Argentine Constitution led lawmakers to choose it for Constitutional Conventions in 1949, 1957 and 1994.

Santa Fe is the capital of its province and the commercial and transport centre of a rich agricultural area producing grain, vegetable oils and meat. The National University of the Littoral began as the Provincial University in 1889 and took its present name in 1919. The Salado has flooded the city repeatedly. A catastrophic flood on 29 April 2003 forced at least 100,000 people to be evacuated. The Santa Fe Belgrano railway station, built in 1891 and named Cultural Heritage, was reopened as a convention centre.
santa-fe-new-mexico: Santa Fe lies at the foothills of the Sangre de Cristo Mountains and is the highest state capital in the United States. Its climate is cold semi-arid, with cool, dry winters and hot summers. The name is Spanish for Holy Faith and is a shortened form of the original La Villa Real de la Santa Fe de San Francisco de Asís. The Tewa call the place P'oegeh, water place, a name that predates European colonisation.

The area was originally occupied by Tanoan peoples who lived in Pueblo villages along the Rio Grande. Tewa built a cluster of homes around the site of today's Plaza sometime after 900 CE, but the Pueblo peoples had abandoned the site for at least 200 years by the time the Spanish arrived in the early 17th century. Juan de Oñate led the first Spanish effort to colonise the region in 1598; the Spanish banished him after his rule was judged cruel to the indigenous population.

Santa Fe was founded in 1610 as the capital of Nuevo México, a province of New Spain, and is the oldest state capital in the United States. The Spanish laid it out by the Laws of the Indies of 1573, around a central plaza with the Palace of the Governors on its north side. It prospered on the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro and the Santa Fe Trail. In 1846 General Stephen W. Kearny led some 1,700 soldiers into the city, and by the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo in 1848 the United States gained New Mexico. Santa Fe became the capital of the territory in 1851 and of the state in 1912.

Santa Fe is the fourth most populous city in New Mexico and the county seat of Santa Fe County. It blends indigenous, Spanish and American influences and has been a UNESCO Creative City in Crafts and Folk Art since 2005. The Plaza and the Palace of the Governors remain at its centre, and its adobe-style Pueblo Revival and Territorial Revival architecture is largely preserved. The city has been associated with science since 1943, when it served as the gateway to Los Alamos National Laboratory.
santa-maria-capua-vetere: Santa Maria Capua Vetere is a town in the province of Caserta, in Campania, and is nicknamed by its people the city of Spartacus. After ancient Capua was destroyed, the town grew up near the Roman amphitheatre and the old basilica of Santa Maria Maggiore, which gave it its old name, kept until 1861. Capua Vetere means Old Capua. Capua's founding date is uncertain, though Velleius Paterculus places it around 800 BCE, and the name probably comes from the Etruscan Capeva, city of marshes.

Villanovan settlements stood in the area before Oscans and Etruscans enlarged them. Under Etruscan rule in the 5th century BCE the city's layout was remodelled, and Oscan speaking peoples who migrated in from inland as cheap labour were granted citizenship in 438 BCE. In the 4th century BCE Capua was the largest city in Italy after Rome. It submitted to Rome for protection against the Samnites in 343 BCE and in 338 BCE became a civitas sine suffragio, keeping its own laws, language and senate. The Via Appia connected it to Rome in 312 BCE.

Capua stayed loyal to Rome in the Second Punic War until the defeat at Cannae. It then allied with Hannibal, after Rome rejected its demand that one of the two consuls be a Capuan, and Hannibal wintered there. Rome retook the city after a brutal siege in 211 BCE: its leaders, among them Vibius Virrius, killed themselves, most of the population was sold into slavery or killed, and its territory became public land. Capua later recovered as one of the richest cities of the empire. It held one of the first and most prestigious gladiatorial schools, where Spartacus trained and began his revolt in 73 BCE, and in 59 BCE Julius Caesar resettled twenty thousand Roman citizens there.

Vandal ravages damaged the city, which became the seat of a Lombard principate. In 841 CE a band of Saracens destroyed it, leaving only the church of Santa Maria Maggiore standing. Most survivors fled and founded the modern town of Capua, while others fortified the amphitheatre. The present town grew slowly around the old basilicas and was an agricultural place; King Robert of Anjou was born there.

The Roman amphitheatre, built under Augustus and restored by Hadrian, is the second largest after the Colosseum. Its longer diameter is 170 metres, and only two of its 80 Doric arcades of four storeys survive, while its underground passages are well preserved. Nearby stand the Arch of Hadrian and a mithraeum, one of the best preserved in the former empire. The basilica of Santa Maria Maggiore is held by tradition to have been founded in the 5th century by Pope Symmachus.
santa-maria-delle-grazie-milan: The name means Holy Mary of Grace. Duke Francesco I Sforza of Milan ordered the construction of a Dominican convent and church on the site of an earlier chapel dedicated to St Mary of the Graces. Guiniforte Solari, the main architect, designed the convent, with its Gothic nave, which was completed by 1469, but construction of the church took decades. Duke Ludovico Sforza decided that the church should serve as the burial place of the Sforza family and rebuilt the cloister and the apse, both completed after 1490. His wife Beatrice was buried in the church in 1497.

The design of the apse has been attributed to Donato Bramante, because his name is inscribed on a piece of marble in the church vaults delivered in 1494, though some dispute that he worked on the church at all. One source gives him the crossing, the dome, the transept apses and the choir with apse in 1492 to 1497. Some documents mention the name Amadeo, probably Giovanni Antonio Amadeo, and the church shares similarities with his design for Santa Maria alla Fontana.

In 1543 a Titian altarpiece of Christ receiving the crown of thorns was installed in the Chapel of the Holy Crown, which is frescoed with Stories of the Passion by Gaudenzio Ferrari; French troops looted the painting in 1797 and it is now in the Louvre. A fresco by Bramantino stands in the small cloister, and Bernardo Zenale painted frescoes of the Resurrection and Passion.

On the night of 15 August 1943 an Allied aerial bombardment struck the church and convent. Much of the refectory was destroyed, but some walls survived, including the one bearing Leonardo's Last Supper, which had been sand-bagged. The painting had been distorted by restorations over the centuries, and the work begun in 1978 and completed in 1999 brought Leonardo's original to light. It also addressed the refectory's environment, since dust, fumes and humidity were identified as the chief causes of the painting's deterioration. The Old Sacristy, designed by Bramante, is now the seat of a Dominican cultural centre that hosts conferences and concerts.
santa-marta: Santa Marta lies on Santa Marta Bay on the Caribbean coast of northern Colombia, 992 kilometres from Bogotá and 93 kilometres from Barranquilla. It is bordered to the north and west by the Caribbean and to the south by the municipalities of Aracataca and Ciénaga. The climate is tropical savanna, with largely uniform temperatures throughout the year, a dry season from December to April and a wet season from May to November.

Before Europeans arrived the region was inhabited by indigenous groups, among them the Tairona, who formed mid-sized and large population centres with stone pathways, terraces and protected waterways. Their economy was mainly agricultural, growing corn, pineapple and yucca, and they collected and processed salt, a significant trading commodity. They traded with other groups along the coast and in the interior, and excavations have recovered pottery, stonework and gold. Understanding of the peoples of the region is limited, in part because Spanish conquistadors destroyed and misrepresented many records.

The Spanish conqueror Rodrigo de Bastidas founded the city on 29 July 1525. It was one of the first Spanish settlements in Colombia and the second oldest in South America. Simón Bolívar spent his last weeks in Santa Marta and died of tuberculosis in 1830, aged 47, at the Quinta de San Pedro Alejandrino. He was buried in the cathedral, and his remains were later moved to Caracas.

Santa Marta is the capital of Magdalena Department and one of the principal cities of Colombia's Caribbean region. The Cathedral Basilica, built in the eighteenth century, once held the remains of Bastidas and Bolívar, and the Quinta de San Pedro Alejandrino stands just outside the city centre. The economy rests mainly on tourism, followed by trade, port activities, fishing and agriculture, with bananas, coffee, mango, cocoa and cassava among the main crops. The Universidad del Magdalena is in the city.
santal-people: The Santal, also spelled Santhal, are an Austroasiatic-speaking Munda people of the Indian subcontinent. They are the largest tribal community in the Indian states of Jharkhand and West Bengal, and are also present in Odisha, Bihar, Assam and Tripura. They are the largest ethnic minority in northern Bangladesh and have a sizeable population in Nepal. Their ethnonym is Hor Hopon, child of human. The name Santal is most likely an exonym, derived from Saont in the Midnapore region of West Bengal, a word meaning plain land.

According to the linguist Paul Sidwell, speakers of Austroasiatic languages probably arrived on the coast of Odisha from Indochina about 4,000 to 3,500 years ago and mixed extensively with local populations. The original homeland of the Santals is not known with certainty. Their folklore says they came from Hihiri, which scholars identify as Ahuri in the Hazaribagh district, and were pushed onto the Chhota Nagpur Plateau and finally to Saont.

The Santals enter the historical record in 1795 as Soontars. The Bengal Famine of 1770 had depopulated the western and south-western parts of Bengal, especially the Jungle Mahals, and the East India Company lost revenue. After the Permanent Settlement of 1790 the Company looked for agriculturalists to clear the land, and British officials turned to the Santals, who were ready to clear forest for settled agriculture. In 1832 a large area of the Raj Mahal hills was demarcated as Damin-i-koh, and Santals migrated there to cultivate it, taking loans from non-Santal moneylenders to buy iron tools, seed grain and oxen.

The community was split between West Bengal and East Pakistan at Partition. After independence the Santals were made one of the Scheduled Tribes in India. In East Pakistan and neighbouring West Bengal they supported the Tebhaga movement, and after the Pakistani military crushed the uprising and burned many Santal homes, many fled to Malda in India. When Jharkhand was separated from Bihar in 2000, the Santal Parganas became a separate division, which the Santals consider their cultural heartland.

Santal society rests on a division between sibling, boeha, and guest, pera. Those in the closest brotherhood, mit orak hor, cannot marry each other, and clans are exogamous. A village council led by a manjhi handles local affairs. The principal festival is Sohrai, and dances are accompanied by two drums, the Tamak and the Tumdak. Santal marriage has seven recognised kinds, of which the most widely practised is kesimek.

The Santals worship nature in sacred groves called Jaher and Sarna, and many consider themselves followers of the Sari and Sarna religion rather than Hinduism. The Ol Chiki script of Santali was invented by Raghunath Murmu, known as Olguru, and Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu are remembered as leaders of the Santhal rebellion.
santander-spain: Santander lies on the northern side of the Bay of Santander, facing the Cantabrian Sea, and owes its existence to the excellent harbour of the bay. The earliest settlers probably chose the north side for practical reasons: it is sheltered from the storms of the Bay of Biscay and has a hillside with good visibility for spotting attackers. Little is known of the earliest settlements.

The place is first mentioned in 1068, in a draft document of King Sancho II. According to the account, Alfonso II the Chaste had founded the Abbey of the Holy Bodies in the 9th century, to house the heads of Saint Emeterius and Saint Celedonius. Alfonso VIII of Castile granted a fuero, or charter, in 1187. The shipyards were ordered by the king to take timber from the Cantabrian forests, and the town had to give the monarchy a ship each year. By the end of the 15th century it had about 4,000 or 5,000 inhabitants. It became a city officially in 1755.

On 3 November 1893 the steamship Cabo Machichaco caught fire while being unloaded at a pier. About 40 tonnes of dynamite in her holds exploded, killing about 590 people, injuring about 2,000 and destroying at least 65 buildings near the harbour.

In the Spanish Civil War the Nationalist uprising of 1936 in Santander was defeated, and the city stayed with the Republican government. Nationalist forces captured it in the Battle of Santander on 26 August 1937. Adam Hoschild counts at least 1,267 people executed after quick trials in the weeks that followed. In 1941 a great fire burned for two days, destroyed the greater part of the medieval town centre and gutted the Romanesque cathedral. Only one person died, a firefighter, but thousands of families were left homeless.

Santander is the capital of the autonomous community of Cantabria. The cathedral keeps its lower church, built around 1200 in a style passing from Romanesque to Gothic. The port remains active, with ferry services to the United Kingdom and Ireland, and the bank Banco Santander was founded in the city.
santarem-para: Santarém lies in the western part of the state of Pará, Brazil, where the Tapajós meets the Amazon, some 600–700 km from both Manaus upriver and Belém downriver. The two rivers run side by side for many kilometres in front of the city without mixing: the Amazon's milky water carries sediment from the Andes, while the Tapajós is warmer and deep blue, a sight locals call the meeting of the waters. The climate is tropical monsoon, with a wet season from November to July and a dry season from August to October.

The Tapajós people, after whom the river is named, led a large agricultural chiefdom here before Europeans arrived. The first written references to their settlement date from 1542, when Francisco Orellana sacked one of their corn plantations.

In 1621 the Portuguese explorer Pedro Teixeira, with Father Cristovão, 26 soldiers and many Indians, set out to explore the upper Amazon and made port at a Tupuliçus settlement near the mouth of the Tapajós, whose people had already met Spanish explorers. The Jesuits took on the work of founding a mission village on the site, which Father António Vieira is known to have visited in 1659. Father João Filipe Bettendorff founded it on 22 June 1661 as the Aldeia do Tapajós, and built the Chapel of Our Lady of Conception.

Francisco da Mota Falcão began a fortress by the river in 1693, and his son Manoel Mota Siqueira finished it in 1697. Square, with bastions at each corner, the Fortress of Tapajós became the nucleus of the growing village. In 1758 the village was given the status of vila and the name Santarém, after the Portuguese city, and on 24 October 1848 provincial law no. 145 made it a city. Attempts to restore the fortress ended with the last in 1867, when six cannons were sent and left in the street; a high school was built on the site in 1900.

Santarém is the second most important city of the state of Pará and the economic centre of its western part, and it leads the Santarém Metropolitan Area with Belterra and Mojuí dos Campos. It is the seat of a Roman Catholic diocese, and most of its people are Catholic. Its economy has passed through cycles dominated by rubber, coffee and gold mining, and more recently soybean growing. Its beaches on the Tapajós, such as those at Alter do Chão, are a tourist attraction, and Alter do Chão hosts the Sairé folklore festival each September.
santarem-portugal: Santarém stands on a plateau on the right bank of the Tagus, 65 km north-east of Lisbon. It is the historic capital of the Ribatejo, and its municipality had 58,671 inhabitants in 2021. The city lies on the Portuguese Way variant of the Way of Saint James. The region has been inhabited since prehistory, first by the Lusitani and then by Greeks, Romans, Visigoths, Arabs and Portuguese Christians.

The foundation of the city is attributed to the Romans, who occupied the region in the 2nd century BCE and named it Scalabis. It was an important commercial post of the mid-Tagus and the administrative capital of the Conventus Scalabitanus of Lusitania. In 61 BCE Julius Caesar ordered a military camp there, and the city took the name Scallabis Praesidium Iulium. In the 5th century Germanic tribes conquered it, and in 460 the Visigoths under Sunerico expelled the Alans. The best-known legend of its foundation concerns Saint Iria, martyred at Tomar, whose body reached Santarém and gave the town the name Sancta Irene, from which Santarém derives.
The Arabs took it in the 8th century and called it Shantarin; under their rule it became an important cultural centre, and the poets Ibn Sara and Ibn Bassam came from it.

The first king of Portugal, Afonso Henriques, conquered the city on 15 March 1147. According to the chronicles he and a small army took it after some men climbed the walls at night and opened the gates; the story is told in the chronicle De expugnatione Scalabis. With the capture of Lisbon that year it was a crucial step in the Reconquista of Portugal. The Almohad ruler Abu Yaqub Yusuf died there in 1184 while besieging it.

Afterwards kings often visited and held cortes in Santarém; Fernando I chose to be buried in the Convent of Saint Francis. In the 15th century expeditions such as the conquest of Ceuta in 1415 were planned in its royal palace. Earthquakes struck in 1531 and 1755, and the Napoleonic invasions brought pillage.

The city's many Gothic buildings have earned it the name Capital of the Portuguese Gothic. Pedro de Meneses, first governor of Ceuta, and the navigator Pedro Álvares Cabral are buried in the Church of the Grace. The railway reached Santarém in 1861, and its economy has remained mainly agricultural.
santiago: Santiago lies in the centre of the Santiago Basin, a flat, bowl-shaped valley of fertile land surrounded by mountains. The main chain of the Andes flanks it to the east and the Chilean Coastal Range to the west, with the Cordón de Chacabuco to the north. The basin measures about 80 kilometres north to south and 35 kilometres east to west, and the Mapocho River flows through the city. A few island hills, among them Cerro Santa Lucía, rise from the plain. The historic centre, the Plaza de Armas, lies at 565 metres.

Archaeological evidence suggests that the first human groups reached the basin around the 10th millennium BCE, nomadic hunter-gatherers who travelled from the coast to hunt guanacos during the Andean snowmelt. By around 800 CE the first permanent settlers had established agricultural communities along the Mapocho, growing maize, potatoes and beans. The villages of the Picunche, whom the Incas called the Promaucae, were under Inca rule from the late 15th century to the early 16th, and the Incas placed a settlement of mitimas in the valley.

The conquistador Pedro de Valdivia, sent by Francisco Pizarro from Peru, arrived in the Mapocho valley on 13 December 1540, after a long journey from Cusco. He founded the city as Santiago del Nuevo Extremo on 12 February 1541, naming it for his home region of Extremadura and for James the Great, patron saint of Spain. It was to be the capital of his governorship of Nueva Extremadura.

The city consolidated as the capital of the Captaincy General of Chile despite food shortages, Indigenous attacks, floods and devastating earthquakes, notably in 1647. It remained the political centre during the Chilean War of Independence, which began with the First Government Junta in 1810 and ended in patriot victory at the Battle of Maipú in 1818. The Universidad de Chile traces its roots to 1622, and the 19th century brought railway construction and major educational and cultural institutions.

Santiago is the capital and largest city of Chile, and its metropolitan area holds over a third of the national population. The presidential palace, the Palacio de La Moneda, stands there, while the National Congress meets mainly in nearby Valparaíso. Few colonial buildings survive because earthquakes regularly strike the country, among them the Church of San Francisco of 1586 and the Casa Colorada of 1769. Its cathedral on the Plaza de Armas was built between 1784 and 1805 under the architect Joaquín Toesca.
santiago-de-compostela: Santiago de Compostela lies in the north-west of the Iberian Peninsula, in the province of A Coruña, at an altitude of about 370 metres. Its climate is oceanic, and the Atlantic winds and surrounding mountains give it some of the highest rainfall in Spain. Santiago is the Galician form of the Vulgar Latin Sanctus Iacobus, Saint James. Compostela probably comes from the Latin compositum tella, a well-ordered burial ground, though folk etymology derives it from Campus Stellae, field of the star.

The area was a Roman cemetery by the 4th century and was occupied by the Suebi in the early 5th. In 585 it passed to the Visigothic Kingdom, and around 750 the bishopric of Iria was incorporated into the Kingdom of Asturias. Between 818 and 842, in the reign of Alfonso II of Asturias, Bishop Theodemar of Iria claimed to have found remains attributed to Saint James the Greater. According to a medieval legend, a bright star guided a shepherd, Pelagius the Hermit, to the burial site. A settlement and pilgrimage centre grew around the place and was called Compostella by the 10th century.

After the centre of Asturian power moved from Oviedo to León in 910, several kings of Galicia and León were crowned there, among them Ordoño IV in 958, Bermudo II in 982 and Alfonso VII in 1111, by which time Compostela was the capital of the Kingdom of Galicia. Viking raiders attacked the town in the 10th century, and in 997 Ibn Abi Aamir, known as al-Mansur, assaulted and partly destroyed it but showed no interest in the relics. In the 12th century, under Bishop Diego Gelmírez, Compostela became an archbishopric and drew a large multinational population, and its shrine became second only to Rome and Jerusalem among Catholic shrines.

Santiago de Compostela is the capital of the autonomous community of Galicia and has 96,260 inhabitants. Its Old Town has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1985. The Obradoiro façade of the cathedral is shown on Spanish euro coins of 1, 2 and 5 cents. The University of Santiago de Compostela was established in the early 16th century.
santiago-de-queretaro: The city lies in central Mexico, in the macroregion of the Bajío, 213 kilometres northwest of Mexico City. In Otomi it is called Maxei or Ndamaxei, meaning ball game and the grand ball game. The name Querétaro most likely comes from k'eri ireta rho, meaning place of the great people. It has a semi-arid climate with mild temperatures year round, and most of its rain falls from June to August.

The area was settled around 200 CE by Mesoamerican groups moving north, and archaeological sites show influence from Teotihuacan. In the later pre-Hispanic period it was populated by the Otomi, who in the 1440s were under the Otomi dominion of Xilotepeque, itself subject to the Aztec Empire. Under Ahuizotl in the late 15th century the Aztecs administered the area directly, as a bulwark against the Chichimeca lands to the north.

The Spanish city of Santiago de Querétaro was founded on 25 July 1531, when Hernán Pérez Bocanegra y Córdoba arrived with the Otomi leader Conín, later named Hernando de Tapia. According to chronicles such as that of Friar Isidro Félix de Espinoza, the Spanish and their allies were fighting Otomi and Chichimeca insurgents on the hill of Sangremal when a total eclipse of the sun occurred. The Chichimeca, who were close to winning, were said to have been frightened, and the Spanish claimed to see Saint James on a white horse carrying a cross. This is why Saint James, Santiago, is the city's patron saint, and a stone cross was set up on the hill.

The settlement was declared a town in 1606, and by 1655 only Spaniards lived in the city proper. In 1656 it was named the Muy Noble y Leal Ciudad de Santiago de Querétaro at the request of Viceroy Luis de Velasco, in recognition of its growth, agriculture, industry and schools. In the 18th century it was informally called the Pearl of the Bajío and the Third City of the Viceroyalty.

It is considered one of the cradles of Mexican independence, largely through Josefa Ortiz de Domínguez, wife of the city's corregidor, who gathered intelligence for the nascent insurgency. On 2 February 1916 President Venustiano Carranza named it the provisional capital because the Constituent Congress was to meet there; the Constitution was enacted there on 5 February of the following year and remains the law of the land.

Querétaro is the capital and largest city of the state of Querétaro. In 1996 its historic centre was declared a World Heritage Site by UNESCO. In the same year the state legislature restored Santiago de Querétaro as the capital's official name. The municipality covers 682.7 square kilometres.
santiago-del-estero: Santiago del Estero lies on the Dulce River and on National Route 9, 1,042 km north-north-west of Buenos Aires, in an extensive but largely semi-arid agricultural region. Its climate lies between the temperate Pampa and the hotter Chaco, with very hot summers and about 600 mm of rain a year. The city is nicknamed Madre de Ciudades, "Mother of Cities". It and its surroundings are home to about 100,000 speakers of the local variety of Quechua, the southernmost outpost of the language of the Incas and one of the few indigenous languages surviving in Argentina.

After a series of exploratory expeditions from Chile beginning in 1543, Santiago del Estero del Nuevo Maestrazgo was founded on 25 July 1553 by Francisco de Aguirre. Little of its colonial architecture survives except several churches. In 1576 the governor of a northern province sent soldiers to find a huge mass of iron that the native peoples were said to use for weapons; the area was called Campo del Cielo. During the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata the city was the capital of the intendency of San Miguel de Tucumán and the first seat of its bishop, though both were later moved, to Salta and Córdoba respectively.

In the 19th century the abundance of quebracho attracted British timber companies and led to extensive deforestation, and the British-owned Central Argentine Railway reached the city in 1884. In 1948 the province elected the Peronist activist Carlos Arturo Juárez as governor, and he remained its central political figure through the second half of the century. The Quiroga Dam, built in 1950 on the Río Dulce, eased the city's chronic water shortage and spurred cotton and olive growing. Textile mills and light industry followed from the 1950s, and the population reached 100,000 in 1970.

Santiago del Estero is the capital of its province and had 252,192 inhabitants in the 2010 census. It houses the Universidad Católica, founded in 1960, and the National University, founded in 1973. Its cathedral, the Santo Domingo Convent and the Provincial Archeology Museum are among its points of interest. The region's musical heritage, with the folk forms chacarera and zamba, is one of its most important cultural aspects. Figures linked to its history include Colonel Juan Francisco Borges, who led the local battalion of the Army of the North in the war of independence, and Francisco René and Mario Roberto Santucho, founders of the Workers' Revolutionary Party and the People's Revolutionary Army.
santo-domingo: Santo Domingo lies on the southern coast of the island of Hispaniola, on the Caribbean Sea, at the mouth of the Ozama River, which divides the city into eastern and western sections. The historic Colonial Zone is on the west side. The land is a coastal plain of flat to gently rolling terrain, with some low limestone hills in the surrounding region. The climate is tropical, with trade winds moderating the heat and humidity, and a rainy season from May to November. Its natural harbour has long made it an important port and commercial centre in the Caribbean.

Before Christopher Columbus arrived in 1492, the Taíno people lived on the island, which they called Kiskeya, meaning mother of all lands, and Ayiti, the land of the high mountains. Columbus later named it Hispaniola. The island then consisted of five chiefdoms, Marién, Maguá, Maguana, Jaragua and Higüey, ruled by the caciques Guacanagarix, Guarionex, Caonabo, Bohechío and Cayacoa.

The Spanish Empire founded Santo Domingo in 1496, and it became the first seat of Spanish colonial rule in the New World, the Captaincy General of Santo Domingo. It is the site of the first university, cathedral, castle, monastery and fortress in the Americas. The Universidad Autónoma de Santo Domingo, established in 1538, is the oldest university in the Americas. From 1936 to 1961 the city was called Ciudad Trujillo, after the Dominican dictator Rafael Trujillo, who named the capital after himself. After his assassination it resumed its original name.

Santo Domingo, officially Santo Domingo de Guzmán, is the capital and largest city of the Dominican Republic, with a city population of about one million and a metropolitan area of more than four million. It is coterminous with the Distrito Nacional, and the presidency, ministries, National Congress and Supreme Court of Justice are in the metropolitan area. The Zona Colonial, bordered by the Ozama, has early 16th-century palatial houses and churches in late medieval style, and has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1990. The Church and Convent of los Dominicos is the oldest Catholic building in continuous use in the Americas and was the headquarters of the first university there.
sao-luis-maranhao: São Luís stands on São Luís Island, in the Baía de São Marcos, an extension of the Atlantic Ocean that forms the estuary of the Pindaré, Mearim, Itapecuru and other rivers. It is the only Brazilian state capital founded by France, and one of three state capitals located on islands. The island lies between two large estuarine systems, the bays of São Marcos and São José, where the tides can exceed seven metres. The climate is hot and semi-humid, with a wet season from January to June and a dry season from July to December.

The site was originally a large village of the Tupinambá. The first Europeans to settle it were the French in 1612, who meant to make it the centre of a colony called Equinoctial France under Daniel de la Touche, Seigneur de la Ravardière, and Admiral François de Razilly. They built a fort named Saint-Louis de Maragnan after King Louis XIII and his saintly ancestor Louis IX, and its construction marks the founding date of 8 September. Portugal conquered the settlement in 1615 at the battle of Guaxenduba and renamed it São Luís. Because the French had little time to build a city, there is some controversy over whether the French or the Portuguese founded it.

The Dutch, as part of their wider invasion of Brazil, occupied the city in November 1641 with a force of 1,000 troops under Jan Cornelisz Lichthart of the Dutch West India Company. They pillaged it, notably Catholic imagery and structures, and fighting continued for 27 months until the Dutch surrendered on 28 February 1644. In 1677 the city became the seat of the new Roman Catholic Diocese of São Luís do Maranhão. Conflict between Jesuits, who opposed Indian slavery, and landowners, who resented the Portuguese authorities, led to Beckman's Revolt, led by the brothers Manoel and Tomás Beckman. Portuguese troops put it down, and the brothers were hanged, drawn and quartered.

The economy rested on exports of sugar cane, cacao and tobacco, and after the outbreak of the American Civil War the region supplied cotton to Great Britain. The wealth was used to modernise the city, and it became the third most populous in the country. By the end of the 19th century agriculture was in decay.

The historic centre, dating from the 17th century, has preserved its original street plan and was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997. São Luís has the largest preserved heritage of colonial Portuguese architecture in Latin America. It is the capital and largest city of the state of Maranhão.
sao-paulo: São Paulo stands on a plateau beyond the Serra do Mar, part of the Brazilian Highlands, at an average elevation of about 799 metres above sea level and only some 70 kilometres from the Atlantic. Two highways, the Anchieta and the Imigrantes, descend the range to the port of Santos. The Tietê River and its tributary the Pinheiros once supplied fresh water and leisure but became heavily polluted by industrial effluent in the later 20th century. The municipality covers 1,521.11 square kilometres.

The oldest archaeological artefacts found in the municipality come from the Morumbi site and are thought to date from about 3500 BCE. In 1532 Martim Afonso de Sousa founded São Vicente, the first Brazilian village, on the coast. The village of São Paulo dos Campos de Piratininga dates from 25 January 1554, when Jesuit priests founded the Colégio de São Paulo de Piratininga to catechise the indigenous peoples. The college of twelve priests included Manuel da Nóbrega and José de Anchieta, and they built a mission on a steep hill between the Anhangabaú and Tamanduateí rivers.

In the colonial period the city was the centre and starting point of the expeditions of the Paulista bandeirantes, settlers who pushed the country's territorial and economic expansion. Its wealth was consolidated in the Brazilian coffee cycle of the mid-19th century. The First and Second World Wars and the Great Depression hit coffee exports and forced rich growers to invest in industry, which drew immigrants, mainly from Italy, and migrants from the north-east. The population grew to 8.5 million inhabitants in 1980.

In 1960 the city passed Rio de Janeiro as the most populous in Brazil. Landmark events of Brazilian history took place there, among them the Cry of Ipiranga, the Modern Art Week, the 1932 Revolution and the Diretas Já movement.

São Paulo is the capital of the state of São Paulo and the largest city in Brazil, with 11,244,369 people at the 2010 census and a metropolitan area of more than 20 million. Portuguese is the main language. The city is known as the most multicultural in Brazil, with the largest Arab, Italian and Japanese communities in the world, and neighbourhoods such as Bixiga, Bom Retiro and Liberdade.
saone: The Saône rises at Vioménil in the Vosges, at the foot of the cliff of the Faucilles, at an elevation of 392 metres, and joins the Rhône at Lyon at 158 metres, at the southern end of the Presqu'île. Its length is 473 kilometres. Its largest tributary is the Doubs; upstream of their meeting at Verdun-sur-le-Doubs the Saône is called the Petite Saône. The Doubs has a slightly larger mean flow, so that some assert it is the Saône that flows into the Doubs, but the Saône has the larger watershed, 11,500 square kilometres against 7,500. With 30,000 square kilometres in all, its basin is the largest of any French river that does not flow directly into the sea, about one eighteenth of metropolitan France.

The name Saône derives from the Gallic river goddess Souconna, also connected with the Celtic tribe of the Sequanes; monastic copyists changed it to Saoconna, which gave Saône. Other recorded ancient names were Brigoulus and Arar. Arar was a doubling of the Indo-European root ar, "water", which according to Julius Caesar reflected how hard it was to tell the direction of so slow a river. The Battle of the Arar was the first major battle of the Gallic Wars. The present name came from a sacred spring, Sauc-Onna, at Chalon, whose name Roman legionaries used for the whole river. Historians later called northern Burgundian lands Burgundia Cisararica or Burgundia Transararica, "on this side of" or "on the other side of" the Saône.

The river has flooded often. Recorded floods include one at Lyon in 580, others in 1602 and 1711, and that of May 1856. The flood of November 1840, estimated at almost 4,000 cubic metres per second, destroyed many homes in the valley; the water reached 8.05 metres at Mâcon and 7.28 metres at Chalon, and plaques marking it can still be seen in the villages affected.

The Saône flows through the Vosges, Haute-Saône, Côte-d'Or, Saône-et-Loire, Ain and Rhône, passing Gray, Auxonne, Chalon-sur-Saône, Tournus, Mâcon and Villefranche-sur-Saône before Lyon. It is navigable over 367 kilometres, from Corre to La Mulatière in Lyon. Canals link it with the Loire, the Yonne, the Marne, the Meuse and the Rhine, all of the Freycinet gauge.
saparmurat-niyazov: Niyazov was born on 19 February 1940 in Gypjak, on the outskirts of Ashgabat, into the Teke tribe of the Turkmens. According to the official version of his biography his father died in the Second World War fighting Germany, while other sources contend that he avoided fighting and was sentenced by a military court. His mother and two brothers were killed in the 1948 Ashgabat earthquake, and he grew up in a Soviet orphanage before the state placed him with a distant relative. In 1967 he received a diploma as an electrical engineer from the Leningrad Polytechnic Institute. He joined the Communist Party in 1962 and rose quickly, becoming First Secretary of the Ashgabat City Committee.

In 1985 Mikhail Gorbachev removed the Turkmen party leader after a cotton-related scandal, and Niyazov took his place as First Secretary. The Turkmen party had a reputation as one of the most hardline in the Soviet Union. On 13 January 1990 he became Chairman of the Supreme Soviet of the Turkmen SSR. He supported the 1991 Soviet coup attempt but, after it collapsed, set about separating Turkmenistan from the Soviet Union, and the Supreme Soviet declared independence and appointed him first president on 27 October 1991. In the election of 21 June 1992 he was the sole candidate. A plebiscite in 1994 extended his term to 2002, and on 28 December 1999 the parliament declared him president for life.

He promoted the Ruhnama, a book of his own writing, as a guide to the people and a basis for native culture, and he introduced a Latin-based Turkmen alphabet to replace Cyrillic. He renamed the months and most days of the week, naming September after the Ruhnama, April after his mother and others after Turkmen heroes, poets and himself. He also named towns, schools and airports after himself and his family. The Ruhnama was required reading in schools, universities and government offices, and part of the driving test. In 2005 he ordered hospitals outside Ashgabat closed and closed rural libraries. His government banned opposition, and the state media supported the cult around him. In 1999 he abolished the death penalty by decree.

Turkmen state television announced on 21 December 2006 that Niyazov had died of a sudden heart attack at the age of 66. He was buried on 24 December in a tomb prepared at Gypjak. His successor Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow restored the old names of months and days in 2008 and replaced the anthem's reference to Niyazov with the people. The Melon Day harvest festival that Niyazov introduced continues.
sapienza-university-of-rome: The university was founded by the papal bull In Supremae praeminentia Dignitatis, issued on 20 April 1303 by Pope Boniface VIII, as a Studium for ecclesiastical studies more under his control than the universities of Bologna and Padua. This made it the first pontifical university. In 1431 Pope Eugene IV reorganised the studium with the bull In supremae, granting masters and students the broadest privileges and decreeing that it should include the four schools of Law, Medicine, Philosophy and Theology. He introduced a new tax on wine to raise funds, and the money bought a palace that later housed the church of Sant'Ivo alla Sapienza.

The sack of Rome in 1527 ended the university's days of splendour: the studium was closed, some professors were killed and others dispersed. Pope Paul III restored it shortly after his election in 1534. In the 1650s it became known as Sapienza, meaning wisdom or knowledge, a name it retains.

The Alessandrina University Library was built in 1667 by Pope Alexander VII. In 1703 Pope Clement XI bought land on the Janiculum with his private funds and created a botanical garden, which became the best known in Europe through the labours of the Trionfetti brothers. Filippo Maria Renazzi wrote the first complete history of the university in 1803-1806.

In 1870 Sapienza stopped being the papal university and became the university of the capital of Italy, and it expanded rapidly afterwards. The new campus, planned by Marcello Piacentini, was completed in 1935.

The main campus is the Città Universitaria, covering 44 hectares near the Tiburtina Station, and the university has 50 libraries, 19 museums and a botanical garden. Its alumni and teachers include Maria Montessori, the future pope Eugenio Pacelli, Luigi Pirandello and Nobel laureates such as Guglielmo Marconi, who taught there in 1935-1937, and Enrico Fermi, who held the chair of theoretical physics from 1926 to 1938. Among its scholars are the mathematician Vito Volterra, the orientalist Giuseppe Tucci and the archaeologist Paolo Matthiae, director of the excavations at Ebla. It is the largest university in Italy.
sappho: Little is known for certain about Sappho's life. She came from a wealthy family on the island of Lesbos and lived at the end of the seventh and the beginning of the sixth century BCE, a contemporary, according to most ancient sources, of the poet Alcaeus and the tyrant Pittacus. Her poetry is the only contemporary source for her life, and the earliest surviving biography dates from the late second or early third century CE, some eight centuries after her time.
Ancient authors drew on statements in her poems that they assumed were autobiographical. Tradition gives her three brothers, Charaxos, Larichos and Eurygios. She was exiled to Sicily around 600 BCE.

Sappho probably wrote about 10,000 lines, of which about 650 survive. Only the Ode to Aphrodite is certainly complete. Her poems were written to be sung and were composed in the Aeolic tradition of Lesbos.

She was one of the first Greek poets to adopt the lyric I, speaking from the viewpoint of a specific person. Her poems explore desire, jealousy and love and often the lives of women, and include poems about family, wedding songs and cult hymns. Ancient authors claimed she wrote chiefly love poetry, but papyri published in 2014 contain ten consecutive poems of which only two are certainly love poems.

Scholars have long debated the setting of her poems: teacher, priestess, chorus leader or participant in the symposium have all been proposed. Several prominent classicists have rejected the view of her as a schoolmistress as unsupported by the evidence.

She was among the Nine Lyric Poets esteemed by the scholars of Hellenistic Alexandria, who arranged her poems in at least eight books, grouped by metre. The latest direct copies, on parchment codex pages, date from the sixth and seventh centuries CE, and around the ninth century her poetry seems to have disappeared. The legend that the Church had it burned arose in the Renaissance. In reality it was probably lost because there was too little demand to copy it from papyrus rolls into codices, and because its Aeolic dialect had come to seem provincial.
According to legend she killed herself by leaping from the Leucadian cliffs for love of the ferryman Phaon. The English words sapphic and lesbian derive from her name and that of her island.
saqqara: Saqqara is the necropolis of the ancient Egyptian capital Memphis, about 30 km south of modern Cairo, and covers an area of around 7 by 1.5 km. To its north lies the Abusir pyramid complex and to its south Dahshur; together with Giza, to the far north, they make up the Pyramid Fields of Memphis, which UNESCO designated a World Heritage Site in 1979. The name may derive from the funerary deity Sokar, though some scholars propose a Berber tribe called the Beni Saqqar, which is not documented anywhere. Medieval authors also call the village Ard as-Sadr, "land of the buckthorn".

The earliest burials of nobles on the plateau date to the First Dynasty, when the royal burial ground was at Abydos. The first royal burials there, underground galleries, are of the early Second Dynasty. The Step Pyramid complex of Djoser of the Third Dynasty, built by the royal architect Imhotep, is the oldest complete stone building complex known in history. Nearly all Fourth Dynasty kings built elsewhere, but under the Fifth and Sixth Dynasties Saqqara was again the royal burial ground. Unas, the last ruler of the Fifth Dynasty, was the first king to adorn the chambers of his pyramid with Pyramid Texts, and courtiers were buried in mastabas near the pyramids of Unas and Teti.

After the Middle Kingdom Memphis was no longer the capital, but under the New Kingdom, when it was an administrative and military centre, many high officials built tombs at Saqqara, among them the general Horemheb, later buried in the Valley of the Kings. Prince Khaemweset, a son of Ramesses II, repaired the Pyramid of Unas and enlarged the Serapeum, the burial place of the mummified Apis bulls. In later periods Saqqara became a destination for pilgrims, and galleries were cut into the rock for large numbers of mummified ibises, baboons, cats, dogs and falcons. The site stayed in use for non-royal burials for more than 3,000 years, well into Ptolemaic and Roman times.

Karl Richard Lepsius mapped the remains in 1842 and 1843 and first numbered the monuments. Auguste Mariette excavated from 1851 to 1855 and discovered the Serapeum, with one undisturbed Apis burial and the tomb of Khaemweset. James Edward Quibell worked there between 1905 and 1914, and the Egypt Exploration Society in the 1950s and 1960s. Excavation has continued: in 2011 a team uncovered almost eight million animal mummies, mostly dogs, in the dog catacomb, and in 2018 a Polish-Egyptian expedition reported graves of noblemen of the Sixth Dynasty.
saqqez: Saqqez is the capital of both the Central District and the county of Saqqez in Kurdistan province. The city stands at an altitude of 1,476 metres, on long plains and hills among the irregular heights of the Zagros Mountains, and the Zarrineh and Simineh rivers and their tributaries cross the area. The mountain setting gives it relatively cold weather and long winters, with hot, very dry summers and cold, snowy winters. Most of its people are Kurds who speak the Sorani dialect of Kurdish.

Saqqez's history goes back to the seventh millennium BCE. Its name is said to derive from the Scythian Eskit and then Sakez; some sources link it instead with the Median ruler Cyaxares, while other historians derive it from Sakez and attribute it to Scythians who settled there in his reign. Finds such as the Ziwiye hoard in Ziwiyeh Castle led experts such as Roman Ghirshman to place the ancient capital of the Median kingdom on the site of the modern city, and some place Izirtu, the capital of the Mannaeans, here.

According to Vladimir Minorsky, Saqqez is the site of the medieval city of Barza. Theophanes the Confessor, who calls it Barzan, records that the Byzantine emperor Heraclius stayed there for seven days in March 628 on his way to Ganzak. Barza was an important crossroads in the medieval period, where the road from Dinavar to Maragheh forked towards Urmia, and in the early 9th century it was the capital of a separate principality. David D'Beth Hillel, who died in 1846, stated that the city had a small Jewish community with one synagogue dating from around 1827.

The census of 2016 counted 165,258 people in the city. Saqqez has long been a place of culture and the arts, and each year at the end of autumn it holds a Kurdish Theater Festival at which theatre groups from across Kurdistan perform. Musicians and singers perform in the Kurdish language, and the city counts several well-known poets among its people.
sarajevo: Sarajevo lies near the geometric centre of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the Sarajevo valley in the middle of the Dinaric Alps, along the Miljacka River, 518 metres above sea level. Forested hills and five major mountains surround it: Treskavica, Bjelašnica, Jahorina, Trebević and Igman. The last four are known as the Olympic Mountains of Sarajevo, because venues for the 1984 Winter Olympics were built on them. The name comes from the Turkish saray, meaning palace or mansion, and scholars disagree on the origin of the ending evo. The official name under Ottoman rule was Saraybosna, the Palace of Bosnia.

One of the earliest settlements in the area is that of the Neolithic Butmir culture, discovered in 1893 at Ilidža by Austro-Hungarian authorities building an agricultural school. The area's flint attracted settlers, and the Butmir people developed distinctive ceramics. The modern city arose in the fifteenth century as an Ottoman stronghold, when the Ottoman Empire extended into Europe. Isa-Beg Ishaković called the town he was going to construct Šeher, Turkish for city. Gazi Husrev-beg established a school of Sufi philosophy in 1537, the first institution that can be classed as tertiary education.

Ottoman rule lasted until 1878 de facto and 1908 de jure, and Austria-Hungary then governed to 1918. Muslims, Orthodox Christians, Roman Catholics and Sephardi Jews shared the city under Ottoman rule while keeping distinct identities, and by 1909 about 50 per cent of its people were Muslim, 25 per cent Catholic, 15 per cent Orthodox and 10 per cent Jewish. In 1914 Gavrilo Princip, a local Young Bosnia activist, assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo, a murder that sparked the First World War. Austro-Hungarian rule ended and the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes was created.

After the Second World War the city became the capital of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina within Yugoslavia, and grew rapidly. It hosted the 1984 Winter Olympics. During the Bosnian War it endured the longest siege of a capital city in modern history, 1,425 days from April 1992 to February 1996. The 1991 census recorded 527,049 people in the city's ten municipalities, 49.2 per cent of them Bosniaks, 29.8 per cent Serbs and 6.6 per cent Croats. The war displaced hundreds of thousands, most of whom have not returned.

Sarajevo is the capital and largest city of Bosnia and Herzegovina and of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the de jure capital of Republika Srpska. All national institutions are there. It is one of the few major European cities with a mosque, a Catholic church, an Orthodox church and a synagogue in the same neighbourhood, and has been called the Jerusalem of Europe. The Gazi Husrev-beg Mosque and the Sarajevo cathedral are among its landmarks.
saraswati: Saraswati is one of the earliest river goddesses of the Indian tradition. In the Rigveda, dated about 1500 to 1000 BCE, she is primarily a deified river embodying abundance, power and fertility. Hymn 6.61 is dedicated entirely to her, and with Ila and Bharati she forms a triad of sacrificial goddesses invoked in Vedic rituals. Her association with inspired thought, linked to sacrifice performed on the banks of the river, already points toward her later role.

In the Brahmanas she is increasingly identified with Vac, the Vedic goddess of speech, and the two merge into the single goddess of later tradition. Her connection to the river then fades, while her association with speech, poetry, music and culture grows. The name is Sanskrit, from saras, meaning pooling water or sometimes speech, and vati, she who possesses.

In classical and medieval Hinduism Saraswati is the goddess of learning, the arts and poetic inspiration, and the inventor of the Sanskrit language. She is linked to the creator god Brahma, as his creation or consort, and in some Vaishnava traditions she is one of Vishnu's consorts. With Lakshmi and Parvati she forms the Tridevi. In Shaktism she is venerated as the creative aspect of the Supreme Goddess, and she is also worshipped as a celibate goddess without a consort.

She is shown as a serene woman in white, the colour of sattva, or goodness, usually seated on a white lotus. She has four arms, holding a book, a rosary, a water pot and the veena, and her mount is a hamsa, a white goose or swan, or a peacock.

Saraswati is worshipped across India, above all on Vasant Panchami, the fifth day of spring, when students honour her as patron of knowledge. Traditionally the day is marked by helping young children learn to write the letters of the alphabet. In Kerala and Tamil Nadu the last three days of Navaratri are Saraswati Puja. Sharada Peeth in Kashmir, dated from the sixth to the twelfth century CE, is one of the earliest known shrines.

In Buddhism she is venerated in many forms, including the East Asian Benzaiten, the Tibetan Yangchenma and the Burmese Thurathadi, and she is the consort of Manjushri, the bodhisattva of wisdom. In Jainism she is the goddess of knowledge, responsible for spreading the Tirthankaras' sermons, and the Jain Saraswati from Mathura, dated 132 CE, is the earliest sculpture of her in any tradition.
sardinia: Sardinia is the second-largest island in the Mediterranean Sea after Sicily, with an area of 24,100 square kilometres. It lies 200 kilometres west of the Italian Peninsula, 200 kilometres north of Tunisia and 16.5 kilometres south of Corsica. Its mountains, woods, plains, rocky coasts and sandy beaches have led to its description as a micro-continent. The name is pre-Latin. It appears as ŠRDN on the Phoenician Nora Stone, and some have speculated that the Nuragic Sards were the Sherden, one of the Sea Peoples.

Humans have lived on the island since the end of the Paleolithic, although authors disagree whether the evidence from Corbeddu Cave, about 20,000 years old, is solid or whether occupation is secure only from about 10,000 years ago. The Nuragic civilization flourished from the 18th century BCE to either 238 BCE or, in some parts, the 2nd century CE, and in Barbagia to the 6th century. The Phoenicians began visiting from about the 9th century BCE, using ports such as Caralis, Nora, Bithia, Sulci and Tharros. In the 6th century BCE the Carthaginians planned to annex it, and a first invasion led by Malchus was foiled by Nuragic resistance, but from 510 BCE the southern and west-central part came under Carthaginian rule.

The Vandals conquered the island in 456, and their rule lasted 78 years. In 530 the Vandal governor Godas declared Sardinia independent of Carthage and negotiated with Emperor Justinian I. When Gelimer sent the bulk of his army and navy to subdue him in 533, Justinian's general Belisarius took Carthage, and Sardinia returned to Byzantine rule, which lasted about 300 years apart from a short period after the Ostrogoths invaded in 551.

In 1297 Pope Boniface VIII created a Kingdom of Sardinia and Corsica and offered it to James II of Aragon. Spanish rule followed, and in 1708 the Austrians occupied the island, although in 1717 Cardinal Giulio Alberoni reoccupied it for Philip V of Spain. In 1861 the parliament of the Kingdom of Sardinia renamed the state the Kingdom of Italy. Italy became a republic in 1946, and Sardinia has been governed since 1948 under a special statute of autonomy.

Sardinia is one of the twenty regions of Italy and one of five with statutory autonomy. Cagliari is its capital and largest city, followed by Sassari. The Sardinian language and the Algherese dialect of Catalan are recognised as protected minority languages. Thousands of nuraghe, Bronze Age buildings, still characterise the prehistoric landscape, alongside tombs, megalithic circles and well temples, and the Phoenicians and Punics left traces on the coasts.
sardis: Sardis, in Lydian Sfar and in Old Persian Sparda, stood in the middle of the Hermus River valley, about 4 kilometres south of the river. Its citadel was built on a steep spur of Mount Tmolus, and a lower town extended to the Pactolus stream, where archaeologists have found installations for processing alluvial metals. The site was occupied for at least 3,500 years, fluctuating between a wealthy city of international importance and a collection of modest hamlets.

Sardis was settled before 1500 BCE. In the 7th century BCE it became the capital of Lydia, whose kings, such as Croesus, ruled an empire reaching the Halys River. The city covered 108 hectares and was protected by walls twenty metres thick, and three enormous burial tumuli at Bin Tepe marked it from a distance. Its artisans specialised in seals and jewellery, and its pottery blended Aegean and Anatolian styles.

After defeating Croesus at the battles of Pteria and Thymbra, Cyrus the Great's Persians followed his army back to Sardis and sacked it after a brief siege. The destruction is vivid in the archaeological record: the fortifications burned in a great fire, and arrowheads and household tools lie in the debris, suggesting that civilians joined the fighting. Sardis was rebuilt and, though never again the capital of an independent state, served as the capital of the Persian satrapy of Sparda and as the end station of the Royal Road. Ionian forces burned it in 499 BCE during the Ionian Revolt.

Alexander the Great received its surrender in 334 BCE. Under Hellenistic rulers the city took on a strongly Greek character, with a gymnasium, theatre, hippodrome and the great Temple of Artemis, and Antiochos III settled Jews there. It passed to Rome in 129 BCE, was one of the seven churches of Asia, and declined from the 600s after being sacked in 615. It was lost to the Seljuk Turks in 1078, retaken in 1097, and probably destroyed by Timur in 1402; by the 1700s only two small hamlets stood there.

The site lies near the village of Sart, near Salihli in Manisa Province, Turkey. Princeton University excavated it from 1910 to 1914, and the Archaeological Exploration of Sardis, founded in 1958, has since uncovered the Roman bath-gymnasium complex, a synagogue in use from the 4th to the 6th century, Byzantine shops and a Lydian area for refining electrum. It was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2025, for its significance as the home of coinage.
sargon-ii: Nothing is known of Sargon II's life before he became king. He was probably born about 770 BCE and cannot have been born later than about 760 BCE. He is generally believed to have taken the throne by overthrowing Shalmaneser V, most likely his brother and a son of Tiglath-Pileser III, and is typically regarded as the founder of the Sargonid dynasty, though he was probably a scion of the incumbent Adaside dynasty. He grew up when rebellion and plague had reduced Assyria's prestige, a decline that Tiglath-Pileser reversed.

The name Šarru-kīn means the faithful king or the legitimate king. Sargon was the first king in more than a thousand years to bear it, and it was probably an assumed regnal name, chosen because of Sargon of Akkad, the conqueror of large parts of Mesopotamia. Late Assyrian texts spell the two names alike, and Sargon II is sometimes called the second Sargon.

His reign began with large-scale resistance in Assyria's heartland, and several peripheral regions regained independence. In early 721 BCE the Chaldean warlord Marduk-apla-iddina II captured Babylon and allied with Elam. Sargon intervened in Mannaea in 718, and in 715 he restored its king Ullusunu against Rusa I of Urartu, whose army had been weakened by the Cimmerians. He also annexed Quwê after its king Urik turned to Midas of Phrygia.

From 717 to 707 BCE he built a new capital, Dur-Sharrukin, about 16 kilometres north-east of Nineveh, at a site with no earlier buildings, which he conceived as an ideal city with proportions based on mathematical harmony; he made it his residence in 706. In 710 he set out to reconquer Babylonia, declaring that Marduk had commanded him to liberate the south, and he won over cities and tribes by diplomacy. The citizens of Babylon proclaimed him king, and he spent three years there while his son Sennacherib oversaw Assyria.

In early summer 705 BCE Sargon led a campaign against Tabal in Anatolia and was killed in battle. The Assyrian army could not recover his body, so he could not be buried, and by Mesopotamian belief he was doomed to wander as a restless ghost. Sennacherib believed his father must have committed some grave sin and distanced himself from him, and Sargon was barely mentioned in later ancient literature.

Sargon called himself a guardian of justice, put conquered peoples on the same footing as native Assyrians, and is not known to have committed atrocities against civilians. He was nearly forgotten until Paul-Émile Botta learned of Dur-Sharrukin in 1843 and excavated its palace; Assyriology did not fully accept him as a real king until the 1860s.
sargon-of-akkad: Sargon's reign is poorly understood, since few commemorative inscriptions can be reliably dated to it, most of them known from later copies, and few archives survive from his time. Like the other kings of his dynasty he does not name his father in his inscriptions; the Sumerian Sargon Legend, written long after his death, calls his father La'ipum. He rose as ruler of the small city of Akkad in central Mesopotamia, which lay in the shadow of its powerful neighbour Kish, though the circumstances of his rise remain unclear. His daughter Enheduanna was a high priestess of the moon god at Ur who composed hymns, among them the Exaltation of Inanna, that were used for centuries.

Sargon's reign began in the last phase of the Early Dynastic period, when Lower Mesopotamia was divided among several city-states and the idea of unifying it was emerging. Lugal-zage-si of Uruk had brought the south, the land of Sumer, under his control. According to datable sources it took Sargon three battles to defeat Lugal-zage-si and his allies and take Uruk, whose walls were razed. The captured king was led to the sanctuary of Enlil at Nippur.
