The date of the conquest is debated, and it is placed around 2300 BCE.

Sargon also led expeditions beyond Lower Mesopotamia, east towards Elam and west towards Mari, though he did not incorporate those lands. Their purpose seems to have been glory, riches, control of trade routes and the restraint of rival powers. His inscriptions summarise his successes as 34 battles. One mentions that he fed 5,400 men at his table each day, usually understood as soldiers bound personally to him, and it names the nine regiments of Akkad. The former kingdoms became provinces under governors, and Akkad remained the capital. His scribes began to write inscriptions in Akkadian as well as Sumerian, and the image of the king changed from a cultic and administrative official to a war hero.

The dates of Sargon's reign are uncertain; they are often estimated at 2334 to 2279 BCE, and other proposals exist. After his death his sons Rimush and Manishtushu succeeded him, in an order that is unknown, and Rimush suppressed revolts in the southern cities. Naram-Sin followed, and then Shar-kali-sharri, whose reign ended in the first half of the 22nd century BCE with the decline of the Akkadian Empire.

Sargon became the archetype of the conquering ruler. Stories of his birth, rise and campaigns were still being composed in the 8th century BCE, and Assyrian and Babylonian kings saw themselves as heirs of his empire. The Neo-Babylonian king Nabonidus excavated the palaces of Sargon and his successors.
sari-iran: Sari lies in the north of Iran, between the northern slopes of the Alborz Mountains and the southern coast of the Caspian, here called the Mazandaran Sea. Excavations in the Hutto cave show settlements around Sari as far back as the 7th millennium BCE. The climate is humid subtropical, with cool, rainy winters and hot, humid summers, and the surrounding land is known for its gardens and citrus groves. Sari is the largest city of Mazandaran.

The Muslim historian Hamdollah Mostowfi attributed the foundation of Sari to the king Tahmoures Divband of the Pishdadian dynasty, and Ferdowsi names the city in the Shahnameh. Local folklore says it was settled when the blacksmith Kaveh, a native of the city, revolted against the tyrant Zahak, and that Fereydun chose to live near him. The city may be the Zadracarta of Greek sources of the Achaemenid era, though other sources place Zadracarta at or near Gorgan. According to Arrian it was the largest city of Hyrcania. It was again a regional capital in the Sasanian era.

In the seventh century Farrukhan the Great of the Dabuyid dynasty rebuilt the city and named it after his son Saruyeh, and Sari again became the capital of Tabaristan, which Amol had been before. After invasions it lost its high standing and was periodically burnt. Shah Abbas the Great settled large numbers of Georgians, Circassians, Armenians and other peoples of the Caucasus in Mazandaran, and made Farahabad his alternate capital to the north of the city. Under Reza Shah in the Pahlavi era the face of the town changed drastically, and the railway station and most of the streets and government buildings date from then.

Sari is the capital of Mazandaran province and of its county and district. Most of its people speak the Mazandarani language, with Persian as the lingua franca. Zoroastrians from Sari who fled to India in the 10th century founded a town called Navu Sari, now Navsari, still a centre of the Parsi community. The clock tower in the Clock Square, built in 1930, is a local landmark, and the tomb towers include the Imamzadeh Abbas. The economy rests on food production, citrus fruit, paper and wood, and Mazandaran Wood and Paper Industries has its works there.
sarissa: A sarissa had two main parts, a long wooden shaft and a metal tip; some may also have had a metal butt at the other end, with which the weapon could be stood in the ground without damage to the shaft. Ash, which is long, flexible and light, and cornel wood, which is shorter but stronger, are the likeliest woods. It replaced the considerably shorter dory.

Ancient writers agree that its length set it apart, but not on the figure: Theophrastus, a contemporary of Alexander the Great, puts the longest at 12 cubits, and Polybius gives 16 cubits in the original design, reduced in practice to 14. In modern units this suggests about 5.8 m in Alexander's time and perhaps 6.3 m later.

The weapon needed both hands, so the phalangite carried only a smaller shield, the pelta, perhaps hung from a neck strap. On the march the sarissas were held upright; levelled for battle, fully five rows of points projected in front of the first rank, while the rear ranks held theirs angled upward, which also deflected arrows. A phalanx so formed was considered practically invulnerable from the front, but it turned with difficulty, and a soldier out of formation had to fall back on a sword or dagger.

Sarissa-armed phalanxes were vital in the early battles of Alexander, including the Battle of Gaugamela, though in his later campaigns he gradually reduced their importance. The surest way to beat such a phalanx was to break its formation or outflank it, as the Romans did at the Battle of Cynoscephalae in 197 BCE. A light cavalry unit of Alexander's army, the sarissophoroi, carried somewhat shorter versions; Nicholas Victor Sekunda argues that the Macedonian cavalry spear is better classed as a xyston.

A leaf-shaped spearhead 51 cm long, found by Manolis Andronikos in a Macedonian tomb at Vergina, shaped much scholarship between 1970 and 2000, but more recent work doubts that it belonged to a sarissa; Sekunda favours a small diamond-shaped iron tip of about 13.5 cm. Earlier estimates put the weight at 5.5 to 6.5 kg, yet Peter Connolly reconstructed a pike 5.8 m long in cherry wood that weighed only 4.05 kg. Scholars also draw on later pikemen, such as the Swiss and the German Landsknecht: preserved English pikes are 5.6 to 5.9 m long, which suggests that the lengths reported for the Macedonian weapon were workable.
sarnath: Sarnath lies eight kilometres northeast of Varanasi, near the confluence of the Ganges and the Varuna. It is also known as the Deer Park, Isipatana and Migadaya. The name comes from Sāranganātha, Lord of the Deer, which refers to a Buddhist legend in which the Buddha, in an earlier life as a deer, offered his life in exchange for that of a doe a king meant to kill; the king was so moved that he made the park a deer sanctuary.

Here, around 528 BCE according to the tradition, the Buddha gave his first teaching to his five original disciples, Kaundinya, Assaji, Bhaddiya, Vappa and Mahanama, the First Turning of the Wheel of Dharma. In the Mahaparinibbana Sutta he named Sarnath as one of four places of pilgrimage, with Lumbini, Bodh Gaya and Kushinagar.

Buddhism flourished at Sarnath from about 600 to 200 BCE, helped by the patronage of kings and wealthy merchants of Varanasi. The Chinese monk Faxian, who travelled in northern India from 400 to 411, saw four large towers and two viharas there. Around 640 Xuanzang reported hundreds of small shrines and votive stupas, a vihara about 61 metres high holding a large Buddha statue, and about 1,500 monks of the Sammatiya school. Under the Pala rulers pilgrims and monks came from all over Asia, and the Gahadavala kings, though Hindu, also supported the monasteries.

The site was plundered in 1194, when Qutb ud-Din Aibak led his men to Varanasi and Sarnath. Some scholars now dispute that Muslim invasions were the main cause of its destruction, arguing that Brahmanical hostility toward Buddhists was responsible. In 1794 workmen of Jagat Singh dismantled a stupa and its relics were thrown into the Ganges. Alexander Cunningham carried out the first systematic excavations in 1835 and 1836 and identified Sarnath as the site of the first sermon. Friedrich Oertel's excavations of 1904 and 1905 uncovered parts of the Ashokan pillar with its lion capital.

The Dhamek Stupa, 39 metres high and 28 metres across, marks the place of the first teaching. The Ashokan pillar was broken in the 12th century, but the Lion Capital of Ashoka, which is in the Sarnath Archaeological Museum, is the State Emblem of India, and the wheel of dharma that topped it appears on the Indian flag. The modern Mulagandha Kuty Vihara was opened in 1931 by the Maha Bodhi Society, with frescoes by the Japanese artist Kosetsu Nosu.

Sarnath is also a pilgrimage site for Jains: the village of Singhpur is believed to be the birthplace of Shreyansanatha, the eleventh tirthankara, and a temple dedicated to him was built in 1824. Several Buddhist countries have built temples and monasteries here.
sarnen: Sarnen lies at an altitude of 471 metres on the northern shore of Lake Sarnen, along the outflow of the Sarner Aa, 20 km south of Lucerne. The lake covers about 7.5 square kilometres. The town is surrounded by chains of mountains, and a protected bog lies nearby; the best-known peak in the neighbourhood is Mount Pilatus, at 2,132 metres. The municipality covers 73.12 square kilometres, of which about 39 per cent is agricultural land and 50.7 per cent forest. It is made up of five sections: Sarnen, Stalden, Wilen, Kägiswil and Ramersberg.

Stone Age and Bronze Age finds show that the Sarnen valley was inhabited from the earliest times. Over the years Sarnen developed into an important trading centre. Ten sites in the municipality are Swiss heritage sites of national significance. Three are religious buildings: the Ossuary of St Michael, the parish church of St Peter and Paul and the Church of St Martin. Others are the double house am Grund and Grundacher, the Hexenturm, the Cantonal Rathaus, the musical collection of the Frauenkloster, the Landenberg armory and the State Archives of Obwalden. The whole small city, the hamlet of Ramersberg and the Kirchhofen area belong to the Inventory of Swiss Heritage Sites.

Sarnen is the capital of the canton of Obwalden and a small regional centre with 10,514 inhabitants in December 2020. Most speak German, and about three quarters of the population belongs to the Roman Catholic Church. The town has grown steadily and is attractive to commuters because of its closeness to Lucerne, which they reach by motorway or railway. Sarnen station is on the Brünig line, a narrow-gauge railway from Interlaken to Lucerne. Companies active in the town include SIKA, a maker of specialty chemicals, and Leister Technologies, which makes heated-air tools.
saronic-gulf: The Saronic Gulf, in Greek Saronikos kolpos, forms part of the Aegean Sea between the peninsulas of Attica and Argolis. It marks the eastern side of the isthmus of Corinth and is the eastern end of the Corinth Canal, which cuts across the isthmus. The Gulf of Megara makes up its northern end. Besides Aegina, Salamis and Poros, it includes the smaller islands of Patroklos and Fleves, and the urban area of Athens lies on its north and east coasts, with the port of Piraeus on the north-eastern edge. Bays in the gulf include Phaleron Bay, Elefsina Bay in the north, Kechries Bay in the north-west and Sofiko Bay in the east.

The volcanic centre of Methana lies to the south-west and forms the north-western end of the Cycladic arch of active volcanoes that includes Milos, Santorini and Nisyros. Hot sulphurous water still rises there and is used by a hydropathic institute. The most recent eruption, of a submarine volcano north of Methana, was in the seventeenth century.

The name is said to come from the mythological king Saron, who drowned at the Psiphaea lake, now Psifta. The Saronic Islands have played a pivotal part in the history of Greece. The Battle of Salamis, fought in 480 BCE in the gulf near modern Piraeus, was a major naval engagement in which the Athenian-led Greek fleet defeated the much larger Persian forces of Xerxes I. The victory was a turning point in the Greco-Persian Wars and contributed to Athens' rise as a dominant power in the classical Greek world. The ancient port of Cenchreae also stood on the gulf.

Beaches line much of the coast, and sailing is popular, as the Attic mainland partly shelters the gulf from the summer meltemi wind. Two notable archaeological sites lie on its shores: the ancient theatre at Epidaurus with its nearby asclepieion, and the Temple of Aphaia on Aegina. The gulf is also a gathering area for short-beaked common dolphins.
sarreguemines: Sarreguemines lies at the confluence of the Blies and the Saar, 79 km east of Metz, in north-eastern France. Its name is a French spelling of the local Lorraine-German Saargemin, meaning "confluence into the Saar". It has railway connections to Strasbourg, Saarbrücken and Metz. Traditionally it was the head of river navigation on the Saar, a depot where boats were unloaded. It is the seat of an arrondissement and a canton, and its inhabitants are called Sarregueminois.

Sarreguemines was originally a Roman settlement and obtained civic rights early in the 13th century. In 1297 the count of Saarbrücken ceded it to the Duke of Lorraine, and it passed with Lorraine to France in 1766. Under French rule its industries developed further, including the production of plush velvet, leather, faience, porcelain and papier-mâché boxes, mainly used as snuffboxes, and the town became known for its artisanal craftsmanship.

The Treaty of Frankfurt, which followed the Franco-Prussian War, transferred it to Germany in 1871, and until 1918 it formed part of the German imperial province of Alsace-Lorraine, still making plush velvet, leather, faience and porcelain. It returned to France after World War I. On 21 to 23 December 1944 the 44th Infantry Division of the United States threw back three German attempts to cross the Blies River, and the defence of the Sarreguemines area continued through February and most of March 1945.
sarsina: Sarsina lies in the Tuscan-Romagnolo Apennines, in the province of Forlì-Cesena. Its ancient name was Sarsina or Sassina, and it stood in the valley of the Savio River. It was the centre of a pasture district, and its milk is frequently mentioned in ancient sources. Inscriptions preserved in the local museum show that the town had strategic importance.

In 266 BCE Roman consuls held a triumph over the Sassinates. In 225 BCE the Umbri and Sassinates are named together as Roman allies providing 20,000 men between them. The town gave a number of recruits to the Praetorian Guard, and the playwright Plautus was a native of Sassina. Devastation towards the end of the 3rd century, perhaps by barbarian tribes, left signs of fire on the floors of some houses, and the Visigoths and the Heruli made further incursions between 409 and 470.

Saint Vicinius of Sarsina was the first bishop, from around 303 to his death in 330. In the 10th century the bishops obtained temporal sovereignty over the city and its district, which became a prince-bishopric, and work on the cathedral began around the year 1000.

From 1327 until 1400 the Ordelaffi of Forlì, the popes and the bishops disputed it. In the fifteenth century it passed to the Malatesta of Cesena and then of Rimini, and Cesare Borgia took it from them, and after his death the Venetians captured it. In 1518 it was enfeoffed to the Pio di Meldola and later passed to the Aldobrandini. In a reprisal in 1944 the German Wehrmacht killed or injured many people and burned public buildings and houses.

Remains of the Roman forum and necropolis can still be seen, along with what was probably a public bath, and an archaeological museum holds finds from the Roman era. The Romanesque cathedral dates from around the year 1000, and beside it stands the Sanctuary of San Vicinio. Besides agriculture and cattle breeding, the sulphur and manganese industries have been principal employments.
sasanian-empire: The Sasanian Empire, officially Ērānšahr, the Empire of the Iranians, was founded and ruled by the House of Sasan from 224 to 651. Ardashir I rose as Arsacid influence declined in the face of internal and external strife, and after defeating Artabanus IV of Parthia at the Battle of Hormozdgan in 224 the dynasty set out to restore the legacy of the Achaemenid Empire. The details of the fall of the Parthians and the rise of the Sasanians are shrouded in conflicting accounts.

Ctesiphon was the capital for all but the first two years, when Istakhr briefly served. At its height the empire controlled all of present-day Iran and Iraq and parts of Arabia, the Caucasus, the Levant, Central Asia and the Indian subcontinent.

The Sasanians competed with Rome more zealously than the Arsacids had, opening a new phase of the Roman–Iranian Wars. Shapur I extended his authority into the north-west of the Indian subcontinent and made the Kushans accept his suzerainty. After the division of the Roman Empire in 395, the Byzantine Empire was Persia's principal western enemy. A largely peaceful period followed the death of Shapur II, with only two brief wars with the Romans, in 421–422 and in 440.

Under Kavad I the empire took Amida on the Tigris in 503 and made peace with the Romans in 506. Khosrow I patronised letters, and had the works of Plato and Aristotle translated into Pahlavi. In the early seventh century Khosrow II's campaign was successful from 602 to 622, but it exhausted the army and treasury, and he overtaxed the population. Between 622 and 627 the Byzantine emperor Heraclius counter-attacked in Anatolia and the Caucasus and sacked the Zoroastrian temple at Ganzak. Weakened by that war, the empire fell to the early Muslim conquests.

The ruler took the title shahanshah, king of kings, and guarded the sacred fire of the national religion, which appears on the reverse of Sasanian coins. Historians believe society had four classes: priests, warriors, commoners and artisans, with the royal princes, petty rulers, great landlords and priests forming a privileged group of grandees. The Azatan, a low aristocracy living on small estates, provided the cavalry backbone of the army.

An orthodox Zoroastrianism was revived. Christians, mainly of the Church of the East, were recognised as an allowable faith by Yazdegerd I in 409, and a large Jewish community flourished, in whose academies the Babylonian Talmud was composed between the third and sixth centuries. Mani spent most of his life within the empire. The economy rested on farming, above all in Khuzestan and Iraq, with the Nahrawan Canal among its irrigation works, and Sasanian merchants came to dominate Indian Ocean trade. Chinese records mention sixteen embassies from Persia between 455 and 555.
saskatchewan: Saskatchewan is bordered by Alberta to the west, the Northwest Territories to the north, Manitoba to the east and Montana and North Dakota to the south. With Alberta it is one of only two landlocked provinces of Canada, and it is the only province without a natural border, since its borders follow the 49th and 60th parallels and the 110th meridian. The overwhelming majority of the population lives in the southern third. The name comes from the Saskatchewan River, which in Cree is kisiskāciwani-sīpiy, swift flowing river.

Indigenous peoples, among them the Cree, Saulteaux, Assiniboine and Sioux, have lived in the region for thousands of years. The first known European to enter it was Henry Kelsey of England in 1690, who travelled up the Saskatchewan River to trade for fur. The first permanent European settlement was the Hudson's Bay Company post at Cumberland House, founded by Samuel Hearne in 1774. Most of the province lay in Rupert's Land, controlled by the Hudson's Bay Company, and in the late 1850s and early 1860s expeditions led by John Palliser and Henry Youle Hind explored the prairie.

Saskatchewan became a province on 1 September 1905, carved out of the North-West Territories. In 1901 there were 19,200 families, and 150,300 only fifteen years later, and women's labour was critical to the survival of family farms and the wheat economy. In the early 20th century the province became a stronghold of Canadian social democracy, and the 1944 provincial election brought North America's first socialist government to office. In 1992 the federal and provincial governments signed a land claim agreement with First Nations in the province.

Regina is the capital and Saskatoon the largest city of Saskatchewan, and roughly half the people live in the two. The economy is based on agriculture, mining and energy. Wheat has long been the best-known crop, and canola production surpassed it in 2017.
satrapy: The word satrap comes through Latin from Greek satrápes, borrowed from an Old Iranian form. In Old Persian it is recorded as xšaçapavan, literally protector of the province, and its Sanskrit cognate is kṣatrapa. Provincial organisation began in the Median era, from at least 648 BCE, and the first large-scale use of satrapies came with the Achaemenid Empire under Cyrus the Great, from around 530 BCE. Before the conquest of Media, emperors had ruled conquered lands through client kings and governors. The twenty-six satraps Cyrus established were never kings but viceroys ruling in the king's name, and Darius the Great gave the satrapies a definitive organisation, raising their number to thirty-six and fixing their annual tribute.

A satrap served as viceroy to the king, with considerable autonomy. He collected taxes, controlled local officials and subject tribes and cities, was supreme judge of the province, and was responsible for the safety of the roads and for putting down brigands and rebels. He had a court that was all but royal and a council of Persians, and he was allowed troops of his own. There were checks on him: his secretary, his chief financial official and the general of the regular army and fortresses were independent of him and reported directly to the king, and the king's emissary, the eye of the king, inspected each year.

When central authority weakened, satraps often enjoyed practical independence, particularly when they were also made generals of the army district, contrary to the original rule. Satrapal rebellions became frequent from the middle of the 5th century BCE, and under Artaxerxes II much of Asia Minor and Syria was at times in open rebellion in the Revolt of the Satraps. The last great rebellions were put down by Artaxerxes III.

Alexander the Great kept the satrapic administration and title, even for Greco-Macedonian officials, and so did his successors, especially in the Seleucid Empire, where provinces were much smaller than under the Persians. In the Sasanian Empire centrally appointed governors called shahrabs ruled royal cities and their districts. The Western Satraps or Kshatrapas, Saka rulers in western India from 35 to 405 CE, bore the title too. The word later came to suggest tyranny or ostentatious splendour, and in modern use it is a pejorative for a subordinate or local ruler.
saturn-mythology: Saturn was described as a god of time, generation, dissolution, abundance, wealth, agriculture, periodic renewal and liberation. The Romans kept the memory of a remote time in which Saturn and Janus reigned on the site of the city before its foundation, and the Capitol was called mons Saturnius. After the Roman conquest of Greece he was conflated with the Greek Titan Cronus, whose myths were adapted for Latin literature, and as early as the 3rd century BCE Jupiter was called his son. His consort Ops, equivalent to Rhea, was a later association, since the goddess was originally paired with Consus; earlier was his link with Lua, a goddess of destruction and loosening who received the bloodied weapons of enemies killed in war.

Ancient writers offered several explanations of the name. Varro derived it from satus, sowing, and Cicero's Balbus from satis, because Time is satiated by the years; a modern alternative connects it with the Etruscan god Satre.

In Roman legend Saturn arrived in Italy dethroned and fugitive after his son Jupiter usurped him, was received by Janus and brought agriculture and civilisation. Virgil describes his reign as a golden age of peace under which he gathered the unruly fauns and nymphs and gave them laws. The temple of Saturn at the foot of the Capitoline Hill was consecrated in 497 BCE and housed the state treasury throughout Roman history; a row of columns from its last rebuilding still stands. His statue was filled with oil and had its feet bound with wool, which was removed only during the Saturnalia.

The Saturnalia, held from 17 to 23 December, marked the harvest and sowing. Social restrictions of Rome were relaxed, and its revels were meant to recall the lost golden age before Saturn's rule was overthrown. Sacrifices to him were made in the Greek rite with the head uncovered, unlike those of other major deities, a custom ancient commentators linked to the god's own veiled image. In the 3rd century CE and later, gladiatorial munera were given near the festival, which Christian writers criticised as a form of human sacrifice.

Little evidence exists for his cult in Italy outside Rome. The Romans equated him with the Carthaginian god Baal Hammon, to whom children were sacrificed, and the poet Tibullus called the Sabbath Saturni dies, from which Saturday derives. The identification with Baal Hammon gave rise to the African Saturn, a cult that was popular until the 4th century and had the character of a mystery religion.
saudi-aramco: The company's origins trace to the oil shortages of the First World War and to the exclusion of American companies from Mesopotamia by the United Kingdom and France under the San Remo Petroleum Agreement of 1920. The United States administration had popular support for an Open Door policy, which Herbert Hoover, secretary of commerce, initiated in 1921. Standard Oil of California was among the American companies seeking new sources of oil abroad. In 1932 its wholly owned subsidiary, the Bahrain Petroleum Company, discovered the first oil field in the Persian Gulf outside Iran.

In 1973, after the United States supported Israel in the Yom Kippur War, the Saudi government acquired a one-quarter participation interest in Aramco's assets and raised it to sixty per cent in 1974. Aramco continued to operate the former assets on the government's behalf until November 1988, when a royal decree created a new company, the Saudi Arabian Oil Company, to take control of them and of the management of the kingdom's oil and gas fields. In 1989 and 1990 high-quality oil and gas were discovered in three areas south of Riyadh.

After the start of the Persian Gulf War in September 1990, Aramco was expected to replace much of the oil lost to the embargo of Iraq and occupied Kuwait. It recommissioned 146 wells at Harmaliyah, Khurais and Ghawar that had been mothballed during the oil price collapse of the 1980s, and daily production rose from 5.4 million barrels in July to 8.5 million in December 1990. From 1990 the company expanded its crude sales in Asia, with agreements with South Korea, the Philippines and China.

In 2001 Saudi Arabia announced a Gas Initiative proposing joint ventures with international companies for gas exploration, and in 2005 Aramco began a five-year plan to spend US$50 billion to raise its daily capacity to 12.5 million barrels. On 15 August 2012 a virus known as Shamoon attacked some 30,000 of its workstations. Its shares began trading on the Saudi Exchange on 11 December 2019.

Saudi Aramco is headquartered in Dhahran, and its operations include exploration, production, refining, chemicals, distribution and marketing. It manages over a hundred oil and gas fields in Saudi Arabia. In the Eastern Province it operates the Ghawar Field, the world's largest onshore oil field, and the Safaniya Field, the world's largest offshore oil field, and it runs the Master Gas System, the world's largest single hydrocarbon network. A significant part of its workforce consists of geophysicists and geologists, who work mostly at the EXPEC Advanced Research Center. The Ministry of Petroleum and Mineral Resources and the Supreme Council for Petroleum and Minerals oversee its activities.
saul: According to the Hebrew Bible, Saul was the son of Kish, of the family of the Matrites, and came from Gibeah. He married Ahinoam, daughter of Ahimaaz, and had at least five sons, among them Jonathan and Ish-bosheth, and two daughters, Merab and Michal. The Books of Samuel give three accounts of his rise. In one he is sent to look for his father's strayed donkeys and is anointed in private by the seer Samuel at Ramah. In another Samuel assembles the people at Mizpah and uses the Urim and Thummim to choose the tribe of Benjamin, the clan of Matri and then Saul. In a third he leads an army to relieve Jabesh-Gilead from the Ammonite king Nahash and is crowned at Gilgal.

After relieving Jabesh-Gilead, Saul is said to have fought the Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites, the kings of Zobah, the Philistines and the Amalekites. With Jonathan he defeated a large Philistine force at the pass of Michmash, though his rash oath that the army should fast nearly cost Jonathan his life. Samuel then rebuked him for offering sacrifice himself, and later told him that God had rejected him as king after he spared the Amalekite king Agag and the best livestock in a war meant to destroy Amalek completely.

From then on the narrative turns largely on his troubled relationship with David, the son of Jesse whom Samuel anointed. Saul, troubled by an evil spirit, took David to play the harp for him, and David became his armour bearer. Scholars note that the text portrays Saul positively before David appears and negatively afterwards, and suggest that the David story came from a source loyal to David's house. The reign length in the Hebrew text, two years, is regarded as faulty; a reign of 20 or 22 years is thought more probable.

Before the Philistine battle at Mount Gilboa, Saul consulted a spirit medium at Endor, and the spirit that appeared as Samuel told him he would lose the battle and his life. First Samuel says he asked his armour bearer to kill him and, when refused, fell on his own sword; Jonathan, Abinadab and Malchishua died with him. A conflicting account in 2 Samuel has an Amalekite claiming to have killed him. Ish-bosheth succeeded him for two years before being murdered. The historicity of Saul's kingdom is debated, since the evidence is mostly biblical. In the Qur'an Talut is traditionally identified with Saul, a divinely appointed king chosen by a prophet.
sava: The Sava is the longest tributary of the Danube and the largest by volume of water. Its headwater, the Sava Dolinka, rises in the Zelenci Pools in the Upper Carniola region of Slovenia, at 833 metres above sea level, and meets the Sava Bohinjka near Radovljica. The river then crosses the Ljubljana Basin, flows into Croatia and passes Zagreb. Below the confluence of the Una it forms the border between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, then turns north-east after the Drina joins and reaches Serbia.

It discharges into the Danube at the Great War Island in Belgrade. Its basin covers 97,713 square kilometres and drains much of the Dinaric Alps through tributaries such as the Drina, Bosna, Kupa, Una and Vrbas. The river's course is sometimes used to describe the northern boundary of the Balkans and the southern border of Central Europe. Before the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1991 it was the longest river lying completely within that country.

The name is believed to derive from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning to press or take liquid, so that it means that which waters the ground. The ancient Greeks called the river Saos, Strabo wrote of the Saüs, and the Romans used the name Savus. Worship of river gods in the area dates to the Late Bronze Age, when the first settlements were founded along the river. The Taurisci associated their river goddess Adsullata with the Savus, and altars or inscriptions to the river god Savus have been found at several places, among them the Zelenci Pools, Emona, Andautonia and Siscia.

The Romans built settlements and forts along the Via Pannonia, the road from Aquileia to the Danube. Upstream of the Kupa confluence these included Emona, Andautonia and Siscia, near modern Ljubljana, Velika Gorica and Sisak. Downstream stood Marsonia, built over a prehistoric settlement, then Cibalae, Sirmium and Singidunum, on the sites of Slavonski Brod, Vinkovci, Sremska Mitrovica and Belgrade.

About 8,176,000 people live in the Sava basin, and Ljubljana, Zagreb and Belgrade stand on the river, with Sarajevo in the basin. The river is navigable to larger vessels for 593.8 kilometres between Belgrade and Sisak, and its valley carries road and rail routes, among them Pan-European Corridor X. In Zagreb in 1964 the most destructive flood of the river put one third of the city under water and killed 17 people, after which a flood-relief canal to the Odra plain was built. The basin holds large alluvial wetlands, and six areas of it are protected under the Ramsar Convention.
savaii: Savaiʻi is the largest and highest island both in Samoa and in the Samoan Islands chain, and the sixth largest in Polynesia. Its classical Samoan name, used in formal oratory and prose, is Salafai. It lies north-west of Upolu, from which it is separated by the Apolima Strait, about 13 km wide, with the small inhabited islands of Manono and Apolima between them. The island is mountainous and fertile and is surrounded by coral reefs, rising to 1,858 metres at Mt Silisili, the highest peak in the country.

Savaiʻi is the largest shield volcano in the South Pacific, and only 3% of it is above water. Its central region holds the Central Savaiʻi Rainforest, about 72,699 hectares, the largest continuous rainforest in Polynesia, dotted with more than 100 volcanic craters. The name is cognate with Hawaiʻi and with Hawaiki in Māori, and shares a root with the original homeland of Polynesian folklore, although Samoans themselves preserve no tradition of having originated elsewhere. The island has been called the Cradle of Polynesia.

Archaeology has uncovered prehistoric settlements inland, including sites at Sapapaliʻi and Vailoa, and star mounds, fortifications and pyramids such as the Pulemelei Mound in Palauli district. In prehistory the village of Safotu was a settlement for Tongans. The missionary John Williams (1796-1839) arrived at Sapapaliʻi in 1830, a village that was also a base for the Malietoa title on Savaiʻi. In October 1839 the island was surveyed by the United States Exploring Expedition under Charles Wilkes.

The Matavanu eruptions of 1905 to 1911 sent lava over the central north coast and destroyed villages including Saleaula. Resistance to colonial rule began on Savaiʻi: the Mau a Pule movement, led by the exiled orator Lauaki Namulauulu Mamoe (died 1915) of Safotulafai, was the beginning of the Mau, Samoa's non-violent movement for political independence.

The island is home to 43,958 people (2016 census), 24% of the population of Samoa, and is divided into six political districts. Its only township and ferry terminal is Salelologa. Faʻa Sāmoa, the traditional way of life based on extended family, chiefly titles (matai) and obligations, remains strong there, and the term Pule is applied to traditional authority. Samoa became independent from New Zealand on 1 January 1962. Falealupo, at the westernmost point, lies just 32 km from the dateline, and the 1926 documentary Moana was filmed at Safune.
savannah: The word derives from the Spanish sabana, itself a loanword from Taíno, where it meant treeless grassland in the West Indies. It entered English as Zauana in a description of the islands of the kings of Spayne from 1555, in which Peter Martyr reported it as the local name for the plain around Comagre, the court of the cacique Carlos in present-day Panama.

The English explorer William Dampier, in his volumes of A New Voyage Round the World published between 1697 and 1705, used the spelling savannah with a final h, which became the British English form. He applied it to dry, sandy ground with tufted grass and palmetto trees on an island in the Bay of Campeche, and to similar country in Sumatra and the Philippines.

A savanna is a mixed woodland and grassland biome in which the trees are spaced widely enough that the canopy does not close. The light reaching the ground supports an unbroken layer of grasses. Four forms are distinguished: savanna woodland, tree savanna, shrub savanna and grass savanna. Savannas are marked by seasonal water, with most rain falling in one season, and by yearly variations in rainfall and dry-season wildfires. Annual rainfall ranges from about 500 to 1,270 millimetres. Savanna covers roughly 20 percent of the Earth's land area, mostly in warm to hot climates in Africa, Australia, South America and India, unlike the prairies of North America and the steppes of Eurasia, which have cold winters.

In East Africa, acacias, baobabs and Combretum are common trees, and the African savanna's animals include giraffe, elephant, buffalo, zebra, hippopotamus and rhinoceros. In Australia kangaroos and wallabies predominate. Ecoregions include the Serengeti, the Brazilian Cerrado, the Pantanal and the Sudd.

The ecosystem appears to be in large part the result of human use of fire. Fire-stick farming seems to have been responsible for the widespread savanna of tropical Australia and New Guinea, savannas in India are a result of human fire use, and Native Americans created woodlands in pre-Columbian North America by periodic burning. Controlled burns kill or suppress tree seedlings, preventing a continuous canopy that would shade out the grass.

The open structure that allows grass to grow also suits grazing, and much of the world's savanna has been changed by sheep, goats and cattle. Large areas of Australian and South American savanna have been cleared of trees to improve pasture, which can raise pasture production two to fourfold. Early pastoralists felled and girdled trees. In the 1950s arboricides for stem injection were developed, and war-surplus heavy machinery was used to push or pull timber.
saverne: Saverne is a commune in the Bas-Rhin department of north-eastern France, 45 kilometres north-west of Strasbourg. It lies on the river Zorn at the foot of a pass over the Vosges Mountains, and the Marne–Rhine Canal and the Paris–Strasbourg railway cross it. Its Latin name was Tres Tabernae Caesaris, Caesar's three taverns, from the three inns that once stood on the way to the Lorraine plateau, where oxen were changed because of the steep climb.

Saverne was an important place in Roman times and, after being destroyed by the Alemanni, was rebuilt by the emperor Julian. After the settlement of the Alemanni it became part of the Germanosphere, and after 870 it belonged to East Francia, which became the Holy Roman Empire. In 1525, during the German Peasants' War, insurgents occupied the town and were driven out by Duke Anton of Lorraine. It suffered heavily in the Thirty Years' War, and its episcopal palace, destroyed then, was later rebuilt. The French annexed the town after 1680.

In 1852 Louis Napoleon converted the episcopal palace into a residence for widows of knights of the Legion of Honour. Saverne was conquered by Imperial Germany after the Franco-Prussian War and returned to France after the First World War. In 1913 it was the scene of the Saverne Affair, which gave rise to the term Zabernism, from the German name Zabern, meaning abuse of military authority or unwarranted aggression.

The town's emblem is a unicorn. Legend says a unicorn's horn was found in one of the ruined castles nearby, though it was more likely a narwhal's tooth. Its principal building is the Château des Rohan, the former residence of the bishops of Strasbourg, rebuilt by Cardinal de Rohan in 1779 and used by the Germans as barracks; it now houses the town museum with its Roman and Celtic collection. Other sights include the 15th-century Château vieux, the parish church of Notre-Dame-de-la-Nativité, a former Franciscan monastery with a cloister decorated with 17th-century frescoes, and the decorated Maison Katz. The ruined castles of Haut-Barr, Grand Geroldseck, Ochsenstein and Greifenstein lie nearby.
savoie: Savoie lies in the French Alps and borders the departments of Haute-Savoie, Ain, Isère and Hautes-Alpes, as well as Italy's Aosta Valley and the Metropolitan City of Turin. Much of it is mountainous, with the Mont Blanc, Vanoise, Beaufortain and Belledonne massifs among its ranges. The Isère river has its source at the Iseran pass, and the department's two main lakes are Lac du Bourget, the largest and deepest lake entirely in France, and Lac d'Aiguebelette.

The other main Alpine valley is the Maurienne, one of the longest intra-alpine valleys in the Alps, which two passes connect to the Tarentaise valley. The col de l'Iseran is the highest pass in Europe, and the col du Mont Cenis was the major commercial route between France and Italy.

The name is widely accepted to come from the Latin Sapaudia or Sabaudia, meaning land covered in fir trees. Savoie was long part of the states of Savoy, though from the sixteenth century France occupied it several times. It was part of the Mont-Blanc department from 1792 to 1815, and partly of the Léman department from 1798 to 1814. France annexed the former Duchy of Savoy in 1860, following the Treaty of Turin, and it became the two departments of Savoie and Haute-Savoie. Moûtiers, the capital of the former province of the Tarentaise, ceased to be a subprefecture under a law that took effect on 10 September 1926.

Chambéry is the prefecture and the most populous commune. Savoie belongs to the region of Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, created on 1 January 2016, and was previously part of Rhône-Alpes. Tourism began to develop towards the end of the nineteenth century, at first mostly in summer, and the popularity of skiing in the twentieth century made Savoie home to the largest number of ski resorts in France, among them Val-d'Isère, Courchevel and Méribel. The department hosted the 1992 Winter Olympics, based in Albertville. Spa treatment has been practised in the region since antiquity, and Aix-les-Bains is one of four places where it continues. The area is known for cheeses such as Beaufort and Reblochon and for dishes such as fondue savoyarde.
savona: Savona is a seaport and municipality in the west of the Italian region of Liguria and the capital of the Province of Savona. It faces the Ligurian Sea, between the sea and the Ligurian Alps, 40 kilometres west of Genoa, and is the main city of the western section of the Italian Riviera. The navigator Christopher Columbus is associated with the town. A cottage in the Savona hills is called Columbus's house, and a house in the neighbourhood is documented as the property of his father Domenico Colombo, where the family lived for many years.

Ligurian tribes lived here in ancient times, and the city, which had been allied to Carthage in the Punic Wars, came under Roman influence about 180 BCE. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire it passed under Lombard rule in 641, being destroyed in the attack. It recovered as a county seat in the Carolingian Empire. In the tenth century its bishops were counts of Savona, and the countship passed to the Marquesses of Montferrat in 981 and to the Marquesses Del Vasto in 1084.

After a long struggle against the Saracens, Savona became independent in the eleventh century as a free commune allied with the Holy Roman Emperor, and its freedom declaration was signed in 1191 in the Torre del Brandale. Two monasteries, one Dominican and one Franciscan, made it a centre of religious culture from the thirteenth to the sixteenth century. It then fought the Republic of Genoa and was definitively conquered in 1528. The Genoese destroyed the upper town and buried the port, and in 1542 they built the Priamar fortress on the site of the old cathedral and old city. Savona shared the fortunes of Genoa until Napoleonic times.

Austrian forces besieged the city between April and mid-May 1800 while a small British naval force blockaded it, and the fortress surrendered on 15 May. From 1809 the city held Pope Pius VII, a prisoner of Napoleon Bonaparte, for a few years. Savona was annexed to the Kingdom of Sardinia-Piedmont in 1815 and later became part of the unified Kingdom of Italy. In 1830 and 1831 Giuseppe Mazzini was imprisoned in the Priamar. In the twentieth century Savona became a regional industrial hub.

The Cappella Sistina beside the Cathedral of the Assumption was built from 1480 to 1483 and holds the mausoleum that Pope Sixtus IV of the Della Rovere family erected for his parents. Cardinal Giulio della Rovere, the future Pope Julius II, built the Palazzo Della Rovere, designed by Giuliano da Sangallo as a university. The Torre Leon Pancaldo, built in the fourteenth century, is the symbol of the town. The Priamar now holds the Museum Centre of Priamar.
saxo-grammaticus: Saxo is thought to have been born in Zealand, on the evidence of the Jutland Chronicle, which first gives him the name Grammaticus, meaning the learned. The Sjælland Chronicle calls him Saxo cognomine Longus, with the byname the tall. Sven Aggesen, a Danish nobleman who wrote a slightly earlier history of Denmark, describes him as his contubernalis, or tent-comrade, which suggests that both may have served in the royal guard, the Hird. Saxo writes that he comes from a warrior family: he follows the ancient right of hereditary service, and his father and grandfather frequented the war camp of Valdemar I. Whether he was a layman or a cleric is uncertain, but either way he was well educated.

Saxo was in the retinue of Absalon, Archbishop of Lund and the foremost adviser to Valdemar I, and received his patronage. In his will Absalon forgives his clerk Saxo a small debt of two and a half marks of silver and tells him to return two borrowed books to the monastery of Sorø. In the preface to his history Saxo writes that Absalon had encouraged him to write a heroic history of the Danes, to glorify the fatherland on the model of Virgil's Aeneid. The work is thought to have been begun about 1185. Saxo wrote the preface last, under Anders Sunesen, who replaced Absalon as archbishop, and in it he warmly praised both archbishops and the reigning king, Valdemar II.

The Gesta Danorum begins with the founders of the Danish people, Dan I of Denmark and Angul, and extends to about the year 1187. The first four books treat the Danes before Christ, the next four their history after Christ, books 9 to 12 Christian Denmark, and books 13 to 16 promote Lund and exploits before and during Saxo's own lifetime. His sources were of questionable historical value: oral tales of the Icelanders, ancient volumes, letters carved on rocks and stone, and the statements of Absalon.

Saxo's world has very warlike values, and he glorifies heroes who made their names in battle far more than those who made peace. His gods are not always good characters. Odin teaches Harald, in Saxo's tale a king of the Danes, the ways of war and then betrays and kills him. Erasmus praised Saxo's Latin, and early in the sixteenth century Christiern Pedersen of Lund printed the work with Jodocus Badius Ascensius.
saxons: The earliest possible record of the Saxons is a reference in Ptolemy's Geographia to a tribe north of the lower Elbe, but the manuscripts differ, some reading Saxones and others Axones, and its interpretation is disputed. The first undoubted use of the name comes from the third to fifth centuries, when it described coastal raiders who attacked the Roman Empire by boat from north of the Rhine. Scholars believe the term was then used something like the much later word Viking and was probably not the name of any specific tribe. The raiders included Frisians, Angles and Jutes, as well as the Anglo-Saxons who became established in Britain. The name has traditionally been derived from the seax, a kind of knife.

The continental Saxons appear as inland opponents of the Franks in the sixth century, after the Franks conquered Thuringia, about 531. They do not seem to have been politically united until the generations of conflict that led to their defeat by Charlemagne. Frankish rulers of Austrasia, Merovingian and Carolingian, fought many campaigns against them. Charlemagne conquered them in the Saxon Wars of 772–804 and forced them to convert to Christianity. He deported 10,000 Nordalbingian Saxons to Neustria. In 804 Saxony became a Carolingian stem duchy.

The dukes of Saxony expanded eastwards at the expense of the Slavic-speaking Wends. They became kings of Germany with Henry I the Fowler in 919 and then emperors, beginning with his son Otto I, in the tenth century, but lost this position in 1024. The duchy was divided in 1180 when Duke Henry the Lion refused to follow Emperor Frederick Barbarossa into war in Lombardy.

Bede, writing about 730, remarks that the continental Saxons had no king but were governed by several satraps, who cast lots for leadership in war and were equal in peacetime. Their territory was divided into Westphalia, Eastphalia and Angria, comprising about one hundred districts called Gaue. Sources on Saxon paganism come only from after their conversion and were written by Christians. The Old Saxon Baptismal Vow required converts to renounce the worship of Thunaer, Wodan and Saxnot, and Charlemagne's capitulary prohibited cremation burial, punishable by death.

The Saxons of Germany no longer form a distinct people, but their name survives in Lower Saxony, which includes most of the original duchy. Old Saxon evolved into Middle Low German and then Low German, the lingua franca of the Hanseatic League.
saxony: The Free State of Saxony is a landlocked state of Germany. It borders Brandenburg, Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia and Bavaria, and its southern and eastern boundaries form part of Germany's frontiers with the Czech Republic and Poland. The land rises from the lowlands of the North German Plain in the north, which include the Leipzig Bay and much of Lusatia, to uplands along the Czech border.

Some of the largest ancient monumental temples of central Europe stood here, dating from the fifth millennium BCE. Since the late 6th century the area was populated by Polabian Slavs, most prominently the Sorbs, and it was conquered by Francia and organized as the Sorbian March. The territory became part of the Holy Roman Empire by the 10th century, and the Margravate of Meissen was founded in 985 as a frontier march. In 1423 Saxe-Wittenberg became subject to the margravate, ruled by the Wettin dynasty, creating a new and powerful state. Although its centre lay far to the southeast of the old Saxony, it came to be called Upper Saxony and then simply Saxony, while the northern Saxon lands became Lower Saxony.

In 1806 Napoleon made the Electorate of Saxony a kingdom, in exchange for military support. At the Congress of Vienna the king was restored but forced to cede the northern part of the kingdom to Prussia, a loss of nearly 60 percent of the territory and 40 percent of the population. Frederick Augustus III abdicated on 13 November 1918, and Saxony became the Free State of Saxony. It was broken up under communist rule and re-established on 3 October 1990, on German reunification.

Dresden is the capital of Saxony and Leipzig its largest city. Dresden's Baroque cityscape and art collections, Leipzig's musical traditions and the mining heritage of the Ore Mountains are among its best-known cultural features.
saxony-anhalt: Saxony-Anhalt is a landlocked state of Germany of 20,555 square kilometres, bordering Brandenburg, Saxony, Thuringia and Lower Saxony. In the north the North German Plain dominates, with the old Hanseatic towns of Salzwedel, Gardelegen, Stendal and Tangermünde in the sparsely populated Altmark, and the fertile Magdeburg Börde beyond it. The Harz mountains lie in the south-west; their highest peak, the Brocken at 1,141 metres, is the highest in northern Germany. The wine-growing area of Saale-Unstrut lies in the south, and the Halle area forms an agglomeration with Leipzig, known for its chemical industry at Leuna, Schkopau and Bitterfeld.

Saxony-Anhalt has a short history as a state and consists mainly of three historical regions: the area around Magdeburg, the formerly independent Anhalt, and a southern part that had once belonged to Saxony and was annexed by Prussia in the nineteenth century. Anhalt takes its name from Anhalt Castle near Harzgerode. In April 1945 the US Army took control of most of the western and northern area; it withdrew to make way for the Red Army, as the London Protocol of 1944 had agreed. The Soviet administration then merged the Free State of Anhalt, Halle-Merseburg, the governorate of Magdeburg and some further territories with the Province of Saxony, and appointed Erhard Hübener to head the new provincial administration at Halle.

The Province of Saxony was renamed the Province of Saxony-Anhalt on 20 October 1946, and after the Allied decision to dissolve the Free State of Prussia it became the State of Saxony-Anhalt on 6 October 1947. Hübener, elected minister-president in December 1946, was the only governor in the Soviet zone who did not belong to the Socialist Unity Party. The state joined the German Democratic Republic in 1949. In 1952 the East German states were dissolved and its territory divided into the districts of Halle and Magdeburg, apart from the area around Torgau, which went to Leipzig. In 1990, during German reunification, the districts were reintegrated as a state, though Torgau did not return and joined Saxony.

Magdeburg is the capital and largest city, and Halle (Saale) the second-largest. The state's constitution was adopted by its Landtag in 1992. Six UNESCO World Heritage Sites in Germany lie in Saxony-Anhalt, among them the Bauhaus sites in Dessau and the Dessau-Wörlitz Garden Realm, and the Nebra Sky Disc is part of UNESCO's Memory of the World register. Many sites tied to Martin Luther's life stand there, including Lutherstadt Eisleben and Lutherstadt Wittenberg.
sayyid-qutb: Sayyid Qutb was born on 9 October 1906 and raised in the village of Musha in Asyut Province, Upper Egypt. His father, a landowner and the administrator of the family estate, was known for his political activism and held weekly meetings to discuss political events and Quranic recitation. Qutb learned melodic recitation there and had memorised the whole Quran by the age of ten. In the United States he worked and studied at Wilson Teachers' College in Washington, D.C., at Colorado State College for Education in Greeley and at Stanford University, and he spent time in Europe on his way home.

Before he left the United States he was still Western in many ways, in his dress and his love of classical music and Hollywood films, and he had read Charles Darwin, Albert Einstein, Lord Byron and Percy Bysshe Shelley in translation. Yet he concluded that major aspects of American life were primitive and shocking, and he saw Americans as numb to faith in religion, art and spiritual values. This experience formed in part the impetus for his rejection of Western values.

Qutb wrote 24 published books and at least 581 articles, including novels, literary criticism and works on education. From 1948 his outlook turned Islamist, beginning with the treatise al-ʿAdāla, and he later denounced his literary works of the 1940s as un-Islamic. His 30-volume Quran commentary, Fi Zilal al-Qur'an (In the Shade of the Qur'an), began to appear in 1954. In Milestones (Ma'alim fi-l-Tariq) he held that there are only two kinds of societies, Islamic and jahili, and that existing Muslim societies are jahili because they gave the legislative attribute of God to others.

He called for a revolutionary vanguard, which scholars have compared with Lenin's, although he rejected all Western ideologies, socialism included. His view of jihad changed from defensive to offensive. In 1950 he published Our Struggle against the Jews, which embraced antisemitic conspiracy theories.

Qutb joined the Muslim Brotherhood in the early 1950s and edited its weekly. He and the Brotherhood welcomed the July 1952 coup led by Gamal Abdel Nasser, but their cooperation soured as the secular nationalism of Nasserism proved incompatible with the Brotherhood's Islamism. He was in prison from 1954 to 1964, and one common explanation for his turn to sharia is the torture and killing of Brotherhood members that he saw there. He was convicted of plotting Nasser's assassination and hanged on 29 August 1966.

Followers describe him as a great thinker and a martyr for Islam, while Western observers and some Muslims see him as a key originator of Islamist ideology. The ulama of Al-Azhar University placed him on their index of heresy as a deviant. His ideas on jahiliyya have influenced Islamist and jihadist movements.
scandinavia: The geography of Scandinavia is varied. It includes the Norwegian fjords, the Scandinavian Mountains that cover much of Norway and parts of Sweden, the flat, low land of Denmark, and the archipelagos and lakes of the east. Finland and Sweden have many lakes and moraines, left by the ice age that ended about ten millennia ago. The region extends north of the Arctic Circle but has relatively mild weather for its latitude because of the Gulf Stream.

The name goes back to the Proto-Germanic compound *Skaðin-awjō, which is also the source of Scania, the southernmost province of Sweden. The earliest identified source for Scandinavia is Pliny the Elder's Natural History of the 1st century CE, which describes Scatinavia as an island.

The Viking Age lasted from about 793 to 1066 CE. Scandinavians raided, conquered, colonised and traded across Europe, and their longships took them to North America, where they were the first Europeans to arrive. Those known as Varangians, mostly from what is now Sweden, travelled east along the river routes into Russia. The expansion produced settlements and realms such as the Danelaw, the Kingdom of Dublin, the Duchy of Normandy and the Kievan Rus', and the Faroe Islands, Iceland and Greenland were settled. The North Sea Empire briefly joined large parts of Scandinavia and Great Britain.

Between the 10th and 13th centuries, as the region became Christian and its states formed, petty kingdoms and chiefdoms were unified into Denmark, Sweden and Norway. The historian Sverre Bagge notes that this division suits the geography, since forests, mountains and empty land separated the three.

Later unions followed, notably the Kalmar Union of Denmark, Norway and Sweden, which lasted over a century until King Gustav I led Sweden out of it. Denmark and Norway then stayed united until 1814. The Treaty of Kiel of 14 January 1814 dissolved that union and ceded Norway to the King of Sweden, but Norwegian resistance led to a constitution drawn up at Eidsvoll and a personal union with Sweden, which ended in 1905. The Scandinavist movement, which stressed a common heritage, peaked in the middle of the 19th century.

In its narrow, local sense Scandinavia comprises Denmark, Norway and Sweden, a subset of the Nordic countries, which also include Finland and Iceland. In English the word is sometimes used for all of them. Danish, Norwegian and Swedish form a dialect continuum and are considered mutually intelligible. Sámi and Finnish, of the unrelated Uralic family, have also been spoken in the region since prehistory.
scania: Scania, called Skåne in Swedish, lies at the south tip of the geographical region of Götaland. To the north it borders the historical provinces of Halland and Småland, to the north-east Blekinge, to the east and south the Baltic Sea, and to the west the Öresund. It extends about 130 kilometres from north to south and covers less than 3 per cent of Sweden's area. Unlike much of Sweden its landscape is generally not mountainous: a large part consists of plains, with lake-rich and densely forested country in the north (Göinge) and rolling hills on the Bjäre and Kulla peninsulas. It has the mildest climate in Sweden.

The names Scania and Scandinavia are considered to have the same etymology. The Romans called the southern tip of what is now Sweden Scania and thought it an island. The origin of the word is uncertain and long debated, though it may derive from a Germanic root related to Old Norse Skáney.

Scania was first mentioned in written texts in the 9th century and came under the Danish king Harald Bluetooth in the middle of the 10th century. As the eastern part of the kingdom of Denmark, it was the focal point of the frequent Dano-Swedish wars for hundreds of years. Lund has held town rights since about 990 and Helsingborg since 1085, and by 1658 ten places in Scania were chartered towns.

By the Treaty of Roskilde in 1658 all Danish lands east of the Öresund were ceded to Sweden. The province was first placed under a Governor-General and was eventually integrated into the Swedish kingdom. Denmark occupied parts of it during the Scanian War of 1676–1679 and again briefly in 1710 during the Great Northern War. The last Danish attempt to regain the lost provinces failed after the Battle of Helsingborg in 1710. Because Scania had had no coat of arms in the Danish era, new provincial arms were created in 1660 for the funeral of Charles X Gustav, based on the arms of Malmö.

Scania is the southernmost of the historical provinces of Sweden and corresponds roughly to Skåne County, created in 1997, with 33 municipalities. Its largest city is Malmö. Since 2000 a road and railway bridge, the Öresund Bridge, has connected it with Denmark. Its trade with other communities along the continental coast has made its culture distinct from other regions of Sweden, and artists and authors have compared its open fields of wheat and rapeseed with Provence and Zeeland.
schaan: Schaan is the northernmost municipality in the Liechtenstein Oberland and covers 26.92 square kilometres, including mountains and forest. It is bordered to the south by Vaduz, to the east by Planken and Triesenberg, and to the north by Eschen and Gamprin. In the west the Rhine forms the natural border with Switzerland, and in the east the town is dominated by the Drei Schwestern mountain range. Schaan has four exclaves within other municipalities, and two enclaves within its main territory, so that it borders Austria in three separate places.

Recent archaeological finds show that Schaan has been inhabited for over 6,000 years. In 15 BCE the Romans under Augustus conquered the territory of present-day Liechtenstein and established the province of Raetia. In the 1st century CE a military road was built from Milan to Bregenz, and settlements arose in what is now Schaan. In 1887 two Roman legionaries' helmets, engraved with the names of Publius Cavidius Felix and Numerius Pomponius, were found buried above Dux.

The most important Roman building in the municipality is Fort Schaan, built in the valley to protect against the ever more frequent Alemannic invasions. Part of its foundations and the gate tower can be seen from St Peter's Church, where excavation found a 5th-century baptistery that suggests early Christianization, and traces of a prehistoric settlement. Alemannic settlement is shown by numerous graves. At that time Schaan consisted of two parts: the Romanized Räter-people had their centre at St Peter, while the Alemannic population settled around Specki. This division survives in two alpine cooperatives, the Alemannic Gritsch and the Rhaeto-Roman Guschg.

Schaan is an important traffic hub and industrial location, and the Hilti Corporation has its headquarters on its outskirts. It lies on the Feldkirch–Buchs railway line between Switzerland and Austria and is served by the Schaan-Vaduz station. The municipality is administered by a mayor and a council of 13, elected every four years since 1975.
scheldt: The Scheldt has its headwaters at Gouy in the Aisne department of northern France. It flows north through Cambrai and Valenciennes and enters Belgium near Tournai. Ghent developed at the confluence of the Scheldt and the Lys, one of its main tributaries, after which the river turns east. Near Antwerp, the largest city on its banks, it flows west into the Netherlands towards the North Sea. Its name derives from an adjective corresponding to Old English sceald, meaning shallow.

Originally two branches left the river there, the Oosterschelde and the Westerschelde. In the 19th century the Dutch built a dyke that cut the river off from the eastern branch and joined Zuid-Beveland to the mainland. The river now continues only into the Westerschelde estuary, passing Terneuzen and reaching the sea between Breskens and Vlissingen.

The estuary has always had commercial and strategic importance. Called Scaldis in Roman times, it was important for the shipping lanes to Roman Britain, and the goddess Nehalennia was venerated at its mouth. The Franks took control of the region about 260 and at first raided the Roman supply routes as pirates, but later became allies of the Romans. With the divisions of the Frankish Empire in the 9th century the Scheldt became the border between its western and eastern parts, which later became France and the Holy Roman Empire. This status held, at least on paper, until 1528.

After Antwerp, then the most prominent harbour in Western Europe, fell back under Spanish control in 1585, the Dutch Republic took Zeelandic Flanders on the left bank and closed the Scheldt to shipping. Trade shifted to Amsterdam and Middelburg and Antwerp was seriously crippled, an important and traumatic element in later relations between the Netherlands and what became Belgium. The Kettle War of 1784 was fought over access, and the river was reopened in 1792.

After Belgium became independent in 1830 the river was to remain open to ships bound for Belgian ports, though the Dutch government demanded a toll until 16 July 1863. In the Second World War the Canadian First Army cleared the German positions in the estuary in the Battle of the Scheldt, and supply convoys could reach Antwerp by November 1944.

The Scheldt is an important waterway, navigable from its mouth up to Cambrai, and the port of Antwerp developed on its banks. Canals, among them the Scheldt-Rhine Canal and the Albert Canal, connect it to the basins of the Rhine, Meuse and Seine and to industrial areas around Brussels, Liège, Lille and Mons.
schenectady-new-york: Schenectady is the county seat of Schenectady County, in eastern New York near the confluence of the Mohawk and Hudson rivers. Albany, the state capital, lies about 24 km to the southeast, and with Albany and Troy the city is one of the three principal population and industrial centres of the Capital District. The name comes from the Mohawk word skahnéhtati, meaning beyond the pines, which was used for the area around Albany.

When Europeans first arrived, the Mohawk Valley was the territory of the Mohawk nation, one of the Five Nations of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, who had held land in the region since at least 1100 CE. In the early 1600s the Mohawks moved their settlements closer to the river, and by 1629 they had taken over territory on the west bank of the Hudson that had belonged to the Algonquian-speaking Mahican. Dutch colonists, many of them from the Albany area, founded Schenectady on the south side of the Mohawk River in the 17th century and laid out farms on strip plots along the river.

After the Revolutionary War the villagers reduced the power of the descendants of the early trustees and gained representative government. Members of the three oldest churches, the Dutch First Reformed Church, St. George's Episcopal Church and First Presbyterian Church, formed a union and founded Union College in 1795; it was the first private nondenominational institution of higher education in the United States. The Mohawk River and the Erie Canal then tied Schenectady to the trade, manufacturing and transport corridor of the Mohawk Valley, and by 1824 more people worked in manufacturing than in agriculture or trade.

General Electric and the American Locomotive Company made the city a manufacturing centre known as the City that Lights and Hauls the World. In the early 20th century it drew immigrants from Eastern and Southern Europe and African Americans leaving the rural South. General Electric's radio station WGY was the second commercial radio station in the United States, and in 1928 its experimental station W2XB began the first regular television broadcasts in the country. The locomotive company's Schenectady plant closed in 1969.

The Stockade Historic District, named after the stockade that once surrounded the colonial settlement, has dozens of Dutch and English colonial houses of the 18th and 19th centuries. It was designated in 1965 as the first historic district in New York State. St. George's Episcopal Church dates from 1735, and the First Reformed Church was formed in the 17th century. Proctors Theatre, built in 1926 as a vaudeville and movie theatre, was the site of one of the first public demonstrations of television.
schengen-agreement: Free movement of people was a core part of the original Treaty of Rome, and from the early days of the European Economic Community nationals of member states could travel from one to another on production of a passport or national identity card. Systematic identity controls nevertheless remained at the border between most member states. Disagreement among them led to an impasse on abolishing border controls within the Community. Belgium, Luxembourg and the Netherlands had already abolished common border controls in 1970 as part of the Benelux Economic Union.

Five of the then ten member states, Belgium, France, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and West Germany, signed the agreement on 14 June 1985 aboard the MS Princesse Marie-Astrid on the Moselle near the town of Schengen, at the tripoint between France, Germany and Luxembourg. It was signed independently of the European Union, in part because member states did not agree whether the Union had the authority to abolish border controls, and in part because those ready to act did not wish to wait for others. It provided for the harmonisation of visa policies, for residents of border areas to cross away from fixed checkpoints, and for passport checks to be replaced by visual surveillance of vehicles at reduced speed, so that vehicles could cross without stopping.

In 1990 the agreement was supplemented by the Schengen Convention, which created the Schengen Area through the abolition of border controls between members, common rules on visas, and police and judicial cooperation. The agreement and convention were enacted in 1995 for only some signatories. At the Amsterdam Intergovernmental Conference, just over two years later, all member states of the Union except the United Kingdom and Ireland had signed. The Amsterdam Treaty incorporated the Schengen rules into European Union law in 1999, with opt-outs for those two states.

Norway and Iceland signed an association agreement in December 1996 and became part of the area through similar agreements with the Union. Switzerland finalised entry in 2009, after a popular referendum accepted an association agreement in 2005. Border controls have been reintroduced temporarily at various times, for example in several countries in 2016.
schengen-area: Before the First World War most countries of the world, including those in Europe, had lax border policies, which made such educational trips as the Grand Tour possible among the wealthy. The first move towards abolishing border controls between members of the European Communities came on 14 June 1985, when five of the then ten EEC members signed the Schengen Agreement: the Benelux countries, France and West Germany. They did so separately from the European Communities, because consensus could not be reached among all member states.

The agreement, on the gradual abolition of checks at the signatories' common borders, was supplemented by the 1990 Schengen Convention. The area originally had its legal basis outside the European Economic Community, in these two international agreements made by a subset of its members.

The Treaty of Amsterdam incorporated the Schengen rules, known as the Schengen acquis, into European Union law, and the change took effect on 1 May 1999. When the treaty was negotiated, only Ireland and the United Kingdom had not signed the agreement. The United Kingdom chose not to join, and Ireland, which wished to keep its Common Travel Area with the United Kingdom, also declined; both negotiated an opt-out. In 1999 the United Kingdom asked to take part in provisions on police and judicial cooperation, which the Council approved on 29 May 2000.

Denmark adopted the Schengen rules on an intergovernmental basis under a specific opt-out. Iceland and Norway, members of the Nordic Passport Union, became associated with the Schengen activities of the Union, and Switzerland was allowed to take part in the same manner in 2008 and Liechtenstein in 2011.

A state that wishes to join is assessed by the European Commission on border control legislation, infrastructure and organisation, personal data protection, visas, deportations and police cooperation. It must take responsibility for controlling the Union's external borders, apply common rules for land, sea and air frontiers, issue uniform Schengen visas, cooperate with the law enforcement agencies of other members and connect to the Schengen Information System. Admission then requires a unanimous decision of the Council of the European Union after consulting the European Parliament.

Some territories have special arrangements: Ceuta, Melilla and Mount Athos are fully inside the area with specific border control arrangements, while the Faroe Islands and Svalbard are excluded. Monaco is administered as part of the area through its open border with France under a 1963 convention. Andorra, San Marino and Vatican City have open or semi-open borders with their neighbours without being formal members.
scheveningen: Scheveningen is one of the eight districts of The Hague and also a subdistrict of that city. It has a long sandy beach, an esplanade, a pier and a lighthouse, and its harbour serves both fishing and tourism. It was never an independent municipality, but it has its own coat of arms, officially recognised by the Hague council in 1984, and it has always kept a strong identity of its own. It once had its own football club in the top Dutch division, Scheveningen Holland Sport, which was forced to merge with ADO Den Haag in the later twentieth century.

The name Sceveninghe first appears around 1280. The first inhabitants may have been Anglo-Saxons, though other historians favour a Scandinavian origin, and fishing was the main source of food and income. On 10 August 1653 English and Dutch fleets fought the Battle of Scheveningen off the coast while thousands watched from the shore. In 1660 Montagu's flagship picked up the English king at Scheveningen to accomplish the Restoration. A road to The Hague was built in 1663.

Storms destroyed the church and half the houses in 1470 and struck again in 1570, 1775, 1825, 1860, 1881 and 1894. After the last, the villagers decided to build a harbour, finished in 1904, since fishing boats with flat bottoms, the bomschuiten, had until then been pulled up the beach. By about 1870 over 150 of them were in use. In 1818 Jacob Pronk built a wooden bathing house on a dune, the start of the resort, and the Kurhaus hotel opened in 1886. Painters including Adriaen van de Velde, Simon de Vlieger and Hendrik Willem Mesdag recorded the village; Mesdag's panorama, 14 m high and 120 m wide, preserved the view of 1881.

The International Skating Union was founded here in 1892. A chess tournament held in the district in 1923 gave its name to the Scheveningen Variation of the Sicilian Defense, played there by several players including Max Euwe.

From 21 April 1960 the pirate station Radio Veronica broadcast from a ship anchored about four miles off the coast, joined later by Radio Noordzee Internationaal and Radio Caroline, until the Netherlands ratified the Treaty of Strasbourg on 1 September 1974. Since the 1970s the fishing industry has declined, most fishermen's houses have been demolished, and some, including original hofjes, have been protected. The old local dress and dialect have largely gone, as have the family nicknames once used to tell apart the many people who shared surnames such as Pronk. Annual events include the New Year's Day winter swim and a competition between Duindorp and Scheveningen dorp to build the largest bonfire tower.
schleswig-holstein: Schleswig-Holstein lies at the base of the Jutland Peninsula between the North Sea and the Baltic Sea, and covers 15,763 km2. It borders Denmark, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Lower Saxony and Hamburg. The state consists of Holstein, the southern part of the former Duchy of Schleswig, Lauenburg and the formerly independent city of Lübeck. The Kiel Canal connects Brunsbüttel on the North Sea with Kiel on the Baltic Sea.

Saxon Holstein became part of the Holy Roman Empire after Charlemagne's Saxon campaigns in the late 8th century, and from 811 the River Eider was its northern border. Between 500 and 1200 Schleswig was part of Denmark. In the 12th century Duke Abel came into conflict with his brother King Eric IV and won autonomy for Schleswig as a duchy. From 1460 the Danish king ruled both Schleswig and Holstein as their duke, although Holstein belonged to the Holy Roman Empire.

In the 19th century both Danes and Germans claimed the duchies, in a dispute called the Schleswig-Holstein Question. Germans wanted both to join the German Confederation and cited the Treaty of Ribe, by which they were to stay forever undivided, while Danes held that the Eider was Denmark's natural border. Holstein was entirely German-speaking, while Schleswig was predominantly Danish-speaking until a shift to German began in the south in the late 18th and early 19th centuries.

In 1848 Denmark tried to annex the area and Prussia invaded, beginning the First Schleswig War, which Denmark won. Prussia and Austria won the Second Schleswig War of 1864, and the territory became the Prussian Province of Schleswig-Holstein rather than the independent state that German Schleswig-Holsteiners had hoped for.

After the First World War the Allies arranged plebiscites in 1920, and the Danish-speaking north returned to Denmark. After the Second World War the province came under British occupation, and on 23 August 1946 the military government reconstituted it as a separate state.

Schleswig-Holstein is the northernmost of the sixteen German states, with its capital at Kiel and other main cities at Lübeck and Flensburg. German is its official language, and Low German, Danish and North Frisian are recognised minority languages. Its culture combines Danish, Frisian and German elements.
schlieffen-plan: The name Schlieffen Plan was given after the First World War to German war plans influenced by Field Marshal Alfred von Schlieffen, who was Chief of the General Staff of the German Army from 1891 to 1906. In 1905 and 1906 he devised an army deployment plan for a decisive offensive against France, in which German forces were to invade through the Netherlands, Luxembourg and Belgium rather than across the common border.

German strategic thinking in those decades was shaped by the Wars of Unification, which had been short and decided by great battles.
