Helmuth von Moltke the Elder, however, had come to doubt that a quick victory over France was possible once it introduced conscription in 1872, and from 1877 he wrote plans that allowed for an incomplete victory settled by diplomats. Schlieffen was appointed in February 1891 as a safe choice, junior and little known outside the General Staff.

Helmuth von Moltke the Younger succeeded Schlieffen on 1 January 1906, beset with doubts about a German victory in a great European war. He kept the idea of a large enveloping manoeuvre, partly because the Japanese victory in the Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905 had weakened Russia. Records of his thinking are fragmentary, and most pre-war planning was secret.

When war came, the German deployment plan, Aufmarsch II, concentrated the army, less 20 per cent to defend Prussia and the coast, on the Belgian border, to force a decisive battle against the French north of their frontier fortifications. France put into effect Plan XVII, an offensive into Alsace-Lorraine and southern Belgium, in the fighting later named the Battle of the Frontiers. The French attacks suffered worse losses than expected and were repulsed.

After the defeat of 1918, official historians of the Reichsarchiv described the plan as a blueprint for victory, and blamed Moltke for ruining it after the First Battle of the Marne, 5–12 September 1914. In 1956 Gerhard Ritter's Der Schlieffenplan: Kritik eines Mythos began a revision, and from the 1970s Martin van Creveld, John Keegan, Hew Strachan and others judged that railways and roads made it impossible to move enough troops far enough and fast enough for a decisive battle if the French retreated.

Much of the Prussian army archive was destroyed in the bombing of Potsdam in April 1945, but some records resurfaced after the fall of the German Democratic Republic, allowing an outline of German war planning for the first time. Terence Zuber argued that the plan was a myth of the 1920s; later scholarship did not uphold this, though it revealed that Schlieffen had been far less dogmatic than presumed.
schmalkalden: Schmalkalden lies in the district of Schmalkalden-Meiningen, in the south-west of Thuringia. It stands on the southern slope of the Thuringian Forest, on the Schmalkalde river, a tributary of the Werra. It is twinned with Fontaine in the Isère in France and with Recklinghausen in Germany.

The place is first mentioned in a deed of 874 as Smalcalta, in the Frankish duchy of Thuringia, and received town privileges about 1180. When Landgrave Henry Raspe of Thuringia died without issue in 1247, it passed to the House of Henneberg-Schleusingen, while the major part of the landgraviate fell to the House of Wettin in Meissen. To secure their acquisition the counts of Henneberg allied with the Landgraviate of Hesse and concluded an inheritance treaty. In 1360, together with Landgrave Henry II of Hesse, they paid off Frederick V, Burgrave of Nuremberg, a son of Elisabeth of Henneberg.

In 1531 the town hall was the site where Protestant princes under the lead of Landgrave Philip I of Hesse established the Schmalkaldic League, to protect their religious and political interests. In 1537 the Smalcald Articles were drawn up there by Martin Luther, Philipp Melanchthon and other reformers. When the Henneberg line became extinct in 1583, its share was inherited by William IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel, who made the town a residence and built Wilhelmsburg Castle, finished in 1590.

The Lordship of Schmalkalden remained an exclave of Hesse. From 1868 it was part of the Prussian province of Hesse-Nassau, until it was incorporated into the Province of Saxony in 1944; in 1945 it became part of the State of Thuringia. The town was heavily damaged by bombing in the war and from 1949 formed part of East Germany with Thuringia. It has its present political configuration since reunification.
schmalkaldic-league: The League was officially established on 27 February 1531 as a defensive religious alliance: its members pledged to defend each other if Emperor Charles V attacked their territories. At the insistence of the Elector of Saxony, membership was conditional on agreement to the Lutheran Augsburg Confession or the Reformed Tetrapolitan Confession. Unlike earlier alliances such as the League of Torgau it had a substantial military, the members agreeing to provide 10,000 infantry and 2,000 cavalry for their mutual protection.

Its formation, together with the advance of Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent in 1532, led Ferdinand of Austria to grant a religious peace, concluded at Nuremberg on 23 July 1532. Supporters of the Reformation obtained religious liberty until the meeting of a council.

In December 1535 the League opened itself to anyone who subscribed to the Augsburg Confession, and Anhalt, Württemberg, Pomerania and the cities of Augsburg, Frankfurt am Main and Kempten joined. It allied with Denmark-Norway in 1538 and gained the Electoral Palatinate in 1545. The members rarely provoked Charles directly, but they confiscated church land, expelled bishops and Catholic princes and helped spread Lutheranism through northern Germany. Martin Luther attended the meeting of 1537, for which he prepared the Smalcald Articles; they were not formally adopted then but entered the Book of Concord in 1580.

For fifteen years the League met no opposition, because Charles was at war with France and the Ottoman Empire. Francis I of France, though he persecuted Protestants at home, supported the princes from 1535 until the Treaty of Crépy in 1544. Once at peace, Charles turned on the League. In the Schmalkaldic War of 1546–1547 its leaders could not agree on a plan of battle; on 24 April 1547 the imperial forces routed them at the Battle of Mühlberg, and Philip of Hesse surrendered in May. Reformers such as Martin Bucer fled to England.

In 1548 Charles forced the League to accept the Augsburg Interim. A Protestant victory in the Second Schmalkaldic War in 1552 made him flee across the Alps, and Ferdinand signed the Peace of Passau, which granted some freedoms to Protestants. Three years later the Peace of Augsburg gave Lutheranism official status in the Holy Roman Empire and let princes choose the religion of their domains, by the principle of cuius regio, eius religio.
scholar-officials: The Chinese term, shi dafu, joins two ranks that were once distinct. In the order ascribed to the Duke of Zhou under the Western Zhou dynasty, the dafu were aristocrats who served as officers, and the shi stood between them and the ordinary people and could hold only low offices. During the Warring States period, as states annexed one another and bureaucracies grew, talented shi gave valuable service to their lords and gained influence, while dafu became an office and ceased to be a hereditary rank. The two merged. In the scheme of the Four Occupations the scholar-officials stood first, above farmers, artisans and merchants.

From the Han dynasty to the end of the Northern and Southern dynasties, officials were chosen through the recommendatory and nine-rank systems, and came mostly from prominent clans such as the Wang clan of Langya and the Cui clan of Qinghe, which supplied officials for generations and intermarried with one another and with the imperial family. The civil service examination was officially established in 587 under the Sui dynasty. In the early Tang dynasty Empress Wu Zetian reformed it by instituting a metropolitan examination, whose graduates were called jinshi; candidates were tested on poems and essays.

The Song dynasty is described as the golden age of the class. Examination had become the main path to office and the bureaucracy replaced the aristocracy. The Song was also the only dynasty to grant scholar-officials a judicial privilege: one who committed a crime faced internal impeachment in place of the ordinary courts, and for a lesser offence only a reprimand. Under the Yuan, Ming and Qing dynasties the fixed form of the eight-legged essay dominated the examinations, and the political climate left officials less free to speak and write. The Qing government abolished the examinations in 1905, and the class gradually disappeared.

Only a few degree-holders became court or local officials. Most stayed in their villages and towns as social leaders: they taught in private schools, organised welfare, helped settle minor disputes, supervised community projects, kept local order, conducted Confucian ceremonies and assisted in collecting taxes. The district magistrate, who was barred from serving in his home district, depended on them for advice, which gave them power to benefit themselves and their clients. In Confucian theory ministers were not mere subordinates and might oppose an unfit ruler. The system offered a path of upward mobility but had no formal safeguard against corruption beyond the moral teaching it examined.
scholasticism: The words scholastic and scholasticism come from the Latin scholasticus, the Latin form of the Greek scholastikos, meaning of or pertaining to schools, so that the scholastics were roughly schoolmen. Its foundations were laid by Boethius through his logical and theological essays. The Carolingian Renaissance brought the first significant renewal of learning in the West: Charlemagne drew scholars from England and Ireland and by a decree of 787 established schools at every abbey in his empire. Among them was Johannes Scotus Eriugena (815–877), who knew Greek and translated works into Latin. Lanfranc and Anselm of Canterbury in the 11th century and Peter Abelard in France are counted among its founders.

Scholasticism was a method of learning more than a philosophy or a theology, with a strong emphasis on dialectical reasoning to extend knowledge by inference and to resolve contradictions. A teacher would choose a book by an established authority and read it with the class. Points where sources disagreed were written down as sententiae, and the two sides were then reconciled by philological analysis, which showed that words could have several meanings, or by logical analysis.

Instruction had several parts. In the lectio a teacher read an authoritative text followed by a commentary, with no questions allowed. The meditatio let students reflect on the text, and in the quaestio they could ask the questions that had occurred to them. Disputations were arranged to resolve controversial questions: each side of an either/or question was argued in turn and the arguments against the chosen position were refuted.

The 13th and early 14th centuries are generally seen as the high period of scholasticism. Universities grew in the large cities, and the Franciscans, founded by Francis of Assisi in 1209, and the Dominicans, founded by St Dominic in 1215, competed for control of them. The Franciscan Bonaventure held that reason can discover truth only when it is illuminated by faith. The Dominicans Albertus Magnus and Thomas Aquinas made more use of Aristotle. Aquinas's Summa Theologica (1265–1274) is considered the pinnacle of scholastic philosophy.

Scholastic methods outlasted the Middle Ages. After the Reformation Calvinists largely adopted the scholastic method of theology, while differing about sources of authority and its content. A revival of medieval scholastic philosophy, sometimes called neo-Thomism, began in the second half of the 19th century.
scipio-aemilianus: Scipio Aemilianus was the second son of Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus, the victor of the Third Macedonian War, and his first wife, Papiria Masonis. He was adopted by his first cousin Publius Cornelius Scipio, a son of Publius Cornelius Scipio Africanus, who had defeated Hannibal. At seventeen he took part in his father's campaign in Greece. Plutarch relates that when he was missing after the Battle of Pydna the whole army searched for him, and that he returned late, covered with the blood of the enemies he had slain.

In 151 BCE, when Roman recruitment for the war in Hispania had collapsed, he asked the Senate to send him there as a military tribune or legate, and his example led others to volunteer. In the Third Punic War he was a military tribune who repeatedly saved Roman forces from disaster. In 147 BCE he was elected consul although under the legal age and was assigned to Africa without the usual drawing of lots. After a year of fighting he took Carthage and made about 50,000 survivors prisoner, roughly one tenth of the city's population. On the Senate's orders he had the city burnt and razed. It was formerly believed that he also salted the ground, but modern scholars have found no evidence of that.

Elected consul again in 134 BCE, he took command in the Numantine War, restored discipline in a demoralized army and besieged Numantia with a circuit of fortifications nine kilometres long. The Numantines were starved into surrender, and Scipio sold the survivors into slavery and destroyed the city. He served as censor in 142 BCE. A patron of writers and philosophers, he gathered the Scipionic circle, which included Polybius, Panaetius, Lucilius and Terence.

Scipio disliked the land reforms of his brother-in-law Tiberius Gracchus, and he became unpopular when he took the side of Rome's Italian allies against the commission applying the land law of Gracchus. He died at home in 129 BCE, and rumours of murder circulated, naming Cornelia, Sempronia, Fulvius Flaccus, Gaius Gracchus and Gaius Papirius Carbo. Modern historians see no strong evidence for any cause but natural death. According to Polybius, Scipio wept at the burning of Carthage and quoted Homer's lines on the fall of Troy, saying he feared the same fate for Rome.
scotland: The mainland of Scotland makes up the northern third of the island of Great Britain, with a total area of 30,977 square miles (80,231 km2). Its only land border, with England, runs for 96 miles (154 km) between the basin of the River Tweed and the Solway Firth. The mainland is divided into the Highlands, a mountainous region in the north and north-west, the Lowlands, a flatter plain across the centre, and the Southern Uplands along the border. Ben Nevis, at 4,413 feet (1,345 m), is the highest peak of the British Isles.

The earliest known evidence of people in Scotland is stone tools of the Hamburgian culture, made by hunter-gatherers who arrived around 14,500 to 14,000 years ago, soon after the ice sheet retreated. Neolithic farmers came about 6000 years ago. Skara Brae on Orkney, the Callanish Stones on Lewis and Maes Howe on Orkney belong to this period, the stone monuments of the third millennium BCE. The Greek sailor Pytheas made the first written reference in 320 BCE, calling the northern tip of Britain Orcas.

The Roman governor Agricola invaded in 79 CE and defeated a Caledonian army at the Battle of Mons Graupius in 83 CE, but within three years the Roman armies had withdrawn to the Southern Uplands. Under Trajan, who reigned from 98 to 117, Roman control had lapsed to the south of a line between the River Tyne and the Solway Firth, where Hadrian later built his wall. The Kingdom of Scotland emerged as a sovereign state in the 9th century and kept its independence from England partly through an alliance with France.

Its extent was largely fixed by the Treaty of York of 1237 with England and the Treaty of Perth of 1266 with Norway. Orkney and Shetland were acquired from Norway in 1472, and Berwick-upon-Tweed was ceded to England in 1482. James VI succeeded to the English and Irish thrones in 1603, and on 1 May 1707 Scotland and England combined as the Kingdom of Great Britain.

Scotland is a country within the United Kingdom, with Edinburgh as its capital and Glasgow as its largest city. The census of 2022 counted 5,436,600 people. A Scottish Parliament was re-established in 1999 with devolved authority over many areas of domestic policy. Scotland keeps its own legal system, education system and religious history. English and Scots are the most widely spoken languages, while Scottish Gaelic is spoken natively mainly in the Hebrides. Its seven World Heritage Sites include St Kilda, the Old Town and New Town of Edinburgh, New Lanark and the Antonine Wall.
scottish-highlands: The Highlands are the northernmost mountain ranges of Great Britain, divided by the Great Glen between the Grampian Mountains to the south-east and the Northwest Highlands. The name also covers the area north and west of the Highland Boundary Fault, which runs from Arran to Stonehaven, though the exact boundary is not clearly defined, particularly in the east. The region lies on ancient Cambrian and Precambrian rocks uplifted in the Caledonian Orogeny, with Lewisian gneiss up to 3 billion years old, and includes Ben Nevis, the highest mountain in the British Isles. The Highlands are the only area in the British Isles with a boreal forest biome, with remnants of the Caledonian Forest.

The region was home to the Caledonians or Picts and became the mainland stronghold of the Hebridean Gaels, whose Gaelic language succeeded that of their neighbours. The cultural distinction between Highlander and Lowlander was first noted towards the end of the 14th century. The clan was the main social unit, and James VI saw clans as a challenge to royal authority. The Statutes of Iona in 1609 began integrating clan leaders into Scottish society. After the Jacobite rising of 1745 the British government banned the bearing of arms and the wearing of tartan, laws mostly repealed by the end of the 18th century. The Black Watch, raised in 1739, was the first Highland regiment of the British Army.

Between about 1760 and 1850 agricultural improvement brought the Highland clearances, in which many tenants were evicted to make way for large-scale sheep farms; in the west and north they were resettled in crofting communities and worked in kelping and fishing. Famine recurred, and potato blight arrived in 1846. The population, around 300,000 in the 18th and early 19th centuries, then declined through emigration, mostly to Canada, the United States, Australia and New Zealand. Crofters, many in the Free Church after 1843, challenged landlords through the Highland Land League in the 1880s, and the Crofters Holdings (Scotland) Act 1886 reduced rents and guaranteed fixity of tenure.

Inverness is regarded as the capital of the Highlands, and the Highland Council has its administrative centre there. The area is among the most sparsely populated in Europe. Scottish Gaelic, once the language of the region, is now largely confined to the Hebrides, and a Highland form of Scottish English predominates. Tartan and the kilt were adopted by elites in the 1820s after the Ossian cycle and Walter Scott's staging of George IV's visit in 1822, and tartan became a major symbol of Scottish identity.
screw: Most screws are tightened by clockwise rotation, which is called a right-hand thread. Left-hand threads are used in exceptional cases, such as the left pedal of a bicycle, where the twisting force would tend to loosen a right-hand screw. The head of a screw is usually larger than the body, which gives a bearing surface and stops the screw from being driven deeper than its length. The cylindrical part below the head is the shank, and the distance between threads is the pitch. Screws are normally made from wire in three steps: cold heading, thread rolling and a coating such as zinc to prevent corrosion.

Fasteners such as dowels, pins, wedges, mortises and tenons, dovetails and nails were widespread before the screw. The screw was one of the last of the simple machines to be invented. By the 1st century BCE wooden screws were in common use around the Mediterranean in presses for olive oil and for grape juice. Metal screws used as fasteners were rare in Europe before the 15th century, if known at all, and did not become common until machine tools for mass production developed toward the end of the 18th century. The first documented screwdriver appears in the Housebook of Wolfegg Castle, written between 1475 and 1490, but screwdrivers probably did not become widespread until after 1800.

Standard thread forms came late. The English engineer Sir Joseph Whitworth created the first standard in about 1841, and the British Standard Fine thread was added in 1908 because his thread was too coarse for some uses. The British Association thread was devised in 1884 and standardised in 1903, and its sizes were defined in metric terms. In the United States the Unified Thread Standard is most common, while in much of the world the ISO metric screw thread has displaced the older systems. Whitworth threads are still used in UK scaffolding and on photographic tripods, and BA threads in railway signalling and in clocks and moving-coil meters.
scythians: The Scythians, also called the Pontic Scythians, were an Eastern Iranic equestrian nomadic people. They migrated from Central Asia to the Pontic Steppe, in present-day Ukraine and southern Russia, during the ninth and eighth centuries BCE, and remained there until the third century BCE. They already practised goldsmithing and bronze-casting, as gold pieces from the eighth-century BCE Aržan-1 kurgan show. Their name comes from the endonym *Skuδa, meaning archers.

Skilled in mounted warfare, they displaced the Agathyrsi and the Cimmerians as the dominant power on the western steppe in the eighth century BCE. From about 750 BCE they settled in the Ciscaucasian Steppe, concentrated in the Kuban valley, where their capital stood until the end of the seventh century BCE. In the seventh century BCE they crossed the Caucasus and often raided West Asia with the Cimmerians.

The sources are Akkadian cuneiform texts, which deal with early Scythian history from the seventh century BCE, and Graeco-Roman writers, above all Herodotus, who cover the whole history but mix in folk tales. Scythian raids destabilised the balance among Assyria, Urartu and Phrygia and spread steppe military technology in West Asia.

In the late sixth century BCE the Scythians left Ciscaucasia and Sauromatian incomers arrived on the Pontic Steppe, giving rise to the Classical Scythian period, with a rise in monumental burials. The Sarmatians later invaded and the Pontic kingdom collapsed, leaving the Scythians in fortified settlements along the rivers and in the two regions called Little Scythia. By the third century CE the remnants were overwhelmed by the Goths, and the last Scythians were absorbed by later populations.

Clan groups formed the basis of society, and clan elders could depose kings. The king came from the dominant tribe, the Royal Scythians. Their herds were about 40 percent horses, 40 percent cattle and 18 percent sheep, with no pigs, and mares' milk was an important food. Trade with the Greek colonies on the Black Sea brought exports of grain, iron, furs, slaves and mounted archers, and by the third century BCE many had become settled farmers.

Mounted archery was their main form of warfare, with the recurved composite bow, and they invented the saddle in the seventh century BCE. Their remains include kurgans, the royal ones holding weapons, horse harness and gold objects in Scythian animal style.
sea-of-azov: The Sea of Azov is a shelf sea about 360 kilometres long and 180 kilometres wide, with an area of 39,000 square kilometres. It joins the Black Sea through the narrow Strait of Kerch, about 4 kilometres wide, and is sometimes regarded as a northern extension of the Black Sea. The Don and Kuban rivers bring sand, silt and shells, which build bays, limans and long narrow spits; the Arabat Spit stretches over 112 kilometres. The inflow keeps the salinity low, almost fresh in places, and the sea is the shallowest in the world, between 0.9 and 14 metres deep. The name Azov probably derives from a settlement whose name comes from the Kipchak Turkish asak or azaq, meaning lowlands.

Traces of Neolithic settlement lie in the area now covered by the sea. In antiquity it was known as the Maeotis Swamp, from the Maeotians who lived by fishing and farming near its northeastern marshes; it remains unclear whether the sea took its name from them or they from it. The marshes around the mouth of the Tanais, today's Don, served as a check on the migration of nomadic peoples from the steppe. Ancient geographers had only a vague idea of its extent: Herodotus judged it as large as the Black Sea, Pseudo-Scylax about half as large, and it was long believed to connect directly with the Arctic Ocean.

The sea was often a theatre of conflict between Russia, seeking naval expansion to the south, and the Ottoman power. In 1695–96 Peter I led two campaigns to take the Turkish fortress of Azov, defended by a garrison of 7,000. The first, in 1695, brought an army of 31 thousand men and 170 cannon to the fortress; after two failed assaults on 5 August and 25 September the siege was lifted. During the Crimean War, British and French forces took Kerch on 12 May 1855 and then besieged Taganrog, which withstood them despite their great superiority in numbers, and their army withdrew around August 1855.

The sea has long been an important waterway, and navigation grew after the Volga–Don Canal was built in 1952, linking it with the Volga. The major ports are Taganrog, Mariupol, Yeysk and Berdyansk. Fishing has long been a major activity, with sturgeon, pike-perch and bream among the valuable species. Dams, over-fishing and pollution have reduced the catch, and the anchovy fisheries have collapsed.
sea-of-japan: The Sea of Japan is almost completely enclosed. The Japanese archipelago separates it from the Pacific Ocean, and like the Mediterranean it has almost no tides. It has a surface area of about 1,050,000 square kilometres, a mean depth of 1,752 metres and a maximum depth of 4,568 metres. It is joined to neighbouring seas by five straits: the Strait of Tartary, La Pérouse Strait, the Tsugaru Strait, the Kanmon Straits and the Korea Strait. All are shallow, which isolates its water and life from the Pacific. The sea has no large islands, bays or capes. Few rivers flow into it, though the four largest rivers of Japan, the Shinano, Ishikari, Agano and Mogami, do.

Its geological history is long. The Japan Sea began to open in the Early Miocene, and the northern and southern parts of the Japanese archipelago separated. The straits formed in recent geological periods, and the Tsugaru and Tsushima straits, the oldest, interrupted the migration of elephants into the Japanese islands about 2.6 million years ago.

For centuries the sea protected Japan from land invasions, particularly by the Mongols. Asian ships had long crossed it, and from the 18th century European ships did too. Russian expeditions of 1733–1743 mapped Sakhalin and the Japanese islands. In the 1780s the Frenchman Jean-François de Galaup, comte de Lapérouse, sailed north across the sea through the strait later named for him. In 1796 the British naval officer William Robert Broughton explored the Strait of Tartary and the coasts of the Russian Far East and the Korean Peninsula. In 1849 the Russian explorer Gennady Nevelskoy found the strait between the mainland and Sakhalin.

American, Canadian and French whaleships hunted in the sea between 1847 and 1892, chiefly for right whales, and then humpbacks. In the peak years of 1848 and 1849 over 170 vessels cruised there in all. The Chinese name for the sea was once the Sea of Whales. Japanese scientific study of the sea began only in 1915 and became systematic from the 1920s.

Several names are in use: Nihonkai in Japan, Donghae, the East Sea, in South Korea, and Yaponskoye more in Russia. Japan holds that the name Sea of Japan has been the internationally accepted term since the early 19th century, while South Korea says that the East Sea was in use before Japanese colonial rule and asks that it be used alongside the other. The International Hydrographic Organization has used the name Japan Sea in its publication on the limits of seas since 1928. Fishing is the dominant economic activity, and Vladivostok, the terminus of the Trans-Siberian Railway, is a major port.
sea-of-marmara: The Sea of Marmara lies entirely within Turkey and links the Black Sea and the Aegean Sea by way of the Bosporus and the Dardanelles, separating the country's European and Asian sides. It covers 11,350 square kilometres, measures roughly 280 by 80 kilometres, and is considered the smallest sea in the world. Its maximum depth is 1,370 metres. The south coast is heavily indented and has the Gulf of İzmit, the Gulf of Gemlik, the Gulf of Bandırma and the Gulf of Erdek.

The surface water averages about 22 parts per thousand of salt, slightly more than the Black Sea and about two-thirds that of most oceans. At the bottom it is much more saline, averaging about 38 parts per thousand, like the Mediterranean, and this dense water does not rise to the surface.

The sea is named after Marmara Island, the largest island on its south side, which is rich in marble, mármaron in Greek. In classical antiquity it was called the Propontis, from the Greek pro, in front of, and pontos, sea, because the ancient Greeks sailed through it to reach the Black Sea. In Greek mythology a storm on the Propontis brought the Argonauts back to an island they had left, which led to a battle in which either Jason or Heracles killed King Cyzicus, who had mistaken them for his Pelasgian enemies.

Two groups of islands lie in the sea. To the north are the Princes' Islands, made up of the inhabited islands Kınaliada, Burgazada, Heybeliada, Büyükada and Sedef Adası, and several uninhabited ones. They are reached by ferry from both shores of Istanbul and form part of its conurbation. To the south are the Marmara Islands, with Marmara Island, Avşa, Paşalimanı and Ekinlik inhabited and 17 largely uninhabited islands, among them the prison island of Imralı. They lie within Balıkesir Province and are reached from Tekirdağ or from Erdek.

The North Anatolian Fault runs under the sea. It has caused several major earthquakes, among them those of İzmit in August 1999 and Düzce in November 1999. The August earthquake is commonly called the Marmara Earthquake, since its epicentre lay under the sea and the places worst affected, by the shaking and a tsunami, lay along its shores. About one third of Turkey's population lives in the basin, and Istanbul, the largest city of the country, stands on the sea.
sea-of-okhotsk: The Sea of Okhotsk covers 1,583,000 square kilometres, with a mean depth of 859 metres and a maximum depth of 3,372 metres. It connects to the Sea of Japan on either side of Sakhalin, through the Gulf of Tartary and through the La Pérouse Strait. It is the coldest sea in East Asia and the southernmost sea in the Northern Hemisphere that freezes over seasonally.

Cold Siberian air forms sea ice over the north-western shelf, where fresh water from the Amur River lowers the salinity of the surface and so raises its freezing point. In a typical winter 50 to 70 percent of the surface is covered, with ice present from about December until early summer. The circulation is cyclonic, and the sea is among the most biologically productive in the world, with walleye pollock, herring, salmon, squid and king crab among its catches.

The Okhotsk culture and the later Ainu people, coastal fishing and hunting peoples, lived on the lands around the sea and in northern Japan. Russian explorers Vassili Poyarkov in 1639 and Ivan Moskvitin in 1645 were the first Europeans to visit it. The Dutch captain Maarten Gerritsz Vries entered from the south-east in 1643 and charted parts of the Sakhalin coast and the Kuril Islands, but did not realise that Sakhalin and Hokkaido were islands. The sea was sometimes called the Sea of Kamchatka.

The port of Okhotsk was the first and foremost Russian settlement on the shore; it gave up commercial supremacy to Ayan in the 1840s. The Second Kamchatka Expedition under Vitus Bering began mapping the whole coast in 1733, and the Russian-American Company almost monopolised commercial navigation in the first half of the nineteenth century. Mamiya Rinzō and Gennady Nevelskoy showed that Sakhalin was an island. American whalers took bowhead whales from 1847, and from 1854 to 1856 an average of over 160 vessels a year cruised the sea.

Japan administered South Sakhalin as Karafuto Prefecture from 1907 to 1949 and held the Kuril Islands until 1945, after which the Soviet Union occupied them. During the Cold War the sea was a base for Soviet ballistic missile submarines and the scene of the Soviet attack on Korean Air Lines Flight 007 in 1983.

With the exception of Hokkaido, the sea is surrounded by territory administered by the Russian Federation. Japan claims the southern Kuril Islands, which it calls the Northern Territories. Its main ports include Magadan in Russia and Abashiri, Monbetsu and Wakkanai on Hokkaido.
sebastian-of-portugal: Sebastian was born on 20 January 1554, the feast of Saint Sebastian, whose name he was given. He was the only child of João Manuel, Prince of Portugal, and Joanna of Austria, and was born two weeks after his father's death, so he was heir apparent from birth. His mother left him soon afterwards to serve as regent of Spain and never saw him again. He succeeded his grandfather, King John III, at the age of three, and a regency followed, first under his grandmother Catherine of Austria and then under his great-uncle Cardinal Henry of Évora.

He grew up under heavy Jesuit influence and became extremely devout, carrying a copy of Thomas Aquinas at his belt. He did not marry, and a plan of Catherine de' Medici to marry him to her daughter Margaret of Valois failed.

During his short personal reign, which began when he attained his majority in 1568, Sebastian strengthened ties with the Holy Roman Empire, England and France and restructured much of the kingdom's administrative, judicial and military life. In 1569 Duarte Nunes de Leão compiled the laws in the Código Sebastiânico, and in 1570 the king ordered that Brazilian Indians should not be used as slaves. During the plague of Lisbon in 1569 he brought doctors from Seville and created two hospitals.

Sebastian dreamed of a great crusade against Morocco, where several Portuguese way stations on the route to India had been lost. His chance came in 1576 when Abu Abdallah Mohammed II Saadi lost his throne and fled to Portugal. In June 1578 an army of 17,000 men, including foreign mercenaries and almost all the country's nobility, sailed from Lisbon.

At the Battle of Alcácer Quibir, also called the Battle of the Three Kings, the Portuguese army was routed by Abd al-Malik at the head of more than 60,000 men. Sebastian was last seen riding headlong into the enemy lines. Philip II claimed to have received his remains and buried them in the Jerónimos Monastery in Lisbon after 1580, but the body could not be identified. His great-uncle Henry succeeded him. The belief that he would return, called Sebastianism, led to four pretenders during the Iberian Union of 1580 to 1640, and he came to be known as the Desired and the Hidden. His reputation in Morocco remained positive as a symbol of chivalry.
second-crusade: After the First Crusade three Crusader states stood in the east, the Kingdom of Jerusalem, the Principality of Antioch and the County of Edessa, with the County of Tripoli added in 1109. Edessa was the most northerly, weakest and least populated, and was exposed to attack from Artuqid, Danishmendid and Seljuk neighbours. Zengi, atabeg of Mosul, took Aleppo in 1128. News of Edessa's fall reached Europe in 1145, and Pope Eugene III issued the bull Quantum praedecessores on 1 December. It met a poor response and was reissued on 1 March 1146. Bernard of Clairvaux preached the crusade at Vézelay on 31 March 1146, where Louis VII and Eleanor of Aquitaine took the cross, and then in Germany, where Conrad III received it at Speyer.

The German army of about 20,000 men left in May 1147 and the French in June, both going overland through Hungary and Byzantine territory. Emperor Manuel I Komnenos feared an attack and posted troops, and the Germans, after a clash at Constantinople, crossed into Anatolia quickly. Later sources, notably Odo of Deuil, accuse Manuel of having the Turks attack the Crusaders, but this is likely an invention of Odo. Both armies were separately defeated by the Seljuks. Louis reached Antioch on 19 March 1148 but refused Raymond of Poitiers's request to attack Aleppo, preferring to finish his pilgrimage to Jerusalem.

On 24 June 1148 the High Court of Jerusalem and the Crusaders met at Palmarea near Acre and chose to attack Damascus, a former ally of Jerusalem. Historians have long called this inexplicable folly, though David Nicolle defends it, arguing that Damascus was the most powerful Muslim state in southern Syria. The Crusaders arrived at Darayya on 23 July 1148 and were pushed back from the orchards by the defenders and Nur ad-Din. They moved to a less defended eastern plain with little food and water. The local lords refused to continue, and the army retreated on 28 July, harassed by Turkish archers all the way.

In the east each side felt betrayed by the other, and the distrust lingered for a generation, to the ruin of the Christian kingdoms. In Iberia the crusade was successful: crusaders from England landed at Porto in June 1147 and helped Afonso I of Portugal take Lisbon after a siege from 1 July to 25 October, and they also helped conquer Sintra, Almada, Palmela and Setúbal. Louis left Jerusalem in 1149, and he and Eleanor, barely speaking, boarded separate ships in April 1149. Bernard of Clairvaux, humiliated, wrote an apology to the pope attributing the failure to the sins of the Crusaders.
second-french-empire: On 2 December 1851 Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte, elected President of the Republic in 1848, dissolved the National Assembly without the constitutional right to do so and restored universal male suffrage. A referendum later that month, which reported 92 percent support, approved a new constitution that made him president for ten years. A second referendum in November 1852 reported 97 percent, though most of the yes votes were manufactured. The Senate re-established the empire on 2 December 1852, and the constitution changed little beyond replacing the word president with emperor and making the post hereditary.

The constitution of 1852 entrusted all executive power to the emperor. The legislative body was elected by universal suffrage but could not propose laws or vote the budget in detail, and the press worked under caution money and official warnings. Napoleon III consolidated three dozen small railway lines into six major companies centred on Paris, and with Georges-Eugène Haussmann rebuilt the capital.

After a general amnesty on 16 August 1859 the regime moved towards a liberal, and later parliamentary, empire. A senatus-consulte of 8 September 1869 replaced personal government with a parliamentary monarchy, and Émile Ollivier headed a ministry from 2 January 1870. A plebiscite on 8 May 1870 brought seven and a half million votes in favour and one and a half million against.

Abroad, the Crimean War ended in 1856 with a peace that excluded Russia from the Black Sea. Napoleon III doubled the area of the overseas empire, with New Caledonia, Cochinchina and a protectorate over Cambodia in 1863. The intervention in Mexico, meant to set up the Second Mexican Empire under Maximilian, ended when the United States demanded French withdrawal; Maximilian stayed and was executed.

France declared war on Prussia on 15 July 1870 and found itself without allies. The French army surrendered at the Battle of Sedan, Napoleon III was taken prisoner, and the Third French Republic was proclaimed on 4 September 1870. France gave up Alsace and Lorraine, and the German Empire was created.

Napoleon III and the Empress Eugénie went into exile in England; their bodies lie in a mausoleum at Farnborough, today St Michael's Abbey. Historians of the 1930s and 1940s disparaged the regime as a precursor of fascism, but later writers have treated it as a modernising one, judging its foreign policy a failure and its domestic legacy more favourably.
second-international: By the 1880s rapid industrialisation, especially in Germany, had created a new urban proletariat, and the extension of the vote made mass parliamentary parties of the working class possible. The strongest was the Social Democratic Party of Germany, founded in 1875 at Gotha by a merger of Marxist and Lassallean groups and led by Wilhelm Liebknecht and August Bebel. French socialism was more divided, among several factions.

The demand for an eight-hour day was taken up by French socialists, and the centenary of the French Revolution in 1889 offered an occasion for a congress. Because of the French divisions two rival congresses met in Paris: the Possibilists, with the British Trades Union Congress, in the Rue de Lancry, and the Marxists, led by Jules Guesde and supported by the SPD, in the Salle Petrelle.

The early congresses were absorbed by the struggle against the anarchists. After their exclusion the International had to face the question of revolution or reform. Eduard Bernstein argued from 1896 that Marx's predictions of collapse had proved wrong and that the movement should embrace gradual reform. In France, the socialist Alexandre Millerand joined the government of Pierre Waldeck-Rousseau in June 1899, causing a great controversy. At Amsterdam in 1904 Jean Jaurès and August Bebel debated, and the congress condemned revisionism and ministerialism.

After the Russo-Japanese War and the Russian Revolution of 1905, preventing war became its central task, and the congresses of Stuttgart (1907), Copenhagen (1910) and Basel (1912) passed ever more urgent resolutions. The containment of the Balkan Wars brought optimism, and by 1913 many leaders believed the threat of war had receded. The International was caught off guard by the crisis of July 1914. Jaurès was assassinated, and the major parties supported their governments in the war, a split between pro-war majorities and an anti-war minority that prefigured the later division between social democracy and communism.

The Second International was a loose federation of autonomous national parties and trade unions, with no executive machinery in its first decade; the London Congress of 1896 affirmed the autonomy of national groups. The Paris Congress of 1900 created the International Socialist Bureau in Brussels, which grew in authority under its secretary Camille Huysmans after 1905 but remained an organ of correlation, not direction.

The conference at Bern in February 1919 failed to revive it, and it was succeeded by the Communist International in 1919 and the Labour and Socialist International in 1923. Lenin called its collapse a betrayal by opportunist leaders; Georges Haupt argued that it came from the International's long-standing contradictions, among them parties with no means of enforcing joint action.
second-schleswig-war: Denmark received its first liberal constitution in 1848, and the movement of the large German majority in Holstein and southern Schleswig to form a united, independent state was suppressed in the First Schleswig War. Holstein was ethnically German and had been a German fief before 1806; Schleswig was a Danish fief with a mixed population speaking Low German, Danish and North Frisian. Two systems of government existed within one state, constitutional monarchy in Denmark and absolutism in the duchies, under one cabinet, which produced deadlock.

On 18 November 1863 King Christian IX signed the November Constitution, which established a shared law of succession and a common parliament for Schleswig and Denmark. The German Confederation saw this as a breach of the London Protocol of 1852. In December Saxon and Hanoverian troops entered Holstein for the Confederation.

Otto von Bismarck had been under great pressure since the constitutional crisis of 1862 over army taxes, and hoped to win Prussian liberals by the liberation of Schleswig. Prussia and Austria alone decided to invade Schleswig rather than only occupy Holstein. On 16 January 1864 Bismarck issued an ultimatum demanding that the November Constitution be abolished within 48 hours, which Denmark rejected, and on 1 February Prussian and Austrian forces crossed the border.

The Danish army numbered about 38,000 men, of whom about 36,000 defended the Danevirke, a task said to need 50,000. Political pressure led to a frontal defence of Jutland at the Danevirke. In a hard winter the waters and marshes at both ends froze and let the Germans bypass the line; an attempt near Missunde failed, but when they appeared in force in its rear the Danish high command ordered it abandoned. The war ended on 30 October 1864 with the Treaty of Vienna.

Denmark ceded Schleswig, except the island of Ærø, together with Holstein and Saxe-Lauenburg to Prussia and Austria, and about 200,000 Danes came under German rule. The Peace of Prague of 1866 promised a plebiscite in north Schleswig, set aside by Prussia and Austria in 1878. After the German defeat in 1918 a plebiscite returned North Schleswig to Denmark.

The war is generally considered a national trauma for Denmark. Sweden-Norway, despite a promise of troops, did not help. Many Danes in the ceded lands were later conscripted into the German army in the First World War. In Prussia the victory led liberals to cease opposing Bismarck, and the Landtag retroactively legalised the taxes he had collected without its consent.
second-world-war: The causes of the war included unresolved tensions after the First World War and the rise of fascism in Europe and militarism in Japan. Under the Treaty of Versailles Germany lost around 13 per cent of its home territory and all its overseas possessions, and had reparations imposed and its armed forces limited. Benito Mussolini's fascist movement seized power in Italy between 1922 and 1925, and Adolf Hitler became chancellor of Germany in 1933. Earlier events included Japan's invasion of Manchuria in 1931, Italy's invasion of Ethiopia from October 1935, the Spanish Civil War, in which Germany and Italy backed General Francisco Franco's Nationalists, and the Second Sino-Japanese War from July 1937.

The war began on 1 September 1939, when Nazi Germany invaded Poland, and the United Kingdom and France declared war on Germany on 3 September. The Soviet Union invaded Poland on 17 September, and the two states partitioned it. In 1940 Germany conquered Norway, Denmark, Belgium, Luxembourg and the Netherlands, and France fell in June. In June 1941 Germany invaded the Soviet Union. In December 1941 Japan attacked American and British territories, including Pearl Harbor, and the United States entered the war. Japan's advance was halted at the Battle of Midway in June 1942.

In early 1943 the Axis were defeated in North Africa and at Stalingrad. In 1944 the Western Allies landed in Normandy while the Soviet Union advanced into Central Europe. Germany surrendered unconditionally on 8 May 1945. The United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki on 6 and 9 August, and Japan signed a surrender document on 2 September 1945.

An estimated 60 million to more than 75 million people died, a majority of them civilians. About 6 million Jews were killed in the Holocaust, together with millions of Slavs and over 130,000 Romani. Germany lost a quarter of its pre-war territory and nine million Germans were expelled from the eastern provinces. German and Japanese leaders were tried for war crimes. The United Nations came into being on 24 October 1945, and the Soviet Union and the United States emerged as rival superpowers, setting the stage for the Cold War. The weakened great powers of Europe saw the decolonisation of Africa and Asia follow, and Italy lost its monarchy and colonial empire.
secretary-general-of-the-united-nations: The role of the secretary-general and of the Secretariat is laid out in Chapter XV, Articles 97 to 101, of the United Nations Charter. The Charter calls the secretary-general the chief administrative officer of the organisation and gives the power to make employment decisions about Secretariat staff. It also empowers the secretary-general to inform the Security Council of any matter which in his opinion may threaten the maintenance of international peace and security. The qualifications, selection process and tenure of the office are open to interpretation and have been established by custom. The secretary-general also chairs the Chief Executives Board for Coordination, which brings together the heads of all UN funds, programmes and specialized agencies.

Appointment is by the General Assembly on the recommendation of the Security Council, so any of its five permanent members can veto a nomination. By precedent the appointee may not be a citizen of a permanent member, and most secretaries-general have been compromise candidates from middle powers with little prior fame. The length of the term is discretionary, but every secretary-general since 1971 has been appointed to a five-year term, and every one since 1961 was chosen for a second term except Boutros Boutros-Ghali, vetoed by the United States in 1996. Incumbents have avoided seeking a third term since 1981, when China cast sixteen vetoes against a third term for Kurt Waldheim.

Many powers are informal, and some holders have taken activist roles while others have been more administrative. Much depends on the use of their good offices, steps taken in public and in private to prevent international disputes from arising, escalating or spreading. Examples include Dag Hammarskjöld's promotion of an armistice between the warring parties of the Arab-Israel conflict, U Thant's role in de-escalating the Cuban Missile Crisis and Javier Pérez de Cuéllar's negotiation of a ceasefire in the Iran-Iraq War. Hammarskjöld is the only holder to have died in office.

Observers have variously called the office the world's most visible bully pulpit or the world's moderator. The official residence, a townhouse at 3 Sutton Place in Manhattan built for Anne Morgan in 1921, was given to the United Nations by Arthur A. Houghton Jr. in 1972; before that, secretaries-general chose where to live.
segou: Ségou lies on the right bank of the Niger in south-central Mali, 235 kilometres north-east of Bamako, and is the capital of the Ségou Region. In the middle of the 19th century four villages called Ségou stood along about 12 kilometres of the bank: Ségou-Koro, Ségou-Bougou, Ségou-Koura and Ségou-Sikoro. The present town is on the site of Ségou-Sikoro.

Its origins are contested. Some derive the name from Sikoro, meaning at the foot of a shea butter tree, others from Cheikou, a marabout said to have founded the city, and others hold that Bozo fishermen coming from the north in the 4th century founded villages along the river. The 11th century brought an influx of Soninke people escaping the collapse of the Ghana Empire, followed by Mandinka.

Around 1650 Kaladian Coulibaly overthrew the ruling Koita dynasty and established a powerful if short-lived kingdom with Ségou-Koro as its capital. His great-grandson Mamary Coulibaly, known as Bitòn, became chief of his tòn, an association of men, after 1700. By 1712 he had used his military strength to displace local elders, and he extended the Bambara Empire over regional commercial centres such as Macina and Djenné; Timbuktu became a tributary. A distinct urban architecture, including mosques, began to emerge at Ségou-Koro.

After Bitòn's death in 1755 the capital moved repeatedly. In 1766 Ngolo Diarra, a former slave and warrior, took control of the empire and moved the capital to Ségou-Sikoro. The Diarra dynasty ruled until the mid-19th century. When Mungo Park passed through in 1797 he described the city, its many canoes on the river, its crowded population and cultivated countryside, as a prospect of civilization and magnificence he had not expected to find in Africa.

On 10 March 1861 the Muslim Toucouleur leader El Hadj Oumar Tall conquered the town, and the military architect Samba Ndiaye rebuilt some of its defences. Oumar died in 1864 and his son Ahmadu Tall succeeded him, facing repeated rebellions and challenges from his brothers. French forces led by Colonel Louis Archinard entered Ségou on 6 April 1890. France at first ruled indirectly, and on 13 March 1893 made the town the capital of a local cercle.

Ségou remains a regional commercial centre, known for its market, its fishing and its pottery; Kalabougou, across the river, is a large pottery district. Bogolan cloth, weaving and sculpture are also among its crafts. Its people include Bambara, Bozo, Malinke, Soninke, Fulani and Toucouleur, and in 2009 it had 130,690 inhabitants. The Office du Niger, which administers a large irrigation scheme in the region, has its headquarters there, and Maryse Condé's novel Segu tells the city's history from 1797 to its defeat by the army of El Hajj Oumar Tall.
seimas: The word Seimas is of Slavic origin, derived from the Polish sejm through the Ruthenian sejmъ. Traces of large meetings of the nobility appear in the negotiations for the Treaty of Salynas in 1398, but the first Seimas is considered to have met at Hrodna in 1445, during talks between Casimir IV Jagiellon and the Council of Lords. As the Muscovite–Lithuanian Wars raged, the Grand Duke needed more tax revenue to finance the army and called the Seimas more often. In exchange for taxation the nobility demanded privileges, including a stronger Seimas.

At first it had no legislative power. It debated foreign and domestic affairs, taxes, wars and the treasury. By the beginning of the 16th century it had gained some legislative powers and could petition the Grand Duke to pass certain laws, which he usually granted in return for the nobility's support in taxation and war.

The first widely elected body in Lithuania after the declaration of independence on 16 February 1918 was the Constituent Assembly, elected on 14–15 April 1920 with a turnout of about 90 per cent. It adopted the Constitution on 1 August 1922, and a land reform. The constitution gave broad powers to the Seimas, elected to a three-year term, which would select the Cabinet and elect the President.

The First Seimas, elected on 10–11 October 1922, could not form a sustainable coalition and was dissolved on 12 March 1923. The Second Seimas, elected in May 1923, was the only regular interwar Seimas to complete its full term. With a slim Christian Democrat majority it continued the land reform, expanded primary and secondary schools and introduced social support, but it saw several short-lived governments.

On 11 March 1990 the Supreme Council of the Lithuanian SSR proclaimed independence from the Soviet Union and renamed itself the Supreme Council of the Republic of Lithuania, regarded as the Fifth Seimas. The present Constitution was approved by referendum on 25 October 1992. The first election under it, on 25 October 1992, was won by the Democratic Labor Party, which took 73 of the 141 seats in the Sixth Seimas.

The Seimas is the unicameral legislature of Lithuania. It enacts laws and amendments to the Constitution, passes the budget, confirms the Prime Minister and the Government and ratifies international treaties. Of its 141 members, 71 are elected in single-seat constituencies and 70 by proportional representation, for four years. The Act of the Re-Establishment of the State of Lithuania was proclaimed on 11 March 1990 in the main hall of its building.
seine: The Seine rises at Source-Seine, about 30 kilometres north-west of Dijon on the Langres plateau, and flows through Paris into the English Channel at Le Havre. Its drainage basin lies in the Paris Basin and covers most of northern France. The river is divided into five parts: the Petite Seine from the sources to Montereau-Fault-Yonne, the Haute Seine to Paris, the Paris waterway, the Basse Seine from Paris to Rouen, and the Seine maritime from Rouen to the sea. Ocean-going vessels can reach Rouen, 120 kilometres from the sea. Because the river is only 24 metres above sea level 446 kilometres from its mouth, it flows slowly and is easily navigated.

The name comes from the Gaulish Sēquana, the Celtic Gallo-Roman goddess of the river, to whom offerings were found at the source. The buried remains of a Gallo-Roman temple lie at the same site, and small statues of the goddess Sequana and other ex-votos found there are now in the Dijon archaeological museum. The source has belonged to the city of Paris since 1864.

On 28 or 29 March 845 an army of Vikings led by a chieftain named Reginherus, possibly another name for Ragnar Lothbrok, sailed up the Seine with siege towers and sacked Paris. On 25 November 885 another Viking expedition, led by Rollo, travelled up the river to attack Paris again. In March 1314 King Philip IV of France had Jacques de Molay, last Grand Master of the Knights Templar, burned on a scaffold on an island in the river in front of Notre Dame de Paris. After the burning of Joan of Arc in 1431 her ashes were thrown into the Seine from the Mathilde Bridge at Rouen, though counter-claims persist without support.

On 9 August 1803 the American engineer Robert Fulton made the first successful test of his steamboat on the Seine beside the Tuileries Garden. The Seine flooded Paris severely in January 1910. In 1944 reaching the Seine was one of the original objectives of Operation Overlord, and the Allies met it within 90 days of D-Day. At the 1900 Summer Olympics the river hosted the rowing, swimming and water polo events.

The Seine is 777 kilometres (483 miles) long, and Paris has 37 bridges across it, among them the Pont Alexandre III and the Pont Neuf. In 1991 UNESCO added the banks of the Seine in Paris to its list of World Heritage Sites. Four large storage reservoirs built since 1950 on the Seine and its tributaries help to keep the river level constant through the city. The river inspired many artists of the 19th and 20th centuries, among them Claude Monet, Camille Pissarro, Georges Seurat and Alfred Sisley.
sejm: The word is an ancient Proto-Lechitic one meaning gathering or meeting. The Sejm traces its roots to the King's Councils, the wiece, which gained authority during the fragmentation of Poland between 1146 and 1295. The Sejm of 1180 at Łęczyca, known as the first Polish parliament, was the most notable, since it established laws constraining the ruler. These early assemblies met only at the king's behest.

After the Sejm of 1493 in Piotrków it became a regularly convening body, to which indirect elections were held every two years. It had two chambers: the Senate, of 81 bishops and other dignitaries, and the Chamber of Deputies, of 54 envoys elected by the local assemblies of landed nobility, the sejmiki, in each province. The nobility made up around 10% of the population, the highest share in Europe, and with the development of the Golden Liberty the powers of the Sejm increased dramatically.

The Union of Lublin in 1569 joined the Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania into the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, and the Sejm gained envoys from the Lithuanian nobility. The Sejm, Senate and King formed the three estates and the supreme deliberating body. Early in the 16th century the Senate had precedence, but from the middle of the century the Sejm became a very powerful representative body of the szlachta. It held final decisions in legislation, taxation, the budget, military funding, foreign policy and the confirmation of nobility.

Until the end of the 16th century unanimity was not required and majority voting was common. Later, as the magnates grew in power, unanimity returned with the right of liberum veto, the free veto. If the envoys did not reach a unanimous decision within the six weeks of a session, its deliberations were void and all its acts annulled. From the mid-17th century any objection by an envoy or senator rejected the other resolutions as well, since a session's resolutions formed one constituent act. From the second half of that century the liberum veto was used to paralyse the Sejm and brought the Commonwealth to the brink of collapse.

The Constitution of 3 May 1791 abolished the liberum veto, although the Sejm needed four years to adopt it. Its acceptance is arguably the reason Habsburg Austria, Russia and Prussia decided to partition the Commonwealth, ending over 300 years of Polish parliamentary continuity. Between 1493 and 1793 a Sejm is estimated to have been held 240 times, with a total debate time of 44 years. Since 1918 the name has referred only to the lower house of parliament.
selenga-river: The Selenga, or Selenge, is formed by the meeting of the Ider, which rises in the Hangyn Mountains of central Mongolia, and the Delger mörön, which comes from the Sangilen Mountains on the border of Mongolia and Tyva. It flows north-east, joins the Orkhon at Suhbaatar and continues north into Russia, turns east towards Ulan-Ude, the capital of Buryatia, and enters Lake Baikal through a lobate delta about 40 km wide. It carries almost half of the river water that flows into the lake.

Its basin is semi-arid, the largest in Mongolia, with harsh winters and warm summers, and the river is frozen from November to April. The name comes from the Mongolian seleh, "to swim", though one view derives it from the Evenki sele, "iron"; Mongolia's Selenge Province is named after it.

Evidence of Paleolithic culture was found in the basin at the end of the 19th century. G. P. Sosnovskii directed a Stone Age study of the valley near Kiakhta in 1928 and 1929, and from 1947 to 1958 an expedition under A. P. Okladnikov found 30 new sites in the Trans-Baikal region. One of them, Ust-Kyakhta-3, was excavated in 1976 and 1978 and yielded more than 40,000 stone artifacts and abundant animal remains; further work there in 2012 found two human tooth fragments, one of which later helped establish a link between Native Americans and their ancestors in East Asia.

The river floods every summer, and twenty-six floods are documented between 1730 and 1900, of which three were catastrophic, in 1830, 1869 and 1897. The first to be recorded in some detail began on 1 August 1830, when the Selenga and its tributaries burst their banks. On 16 August Verkhneudinsk, now Ulan-Ude, was flooded to a depth of 420 centimetres. The flood destroyed fifty-four buildings in Selenginsk, and the town was afterwards moved to higher ground on the left bank. There were heavy losses of pasture and hayfields.

The wetlands of the delta, in Buryatia, are a Ramsar site and an Important Bird Area, habitat of the Siberian Baikal sturgeon, which breeds in the river, and of over 170 species of birds. The Irkutsk Hydroelectric Power Station, built on the Angara between 1950 and 1956 to raise the level of Lake Baikal by 1.5 metres, has made part of the delta waterlogged. The Selenge-Orkhon forest steppe, an ecoregion of scattered forests and mountain ranges, takes in the basins of the Orkhon and the Selenga.
seleucid-empire: Alexander the Great died in 323 BCE without an adult heir, and at the Partition of Babylon his generals became satraps of his vast realm. Seleucus received Babylonia after the Partition of Triparadisus in 320 BCE, but Antigonus forced him out of Babylon around 315 BCE and he fled to Egypt. After Ptolemy I Soter and Seleucus defeated Demetrius at Gaza in 312 BCE, Seleucus returned, and in August 311 BCE his army took the citadel of Babylon. Seleucus then declared himself strategos autokrater of Asia, and the Seleucid state dates its founding to 312 BCE.

In 305 BCE Seleucus marched to the Indus against Chandragupta Maurya. The war ended in an understanding sealed by a marriage relationship, and Alexander's conquests along the Indus passed to the Maurya Empire. After he and Lysimachus defeated Antigonus at Ipsus in 301 BCE, Seleucus took eastern Anatolia and northern Syria, and founded Antioch on the Orontes and Seleucia on the Tigris. The empire reached its largest extent after he defeated Lysimachus at Corupedion in 281 BCE; he was assassinated by Ptolemy Ceraunus as he landed in Europe.

His successors faced repeated wars with Ptolemy II and a Celtic invasion of Asia Minor, and under Antiochus II Theos provinces broke away: Bactria and Sogdiana under Diodotus, Cappadocia, and Parthia, where the Parni of Arsaces killed the satrap Andragoras. Antiochus III the Great, who took the throne in 223 BCE, lost at Raphia in 217 BCE but then restored Parthia and Bactria to at least nominal obedience on his anabasis through the east. His war with Rome ended at the Battle of Magnesia, after which the Seleucids paid reparations and gave up claims west of the Taurus Mountains.

Later civil wars weakened the crown. The Maccabees established independence by 143 BCE, Demetrius II was captured by the Parthians in 139 BCE, and by then the whole Iranian Plateau was lost. By 100 BCE little remained beyond Antioch and some Syrian cities. Tigranes the Great of Armenia invaded Syria in 83 BCE, and Pompey ended the dynasty in 63 BCE.

The empire held Greeks, Assyrians, Armenians, Persians, Medes, Jews and many others. Its kings tolerated local customs while controlling local elites, and they founded Greek cities and settlements that drew migrants from Greece. These settlers, a small minority of the population, served in the army and government and seem to have rarely married non-Greeks. The army fought in the Greco-Macedonian style, with a phalanx of pikemen supplemented by native and mercenary troops. Most of the population worked in agriculture on land held by temples, cities and royal estates, much of it inherited from the Achaemenid system.
selim-ii: Selim was born on 28 May 1524 in the Topkapı Palace, Constantinople, the second surviving son of Suleiman and Hürrem Sultan. In 1542 he became governor of Karaman, with Konya as his seat, and after the death of his brother Şehzade Mehmed in November 1543 he was appointed governor of Saruhan, residing in Manisa. The execution of his elder half-brother Şehzade Mustafa on Suleiman's order in September 1553 left Selim and his brother Bayezid as the main contenders for the throne. Their rivalry ended when Bayezid marched on Konya in 1559 and Selim, with troops sent by Sokollu Mehmed Pasha, won the engagement.

Selim took the throne on 29 September 1566. Sokollu Mehmed Pasha kept Suleiman's death secret until Selim reached the army at Belgrade, where the allegiance ceremony was held. The soldiers, refused an accession payment, revolted in Istanbul until Selim's sister Mihrimah Sultan paid the Janissaries from her own fortune. Sokollu, grand vizier from 1565 until his assassination in 1579, persuaded Selim to make peace with the Habsburgs, and the Treaty of Edirne of 1568 had Maximilian II recognise Ottoman conquests in Hungary and keep paying tribute. Sokollu opposed the Cyprus campaign, but Selim ordered it.

Elsewhere the reign met mixed fortunes. In 1567 the Zaydi imam al-Mutahhar ibn Yahya Sharaf al-Din rose in Yemen and took Sana'a and Ta'izz; Ottoman forces recovered Aden, Ta'izz and much of the highlands, and a peace at Kawkaban in May 1570 brought recognition of Ottoman suzerainty. A fleet intended for Aceh, which had asked for help against the Portuguese, was diverted to Yemen, and only two ships with cannon and gunsmiths arrived. An attempt on Astrakhan in 1569 failed, and a canal between the Don and Volga was left unfinished. The Ottomans also pressed for Henry of Valois's election in Poland in 1573. Venice ceded Cyprus in a peace of 7 March 1573 and agreed to pay 300,000 ducats.

Selim died on 15 December 1574. His wife Nurbanu Sultan kept the death hidden for several days so that her son Murad could arrive and claim the throne unopposed. Murad III later had five of Selim's young sons executed. Selim was buried in Hagia Sophia. He wrote poetry under the pen name Selimi, supported poets, and restored the stipend of Mahidevran, mother of Mustafa. The Selimiye Mosque in Edirne, built by Sinan between 1569 and 1575, is the largest of all Ottoman mosques, and Sinan also renovated Hagia Sophia between 1572 and 1574.
semarang: Semarang lies on the northern coast of Java, bounded by the Java Sea to the north and by Kendal, Demak and Semarang regencies to the west, east and south. Its coastline is 13.6 kilometres long, and its elevation ranges from 0.75 to 348 metres above sea level. It is the capital and largest city of Central Java province, and its population is predominantly Javanese with a significant Chinese presence.

The history of the place goes back to the 9th century, when it was known as Bergota. At the end of the 15th century the Demak Sultanate appointed an Islamic scholar, Ki Ageng Pandan Arang, to build an Islamic school in this fishing village. On 2 May 1547 Sultan Hadiwijaya of Pajang declared him the first bupati of Semarang, which created the city administratively and politically. In 1678 Sunan Amangkurat II promised control of Semarang to the Dutch East India Company as a debt payment, and on 5 October 1705 Susuhunan Pakubuwono I gave the company extensive trade rights in return for wiping out Mataram's debt, making it officially a company city.

The early Dutch settlement was a pentagonal fortress with five towers, beside a Muslim quarter called Kauman and a Chinese quarter; only the Dutch quarter counted as the city. The Great Mail Road of 1847 connected the northern coastal cities of Central and East Java, and railways followed at the end of the 19th century. The mail and railway projects brought an economic boom in the 1870s, but the Javanese kampongs reached as many as 1,000 inhabitants per hectare, and cholera, tuberculosis, dysentery, typhoid and malaria were rife. The city doctor Willem T. de Vogel and the councilman Hendrik Tillema campaigned to extend the city into the healthier hills to the south. By the 1920s the city had doubled in size.

In 1918 the Indonesian People's Hall was established by Sarekat Rakyat as a centre for political and social activity; the Dutch closed it in 1927. Japan occupied the city in 1942. After the Proclamation of Indonesian Independence reached Semarang on 17 August 1945, a local government under the Republic was set up, and the Five Days Battle between Indonesian forces and Japanese soldiers followed in October 1945.

Semarang was designated a city on 1 March 1906. It is a municipality of 16 districts, covers 373.78 square kilometres, and remains an important regional centre and port. It had a population of 1,653,524 at the 2020 census.
semiramis: The historical Shammuramat, the Akkadian form of the name, was the Assyrian wife of Shamshi-Adad V, who ruled from 824 to 811 BCE. She ruled the Neo-Assyrian Empire as regent for five years, until her son Adad-nirari III came of age. She governed at a time of political uncertainty after a destructive civil war, which may partly explain why Assyrians accepted rule by a woman. In the city of Aššur she had a stele inscribed naming her as queen of Shamshi-Adad, mother of Adad-nirari and daughter-in-law of Shalmaneser. It has been speculated that her achievements were retold over generations until she became a figure of legend.

According to Diodorus Siculus, who drew mainly on Ctesias of Cnidus, Semiramis was the daughter of the fish-goddess Derketo of Ascalon and a mortal. Doves fed her until the royal shepherd Simmas adopted her. She married Onnes, a general under King Ninus, and advised the king, and at the Siege of Bactra she led soldiers to seize a key defensive point.

Ninus fell in love with her and Onnes hanged himself. After Ninus died of an arrow wound she disguised herself as their son Ninyas, and Diodorus says she reigned 42 years, restored Babylon with a high brick wall and built palaces including Ecbatana. She attacked King Stabrobates of India with false elephants made of buffalo skins over camels, but was wounded and her army mostly destroyed.

About 80 ancient writers recorded legends of her. Herodotus ascribed to her the banks that confined the Euphrates, and her name was applied to monuments whose origins were forgotten, even the Behistun Inscription of Darius. In Armenian tradition, which portrays her negatively, she asked the handsome King Ara to marry her, and when he refused she marched against Armenia, where Ara was slain despite her orders to capture him alive. She is credited with founding Van, called Shamiramagerd.

Semiramis was generally viewed positively before the rise of Christianity. In the Middle Ages she became associated with lust, and a story from Pompeius Trogus, later spread by Orosius, claims an incestuous relationship with her son. Dante places her among the lustful in the Second Circle of Hell, while Christine de Pizan included her in The Book of the City of Ladies, and she was commonly found on the Nine Worthies list for women.

She appears in plays by Voltaire and Calderón and in an opera by Rossini, and Margaret I of Denmark and Catherine the Great were called the Semiramis of the North. In 1853 Alexander Hislop's The Two Babylons made her a figure in a claimed conspiracy, a view that scholars such as Lester Grabbe have rejected. Armenians and Assyrians still use Shamiram as a girl's name.
semitic-languages: The Semitic languages are a branch of the Afroasiatic language family. They occur in written form from a very early date: Akkadian, also known as Assyrian and Babylonian, and Eblaite texts, written in a script adapted from Sumerian cuneiform, appear from about 2600 BCE in Mesopotamia and the north-eastern Levant respectively. Egyptian, from about 3000 BCE, is a sister branch of Afroasiatic, related to Semitic but not part of it. Amorite appeared about 2100 BCE, followed during the 2nd millennium BCE by the Canaanite languages, including Hebrew and Phoenician, by Aramaic, and by Ugaritic. Where Semitic-speaking peoples originated is still debated: Mesopotamia, the Levant, Ethiopia, the Arabian Peninsula and North Africa have all been proposed.

The Semitic languages are notable for their nonconcatenative morphology. Word roots are sets of consonants, usually three, and words are formed by filling in vowels between them. In Arabic the root k-t-b, dealing with writing, gives kitāb, book, and kataba, he wrote; Hebrew uses the same root in katav, he wrote, and michtav, letter. Most Semitic scripts are abjads, which omit some or all vowels. The Geʽez script of Ethiopia and Eritrea is technically an abugida, and Maltese is the only Semitic language written in the Latin script. The reconstructed word order of Proto-Semitic is verb–subject–object, which Classical Arabic and Biblical Hebrew keep.

Scholars have accepted the similarity of Hebrew, Arabic and Aramaic since medieval times. Guillaume Postel published a comparison of them in Latin in 1538, but did not name the group. The term Semitic was created by the Göttingen school of history, first by August Ludwig von Schlözer in 1781, from Shem, one of Noah's three sons in the Book of Genesis, and Johann Gottfried Eichhorn popularised it in 1795. Classical Syriac, an Aramaic dialect of about 200 CE, became a literary language of early Christianity. Classical Arabic is the language of the Quran, and Maltese descends from the extinct Siculo-Arabic of Sicily.
sendai: Sendai stretches from the Pacific Ocean to the Ōu Mountains, which form the east and west borders of Miyagi Prefecture. Its eastern part is a plain, its centre hilly and its west mountainous, and the highest point is Mount Funagata at 1,500 metres. Unusually for a large Japanese coastal city, the city core stands on a terrace 40 to 60 metres above sea level. The area was inhabited as early as 20,000 years ago, though the history of Sendai as a city begins with Date Masamune. It became a designated city in 1989 and has five wards, whose names deliberately avoid directions.

Date Masamune was unhappy with his previous stronghold at Iwadeyama, in the north of his territories and hard to reach from Edo. Sendai lay in the centre of his newly defined lands on the major road from Edo, and Tokugawa Ieyasu gave him permission to build a new castle on Aobayama after the Battle of Sekigahara. The name had been written with characters meaning a thousand generations, and Masamune changed it to characters meaning a hermit and a platform. The characters come from a Chinese poem praising a palace of the Han emperor Wen, and tradition says Masamune chose them so that the castle would prosper like a mountain inhabited by an immortal hermit.

In 1613 Masamune built a galleon to send an embassy headed by Hasekura Tsunenaga to the Pope in Rome. The embassy established relations with the Holy See, but the suppression of Christianity in Japan frustrated Masamune's plans. The first railway between Sendai and Tokyo, now the Tōhoku Main Line, opened in 1887 and put the area within a day's travel of Tokyo. Tohoku Imperial University was founded in 1907 and became the first Japanese university to admit women in 1913. After the Second World War the city was rebuilt as a transport and logistics hub for the region.

Sendai is the capital of Miyagi Prefecture and the largest city of the Tōhoku region. It is known as the City of Trees, because of the zelkova trees along Jōzenji Street and Aoba Street, and its Tanabata Festival is the largest in Japan. The ruins of Sendai Castle stand on Aobayama, and the Zuihōden is the tomb of Date Masamune. The Ōsaki Hachimangū shaden, built by Masamune in 1607, is a National Treasure. On 11 March 2011 coastal areas of the city suffered severe damage from a magnitude 9.0 offshore earthquake and the tsunami it caused.
seneca-the-younger: Seneca's father, Seneca the Elder, was a Spanish-born Roman knight who had gained fame as a writer and teacher of rhetoric in Rome, and his brother Annaeus Mela was the father of the poet Lucan. His early career as a senator seems to have been successful, and he was praised for his oratory. According to Cassius Dio, the emperor Caligula was so offended by his success in the Senate that he ordered him to commit suicide, and Seneca survived only because he was seriously ill and Caligula was told that he would soon die anyway.

From 54 to 62 Seneca advised Nero together with the praetorian prefect Sextus Afranius Burrus, and he was appointed suffect consul in 56. His satire Apocolocyntosis lampoons the deification of Claudius. Tacitus and Dio suggest that Nero's early rule, while he listened to Seneca and Burrus, was quite competent. After Burrus died in 62 Seneca's influence declined rapidly, and Tacitus reports that Nero refused his requests to retire in 62 and 64. He lived quietly on his country estates, rarely visiting Rome.

Seneca wrote mostly on ethics, with one work, Naturales Quaestiones, on the physical world. Many upper-class Romans found in Stoicism an ethical framework for political involvement. He was once regarded as eclectic, but modern scholarship sees him as a fairly orthodox Stoic, albeit a free-minded one. Among his later works are the Letters to Lucilius, which set out his philosophical thought.

His plays are tragedies, and ten are attributed to him, of which probably eight are his. Their intense emotions and grim tone seem the opposite of his Stoic beliefs, and until the 16th century he was often thought to be two people, a philosopher and a dramatist. Many scholars have held that they were written for recitation only, while others think they were meant for performance.
