In 65 Seneca was caught up in the aftermath of the Pisonian conspiracy, and Nero ordered him to kill himself, though it is unlikely that he took part. He cut several veins, and his wife Pompeia Paulina tried to share his fate but was saved on Nero's order. According to Tacitus, his age and diet made him bleed slowly, and he also took poison, which was not fatal. The early Christian Church thought well of him, and Tertullian called him our Seneca. In the later Middle Ages he was read mostly through the Letters to Lucilius, and Petrarch quoted him more than any authority except Virgil. His suicide has been a popular subject in art.
senegal: Senegal lies on the western coast of Africa between latitudes 12° and 17°N. It almost completely surrounds the Gambia, which separates the southern region of Casamance from the rest of the country. The landscape consists mainly of the rolling sandy plains of the western Sahel, rising to foothills in the southeast, where the highest point, the Baunez ridge, reaches 648 metres. The Senegal River forms the northern border and gives the country its name, and the Gambia and Casamance rivers also cross it. The capital Dakar lies on the Cap-Vert peninsula, the westernmost point of continental Africa. The dry season runs from December to April, with hot, dry harmattan winds.

Archaeological findings indicate that Senegal was inhabited in prehistoric times and continuously occupied by various ethnic groups. Kingdoms were created between the 6th and 14th centuries, among them Takrur in the 6th century, Namandiru and the Jolof Empire in the 13th and 14th centuries, and eastern Senegal was once part of the Ghana Empire. Islam was introduced by the Toucouleur and Soninke through contact with the Almoravid dynasty, and the Serers in particular resisted it. Between 1300 and 1900 close to one-third of the population was enslaved, typically after capture in warfare.

The Jolof Empire grew more powerful in the 14th century, uniting Cayor and the kingdoms of Baol, Siné, Saloum, Waalo, Futa Tooro and Bambouk. It was a voluntary confederacy rather than a state built on conquest, founded by Ndiadiane Ndiaye, and it collapsed around 1549 after the defeat and death of Lele Fouli Fak at the hands of Amari Ngone Sobel Fall.

The Portuguese landed on the coast in the mid-15th century, followed by traders from other countries, including the French. In 1677 France gained control of the island of Gorée, a minor hub of the Atlantic slave trade. From the 1850s the French expanded onto the mainland under Governor Louis Faidherbe, taking over all the kingdoms except the Serer kingdoms of Sine and Saloum. Senegal became independent in 1960.

Dakar is the capital and largest city, and was once the capital of all French West Africa. Senegal is a semi-presidential republic. French is the official language, ratified in 1960, but over 30 languages are spoken, and Wolof is the most widely spoken, serving as a lingua franca alongside French. The largest ethnic groups are the Wolof, Fula and Serer, and Senegalese people are predominantly Muslim. Griots, whose profession is passed down through generations, have kept West African history alive through words and music. Senegal is a member of the African Union, the United Nations and the Economic Community of West African States.
senegal-river: The Senegal River is 1086 kilometres long and drains a basin of 270,000 square kilometres. Its headwaters, the Bafing and the Semefé (Bakoye), both rise in Guinea and meet at Bafoulabé in Mali. From there the river flows west and then north through the Talari Gorges and over the Gouina Falls, past Kayes, and receives the Falémé River at Bakel. It then crosses semi-arid land, forming the border between Senegal and Mauritania, and takes in the Gorgol at Kaédi.

Below Kaédi it divides into two branches, the main river and the Doué, which rejoin a few kilometres downstream of Podor and enclose a long strip of land called the Île à Morfil. The river passes Richard Toll and Rosso and turns south around the island on which Saint-Louis stands, separated from the Atlantic by a thin strip of sand, the Langue de Barbarie.

Early Mediterranean writers knew of the river: Pliny the Elder called it, or some other river, Bambotus, and Ptolemy called it Nias. Hanno the Carthaginian visited it around 450 BCE. From about 800 CE the Trans-Saharan trade between Morocco and the Ghana Empire restored contact, and the Arab geographers al-Masudi (957), al-Bakri (1068) and al-Idrisi (1154) gave some of the earliest descriptions. Some of them believed the upper Senegal and the upper Niger formed a single river, the Western Nile, and later writers called it the Nile of Ghana. Because it reached into the gold-producing Ghana Empire and later the Mali Empire, traders called it the River of Gold, and European maps from the 14th century, among them the Hereford Mappa Mundi, drew it.

Europeans sought its mouth from 1291, when the Genoese Vivaldi brothers sailed down the coast and were not heard of again. Under Prince Henry the Navigator, Gil Eanes passed Cape Bojador in 1434. In 1445 Nuno Tristão reached the Langue de Barbarie, and Dinis Dias was the first known European since antiquity to reach the river's mouth. Between 1448 and 1455 the captain Lourenço Dias opened regular trade with the Wolof states of Waalo and Cayor, exchanging horses and Mediterranean goods for gold and slaves.

In 1972 Mali, Mauritania and Senegal founded the Organisation pour la mise en valeur du fleuve Sénégal to manage the river basin, and Guinea joined in 2005. Two large dams stand on the river: the Manantali Dam in Mali, and the Maka-Diama Dam on the Mauritania-Senegal border near the sea, which keeps salt water from moving upstream. The river's aquatic life is closely linked to that of the Gambia River basin.
senlis: Senlis stands on the river Nonette, 40 km north of Paris, between the forests of Chantilly and Ermenonville to the south and Halatte to the north. The highest point of the town, 140 metres, lies in the heart of the forest of Halatte, and the lowest on the banks of the Nonette. The area is a vast limestone plateau of the Lutetian, covered mostly in silt.

The town was known in early imperial times as Augustomagus and later as Civitas Silvanectium, the city of the Silvanectes. In the 3rd century a defensive wall seven metres high was built round it in response to Frankish incursions; about half of it still stands, and it remained in use into the 13th century. A Roman amphitheatre seating as many as 10,000 people stood about 500 m west of the walled town, and its remains are still visible. Monarchs of the early French dynasties lived at Senlis, drawn by the venison of the Chantilly forest, and built a castle on the foundations of the Roman settlement.

Senlis came into the ownership of Hugh Capet in 981. In 987 Archbishop Adalbero of Reims called an assembly and asked it to choose Hugh as king of France; he was crowned at Noyon. Under Capetian rule Senlis became a royal city and remained one until the reign of Charles X.

It reached its height in the 12th and 13th centuries as trade in wool and leather increased and vineyards were planted; a second set of ramparts, larger and higher than the Gallo-Roman ones, was built under Philip II, and King Louis VII granted a municipal charter in 1173. The Bailiwick of Senlis was created in 1265. The Hundred Years' War devastated the town, though it escaped destruction despite a siege by the Armagnacs, and in 1493 Charles VIII signed the Treaty of Senlis there with Maximilian I of Austria. In early September 1914 the Germans occupied the town and executed its mayor, Eugène Odent, with six other civilian hostages.

The cathedral, a Gothic church and national monument, was built between 1153 and 1519; its spire dates from the 13th century, and the southern portal of the 16th century is the work of Martin Chambiges. The former bishopric was abolished by the Concordat of 1801. The royal castle, whose present building dates from the 12th century under Louis VII, stands beside the priory of Saint Maurice. St Vincent Abbey was founded in 1065 by Queen Anne of Kiev. The town has museums of art and archaeology, of hunting and of the Spahis, and its old streets have often served as a film setting.
sens: Sens lies on the Yonne, 120 km south-east of Paris, at the point where the Vanne empties into that river. It stands at the extreme north-west of the present region of Bourgogne-Franche-Comté, on the border of Île-de-France, Grand Est and Centre-Val de Loire. The hills of Paron and Saint-Martin-du-Tertre border it to the west and the forest of Othe to the east, while the Yonne valley leads north towards the Brie.

The city is said to have been one of the oppida of the Senones, one of the oldest Celtic tribes in Gaul. The Battle of the Allia, fought around 387 BCE between the Senones under Brennus and the Roman Republic, involved the same people. Julius Caesar mentions Agedincum several times, and in 53 BCE he wintered six legions at a place south of the city called the camp of Caesar. The Roman town was built in the first century BCE and walled in the third; parts of the walls remain, and the city keeps the skeleton of its Roman street plan. After the reorganisation of the empire in 375 it became the chief town of Lugdunensis Quarta.

The bishop of Sens became an archbishop as early as the mid-5th century, and in the Middle Ages the archbishops held the role of primate of Gaul and Germany. The archdiocese ruled over the dioceses of Chartres, Auxerre, Meaux, Paris, Orléans, Nevers and Troyes, summarised by the acronym CAMPONT. From 1135 the cathedral, dedicated to Saint Stephen, was rebuilt as one of the first Gothic cathedrals.

Louis IX of France held his wedding to Marguerite of Provence there in 1234. The town witnessed the trial of Peter Abelard, sheltered Pope Alexander III for a time and received Thomas Becket during part of his exile between 1162 and 1165. William of Sens was the principal architect of Canterbury Cathedral. During the Wars of Religion, in 1562, 100 of the town's Huguenot residents were killed in the Massacre of Sens.

Sens is a sub-prefecture and the second largest city of the Yonne department, with 27,106 inhabitants in 2023. Its main sights are the cathedral, the Archbishops' Palace, the churches of St Maurice and St Pierre le Rond, the House of Abraham and a museum. The Hôtel de Ville was completed in 1904.
senusret-iii: Khakaure Senusret III, also written Senwosret III or Sesostris III, was the fifth king of the late Twelfth Dynasty of the Middle Kingdom. He was the son of Senusret II and Khenemetneferhedjet I. Three wives are known for certain, Itakayt, Khenemetneferhedjet II and Neferthenut, all known mainly from their burials beside his pyramid at Dahshur. His son Amenemhat III succeeded him.

His military campaigns were followed by an era of peace and prosperity that reduced the power of regional rulers and revived craftwork, trade and urban development. In Nubia he built massive river forts including Buhen, Semna, Shalfak and Toshka, and carried out at least four major campaigns, in his Years 8, 10, 16 and 19. The campaign of Year 19 was less successful: the Nile ran lower than normal, and the king's forces withdrew to avoid being trapped in hostile territory.

A stela at Semna dated to the third month of Year 16 records that he made his southern boundary at Heh, further south than his fathers, and charged his successors to hold it, calling any who abandoned it no son of his. A statue of the king was set at the border.

He cleared a navigable canal through the first cataract of the Nile, documented by rock inscriptions near Sehel Island. Late in his reign he built at Abydos, where he founded the planned town of Wah-Sut, a mortuary temple and a second tomb cut into the rock. A stela of his official Sebek-khu records the earliest known Egyptian military campaign in the Levant.
A double-dated papyrus joins his Year 19 with Year 1 of Amenemhat III, which is generally taken as proof of a coregency, though Pierre Tallet and Harco Willems doubt that it ever occurred.

His pyramid complex at Dahshur, north-east of the Red Pyramid, far surpassed earlier Twelfth Dynasty pyramids in size. Its base is 105 metres and its height 78 metres, with a granite-lined burial chamber. Six smaller pyramids for royal women stood around it. Some have suggested that he was in fact buried in his complex at Abydos, making the pyramid a cenotaph.

Senusret III was among the few Egyptian kings deified and honoured with a cult in his own lifetime. A cycle of six songs in his honour, preserved among the papyri of Illahun, compares him to the goddess Sekhmet, and his cult at south Abydos lasted roughly 300 years. Later generations worshipped him as a deity at Semna, and he is regarded as one of the sources of the legend of Sesostris.
seoul: Seoul lies in the north-west of South Korea, in mountainous and hilly terrain, with Bukhansan on its northern edge. The Han River roughly divides it into northern and southern halves, and the city proper covers 605.25 square kilometres. Four main mountains stand in the centre: Bugaksan, Inwangsan, Naksan and Namsan. The Seoul Fortress Wall, which historically bounded the city, runs over these heights.

People lived in the area 30,000 to 40,000 years ago. Around 4,000 BCE they lived in huts with lowered floors called umjip, and around 1,500 BCE communities began to farm at scale and enter the Bronze Age. After the fall of Wiman Joseon (194 to 108 BCE), refugees went south to the Han River basin, bringing the culture and technology of the Chinese Warring States and speeding the region's entry into the Iron Age.

Baekje, founded in 18 BCE as one of the statelets of the Mahan confederacy, became the dominant local power by the 2nd century CE. Its capital, Wiryeseong, is believed to have lain in what is now south-eastern Seoul, though its exact site is uncertain. In July or August 553 Silla took the region from Baekje, and it became part of the new Sin Province. Later names include Bukhansan-gun under Goguryeo, Namgyeong under Goryeo and Hanseong under Joseon.

Seoul was designed as a capital in the late 14th century, and the Joseon dynasty built the Five Grand Palaces there: Changdeokgung, Changgyeonggung, Deoksugung, Gyeongbokgung and Gyeonghuigung. In the early 20th century the city was occupied by the Empire of Japan. In the Korean War it changed hands four times and was left mostly in ruins, and it has since been rebuilt and rapidly urbanized.

Seoul is the capital and largest city of South Korea, with about 9.6 million residents. It is divided into 25 districts, called gu. The Constitutional Court of Korea declared in 2004 that Seoul must remain the national capital as an unwritten constitutional custom, though many ministries have moved to Sejong City. Five UNESCO World Heritage Sites lie in the Seoul Capital Area, among them Changdeokgung, Jongmyo and the Royal Tombs of the Joseon dynasty.
septuagint: Biblical scholars agree that the first five books of the Hebrew Bible were translated into Koine Greek by Jews living in the Ptolemaic Kingdom, probably in or around Alexandria, and can be dated with confidence to the mid- or late 3rd century BCE. The remaining books were presumably translated in the 2nd century BCE. Few people could read Hebrew in the Second Temple period, and Koine Greek and Aramaic were the lingua francas of the Jewish community, so the translation met a need.

According to tradition, Ptolemy II Philadelphus sent seventy-two translators, six from each of the Twelve Tribes, from Jerusalem to Alexandria to translate the Torah for the Library of Alexandria. The story is told in the Letter of Aristeas to his brother Philocrates, which some scholars regard as pseudepigraphical, and was repeated by Philo, Josephus and the Babylonian Talmud.

The name derives from the Latin phrase for the version of the seventy translators, and it was not until Augustine of Hippo that the Greek translation was called Septuaginta. The Greek text was produced within Hellenistic Judaism and completed by 132 BCE, though it continued to be revised in Jewish and Christian communities through the fourth century CE.

The Septuagint is not a single unified corpus but a collection of ancient translations of the Tanakh along with other Jewish texts now called apocrypha. The canon of the Hebrew Bible was still evolving while it was written, and the books were translated by different people, in different places and for different purposes, in styles that range from literal to paraphrase. Samuel and Kings form one four-part book, Of Reigns, and Chronicles is titled Of Things Left Out. Books found in it but not in the Hebrew Bible include Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, the additions to Daniel and Esther, and 1 to 4 Maccabees.

Most Jews abandoned it around the 2nd century. The earliest gentile Christians had used it out of necessity, since it was the only Greek Bible and most could not read Hebrew, and its association with a rival religion may have made it suspect. Differences between it and the contemporary Hebrew scriptures were also discovered, and Greek-speaking Jews tended to prefer other versions, such as that of Aquila. The New Testament writers freely used the Greek translation when citing the scriptures. It formed the basis of the Old Latin versions and of the Old Church Slavonic, Armenian, Georgian and Coptic versions of the Old Testament. Origen's Hexapla produced the first major Christian recension.
serbia: Serbia lies in the Balkans and the Pannonian Basin. It covers 88,499 square kilometres including the disputed territory of Kosovo, or 77,589 square kilometres excluding it. It has eight neighbouring countries, more than any other European country except Germany. The Pannonian Plain covers the northern third of the country, central Serbia is chiefly hills traversed by rivers, and mountains dominate the southern third.

Elevation ranges from 2,169 metres at the Midžor peak in the Balkan Mountains to just 17 metres near Prahovo in the Timok Valley. Karst topography is prominent in the Dinaric Alps and the Carpathian Mountains, and the country hosts about 1,500 deep caves.

A hominid jaw fragment from Mala Balanica Cave is believed to be up to 525,000 years old. Around 6500 BCE the Starčevo and Vinča cultures were present near modern Belgrade, and Lepenski Vir and Vinča-Belo Brdo lie along the Danube. The Celtic Scordisci settled the area in the 3rd century BCE and built fortified settlements, including Singidunum (present-day Belgrade) and Naissos (present-day Niš). The Romans conquered much of the territory from the 2nd century BCE, and some historians believe 18 Roman emperors were born there, among them Constantine the Great.

Slavs migrated into Byzantine territory in large numbers by the 6th century. The first Serbian proto-state was established in the 7th century and had become a more stable principality by the beginning of the 9th century, remaining a Byzantine vassal state throughout. It was conquered and annexed by the Byzantine Empire in the late 10th century. The Serbian Kingdom lasted from 1217 to 1346, followed by the Serbian Empire from 1346 to 1371 and the Serbian Despotate from 1402 to 1459.

Serbia is a parliamentary republic under a constitution adopted in 2006, after the dissolution of the State Union of Serbia and Montenegro. The National Assembly has 250 deputies elected for four years. The 2022 census counted a population of 6,647,003, excluding Kosovo, of whom 80.6% were Serbs; Hungarians (2.8%) and Bosniaks (2.3%) are the largest minorities.

The country has five World Heritage sites, among them Stari Ras, the Studenica Monastery and the Roman palace complex of Felix Romuliana, and six traditions on the intangible heritage list, including the slava and kolo dance. Its cultural identity was shaped by its position as a frontier between the Byzantine Empire and Western Christianity, and later between the Ottoman and Habsburg empires.
serbs: The origin of the name Serb is unclear. The most prominent theory holds that it is of Proto-Slavic origin, meaning family kinship or alliance, and ultimately rooted in a word for sipping or breast-feeding, so that it carries the idea of milk kinship and brotherhood. Early Slavs, especially the Sclaveni and Antae, including the White Serbs, invaded and settled Southeastern Europe in the 6th and 7th centuries. Until the late 560s they mainly raided across the Danube, but large-scale settlement overwhelmed the Danube and Sava frontier in the late 6th and early 7th centuries. The region of Raška was the centre of Serb settlement, and Serb tribes also occupied most of modern Herzegovina and Montenegro.

The first Serb states, Serbia (c. 780–960) and Duklja (10th century to 1186/9), were formed chiefly under the Vlastimirović and Vojislavljević dynasties. As Duklja declined in the late 11th century, Raška gained independence and became the most powerful Serbian state. Grand Prince Stefan Nemanja, (r. 1166–96), founded the Nemanjić dynasty, which ruled Serbia until the 14th century. His son Stefan Nemanjić became the first recognised king, and his younger son Rastko founded the Serbian Orthodox Church in 1219 and became known as Saint Sava.

Under the Ottomans, the devshirme took Christian boys from the Balkans, many of them Serbs, from their families, converted them by force to Islam and trained them for the Janissary corps. Some Serbs who converted rose to the highest ranks, among them the grand vizier Sokollu Mehmed Pasha. The Serbian Revolution (1804–1817) began with the First Serbian Uprising under Karađorđe Petrović, which created an independent state for almost a decade until the Ottomans crushed it in 1813. The Second Uprising under Miloš Obrenović won substantial autonomy in 1815–1816, the last Ottoman troops withdrew in 1867, and full international recognition of independence came at the Congress of Berlin in 1878.

Serbs are predominantly Eastern Orthodox Christians, traditionally affiliated with the Serbian Orthodox Church. During the centuries of Ottoman rule it remained the only permitted Serb institution, and through its monasteries and clergy it preserved the Serbian language, literacy and national consciousness. When the Principality of Serbia became independent, Orthodoxy became crucial in defining national identity, since language was shared with other South Slavs.

Serbs are noted for icon painting, frescoes, literature, music and medieval architecture, shaped by Byzantine tradition. The gusle, a bowed single-stringed instrument, accompanies a centuries-old oral tradition of epic songs, most of which centre on the Ottoman occupation and the struggle for liberation. The Kosovo Myth is a central national myth that symbolises martyrdom and the defence of the homeland against the Ottomans.
serfdom: Institutions similar to serfdom existed in antiquity; the status of the helots of Sparta resembled that of medieval serfs. By the 3rd century CE the Roman Empire faced a labour shortage, and large landowners relied increasingly on free tenant farmers, later called coloni, instead of slaves. Diocletian's tax system assessed both land and its inhabitants, so it became administratively inconvenient for peasants to leave the land where they were counted. Medieval serfdom really began with the breakup of the Carolingian Empire around the 10th century, when powerful lords encouraged it as a source of agricultural labour. The word serf comes from Middle French, from Latin servus, and serfdom was coined only in 1850.

A serf lived on and worked a parcel of land within the manor of a lord, who owed protection and justice in return. Unlike a slave, a serf could not be sold individually, although serfs passed with the land when it was sold. A serf could not leave without permission and had no saleable title to the land. A freeman usually became a serf through force or necessity, sometimes in a ceremony of bondage, and children inherited the status.

Serfs paid dues mainly in seasonally appropriate labour on the lord's demesne and in produce, and Easter eggs or a Christmas goose might be owed on top. They had rights in land and could take their disputes to the manorial court. A well-off serf might buy his freedom, and in England one who reached a chartered borough and lived there a year and a day became free.

Serfdom varied greatly in time and place. In Poland the labour owed was commonly a few days a year per household in the 13th century, one day a week in the 14th, four in the 17th and six in the 18th. Serfdom began to disappear west of the Rhine in the later Middle Ages while it spread through eastern Europe, becoming dominant there around the 15th century. The decline in the west has sometimes been attributed to the Black Death. In Russia it became the dominant relation between peasants and nobility in the 17th century.

Abolition came by stages. France abolished serfdom in Crown lands in 1779 and formally on 4 August 1789. Joseph II issued the Serfdom Patent for the Habsburg monarchy in 1781, though dues and unpaid labour continued until the revolutions of 1848. Prussia abolished it in 1807, and Alexander II freed Russia's privately held serfs in 1861, with owners compensated through taxes on the freed serfs. The United Nations 1956 Supplementary Convention on the Abolition of Slavery prohibits serfdom.
sergei-eisenstein: Sergei Mikhailovich Eisenstein was born on 22 January 1898 in Riga, then in the Russian Empire, to a middle-class family. His father, the architect Mikhail Osipovich Eisenstein, came from a Jewish family but had converted to the Russian Orthodox Church before his marriage in 1897. His mother took Sergei to Saint Petersburg in 1905. He was raised an Orthodox Christian and later became an atheist. At the Petrograd Institute of Civil Engineering he studied architecture and engineering, but in 1918 he left to join the Red Army in the Russian Civil War. In Minsk in 1920 he saw Kabuki theatre and studied Japanese, learning about 300 kanji characters, which he cited as an influence on his pictorial development.

In 1920 Eisenstein moved to Moscow and worked in the theatre for Proletkult, an experimental institution that aimed at a revolutionary working-class aesthetic. In 1923 he began as a theorist with the essay The Montage of Attractions. His first full-length film was Strike in 1925, followed in the same year by Battleship Potemkin, which was acclaimed around the world, and by October: Ten Days That Shook the World, made for the tenth anniversary of the Revolution. His attention to camera angles, crowd movements and montage drew criticism in the Soviet film community and led to self-criticism and promises to conform to socialist realism.

In 1930 Paramount Pictures gave him a short contract in Hollywood, but his projects failed to impress the studio and it ended by mutual consent. He then made a film in Mexico, Que viva Mexico, financed by the author Upton Sinclair and other investors. It ran far beyond the three or four months agreed, and Sinclair shut down production, leaving the footage in the United States, where others edited it into films that Eisenstein never saw. Alexander Nevsky, made in 1938 with music by Sergei Prokofiev, was received well in the Soviet Union and the West and won him the Order of Lenin and the Stalin Prize.

During the war he worked on the film about Tsar Ivan IV, with Prokofiev scoring it. Ivan the Terrible, Part I won a Stalin Prize. Part II was criticized by various authorities and went unreleased until 1958, and the footage of the unfinished Part III was confiscated and mostly destroyed.

Eisenstein suffered a heart attack on 2 February 1946 and died of a second on 11 February 1948, aged 50. His ashes were buried in the Novodevichy Cemetery in Moscow. He was a pioneer in the theory and practice of montage.
sergei-witte: Sergei Yulyevich Witte was born on 29 June 1849. His father, from a Lutheran Baltic German family, converted to Russian Orthodoxy on marrying Yekaterina Fadeyeva, and Sergei was raised on the estate of his mother's parents. He studied at Novorossiysk University in Odessa, graduating at the top of his class in 1870. He had planned an academic career in mathematics, but his relatives thought it unsuitable for a noble, and he was persuaded to enter the railways.

After six months of training on the Odessa Railways he became chief of the traffic office. A wreck in late 1875 cost many lives and led to a four-month prison sentence, but in the Russo-Turkish War he directed the Odessa Railways and attracted the notice of Grand Duke Nicholas Nikolaevich, who commuted the sentence to two weeks.

From 1889 to 1891 Witte was Director of Railway Affairs in the Finance Ministry, expanding the railways under state control and assigning staff by merit rather than patronage. Appointed Minister of Finance in August 1892, he held the post for eleven years and nearly doubled the empire's revenues. He accelerated the construction of the Trans-Siberian Railway, established a state alcohol monopoly in 1895 and, in 1896, placed the ruble on the gold standard, which increased investment and the inflow of foreign capital. In 1896 he concluded the Li-Lobanov Treaty with Li Hongzhang, which gave Russia the right to build the Chinese Eastern Railway.

Under pressure from the landed gentry and his enemies at court, he was moved in August 1903 to the chairmanship of the Committee of Ministers, a post with no real power. In 1905 the tsar sent him to the United States to negotiate the end of the Russo-Japanese War at Portsmouth, New Hampshire, where he is credited with negotiating well for Russia, and he was made a count.

On 9 October 1905 Witte told Nicholas II that the country faced a catastrophic revolution and offered two choices: a military dictator or broad reforms. He framed the October Manifesto, and on 20 October 1905 he was appointed the first chairman of the Council of Ministers, effectively prime minister. With his Council he designed Russia's first constitution, but within months court opposition discredited him as a reformer, and he resigned before the First Duma met on 10 May 1906. He remained a member of the State Council but never again held an administrative post. Witte died in St Petersburg in 1915. His memoirs, completed in 1912, were published in translation in 1921.
sergipe: Sergipe covers 21,910 square kilometres and borders Bahia to the south and west and Alagoas to the north. The São Francisco River forms its northern boundary. Inland the state is almost entirely savanna, called caatinga, while the coastline has mangroves, swamps and sandy beaches. The rivers that drain the southern half into the Atlantic are obstructed by sandbars at their mouths, so there are no good ports on the coast. The name comes from an Old Tupi word meaning in the river of the siri, a species of crab.

The region was home to numerous Indigenous peoples, including the Kanindé, the Aratus and the Tupi. Gaspar de Lemos briefly landed there in 1501, and the Portuguese Crown declared it part of the Captaincy of Bahia. It was one of the last coastal regions of Brazil whose Indigenous population resisted Portuguese rule, and it was fully brought under it after about two decades of warfare, during which thousands of Indigenous people were killed and thousands more enslaved to work on sugar plantations. The first Portuguese settlement was at São Cristóvão, then called Sergipe D'El-Rey.

Sergipe was invaded several times by the Dutch and often raided by French buccaneers, who were drawn by its king-wood, a prized commodity. The territory belonged to Dutch-controlled Brazil until the Portuguese regained control in 1645. By 1723 Sergipe, still part of Bahia, produced a third of Bahia's sugar. Land unsuitable for sugarcane was used for livestock, and Sergipe supplied draft animals to farms in Bahia and Pernambuco.

John VI of Portugal signed a decree separating Sergipe from Bahia on 8 July 1820. It kept its separation after the independence of Brazil in 1822, first as a captaincy and then as a province. On 17 March 1855 the provincial president moved the capital from São Cristóvão, inland, to Aracaju on the coast. Sergipe became a state when the Republic of Brazil was proclaimed in 1892.

Sergipe is the smallest Brazilian state by area, larger only than the Federal District, with Aracaju as its capital and largest city. São Cristóvão, the fourth oldest town in the country and the state capital until 1855, has a main square, São Francisco Square, that became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2010.
sesame: Sesame, Sesamum indicum, is a plant also called benne. Most of the other species of its genus are wild and native to sub-Saharan Africa, while the cultivated type originated in India. It was described by Carl Linnaeus in 1753, and its epithet means of India. The seeds, which are white or black and grow in pods, have one of the highest oil contents of any seed. The plant tolerates drought and heat and will grow where other crops fail, so subsistence farmers at the edge of deserts have grown it. The word sesame comes through Latin and Greek from ancient Semitic languages such as the Akkadian šamaššamu.

Sesame is considered the oldest oilseed crop known to humanity. Charred remains dated to about 3500 to 3050 BCE show that it was domesticated in the Indian subcontinent at least 5,500 years ago. The archaeobotanist Dorian Q. Fuller states that sesame was traded between Mesopotamia and the Indian subcontinent by 2000 BCE, and the Indus Valley civilization may have exported sesame oil to Mesopotamia, where it was called ilu in Sumerian and ellu in Akkadian. Some believe it may instead have originated in Ethiopia.

Egyptians called it sesemt, and it appears in the list of medicinal drugs of the Ebers Papyrus of about 1550 BCE. Baskets of sesame were found among the grave goods of King Tutankhamen, which suggests it was present in Egypt by 1350 BCE. It was grown and pressed for oil at least by 750 BCE in the empire of Urartu.

The seeds are a common ingredient in many cuisines, made into tahini paste and halva in the Middle East and a part of the spice mixture za'atar. Enslaved West Africans brought sesame to colonial America in the 17th century and grew it as a subsistence crop. In Southern Italian cuisine sesame sweets such as giurgiulena remain from the Arabic period. In the early twentieth century sesame oil was a compulsory ingredient of margarine in Europe, because its presence made it simple to detect margarine used to adulterate butter. Around 1920 Burma exported about 197,400 tons of the oil a year.
sevastopol: Sevastopol lies at the south-western tip of the Crimean Peninsula, on the Heracles Peninsula, on the coast of the Black Sea. Much of the city is gathered around the long Bay of Sevastopol, and its navigable harbours made it an important port and naval base throughout its history. Its name joins the Greek sebastós, venerable, and pólis, city, and probably honours Empress Catherine II, who founded it. In the west of the city stand the well-preserved ruins of the ancient Greek port of Chersonesos, founded in the 5th century BCE by settlers from Heraclea Pontica.

Sevastopol was founded in June 1783, in the area of the ruined Greek city of Chersonesus, as a base for a naval squadron under the name Akhtiar, White Cliff, by Rear Admiral Thomas MacKenzie, a Scot in Russian service. In February 1784 Catherine the Great ordered Grigory Potyomkin to build a fortress and call it Sevastopol, and Captain Fyodor Ushakov, commander of the port from 1788, carried out the plans. The name Sevastopol was restored on 29 April (10 May) 1826.

In the Crimean War the allies chose Sevastopol as Russia's main Black Sea naval base. They landed in September 1854 and settled into a siege marked by brutal conditions on both sides. The city fell after eleven months, and the Treaty of Paris of 30 March 1856 forbade Russia to base warships in the Black Sea. In the Second World War it withstood intensive German bombardment in 1941-42, in which the Germans used the 80-cm railway gun Schwerer Gustav, and after 250 days of fierce fighting fell to Axis forces in July 1942. The Red Army liberated it on 9 May 1944.

In the Soviet era it was a closed city. In 1954 Sevastopol and the rest of Crimea were transferred from the Russian SFSR to the Ukrainian SSR. Russia annexed Crimea, with Sevastopol, in March 2014; the annexation is not recognised internationally.

Sevastopol is the largest city of Crimea and a major Black Sea port, with a population mostly of ethnic Russians and a substantial minority of Ukrainians. Because of its military history most of its streets are named after Russian and Soviet military heroes, and hundreds of monuments and plaques recall its military past.
seven-wonders-of-the-ancient-world: After the conquests of Alexander the Great in the 4th century BCE, Hellenistic travellers gained access to the civilizations of the Egyptians, Persians and Babylonians, and began to list the landmarks that impressed them. The ancient Greeks spoke not of wonders but of theamata, meaning sights or things to be seen, so the list was the ancient counterpart of a travel guidebook. Later the word for wonder, thaumata, was used instead.

The first known list of seven dates to the 2nd to 1st century BCE, and at least eight full lists and ten partial lists are known. Diodorus Siculus mentioned only the Walls of Babylon and the Pyramids. The epigrammist Antipater of Sidon, who lived around or before 100 BCE, listed six of the present wonders and put the walls of Babylon where the Lighthouse of Alexandria now stands. Lists by Herodotus and by the poet Callimachus of Cyrene survive only as references.

The seven names now generally given are the Great Pyramid of Giza, the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, the Statue of Zeus at Olympia, the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, the Colossus of Rhodes and the Lighthouse of Alexandria. This canonical list was first established in the 1572 publication Octo Mundi Miracula from a combination of historical sources. Two wonders stood in Greece, two in Turkey, two in Egypt and one in Iraq. Five of the seven celebrate Greek construction; the exceptions are the pyramids and the Hanging Gardens.

Only the Great Pyramid survives, and it lost its white stone facing around 1300 when local communities removed it for building. The Colossus, finished after 280 BCE, fell to an earthquake in 226 or 225 BCE, so all seven stood together for less than sixty years. The Temple of Artemis and the statue of Zeus were destroyed by fire, and the Lighthouse and the tomb of Mausolus by earthquakes.

Sculptures from the tomb and the temple are in the British Museum. Scholars debate the nature of the Hanging Gardens and whether they existed. Later lists added Roman and Christian sites, and Gregory of Tours named the Temple of Solomon and Noah's Ark. Wilhelm Heinrich Roscher found 22 distinct places across 18 classical lists in 1906.
seville: Seville lies on the lower reaches of the River Guadalquivir in the southwest of the Iberian Peninsula, in a fertile valley, at an average height of 7 metres above sea level. Its port, about 80 kilometres from the Atlantic, is the only river harbour in Spain. The summers are very hot and dry.

The city is about 2,200 years old. The original core dates to the 8th century BCE, when the site was on an island in the Guadalquivir, and the Phoenicians and the Tartessians called it Hisbaal. It was founded as the Roman city of Hispalis, and after the Islamic conquest of 711 was called Ishbiliyah. It was the seat of the Wali of Al-Andalus until 716, when the capital moved to Córdoba. After the Caliphate of Córdoba collapsed in the early 11th century it became the centre of the independent Taifa of Seville, and it was later ruled by the Almoravids and the Almohads, who built its main mosque in the 12th century. It was incorporated into the Crown of Castile in 1248.

Following the voyages of Columbus, Seville was chosen in 1503 as the headquarters of the Casa de Contratación, which made it the gateway to the Indies, though ships had to sail about 80 kilometres up the Guadalquivir to reach it. In the 16th century it was one of the largest cities in Western Europe. Worsening drought in the river gradually moved the trade away to the Bay of Cádiz, which received the fleets of the Indies in 1680 and the Casa de Contratación in 1717.

Seville is the capital of Andalusia and of the province of Seville. Its old town contains a UNESCO World Heritage Site made up of three buildings: the Alcázar, the Cathedral and the General Archive of the Indies. Its motto, NO8DO, is popularly read as a rebus for the Spanish No me ha dejado, She has not abandoned me.
sewing-needle: A sewing needle for hand-sewing is a long slender tool with a point at one end and an eye to hold the thread. The earliest were made of bone or wood, and modern ones are made of high-carbon steel wire, plated with nickel or gold against corrosion. Needles have come in many kinds for their uses: sharps for general sewing, embroidery needles with longer eyes, quilting needles, tapestry needles with blunt tips for loose weaves, leather needles with a triangular point, and long upholstery needles that may be straight or curved. Sizes are not standardised, and within a class a higher number means a shorter, thinner needle.

The first sewing was probably the tying together of animal skins, with shards of bone as needles and sinew or plant material as thread. The early limit was making an eye small enough not to damage the material. Bone awls from Blombos Cave in southern Africa date to 73,000 to 70,000 years ago, and a point that may come from a bone needle, found in Sibudu Cave, to 61,000 years ago.

Later needles are better dated. A bone needle from Potok Cave in Slovenia belongs to the Aurignacian, 47,000 to 41,000 years ago. Ivory needles about 30,000 years old come from Kostenki in Russia, and 8,600-year-old needles from Ekşi Höyük in western Anatolia. Flinders Petrie found copper needles at Naqada in Egypt from 4400 to 3000 BCE, and iron needles from the third century BCE were found at the oppidum of Manching. Needles apply the wire-making technology that appeared in the second millennium BCE.

Native Americans used needles from natural sources. The agave leaf, soaked until only long fibres and a sharp tip remained, gave both needle and thread. Steel-making from China reached Spain in the tenth century in the form of the Catalan furnace and later Germany and France. England began making needles in 1639 at Redditch, with the drawn-wire technique still in common use, and about 1655 a Guild of Needlemakers was established in London. In Japan the Festival of Broken Needles, Hari-Kuyo, dates back to the 1600s.
sextus-pompey: Sextus Pompeius Magnus Pius was the son of Pompey by his third wife, Mucia Tertia, with an elder brother, Gnaeus Pompeius, and a sister, Pompeia. When Julius Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49 BCE, Gnaeus followed their father to the East while Sextus stayed in Rome in the care of his stepmother, Cornelia Metella. After the defeat at the Battle of Pharsalus in 48 BCE the two met Pompey on Lesbos and fled with him to Egypt, where Sextus watched his father killed by treachery on 29 September of that year.

He then joined the resistance to Caesar in the African provinces alongside Metellus Scipio, Cato the Younger and his brother. Caesar defeated the Pompeius brothers at the Battle of Munda in Hispania in 45 BCE. Gnaeus died soon afterwards in a last stand at Lauro; Sextus escaped and raised another army in Spain.

After Caesar's death Mark Antony moved that Sextus be recalled, paid 50 million Attic drachmas for his father's confiscated property and given command of the whole Roman navy. He accepted, but went no further than Massilia before returning to Sicily. When the Second Triumvirate began its proscriptions, many of the proscribed fled to him, and after the battles of Philippi in 42 BCE survivors of the party of Brutus and Cassius did the same. With the whole island as his base he built an army and a strong navy.

In 40 BCE his admiral, the freedman Menas, seized Sardinia from Octavian's governor Marcus Lurius. By the Pact of Misenum in 39 BCE the triumvirs recognised his control of Sicily and Sardinia in exchange for keeping the grain supply to Rome open and his pirates in check. The peace was short. Each side accused the other of breaking it, and Menas betrayed Sardinia to Octavian. Sextus defeated Octavian at sea off Messina in 37 BCE.

Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa spent a winter building and training a fleet near Lake Avernus. He fought Sextus at Mylae in August 36 BCE, Marcus Aemilius Lepidus and Titus Statilius Taurus invaded Sicily, and after Naulochus Sextus fled to Asia Minor. Captured in 35 BCE, he was put to death without trial at Miletus by Marcus Titius, whom he had once spared, either on Titius's own initiative or possibly on the orders of Antony or Plancus. Plutarch gives him a minor role in the fall of the Republic; Appian treats him as a central figure who might even have emerged as the final victor.
seychelles: Seychelles is an archipelago of 115 islands in the Indian Ocean, with its capital and largest city, Victoria, about 1,500 kilometres east of mainland Africa. The islands lie northeast of Madagascar. The inner islands, 42 granitic and 2 coralline, occupy the shallow Seychelles Bank and hold 54% of the land area. The granitic islands rest on a submerged granite block, the Seychelles microcontinent, which lay between Madagascar and India before the breakup of Gondwanaland. Alfred Wegener cited this granite as evidence of continental drift.

The islands were uninhabited before sustained outside contact. Arab sailors knew of them through Indian Ocean trade routes, and scholars identify them with the Zarin islands described by al-Mahri. Europeans learnt of them in the early 16th century. The first sighting was made on 15 March 1503 by Thomé Lopes, during Vasco da Gama's fourth Portuguese India Armada. The earliest recorded landing was in January 1609, by the crew of the Ascension under Captain Alexander Sharpeigh, on a voyage of the British East India Company.

France began to take control in 1756, when Captain Corneille Nicholas Morphey laid a Stone of Possession on Mahé. The islands were named after the French politician Jean Moreau de Séchelles and formed part of the colony of Isle de France. In August 1770 the ship Thélémaque landed 15 white settlers and 13 African and Indian slaves on Ste. Anne Island. Enslaved Africans were then brought to work the plantations.

In 1794 the senior administrator, Jean-Baptiste Quéau de Quinssy, negotiated with the British frigate HMS Orpheus and kept the islands under French control as neutral territory. Britain took control after invading Isle de France in December 1810, formalised by the Treaty of Paris of 1814. Slavery was prohibited in 1835, and indentured labourers from India were later employed. Seychelles became a separate crown colony from Mauritius in 1903. It gained independence as a republic in 1976, and a coup in 1977 ousted its first president, James Mancham.

Seychelles is a republic whose president is both head of state and head of government. French, English and Seychellois Creole are official languages, and the Creole, a French-based language, is the most widely spoken. The population was estimated at 100,600 in 2022, making it the smallest African country by area and the least populated sovereign African state. Most people descend from African, French, Indian and Chinese immigrants. It belongs to the United Nations, the African Union and the Commonwealth of Nations.
shaanxi: Shaanxi covers more than 205,000 square kilometres and borders Inner Mongolia to the north, Shanxi and Henan to the east, Hubei, Chongqing and Sichuan to the south, and Gansu and Ningxia to the west. It is divided into northern Shaanxi on the Loess Plateau, central Shaanxi or Guanzhong, where most of the population lives, and the mountainous south beyond the Qinling Mountains. The Wei River valley between them is a cradle of early Chinese civilisation. The name means west of Shan and is attested around 1000 BCE, when the dukes of Shao and Zhou marked their borders along the Shan plateau.

Thirteen dynasties established their capitals in Shaanxi over more than 1,100 years, from the Zhou to the Tang. Fossils of Lantian Man, a subspecies of Homo erectus about a million years old, were found near Xi'an. After the fall of the Qin the region was briefly governed as the Three Qins, which is the origin of one of its two abbreviations, Qin, the other being Shaan. Under the Han the Northern Silk Road connected Xi'an westward to Kashgar. The Ming founded the Shaanxi Provincial Administration Commission in 1376, which also covered Gansu and Ningxia. On 23 January 1556 an earthquake near Hua Shan killed an estimated 100,000 people.

From late 1935 to early 1947 Yan'an, at the end of the Long March, was the base of the Chinese Communist Revolution, and the Communists formed the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region in parts of Shaanxi. The People's Government of Shaanxi was established in Xi'an on 10 January 1950.

The capital and largest city, Xi'an, includes the sites of the former capitals Fenghao and Chang'an. It is the oldest of China's Four Ancient Capitals and the eastern terminus of the Silk Road. Xianyang, capital of the Qin dynasty from 221 to 206 BCE, lies just north across the Wei River. The population is about 37 million, and the vast majority are Han Chinese, with Hui, Manchu and Mongol minorities. Mandarin is the main language.
shaduf: One theory holds that the shadoof was invented in Mesopotamia as early as the time of Sargon of Akkad, around the 24th and 23rd centuries BCE. The Minoans are believed to have adopted it next, with evidence of its use from around 2100–1600 BCE. Its appearance in Upper Egypt is placed most likely in the 18th Dynasty. Some historians believe instead that the Egyptians invented it along the Nile, citing tomb drawings of shadoofs at Thebes from 1250 BCE. A third theory places its origin in India at about the same time as in Mesopotamia, because it was so widespread there, but little other evidence supports it.

The pole is hung on its frame about one-fifth of its length from one end. The vessel on the long arm may be a bucket, a skin bag or a reed basket coated with bitumen, and some have an uneven base or a tie at the top so that the water runs out at once. The operator pushes the vessel down with his own weight, and the counterweight raises it full without effort. The water is emptied into runnels that carry it along irrigation ditches. The frame may be one post or a pair, and the vessel may hang from a rope or from a thinner stick.

The device lifts water from 1 to 6 metres, and its efficiency has been calculated at 60 per cent. A study in Nigeria, which measured effort by heart rate, found that suitable adjustments reduced the energy the operator spent from about 109 to 71 watts.

In ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia shadoofs set in tiers, one above another, raised water to higher levels by the work of several people. In Egypt under the Middle and New Kingdoms, pleasure gardens watered by shadoof became a mark of luxury residences and a symbol of status. Women have often worked it, since it is easy to use.

The name comes from the Arabic šādūf; in English it is also called a well sweep or swape. The ancient Greeks knew it as the kēlōn or kēlōneion, the Chinese call it jiégāo, and its Hungarian name, gémeskút, means heron well. Today it is very common in rural India and Pakistan, and in Europe in Ukraine, Belarus, Poland and Germany. On the Great Hungarian Plain it is considered a symbol of the region.
shahnameh: Ferdowsi began the Shahnameh in 977 and completed it on 8 March 1010. It is a poetic recasting of what he, his contemporaries and his predecessors regarded as the account of Iran's ancient history, and many such accounts already existed in prose, among them the Shahnameh of Abu-Mansur. Traditional Iranian historiography holds that Ferdowsi grieved at the fall of the Sasanian Empire and wrote to preserve the memory of Persia's golden days, though some scholars have challenged this view. Josef Markwart and Theodor Nöldeke argued that much of the epic's world reshaped Parthian history, and that Rostam had Parthian origins.

The mythical age is short, about 2,100 verses or four per cent of the whole. After an opening in praise of God and Wisdom it gives the creation of the world as the Sasanians believed it, then the first man and king, Keyumars, and Hushang, who accidentally discovered fire. Almost two thirds of the poem belong to the heroic age, from Manuchehr's reign to the conquest of Alexander the Great, in which myth and legend are combined; its stories include Zal and Rudaba, Rostam and Sohrab, and Rostam and Esfandyar.

A brief mention of the Arsacid dynasty leads to Ardashir I, founder of the Sasanian Empire, and from there Sasanian history is told with a good deal of accuracy, while the Arab conquest is narrated romantically.

Later works in Persian followed the Shahnameh in style and method, but none matched its fame, and some experts hold that Modern Persian remains much the same language as in Ferdowsi's day because of works like it. The Shirvanshah dynasty took many of its names from the poem, and the Qarakhanid dynasty called itself the family of Afrasiab.

Illustrated copies are among the most sumptuous examples of Persian miniature painting. The Baysonghori Shahnameh, made in 1430, is preserved at Golestan Palace and was inscribed in UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 2007. Turner Macan published the first complete edition in 1829, and Arthur and Edmond Warner translated the whole work into English in nine volumes between 1905 and 1925.
shandong: Shandong lies on the eastern edge of the North China Plain and in the lower reaches of the Yellow River, and extends into the sea as the Shandong Peninsula. It borders the Bohai Sea to the north, Hebei to the northwest, Henan to the west, Jiangsu to the south and the Yellow Sea to the east. The name means east of the mountain, and refers to its position east of the Taihang Mountains; it came into use when the Jin dynasty established the military command offices of Shandong East Circuit and Shandong West Circuit in 1168. The province is a centre of Taoism, Chinese Buddhism and Confucianism, and Mount Tai has one of the longest histories of continuous religious worship in the world.

A succession of Neolithic cultures lived in Shandong, among them the Houli, Beixin, Dawenkou, Longshan and Yueshi cultures. The Qin dynasty conquered Qi and founded the first centralised Chinese state in 221 BCE, and the Han dynasty then created commanderies under the Qingzhou and Yanzhou inspectorates. The Ming dynasty created the modern province, and in 1376 moved its capital from Qingzhou to Jinan, which remained the capital for seven centuries.

After the Second Opium War the Qing court opened Cheefoo as a trade port, and Western powers established consulates, missionaries and factories there. In the 1880s Shandong became the base of the Beiyang Fleet, which the Imperial Japanese Navy defeated in 1894. After the killing of two German Catholic missionaries in the Juye Incident, the Qing government had to cede Qingdao to the German Empire, and in 1898 Weihaiwei went to Britain. During the warlord era the Fengtian clique installed Zhang Zongchang as military governor in April 1925; he ruled until 1928 and was succeeded by Han Fuju. The Jiaozhou–Jinan Railway, constructed by Germans from 1899 to 1904, connects Jinan with Qingdao and remains the main east–west line across the province.

Shandong is a coastal province of eastern China with Jinan as its capital, and the 2020 census counted 101.5 million people. Qufu, the birthplace of Confucius, later became the centre of Confucianism, and the Buddhist temples in the mountains south of Jinan were once among the foremost in China. Shandong cuisine is one of the eight great traditions of Chinese cooking. Its literature largely reflects Confucianism, and classics such as the Analects, Mencius and the Zuo Zhuan come from the province. Qingdao keeps German-era architecture.
shanghai: Shanghai lies on the Yangtze Estuary of China's east coast, with the Yangtze River to the north, Hangzhou Bay to the south and the East China Sea to the east. The Huangpu River bisects the city. The land is an alluvial plain formed by the Yangtze's deposition and by land reclamation, and most of it is flat, with an average elevation of four metres. The soil is soft, so skyscrapers have to be built on deep concrete piles to avoid sinking.

The western part of the area was inhabited 6,000 years ago. In the Spring and Autumn period it belonged to the Kingdom of Wu, which was conquered by Yue and then by Chu. The name Shanghai, on the sea, is first found in the 11th-century Song dynasty, and in 1280 the place was renamed Shanghai.

Originally a fishing village and market town, Shanghai grew to prominence in the 19th century through trade and its port. It was one of five treaty ports forced open to European trade after the First Opium War, and the Shanghai International Settlement and the French Concession were set up there. In the 1930s it was a primary commercial and financial hub of Asia. In the Second World War it fell under Japanese rule after the Battle of Shanghai, and the Communists took it during the Chinese Civil War. The reform and opening up supported by Deng Xiaoping led to extensive redevelopment by the 1990s, especially in the Pudong New Area.

Shanghai is one of the four municipalities under the direct administration of the Central People's Government and is divided into 16 districts. Its historic sites include the City God Temple, Yu Garden and the row of early 20th-century buildings along the Bund.
shanxi: Shanxi lies on a plateau made up of higher ground to the east, in the Taihang Mountains, and to the west, in the Lüliang Mountains, with a series of valleys in the centre through which the Fen River runs. The name means west of the mountains, a reference to its position west of the Taihang range. The Great Wall forms most of the northern border with Inner Mongolia, and the province also borders Hebei to the east, Henan to the south and Shaanxi to the west. The highest peak is Mount Wutai, at 3,058 metres, and the total area is 156,700 square kilometres.

The state of Jin, which existed in what is now Shanxi during the Spring and Autumn period (c. 770 – c. 481 BCE), gave the province its one-character abbreviation, Jin. Jin split into three states, Han, Zhao and Wei, in 403 BCE, a date sometimes taken as the start of the Warring States period, and all of them had fallen to the state of Qin by 221 BCE. The Han dynasty ruled the region as Bingzhou. During the Sixteen Kingdoms period several regimes controlled it in turn, followed by the Northern Wei (386–534), a Xianbei kingdom with one of its early capitals at present-day Datong.

Under the Ming and Qing dynasties Shanxi merchants, also called Jin merchants, dominated China's commerce and finance, a phenomenon that lasted for centuries from the Song to the Qing. Their networks reached Russia, Japan, Korea, Central Asia, Southeast Asia and South Asia. They controlled the overland tea trade with Russia and Mongolia, monopolised trade routes across the Great Wall and handled the Qing government's tax remittances between provinces.

After the Qing collapsed, Shanxi was governed for nearly four decades by Yan Xishan and kept a high degree of de facto autonomy within the Republic of China. When Japan invaded in 1937, Shanxi was one of the first areas attacked, and Yan invited Communist forces to re-enter the province. They arrived in time to help defeat a stronger Japanese force at the Pingxing Pass, in the Battle of Pingxingguan.

Shanxi is a province of North China whose capital and largest city is Taiyuan. The population is more than 99 per cent Han Chinese, and the dominant local language, Jin Chinese, is the only major Sinitic variety in northern China that is not classified within the Mandarin group. The province holds roughly one third of China's coal reserves. It has by far the largest number of historic buildings of any Chinese province, over 28,000 ancient structures, and three UNESCO World Heritage Sites: Pingyao Ancient City, the Yungang Grottoes and Mount Wutai.
shenyang: Shenyang lies in the central part of Liaoning province. Its western districts are on the alluvial plain of the Liao River system and its eastern part reaches into the forested hinterland of the Changbai Mountains. The name means the yang side of the Shen River, the old name of the Hun River, which runs on the southern side of the city; in Chinese naming custom a river's north bank is the sunny, or yang, side. Humans lived here as early as 8,000 years ago, and the remains of the Xinle culture, a late Neolithic society over 6,800 years old, are kept in a museum in Huanggu District.

In the 14th century the city came under the Ming dynasty, for which it was an important military stronghold. In 1625 the Jurchen leader Nurhaci captured Shenyang and moved his whole administration to it. The Manchu name was Simiyan hoton, and in 1634 the official name became Mukden, or Shengjing, meaning rising capital, from the Manchu word mukdembi, to rise. The imperial palace was built from 1626 on Nurhaci's orders, with more than 300 rooms and 20 gardens.

After the First Sino-Japanese War Japan obtained the Liaodong Peninsula by the Treaty of Shimonoseki in 1895 but had to give it up under the Triple Intervention. A secret treaty of 1896 allowed Russia to build a railway through Manchuria, and after the Boxer Rebellion of 1900 Russian forces occupied most of Manchuria, making Mukden a Russian stronghold. The Battle of Mukden of 1905 was fought south of the city, and Japanese influence grew afterwards. In 1914 the city took back the name Shenyang, though Mukden stayed in use in English and in Japan for decades.

The Mukden incident of 1931 led to the Japanese invasion and occupation of the rest of Manchuria and the puppet state of Manchukuo. The Red Army occupied the city in August 1945, and British and American reports say Soviet troops looted and terrorised its people. The Communists captured it in 1948 after the Liaoshen campaign.

Shenyang is the capital of Liaoning province, with 9,070,093 residents at the 2020 census. It has been a centre of heavy industry since the 1930s, and many factories were built in Tiexi district in the first five-year plan, 1951 to 1956. After the 1980s heavy industry declined and hundreds of thousands of workers were laid off. It is the railway hub of north-eastern China.
shenzhen: Shenzhen lies on the east bank of the Pearl River estuary on the central coast of Guangdong. It borders Hong Kong to the south, Dongguan to the north, Huizhou to the northeast and Macau to the southwest. Although it sits about a degree south of the Tropic of Cancer, it has a warm, humid subtropical climate shaped by the monsoon and the Siberian anticyclone, with mild winters and a rainy season that lasts until late September or early October.

The city roughly follows the administrative boundaries of the historical Bao'an County. Its name means deep ditch in the local vernacular, from words used for irrigation ditches. The earliest recorded mention of the name dates from 1410, under the Ming dynasty, but no market town was established there until the Qing dynasty.

Humans have lived in the area for some 6,700 years, with the oldest evidence from the mid-Neolithic period. Historic counties were first established there about 1,700 years ago, and the towns of Nantou and Dapeng were built over 600 years ago. After the Second Opium War the United Kingdom seized Hong Kong Island and was leased the New Territories, which fixed the modern boundary between Hong Kong and the area of Shenzhen, then a village on the border.

In 1953 the Bao'an County government moved to Shenzhen, which was closer to the Kowloon–Canton Railway and had a larger economy than Nantou. From the 1950s to the end of the 1970s the county received a large influx of refugees trying to reach Hong Kong; between 100,000 and 560,000 are said to have lived there. The place became a city by 1979. In May 1980 the Central Committee designated it the first special economic zone in China, as part of the reform and opening up promoted by Deng Xiaoping, an experiment in market capitalism within a community guided by socialism with Chinese characteristics. It then had a population of 30,000.

Shenzhen is a prefecture-level city with nine districts and one new district. Its permanent population was recorded as 17,560,000 in 2020, many of them migrants from other parts of China, so that the population is younger than that of most Chinese cities. Before the zone was established the local communities spoke Cantonese or Hakka, and the main local cuisine is Cantonese.

The city is a centre of the technology and manufacturing industries, and is home to the Shenzhen Stock Exchange and companies such as Huawei, Tencent and DJI. Its port is one of the large container ports of the world. The Shenzhen Metro, a rapid transit system, serves the city, and the city is part of the Pearl River Delta Metropolitan Region together with Guangzhou, Hong Kong and Macau, among others.
shikoku: Shikoku is 225 kilometres long and between 50 and 150 kilometres wide, and lies south of Honshu and north-east of Kyushu. With its surrounding islands it covers about 18,800 square kilometres. Mountains running east and west divide it into a narrow northern zone facing the Seto Inland Sea and a larger, sparsely populated southern part facing the Pacific Ocean. Mount Ishizuchi in Ehime, at 1,982 metres, is the highest mountain. The major river is the Yoshino, which runs 196 kilometres from near Mount Ishizuchi to the sea at the city of Tokushima. Unlike Japan's other main islands, Shikoku has no active volcanoes, although a major volcanic caldera near Mount Ishizuchi was active around 14 million years ago.

The island's ancient names include Iyo-no-futana-shima, Iyo-shima and Futana-shima. Its present name, meaning four provinces, refers to the four former provinces that make it up: Awa, Tosa, Sanuki and Iyo. Shikoku has historically been quite isolated and therefore kept the original characteristics of Japan for longer, especially in vegetation and some architectural techniques. Until the Great Seto Bridge network opened in 1988, the central part of the island was isolated from the rest of Japan.

Shikoku is known for a pilgrimage of 88 temples, established by the Heian-period Buddhist priest Kūkai, a native of present-day Zentsūji in Kagawa Prefecture. According to legend Kūkai still appears to pilgrims. Pilgrims wear white jackets bearing the characters dōgyō ninin, meaning two travelling together. Because of wheat production, Sanuki udon became an important part of the diet in Kagawa Prefecture, formerly Sanuki Province, in the Edo period.

Shikoku is the smallest of Japan's four main islands and has the smallest population, about 3.4 million. It consists of four prefectures: Ehime, Kagawa, Kōchi and Tokushima. Matsuyama, the capital of Ehime Prefecture, is the largest city, and most inhabitants live in the north. Three expressways, which together form the Honshū–Shikoku Bridge Project, connect the island to Honshu. Annual festivals include the Awa Odori in Tokushima, held in August at the time of the Obon festival, and the Yosakoi festival in Kōchi.
shinto: Shinto has no single founder, no canonical text and no central authority, so beliefs and practices vary widely. One proposed broad definition is that Shinto is a belief in kami, the supernatural beings that practitioners hold to inhabit all things, including forces of nature and prominent places. They are not regarded as omnipotent, omniscient or necessarily immortal, and the dead may become kami. Kami are worshipped at household shrines called kamidana and at public shrines called jinja, where priests known as kannushi offer food and drink. Shinto stresses ritual over doctrine, and above all purity: humans are seen as fundamentally pure, and pollution, or kegare, is a temporary condition removed by rites of purification.

Kami veneration has been traced back to the Yayoi period, from 300 BCE to 250 CE, when bronze bells, weapons and mirrors seem to have played a role in ritual. Historians debate when it is suitable to speak of Shinto as a distinct religion. Buddhism reached Japan at the end of the Kofun period and spread quickly, and the two merged so closely, in a process called shinbutsu-shūgō, that kami came to be seen as part of Buddhist cosmology.

The earliest written tradition of kami worship is in the 8th-century Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, which were commissioned by ruling elites to legitimise and consolidate their rule. They describe a universe in three parts: the Plane of High Heaven, where the kami live, the world of humans, and the Nether World. Although never of great importance to Japanese religious life, their accounts were proclaimed factual by the government in the early 20th century.

Japan has around 100,000 public shrines, about 80,000 of them affiliated with the Association of Shinto Shrines, which shrines formed in 1946. Festivals, called matsuri, mark the seasons of the agricultural year and give thanks to the kami, while rites of passage include a child's first visit to a shrine and weddings. Shinto was formally separated from the state during the U.S. occupation after World War II. A new constitution separated religion from the state, and the emperor declared that he was not a kami.

Numerically Shinto is the largest religion in Japan, with Buddhism second, but most people take part in both. Many Japanese say they have no religion, partly because they dislike the connotations of the Japanese word shūkyō, which suggests sect doctrine. Aspects of Shinto have been taken into new religious movements such as Tenrikyo and Oomoto.
shiraz: Shiraz is the capital of Fars province, historically known by the exonym Persia proper. It lies in a green plain at the foot of the Zagros Mountains, 1,500 metres above sea level, and has been a regional trade centre for over a thousand years. The earliest reference to the city, as Tiraziš, is on Elamite clay tablets dated to 2000 BCE, and tablets from the Persepolis treasury archives mention major workshops there. The name became Old Persian Širājiš and then the modern Persian Shirāz.

The Arab Muslim army conquered Fars in expeditions between 640 and 653 and captured the area around Shiraz in 641. Because the Sasanian capital Istakhr was deeply associated with the Sasanian Empire and the Zoroastrian religion, the Arabs sought to establish a rival cultural and administrative centre in nearby Shiraz. It was founded or restored in 693 by Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Thaqafi, brother of the Umayyad viceroy al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, or by the latter's kinsman Muhammad ibn Qasim. In the 13th century it became a leading centre of the arts and letters, through its ruler's encouragement and the presence of Persian scholars and artists.

Ismail I, founder of the Safavid dynasty, captured Shiraz in 1504. After the fall of the Safavids the city declined, and a revolt of its governor against Nader Shah ended with a siege of many months and a sack. By Nader Shah's murder in 1747 most of its historical buildings were damaged or ruined, and its population had fallen to 50,000, a quarter of that in the 16th century. Karim Khan, de facto ruler of Iran from 1760 until 1779, made Shiraz his capital.

Shiraz is the fifth-most-populous city of Iran, with 1,995,500 inhabitants at the 2021 census. It is known as the city of poets, gardens, wine, nightingales and flowers. Hafez and Saadi were born there, and their tombs lie on the north side of the present city. The Eram garden is among its old gardens, and the Arg of Karim Khan, the citadel, stands beside the Vakil Bazaar and Vakil Bath. Shiraz has historically had major Jewish and Christian communities.
shiva: The name Shiva means auspicious, propitious or gracious. In the Rig Veda (c. 1700 to 1100 BCE) the word is an adjective applied to several deities, among them Rudra, a fearsome god of the roaring storm. Shiva is associated with Rudra, and the Hindu scriptures treat the two as the same figure. The Shiva of later Hinduism is, however, regarded as an amalgamation of various older Vedic and non-Vedic deities into a single god, a process linked to the Hindu synthesis of post-Vedic times. How this composite figure formed is not well documented and has attracted much speculation.

Some authors have read Mesolithic rock paintings at Bhimbetka as depictions of Shiva, but Howard Morphy holds that in context they more probably show hunting parties with animals. The Yajurveda gives both terrifying (rudra) and benign (shiva) attributes, and later texts such as the Atharvashiras Upanishad declare that all gods are Rudra.

For Shaivas, the followers of Shaivism, Shiva is the Supreme Lord who creates, protects and transforms the universe. In the Shakta tradition the Goddess is the equal and complementary partner of Shiva. Within the Trimurti he is the destroyer or transformer beside Brahma the creator and Vishnu the preserver, though ancient and medieval texts also contain many triads that do not include him.

Shiva is a god of ambiguity: fierce and benevolent, an ascetic yogi on Kailasa and a householder with his wife Parvati and their children Ganesha and Kartikeya. His attributes include the third eye, with which he burned Kama, desire, to ashes, the crescent moon in his hair, the river Ganga flowing from his matted locks and the trident. He is shown as Nataraja, Lord of Dance, and is usually worshipped in the aniconic form of the linga, which the Linga Purana presents as the manifested sign of the signless.

Shiva is revered across India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Indonesia, especially Java and Bali, where he is known as Batara Guru, a spiritual teacher blended with local spirits and heroes. His worship spread in Central Asia under the Kushan and Hephthalite empires, and wall paintings from Penjikent in Sogdia show him with a halo, a sacred thread and a tiger skin.

The Siva Sutta shows him conversing with the Buddha, and he appears as Mahakala in Vajrayana, as Maheshvara in Mahayana and as Ishana in Theravada Buddhism, in most forms ranked below Mahabrahma or Sakra. The Japuji Sahib of the Guru Granth Sahib names Shiva beside Vishnu and Brahma.
siberia: Siberia is a geographic and historic concept, not a political entity, so it has no single precise border. It stretches from the Ural Mountains to the Pacific Ocean and from the lands inside the Arctic Circle to the northern borders of Kazakhstan, Mongolia and China, and it covers over 13.1 million square kilometres, about three-quarters of Russia's area. Great rivers such as the Ob, the Yenisey and the Lena cross it. The climate runs from Arctic to temperate, with long, extremely cold winters; the January average is −25 °C.

Many nomadic groups lived in parts of Siberia over the millennia, among them the Xiongnu, the Huns, the Scythians and the Nenets. Later states reaching into the region included the Turkic khaganates, the Kyrgyz Khaganate, the Mongol Empire and the Khanate of Sibir. The Russian conquest began with the fall of the Khanate of Sibir in 1582. By the mid-17th century Russia controlled areas reaching the Pacific, and some 230,000 Russians had settled in Siberia by 1709.

Siberia became a destination for internal exiles, with more than 800,000 people exiled in the 19th century. The Trans-Siberian Railway, built in 1891–1916, tied the region to industrialising Russia, and around seven million Russians moved to Siberia between 1801 and 1914. In the Soviet period the Gulag administered penal labour camps, many of them in Siberia; according to semi-official Soviet estimates, more than 14 million people passed through the camps and prisons between 1929 and 1953.

Siberia holds roughly a quarter of Russia's population. Its largest cities are Novosibirsk, Krasnoyarsk and Omsk. More than 85 per cent of its people are of European descent, chiefly Russian, and the predominant religious group is the Russian Orthodox Church. Indigenous peoples include the Yakuts, Tuvans, Altai, Khakas and Buryats, and Siberia is traditionally regarded as the archetypal home of shamanism. The Trans-Siberian Railway still runs from Moscow to Vladivostok.
sicily: Sicily is roughly triangular, which gave it the ancient name Trinacria, from the Greek for having three headlands. The Strait of Messina, about 3 km wide in the north and about 16 km wide in the south, separates it from Calabria. The island covers 25,711 km2, and the Autonomous Region of Sicily, which includes the smaller islands of Lipari, Egadi, Ustica and Pantelleria, covers 27,708 km2. Inland the terrain is mostly hilly and intensively cultivated, and the mountain ranges of Madonie, Nebrodi and Peloritani along the north coast extend the mainland Apennines. Mount Etna dominates the east coast, and the fertile soil is the result of past volcanic eruptions.

Humans first colonized Sicily towards the end of the Late Pleistocene, around 16,000 years ago, and dolmens date to the second half of the third millennium BCE. The original classical-era inhabitants were three peoples: the Sicani, the Elymians and the Sicels. Thucydides writes that the Sicani, the earliest, arrived from the Iberian Peninsula. The Elymians are thought to have come from the Aegean. The Sicels, whose name the island bears, are thought to have originated in Liguria and arrived from mainland Italy in 1200 BCE, forcing the Sicani to the middle of the island. By around 750 BCE there were three Phoenician and about twelve Greek colonies along the coasts, and Sicily became a centre of Magna Graecia.

The Sicilian Wars of 580-265 BCE were fought between Carthaginians and Greeks, and the Punic Wars of 264-146 BCE between Rome and Carthage. The name Sicilia was given to the Roman province in 241 BCE. Later rulers included the Vandals, the Ostrogoths, the Byzantine Empire and the Emirate of Sicily. The Norman conquest created the County of Sicily in 1071 and the Kingdom of Sicily in 1130. After the Sicilian Vespers in 1282 the island was ruled by the Crown of Aragon and then Spain. In 1816 the kingdom joined with Naples to form the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, and after Garibaldi's Expedition of the Thousand and a plebiscite the island joined Italy in 1860.

Sicily is one of Italy's twenty regions and one of its five autonomous ones, with special status granted on 15 May 1946. Its capital is Palermo. It has seven UNESCO World Heritage Sites, among them the Valle dei Templi at Agrigento, the Roman mosaics of the Villa Romana del Casale, the Aeolian Islands and the Late Baroque towns of the Val di Noto. Millions of people of Sicilian origin live abroad, the result of emigration that began after Italian unification, first to the United States between the 1880s and the 1920s.
siege-engine: Siege engines ranged from the size of a small house to that of a large building. Some were built in place to attack from a distance, while others stood on wheels so that they could be advanced to the walls.
