From antiquity until the development of gunpowder they were made largely of wood, bound with rope or leather and possibly strengthened with a few pieces of metal at points of stress. Those that threw projectiles built up force by tension, by torsion or, in the trebuchet, by human power or a counterweight.

The earliest siege engines appear to be simple movable roofed towers, used with scaling ladders, depicted during the Middle Kingdom of Egypt. The Assyrians used battering rams, and in Kush siege towers and rams were built from the 8th century BCE. The Carthaginians used towers and rams against the Greek colonies of Sicily, which influenced Dionysius I of Syracuse, who developed a catapult in 399 BCE. Philip II of Macedonia and Alexander the Great were the first rulers to use siege engines to a large extent. The Helepolis of Demetrius Poliorcetes, of 304 BCE, was nine stories high, plated with iron, 40 metres tall and weighed 180 tonnes.

The Romans preferred to build earthen ramps or simply to scale the walls, their soldiers working under shelters called vineae. Roman legions first used siege towers around 200 BCE, and the onager was the main Roman invention in the field. In China the earliest documented siege artillery, a levered traction catapult and a large siege crossbow, is described in the Mozi, a Mohist text of about the 4th to 3rd century BCE.

Medieval armies used catapults such as the mangonel, the ballista, the traction trebuchet, first designed in China in the 3rd century BCE, and the counterweight trebuchet, first described by Mardi bin Ali al-Tarsusi in the 12th century though of unknown origin. Besiegers could also starve a castle out, set fires against its walls, dig mines under the foundations or throw diseased animals and human corpses over the walls to spread disease.

With gunpowder came the cannon, the petard and the mortar, which proved so effective that fortifications had to be built low and thick, as in the designs of Vauban. Specialised siege artillery culminated in the two world wars, with guns such as Big Bertha and the German Schwerer Gustav, a railway gun of 80 cm calibre. Such guns took so long to move and deploy that they were vulnerable to air attack and unsuited to rapid warfare.
sierra-leone: Sierra Leone lies on the south-west coast of West Africa, bordered by Guinea to the north and east, Liberia to the south-east and the Atlantic Ocean to the west. It has about 400 km of coastline. The east is a plateau with high mountains, where Mount Bintumani reaches 1,948 m, and lowland plains of forest, bush and farmland cover about 43% of the land. Freetown stands on a mountainous coastal peninsula. The name comes from the Lion Mountains near Freetown, which the Portuguese explorer Pedro de Sintra named Serra Leoa, meaning lioness mountains, in 1462.

The area has been inhabited for at least 2,500 years. Iron technology was adopted by the 9th century and agriculture established on the coast by about 1000 CE. Dense rainforest and swamps, and the tsetse fly, whose disease killed the horses and zebu cattle of the Mandé people, protected the region against invasion by the Mandinka Empire and limited the influence of the Mali Empire. Susu traders brought Islam in the 18th century.

European contact began in the 15th century. Traders from the Dutch Republic, England and France set up stations that came to deal mainly in slaves, brought to the coast by traders from the interior. In 1808 the coastal Sierra Leone Colony was founded as part of the British Empire, to resettle Africans returning after the abolition of the slave trade, and in 1896 an inland Protectorate was created. Independence came in 1961 under Prime Minister Sir Milton Margai. A constitution of 1971 made the country a presidential republic under Siaka Stevens. In 1991 a civil war began between the government and the Revolutionary United Front. It lasted 11 years and ended in 2002 after intervention by ECOMOG forces and then the United Kingdom.

Freetown is the capital and largest city. The country is a presidential republic, and English is the official language, while Krio, derived from English and several African languages, is spoken across the country. About 18 ethnic groups live there, the Temne and Mende being the largest, and the Creole people descend from freed African-American and Afro-Caribbean slaves and liberated Africans. Bunce Island, near Freetown, holds the ruins of a slave fortress of the Atlantic slave trade.
sigmund-freud: Sigmund Freud was born Sigismund Schlomo Freud on 6 May 1856 in the Moravian town of Freiberg, in the Austrian Empire, now Příbor in the Czech Republic. He was the first of eight children of Ashkenazi Jewish parents who both came from Galicia. His father, Jakob Freud, was a wool merchant, and his mother, Amalia Nathansohn, was Jakob's third wife. The family was struggling financially and living in a rented room when he was born. He was born with a caul, which his mother saw as a good omen.

Freud took almost nine years to finish his medical studies, because of his interest in neurophysiological research, including the sexual anatomy of eels, and in philosophy under Franz Brentano. He entered private practice in neurology for financial reasons and received his doctorate in medicine in 1881, aged 25. In the 1880s he worked chiefly on the anatomy of the brain. In 1891 his monograph Zur Auffassung der Aphasien entered the debates about aphasia, coined the term agnosia and counselled against too locationist a view of neurological deficits.

He was also an early researcher of cerebral palsy, then called cerebral paralysis, and showed that the disease existed long before other researchers studied it. He suggested that William John Little, who first identified it, was wrong that lack of oxygen at birth was a cause, and proposed instead that birth complications were a symptom. Freud died on 23 September 1939.

Freud founded psychoanalysis, a clinical method that treats conflicts in the psyche through dialogue between patient and analyst. He introduced free association, the interpretation of dreams and the analysis of transference. He widened the idea of sexuality to include infantile stages, which led to the Oedipus complex, and developed a theory of the unconscious and a model of the mind with id, ego and superego. His later work offered an interpretation and critique of religion and culture.

His books include The Interpretation of Dreams (1899), Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality (1905), Totem and Taboo (1913), The Ego and the Id (1923), The Future of an Illusion (1927), Civilization and Its Discontents (1930) and Moses and Monotheism (1939). His talking cure gave the basic format for later psychotherapy. The neo-Freudians, among them Alfred Adler and Karen Horney, rejected his theory of instinctual drive, and Jacques Lacan approached psychoanalysis through linguistics and literature. His legacy remains controversial.
sikhism: Sikhism, also called Sikhi, developed from the teachings of Guru Nanak (1469–1539), the first guru, and the nine gurus who followed him. Nanak was born in the village now called Nankana Sahib, in present-day Pakistan, to Punjabi Khatri Hindu parents. The hagiography Puratan Janamsakhi, composed more than two centuries after his death, says that after a disappearance of three days he declared, "There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim". In 1526 he started a small commune at Kartarpur, and his disciples came to be known as Sikhs, a word meaning students or disciples.

In 1539 Nanak chose his disciple Lahiṇā, who became Guru Angad, as successor rather than either of his sons. The Mughal emperors tortured and executed two gurus, Guru Arjan (1563–1606) and Guru Tegh Bahadur (1621–1675), who refused to convert to Islam. In 1699 Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa, an order meant to protect freedom of conscience, whose members express the qualities of the sant-sipāhī, the saint-soldier.

Sikhs hold that only one God exists, present in everything, a oneness expressed in the phrase Ik Onkar. The word for God is Waheguru. Central practices are remembrance of the divine name (simran), selfless service (sevā), honest work and sharing with those in need. Nanak is quoted as saying, "Truth is the highest virtue, but higher still is truthful living." Sikhism rejects the claim that any religious tradition has a monopoly on truth, and Sikhs do not actively proselytise, though voluntary converts are generally accepted.

The Khalsa is the name Guru Gobind Singh gave to Sikhs fully initiated in the ceremony of ammrit sañcār, in which sweetened water is stirred with a double-edged sword. Baptised Sikhs wear the five Ks, which include the kesh, uncut hair, so that most religious Sikh men wear a turban. Gurdwaras are open to all.

The central scripture is the Guru Granth Sahib. Guru Gobind Singh decreed in 1708 that it would be the final and perpetual guru, closing the line of human gurus, and Sikhs regard it as the eleventh and eternally living guru. Its earlier form, the Ādi Granth, was compiled primarily by Bhai Gurdas under Guru Arjan in 1603 and 1604. It contains the hymns of the gurus and of thirteen Hindu and two Muslim bhagats of the Bhakti tradition, among them Kabir and the Sufi saint Farid. It is written as poetry for recitation in thirty-one ragas. The Dasam Granth, containing texts attributed to Guru Gobind Singh, does not have the same authority.
silk: Silk is a natural protein fibre, composed mainly of fibroin with a smaller coating of sericin, most commonly made from the cocoons of insect larvae. The best-known silk comes from the mulberry silkworm, Bombyx mori, reared in captivity in a process called sericulture. The production of silk originated in central China in the Neolithic period. The earliest evidence is the silk protein fibroin found in soil from two tombs at Jiahu in Henan, about 8,500 years old, and the earliest surviving silk fabric, from about 3630 BCE, wrapped the body of a child at a Yangshao culture site in Henan.

Silk production remained confined to China until the Silk Road opened, at some point in the latter part of the 1st millennium BCE, and China kept a virtual monopoly on it for another thousand years. Wild silks were spun in China, South Asia and Europe from ancient times, but always on a far smaller scale.

The Roman Empire knew of silk and traded in it, and Chinese silk was the most highly priced luxury good it imported. Under the emperor Tiberius, sumptuary laws forbade men to wear silk, but they proved ineffectual. The secret of silk-making reached Europe only around 550, by way of the Byzantine Empire; contemporary accounts say monks working for the emperor Justinian I smuggled silkworm eggs from China to Constantinople inside hollow canes. The best looms and weavers worked inside the Great Palace there, and the cloth was used for imperial robes and as diplomatic gifts.

Italy was the leading producer in the medieval period, beginning at Catanzaro in the 11th century. Bengal was the leading exporter of silk between the 16th and 19th centuries, and silkworms were brought to Oaxaca from Spain in the 1530s.

Silk is not spun like other natural fibres. The cocoons are soaked in boiling water to remove the sericin and free the end of the filament, which is then reeled off in one continuous length. A caterpillar spins about one mile (1.6 km) of filament in two or three days, and since one thread is too fine for commercial use, three to ten strands are twisted together. The flat surfaces of the fibrils reflect light at many angles, which gives silk its natural sheen. It was used for clothing and furnishings, and also in parachutes and bicycle tyres.
silver: Silver was known in prehistoric times. Copper, silver and gold occur in elemental form in nature and were probably the first primitive forms of money, replacing simple barter. Unlike copper, silver did not lead to the growth of metallurgy, because of its low structural strength; it was used mostly for ornament or as money. Native silver was much scarcer than native gold, and in Egypt silver was more expensive than gold until about the fifteenth century BCE.

The discovery of cupellation, which extracts silver from its ores, changed this. Slag heaps in Asia Minor and on the Aegean islands show silver being separated from lead as early as the 4th millennium BCE, and Sardinia was one of the earliest extraction centres in Europe, in the early Chalcolithic. The techniques spread widely only later.

Silver is a soft, ductile and malleable metal, slightly less malleable than gold, with a brilliant white lustre that takes a high polish; the name of the metal has become the name of a colour. It is one of the seven metals of antiquity and sits in group 11 of the periodic table with copper and gold. Because pure silver is so soft, silver used for jewellery, coinage and household objects is usually alloyed with copper.

The English word comes from Old English seolfor and siolfor, with cognates in Old High German silabar, Gothic silubr and Old Norse silfr. The chemical symbol Ag comes from the Latin argentum, from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning 'white' or 'shining'.

The earliest known coins were minted in the kingdom of Lydia in Asia Minor around 600 BCE, of electrum, a natural alloy of gold and silver. Silver standards, in which the unit of account is a fixed weight of silver, were then widespread until the 20th century. Notable silver coins include the Greek drachma, the Roman denarius, the Islamic dirham, the karshapana of ancient India, the rupee of the Mughal Empire and the Spanish dollar.

Apart from coinage, the major use throughout most of history was in jewellery and general-use items such as table silver. In Hesiod's Works and Days the successive ages of humanity are named after metals, among them silver, and Ovid, in the Metamorphoses, describes a silver age that excels bronze but is excelled by gold.
sima-qian: Sima Qian was born at Xiayang in Zuopingyi, near present-day Hancheng in Shaanxi. His father, Sima Tan, was appointed grand historian at the imperial court, a relatively low-ranking post whose main duty was to draw up the yearly calendar, identifying ritually auspicious and inauspicious days, and which also involved recording events at court and across the country.

In 126 BCE, at about the age of twenty, he made an extensive tour of Han China. Starting from Chang'an, he went south across the Yangtze to the Changsha Kingdom, where he visited the Miluo River, traditionally the place where the poet Qu Yuan drowned himself. He visited the grave of the general Han Xin at Huaiyin and Qufu, the hometown of Confucius, where he studied ritual.

After his travels Sima became a Palace Attendant to Emperor Wu of Han. His father had conceived a complete history of China but left only preparatory sketches, and summoned his son to continue it. Sima Qian succeeded him as grand historian and in 105 BCE was among the scholars chosen to reform the calendar. The resulting Taichu calendar, promulgated in 104 BCE, is the first Chinese calendar whose full method of calculation has been preserved.

In 99 BCE he became embroiled in the Li Ling affair. The general Li Ling had been defeated and captured in a campaign against the Xiongnu, and every official condemned him. Sima alone defended him, though Li had never been his friend. Emperor Wu took this as an attack on his brother-in-law Li Guangli and sentenced Sima to death. Execution could be commuted by money or by castration; lacking the money, Sima chose castration and spent three years in prison. On his release he lived on as a palace eunuch to finish his history, rather than die as a disgraced gentleman-scholar was expected to.

The Shiji, or Records of the Grand Historian, runs to over 500,000 characters in 130 chapters and covers more than two thousand years, from the Yellow Emperor to the reign of Emperor Wu. It combined basic annals of sovereigns, tables, treatises on music, ritual and economics, house chronicles and ordered biographies. Earlier histories had recounted particular events or regions. Sima treated the known world and was the first Chinese historian to treat the Xiongnu as human beings implicitly the equals of the Han. His Letter to Ren An is admired as prose. His grandson Yang Yun released the work during the reign of Emperor Xuan.
simferopol: Simferopol lies in the south-central Crimean Peninsula on the Salhir River, near the artificial Simferopol Reservoir, which supplies the city's drinking water and has the biggest earth dam in Europe. It has a humid subtropical climate. The city is a political, economic and transport hub of the peninsula and has a major railway station.

Its name comes from the Greek Sympheropoli, meaning city of common good or usefulness. In Crimean Tatar the city is Aqmescit, the white mosque. The colour does not describe a building: Turkic peoples give a colour to each cardinal point, and white is the west, so the name means the Western Mosque.

The Crimean Scythians lived in the area from the 3rd century BCE to the 4th century CE, and the remnants of their capital, Scythian Neapolis, lie within the city. The Crimean Tatars later founded Aqmescit, which was for a time the residence of the Qalğa-Sultan, the second most important office in the Crimean Khanate after the Khan.

After Catherine II annexed the Crimean Khanate in 1784, the new city of Simferopol was founded on the site of Aqmescit, in line with her Greek Plan of Greek place names for the new southern lands. It became the administrative centre of the Taurida Governorate in 1802. After the Crimean War of 1854-1856 more than 30,000 Russian soldiers were buried near the city. In 1870 about 57 per cent of the population were Eastern Orthodox, with Jewish, Karaite, Catholic and other communities beside them.

The Red Army took the city on 13 November 1920, and it became capital of the Crimean Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic in 1921. German forces occupied it from 1 November 1941 to 13 April 1944 and killed over 22,000 local people, mostly Jews, Russians, Krymchaks and Romani, including an estimated 14,300 from 9 December 1941. On 18 May 1944 the city's Crimean Tatars were deported with their whole nation to Central Asia. Crimea was transferred to the Ukrainian SSR on 26 April 1954. After 1991 Simferopol was capital of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea. Russia annexed Crimea in 2014; the city is internationally recognised as part of Ukraine.
simon-bolivar: Simón Bolívar was born on 24 July 1783 in Caracas, the youngest of four children of Juan Vicente Bolívar y Ponte and María de la Concepción Palacios y Blanco, in a wealthy creole family. His father died of tuberculosis in 1786 and his mother in 1792, and he was raised partly by an enslaved woman named Hipólita, whom he viewed as both a motherly and a fatherly figure. In 1799 he was sent to Madrid, where he married María Teresa Rodríguez del Toro y Alaysa in 1802; she died of yellow fever in 1803. On a second journey to Europe he reached Rome, where he swore to end Spanish rule in the Americas.

After Napoleon's invasion of the Iberian peninsula, Venezuelan creoles sought their own government, and Bolívar helped secure Francisco de Miranda's election to the congress that declared Venezuela independent on 5 July 1811, creating the first Republic of Venezuela. The republic fell in 1812, and Bolívar went into exile in Curaçao and Cartagena. After Spanish forces subdued New Granada, he wrote the Jamaica Letter in 1815 in Kingston, laying out his ideology and vision of the future of the Americas.

In Haiti Alexandre Pétion, after Bolívar pledged to free every slave in the areas he occupied, gave him money and military supplies. In February 1819 the congress at Angostura elected him president. In May he marched over the Andes with more than 2,000 soldiers, and on 7 August 1819 the Royalists were routed at the Battle of Boyacá. Allies and Bolívar defeated the Spanish in Venezuela and Panama in 1821, Ecuador in 1822, Peru in 1824 and Bolivia in 1825, and Venezuela, New Granada, Ecuador and Panama were merged into Gran Colombia.

In his final years Bolívar became disillusioned with the republics and was successively removed from his offices. He left Bogotá on 8 May 1830 intending to go into exile in England, but with his health failing and no ship available he was taken to the Quinta de San Pedro Alejandrino near Santa Marta, where he died of tuberculosis on 17 December 1830, aged 47. In 1842 his remains were returned to Caracas, and in 1876 they were moved to the National Pantheon of Venezuela. He is regarded as a hero and national and cultural icon throughout Latin America, and Bolivia and Venezuela, as the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, are named after him.
simone-de-beauvoir: Beauvoir was born on 9 January 1908 in Montparnasse, in Paris. Her father, Georges Bertrand de Beauvoir, was initially a lawyer but aspired to be an actor, and her mother, Françoise, was a devout Catholic and a banker's daughter. The promised dowry was lost when Françoise's father was jailed. Her parents were often absent, and she was raised chiefly by a nanny, Louise. She had a younger sister, Hélène, born on 6 June 1910. Intellectually precocious and encouraged by her father, she wrote that the contrast between her father's individualism and pagan standards and her mother's rigid conventional morality made her life an endless disputation, the main reason she became an intellectual.

After her studies Beauvoir saw teaching as a way to earn her own living. She did her practice teaching at the same secondary school as Maurice Merleau-Ponty and Claude Lévi-Strauss, and from 1929 to 1943 she taught at lycées in Marseille, Rouen and Paris until she could live on her writing. She then became a public intellectual. Her first novel, She Came to Stay, appeared in 1943, followed by The Blood of Others (1945), which tells a love story between two young students in the French Resistance during the Second World War.

With Jean-Paul Sartre and Maurice Merleau-Ponty she co-founded Les Temps Modernes, a monthly political journal that carried communists, Catholics, Gaullists and socialists, whose first issue appeared on 1 October 1945. Sartre and Merleau-Ponty later quarrelled, and Beauvoir sided with Sartre. She remained an editor until her death and in later years held the editorial meetings in her flat.

Her first philosophical essay, Pyrrhus et Cinéas (1944), was followed by The Ethics of Ambiguity (1947), in which she argues that the freedom of the self requires the freedom of others. The Second Sex (1949) turned the existentialist principle that existence precedes essence into a feminist one: One is not born, but rather becomes, woman. It articulated the distinction between biological sex and the social construction of gender, and showed how sexual difference is used to trap women in the role of the Other. The Mandarins (1954), a roman à clef about Sartre's and Beauvoir's circle after the war, won the Prix Goncourt.

Beauvoir at first denied being a feminist but later admitted it. The Second Sex opened the way for second-wave feminism, and Kate Millett, Shulamith Firestone, Juliet Mitchell, Ann Oakley and Germaine Greer read it in translation and acknowledged their debt to her. Betty Friedan said that reading it in the early 1950s led to her own analysis of women's existence.
sindh: Sindh lies in the south-east of Pakistan and is bounded by the Arabian Sea to the south, Balochistan to the west and Punjab to the north; to the east it shares a border with the Indian states of Gujarat and Rajasthan. Its landscape is mostly alluvial plain on either side of the Indus River, with the Thar Desert in the east and the Kirthar Mountains in the west. The name Sind is a Persian derivative of the Sanskrit sindhu, meaning river, and the Greeks under Alexander the Great called the Indus Indos. The spelling Sindh replaced the older Sind in 1988.

Settled life began around Sindh and Punjab some 9,000 years ago and developed into the Indus Valley Civilisation. Mohenjo-daro, built around 2500 BCE, was one of the largest settlements of that civilisation, with standardised bricks, street grids and covered sewerage. It was abandoned in the 19th century BCE as the civilisation declined, and was not rediscovered until the 1920s. Around 1000 BCE the Indo-Aryan kingdom of Sindhu-Sauvira emerged and lasted until the Achaemenids captured the region in 518 BCE, after whom came the Macedonians, Mauryans, Indo-Greeks, Indo-Scythians, Guptas and Sasanians.

The first Muslim naval raids came in 636 under the caliph Umar. Arab forces conquered Sindh in 712 under the Umayyad Caliphate and made it a province, which laid the foundations of the Muslim period in South Asia. The Habbari Emirate emerged in the 9th century, and between the 11th and 16th centuries the Soomra, Samma and Arghun dynasties ruled, mostly as vassals of the Delhi Sultanate. Akbar, himself born at Umerkot in Sindh, sent an army in 1591 to 1593 to take lower Sindh from the Tarkhan dynasty. Mughal rule ran from the provincial capital Thatta, while the Kalhora dynasty held upper Sindh from Khudabad. The Talpur dynasty ruled from 1783, and the East India Company later captured the province.

Sindh became a separate province in 1936. After the Lahore Resolution of 1940 it was the first province to endorse the Pakistan Movement, and it joined the Dominion of Pakistan in 1947. It was merged into West Pakistan in 1955 and restored as a province in 1970.

Karachi, on the southern coast, is the provincial capital and the largest city. Sindhi, spoken by about 60 per cent of the population at the 2023 census, is the most widely spoken language, and about 90 per cent of residents are Muslim. Sufism is an important marker of Sindhi identity for Muslims and Hindus alike, and the poet Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai lived here. Two World Heritage Sites lie in the province, Mohenjo-daro and the Makli Necropolis near Thatta.
singapore: Singapore lies about one degree of latitude, 137 kilometres, north of the equator, off the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula. Its territory is a main island, also known as Pulau Ujong, over 60 satellite islands and one outlying islet, and two man-made connections, the Johor–Singapore Causeway and the Tuas Second Link, join it to Johor in Malaysia. The highest natural point is Bukit Timah Hill, at 163.63 metres. Land reclamation has raised the land area from roughly 580 km2 in the 1960s to 770 km2. The name is an anglicisation of the Malay Singapura, from the Sanskrit for 'lion city', and the island was earlier known as Temasek.

According to the Malay Annals, the Kingdom of Singapura was founded in 1299 by Sang Nila Utama, although historians debate the accounts. In the 14th century, as Temasek, Singapore was a trading port under the influence of both the Majapahit Empire and the Siamese kingdoms. Around the end of that century its ruler Parameswara was attacked, by either the Majapahit or the Siamese, and moved to Malacca, where he founded the Sultanate of Malacca. Portuguese raiders burned the settlement in 1613, and the island then faded into obscurity for two centuries, nominally part of the Johor Sultanate.

Stamford Raffles arrived on 28 January 1819, when around 150 people lived on the island, 120 of them Malays. With the help of the Temenggong of Johor, he brought Tengku Long back from exile and recognised him as Sultan Hussein, and in the Treaty of Singapore of 6 February 1819 the Sultan granted the British the right to establish a trading post. Singapore came under direct British control in 1867 as part of the Straits Settlements, was occupied by Japan in 1942, gained self-governance in 1959 and joined Malaysia in 1963. It was expelled from the federation two years later and became independent in 1965.

Singapore is a parliamentary republic based on the Westminster system. Its population was 6,110,200 in 2025, of whom 3,660,200 were citizens. The 2020 census reported 74.3% of residents of Chinese descent, 13.5% Malay and 9.0% Indian. English, Malay, Mandarin and Tamil are the four official languages, and 78.7% of resident households live in public housing developed by the Housing and Development Board.
skopje: Skopje lies in the north of North Macedonia, in the centre of the Balkan peninsula and about halfway between Belgrade and Athens. The city was built in the Skopje Valley, which runs west to east along the Vardar river and is about 20 km wide. Mountain ranges to the north and south limit its expansion, so the city spreads along the Vardar and the Serava, a small river that comes from the north. Within its administrative boundaries it stretches for more than 33 km but is only 10 km wide.

The name is first attested in Ptolemy's Geography, c. 150, as Scupi, a city of Roman Dardania. The Macedonian Skopje is the local Slavic rendering of that name, Shkup is the Albanian form, and Üsküb is the Ottoman Turkish one, which Western languages adapted as Uskub or Uskup and used until 1912.

The earliest traces of settlement, from the Chalcolithic period (4th millennium BCE), come from the rocky promontory on which Skopje Fortress stands. The Roman city of Scupi was founded in the late 1st century under Domitian and abandoned in 518 after an earthquake destroyed it. It was rebuilt under Justinian I. The city later belonged to the First Bulgarian Empire, to the Byzantine Empire and to the Second Bulgarian Empire, before it passed to Serbia.

Before the Austro-Turkish war and the great fire of 1689, Skopje was one of the biggest cities of the Balkans, with a population estimated at between 30,000 and 60,000. The fire was set by the retreating Austrian forces and was followed by a long decline: the city had only 10,000 inhabitants in 1836. Growth resumed after 1850, and the population reached 32,000 in 1905. Annexed by Serbia in 1912 after the Balkan Wars, Skopje was held by Bulgaria in 1915-1918 and again in 1941-1944, and in between formed part of Yugoslavia.

The earthquake of 1963 destroyed 80 per cent of the city. Its reconstruction was directed mainly by the Polish architect Adolf Ciborowski, who had already planned the rebuilding of Warsaw after World War II. He divided Skopje into zones for particular activities: parks along the Vardar, high-rise housing and shopping centres between the main boulevards, and individual housing and industry in the suburbs. Population density was kept low to limit the effects of a future earthquake.

The 2021 census counted 526,502 inhabitants, roughly a quarter of the country's population. Ethnic Macedonians form the majority, with Albanians a significant minority. The city is the seat of the Ss. Cyril and Methodius University, the Macedonian Academy of Sciences and Arts and the National Theatre.
skype: Skype was founded in 2003 by Niklas Zennström from Sweden and Janus Friis from Denmark, and its software was created by Estonian developers. Friis and one of the Estonians, Toivo Annus, are credited with the idea of cutting the cost of voice calls by using a peer-to-peer protocol like that of Kazaa. An early alpha version was tested in the spring of 2003, and the first public beta was released on 29 August 2003. The name came from the words sky and peer-to-peer, which became Skyper. Some domain names for Skyper were already taken, so the final r was dropped.

Skype was a proprietary telecommunications application best known for videotelephony, videoconferencing and voice calls. It also offered instant messaging, file transfer and paid calls to landline and mobile telephones over traditional networks. Registered users had a unique Skype ID and could hold voice chats between pairs of users and conference calls using a proprietary audio codec. It originally ran as a hybrid of peer-to-peer and client-server systems. An early web page described it as highly secure with end-to-end encryption, but its protocol was never made public, so the claim could not be independently verified.

In September 2005 eBay agreed to acquire Skype Technologies, based in Luxembourg. In 2009 eBay sold 65 per cent of it to Silver Lake, Andreessen Horowitz and the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board. Microsoft acquired it on 10 May 2011 for 8.5 billion US dollars and used it to replace its own Windows Live Messenger, which it discontinued in April 2013. In 2011 most of the development team and 44 per cent of the division's employees were in Tallinn and Tartu, in Estonia.

At the end of 2010 there were over 660 million registered users worldwide. In February 2012 there were 34 million users online at one time, and by January 2013 more than 50 million. In 2011 its free version was reported to be used increasingly by teachers and schools for global education projects and language learning. Microsoft retired Skype in favour of Microsoft Teams on 5 May 2025.
slavery: Slavery predates written records and has existed in many cultures. It is rare among hunter-gatherers, because it requires economic surpluses and a substantial population density, and became widespread only with the invention of agriculture in the Neolithic Revolution about 11,000 years ago. It was practised in almost every ancient civilisation, through debt bondage, punishment for crime, the enslavement of prisoners of war, child abandonment and the enslavement of slaves' offspring.

The English word slave came through Old French esclave from Byzantine Greek sklábos. According to a widespread view, known since the 18th century, this derives from the self-name of a Slavic tribe, because its people were often captured and enslaved; the view has been disputed since the 19th century.

Slavery is the ownership of a person as property, especially with regard to their labour, and typically involves compulsory work, with place of work and residence dictated by the holder. Many cases of enslavement followed a breach of the law, indebtedness, military defeat or the pursuit of cheaper labour; others were instituted along lines of race or sex. In chattel slavery the slave is legally the personal property of the owner and can be bought and sold like livestock. Depending on era and country, slaves sometimes had limited legal rights: a 1686 statute in the Province of New York punished those who deliberately killed slaves.

Chattel slavery was widely accepted, and in ancient Greece and the Roman Empire was considered a keystone of society. Other examples are medieval Egypt, Sub-Saharan Africa, Brazil, the antebellum United States, Cuba and Haiti. In the Senegambia region between 1300 and 1900 close to one-third of the population was enslaved, and in early Islamic states of the western Sahel, including Ghana, Mali, Segou and Songhai, about a third.

Economists have argued that slavery becomes desirable where land is abundant and labour scarce, and that slavery and then serfdom declined in Europe as the population grew, then returned in the Americas and Russia where large areas had few inhabitants. It was common where tasks were simple and easy to supervise, as on large plantations of sugarcane and cotton.
slavs: The oldest mention of the Slavic name is from the 6th century, when Procopius wrote Sklaboi and related forms in Byzantine Greek and his contemporary Jordanes wrote Sclaveni in Latin. It is usually derived from slovo, word, so that it meant people who speak the same language, in contrast to the Slavic word for Germans, němьcь, meaning mute people.

Roman sources of the 1st and 2nd centuries refer to early Slavic peoples as Veneti, living east of the Suebi and west of the Sarmatians between the upper Vistula and the Dnieper. The Slavs, called Antes and Sclaveni, first appear in Byzantine records in the early 6th century, emerging from the area of the Carpathian Mountains, the lower Danube and the Black Sea to invade the Danubian provinces of the Eastern Empire under Justinian I.

The westward movement of Germanic tribes in the 5th and 6th centuries, together with that of the Huns and later the Avars and Bulgars, began the great migration of the Slavs, who settled lands the Germanic tribes had left. They moved west towards the Oder and the Elbe-Saale line, south into Bohemia, Moravia, the Pannonian plain and the Balkans, and north along the upper Dnieper. By the end of the 6th century they had settled the Eastern Alps.

In the 7th century the Frankish merchant Samo supported the Slavs against their Avar rulers and became ruler of Samo's Empire, the first known Slav state in Central Europe. The First Bulgarian Empire was founded in 681 as an alliance of the ruling Bulgars and the numerous Slavs, and Old Church Slavonic became its official language in 864. The Principality of Serbia dates from the 8th century, and the Duchy of Bohemia and Kievan Rus' from the 9th.

From the mid-19th century a pan-Slavic movement stressed the common heritage of the Slavic peoples, especially in the Balkans, where South Slavs had long been ruled by other empires. In 1918 the Slavs established Czechoslovakia, the Second Polish Republic and the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes.

Procopius, in 545, described the Sclaveni and Antae as having once shared the name Sporoi. He wrote that they lived under a democracy, believed in one god, the maker of lightning, to whom they sacrificed, and lived in scattered housing, often changing settlement. In war they were mainly foot soldiers with shields, spears and bows and little armour.
slovakia: Slovakia covers about 49,000 km2 and is mostly mountainous, with the Carpathian Mountains across most of the northern half. The Tatra Mountains hold 29 peaks above 2,500 metres, and Gerlachovský štít, at 2,655 metres, is the highest point in the country. The largest lowland is the Danubian Lowland in the southwest, followed by the Eastern Slovak Lowland in the southeast. Forests cover 41% of the land, nine national parks cover 6.5%, and hundreds of caves lie under the mountains, five of them on UNESCO's World Heritage list. The name means the Land of the Slavs, and the present Slovak form Slovensko is first attested in 1675.

The oldest human artefacts, stone tools dated to 270,000 BCE, come from near Nové Mesto nad Váhom, and a Neanderthal cranium of about 200,000 BCE was found near Gánovce. Slavs arrived in the 5th and 6th centuries, and parts of the territory came under the Avar Khaganate before the Principality of Nitra was annexed by the Principality of Moravia, later Great Moravia. The land passed into the Principality of Hungary, which became the Kingdom of Hungary in 1000. The Mongol invasion of 1241 and 1242 destroyed much of it, and the south was part of Ottoman provinces in the 16th and 17th centuries.

The Slovak Uprising of 1848 did not achieve its aim but helped to cement a Slovak national identity. Czechoslovakia was proclaimed in 1918, with its borders set by the Treaty of Saint Germain in 1919 and the Treaty of Trianon in 1920. The first Slovak Republic, established in 1939 as a one-party clerical fascist client state under Nazi Germany, joined the Axis in 1940. Czechoslovakia became a communist state after the Soviet-backed coup of 1948, the Prague Spring was suppressed by the Warsaw Pact invasion in August 1968, and the Velvet Revolution of 1989 ended communist rule.

Slovakia became independent on 1 January 1993 after the peaceful dissolution of Czechoslovakia, and its constitution, ratified on 1 September 1992, took effect that day. It is a parliamentary democratic republic with a directly elected president of limited powers and a 150-seat National Council. It joined the European Union and NATO in 2004, the Schengen Area in 2007 and the eurozone in 2009.

The 2021 census recorded 83.8% Slovaks and 7.8% Hungarians, the largest minority, and 55.8% of the population identified as Catholic. About 90,000 Jews lived in Slovakia before the Second World War, and most were murdered in the Holocaust; about 2,300 remain.
slovenia: Slovenia covers 20,271 km2 and is mostly mountainous and forested. Four major European geographic regions meet there: the Alps, the Dinarides, the Pannonian Plain and the Mediterranean Sea. The highest peak, Triglav, at 2,864 metres, appears on the national coat of arms and flag. The Adriatic coastline stretches approximately 47 kilometres, the southwest has a limestone Karst Plateau of underground rivers, gorges and caves, and the landscape of the northeast is essentially flat. The name means land of the Slavs.

Evidence of habitation dates to around 250,000 years ago. A pierced cave bear bone from Divje Babe cave near Cerkno, dated to 43100 ± 700 years before present, is considered a kind of flute and possibly the oldest musical instrument discovered. Pile dwellings over 4,500 years old in the Ljubljana Marsh are a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the Ljubljana Marshes Wooden Wheel is the world's oldest wooden wheel. In Roman times the area was divided between Venetia et Histria and the provinces of Pannonia and Noricum, with posts at Emona (Ljubljana), Poetovio (Ptuj) and Celeia (Celje). In 394 the Battle of the Frigidus took place in the Vipava Valley, where Theodosius I defeated the usurper Eugenius.

Slavic tribes migrated to the Alpine area in the early Middle Ages. From 623 or 624 King Samo united the Alpine and Western Slavs against the Avars, and after his death around 658 the ancestors of the Slovenes formed Carantania and Carniola. Charlemagne decisively defeated the Avars in 803. The Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes was formed in December 1918 and became known as Yugoslavia in 1929. Nazi Germany, Fascist Italy, Hungary and the Independent State of Croatia partitioned Slovenia in 1941.

Slovenia was established in 1945 as one of six republics of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and modern Slovenia emerged in June 1991, when it declared independence and became a sovereign state after the brief Ten-Day War. It is a parliamentary republic whose head of state is a president elected for five years, and legislative power rests mainly with the 90-member National Assembly. In 2007 it was the first new member state of the European Union to adopt the euro. The population is about 2.1 million, and Slovenes make up 83.1% of the inhabitants. Four sites are on UNESCO's World Heritage list, among them the Škocjan Caves and the Idrija Mercury mining site.
smolensk: Smolensk stands on the Dnieper River, 360 kilometres west-southwest of Moscow, and is the administrative centre of Smolensk Oblast. In the early medieval period it lay on the route from the Varangians to the Greeks. Rus' travellers sailed up the Western Dvina and portaged their boats to the upper Dnieper, and at Smolensk they are supposed to have mended leaks with tar, which one explanation gives for the name. Others derive it from the Smolnya River or from a Slavic tribe, the Smolyans. The Byzantine emperor Constantine Porphyrogenitus described the city around 950 as a key station on the route.

The Ustyug Chronicle of the 16th century first mentions Smolensk under 863, and the Primary Chronicle names it as the centre of the Krivichi. After Oleg the Wise took Kiev in 882, it became part of Kievan Rus'. The Principality of Smolensk was founded in 1054 and by the end of the 12th century was one of the strongest in Eastern Europe, its princes often holding the Kievan throne. The Svirskaya church of 1197 was admired as the most beautiful building east of Kiev. The city had its own veche from the start.

Spared by Mongol armies in 1240, Smolensk paid tribute to the Golden Horde and became a pawn between Lithuania and Moscow. Vytautas the Great of Lithuania took it in 1395, 1404 and 1408, and Vasily III of Russia took it in 1514. Boris Godunov fortified it, building the stone kremlin of 1597-1602, the largest in Russia. The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth captured it in 1611 after a siege of twenty months and kept it through the Smolensk War that began in 1632. Russia retook it on 23 September 1654, and the Truce of Andrusovo in 1667 ended Polish claims.

Smolensk was the seat of a governorate from 1708. In August 1812 Napoleon entered the city after a battle in which total losses were estimated at 30,000, and the Eagles monument of 1912 marks the centenary. German forces occupied it in 1941-1943. Some 18 kilometres away, at Katyn in 1940, the NKVD murdered some 22,000 Polish prisoners of war. The population was 316,570 in the 2021 census.
soap: Toilet soaps are made by saponification, in which an alkaline solution, often lye, breaks down the triglycerides of vegetable or animal oils and fats into salts of fatty acids and frees glycerol. Sodium soaps, made with soda lye, are firm, while potassium soaps, made with potash lye, are softer or often liquid. Soap made from pure olive oil is sometimes called Castile soap or Marseille soap. Soap cleans by gathering oil and dirt into tiny spheres called micelles, which the water then carries away.

Proto-soaps, which mixed fat and alkali for cleansing, are mentioned in Sumerian, Babylonian and Egyptian texts. The Ebers papyrus of about 1550 BCE shows that the Egyptians made a soap-like product as a medicine from animal fats or vegetable oils and trona. True soaps differed from these: they foamed, were made deliberately and could be hard or soft, because their makers understood sources of lye. It is uncertain who invented true soap, which may have arisen independently in various societies.

The Romans cleaned the body by rubbing oil into the skin and scraping it off with a strigil, and they did not use soap until at least the first century CE. Pliny the Elder describes soap as an invention of the Gauls, made from tallow and ashes. In the second century CE the physician Galen described soap-making with lye and rated Germanic soaps the best and those of Gaul second.

During the Islamic Golden Age hard, pleasantly scented toilet soap was produced in West Asia and North Africa, and soap-making became an established industry. Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi gave recipes, and in Syria soap was made from olive oil, alkali and lime and exported to the rest of the Muslim world and to Europe.

In Europe the soapmakers of Naples formed a guild in the late sixth century, and by the 15th century soap was made on an industrial scale in Antwerp, Castile, Marseille, Naples and Venice. In England a soap tax kept soap a luxury until it was repealed in 1853. Industrially made bar soaps became available in the late 18th century, and William Hesketh Lever and his brother bought a soap works in Warrington in 1886, which became Lever Brothers and later Unilever.
sochi: Sochi lies on the Sochi River along the Black Sea, in the North Caucasus of southern Russia. Greater Sochi is elongated along the coast for 145 kilometres and is about 1,603 kilometres from Moscow. It has a humid subtropical climate, with daytime temperatures of 25 to 29 °C in July and August and about 10 °C in January and February. The Caucasus Nature Reserve, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, lies just to the north, and the city has the region's most northerly tea plantations.

The name is the Russified form of a Circassian name that comes from the Ubykh Ş̂uaça, a compound of the words for sea and side, and roughly means seaside or coast. Georgian sources offer another derivation, from the Georgian word for the fir tree.

In antiquity the Zygii, a Proto-Adyghe people, lived in the area under the Kingdom of Pontus and then the influence of the Roman Empire. From the 6th to the 11th century it belonged successively to the Georgian kingdoms of Lazica and Abkhazia, which built about a dozen churches within the present city boundaries; the northern wall of an 11th-century Byzantine basilica still stands in the Loo microdistrict. The Christian settlements along the coast were later destroyed by invading Alans, Khazars, Mongols and other nomadic powers whose control was slight.

Russia occupied the coastline in 1829 as a result of the Russo-Circassian War and the Russo-Turkish War of 1828 to 1829, but the Circassians did not accept Russian control and kept resisting the new outposts. Supplying weapons to them from abroad caused a diplomatic conflict between the Russian and British empires in 1836 over the mission of the Vixen. Lazarevskoye was founded as a Russian military outpost in 1839 and named after Admiral Mikhail Lazarev. The Michael Archangel Cathedral, built in 1873 to 1891, commemorates the end of the Caucasian War.

In the Russian Civil War the coast saw armed clashes among the Red Army, White forces and the Democratic Republic of Georgia. A railway from Tuapse to Georgia, running within a kilometre or two of the shore, opened in 1923. After the Crimean resorts passed from the Russian SFSR to the Ukrainian SSR in 1954, Sochi became the unofficial summer capital of the country. In 1961 Soviet officials formed Greater Sochi, stretching 140 kilometres from the southern part of Tuapse to Adler.

Sochi is the largest resort city in Russia, with sanatoriums, hotels and beaches along its coast, and it is divided into four city districts. It hosted the Winter Olympic and Paralympic Games in 2014, with the alpine and Nordic events at the ski resort of Rosa Khutor in Krasnaya Polyana.
socialism: The history of socialism has its origins in the Age of Enlightenment and the French Revolution of 1789, although it has precedents in earlier movements and ideas. Pierre Leroux claimed to have first used the word socialism, in the Parisian journal Le Globe in 1832. He was a follower of Henri de Saint-Simon, one of the founders of what would later be labelled utopian socialism. The utopian socialists condemned liberal individualism for failing to address the poverty, oppression and wealth inequality of the Industrial Revolution. Saint-Simon proposed economic planning and scientific administration, while Robert Owen proposed cooperatives.

Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels wrote The Communist Manifesto in 1847 and 1848, just before the Revolutions of 1848, and called their position scientific socialism. In the last third of the 19th century parties dedicated to democratic socialism arose in Europe, drawing mainly on Marxism. For one week in December 1899 the Australian Labor Party formed the first socialist government in the world, when it was elected in the Colony of Queensland under Premier Anderson Dawson.

Socialism encompasses diverse economic and social systems characterised by social ownership of the means of production, which can be public, community, collective, cooperative or employee ownership. Systems are divided into non-market forms and market socialism, which retains monetary prices and factor markets. In his Dictionary of Socialism (1924), Angelo S. Rappoport analysed forty definitions and found common elements: criticism of the social effects of private ownership of capital, a view that the solution is some form of collective control, and agreement that the result should be a society based on social justice. Major movements include anarchism, communism, the labour movement, Marxism, social democracy and syndicalism.

By the early 1920s communism and social democracy had become the two dominant tendencies within the international socialist movement. In the first half of the 20th century the Soviet Union and the communist parties of the Third International came to represent socialism as a centrally planned economy directed by a state that owns all the means of production, although other trends condemned what they saw as its lack of democracy. The People's Republic of China, founded in 1949, introduced socialism through a state-led economy, land redistribution and the Anti-Rightist Movement, followed by the Great Leap Forward.

Elsewhere reformist social democrats and democratic socialists came to power through the ballot box. In the UK, Herbert Morrison said that socialism is what the Labour government does, while Aneurin Bevan argued that it requires the main streams of economic activity to be brought under public direction. Such governments established mixed economies with partial nationalisation and social welfare, as in the Nordic model.
socialist-party-of-albania: The Party of Labour of Albania, founded by Enver Hoxha, had ruled the country for over four decades. Hoxha's successor, Ramiz Alia, was forced to introduce limited reforms in the late 1980s, and on 11 December 1990 he announced that the party had given up its monopoly of power. It won the Constitutional Assembly election of 1991, the first free elections held in Albania in almost 80 years, by which time it was no longer a Marxist-Leninist party. At an extraordinary congress held from 10 to 13 June 1991 it reorganised itself as the Socialist Party in order to survive in the new system.

Fatos Nano, a man from the intelligentsia, was elected the first chairman. He helped to reform the old communist party and brought it into the Socialist International. In 2004 a faction led by Ilir Meta broke away and formed the Socialist Movement for Integration. On 10 October 2005, after losing the parliamentary election of that year, Nano resigned and was succeeded by Edi Rama.

Under Rama the party formed the Alliance for a European Albania, which united several parties and won the parliamentary election of 2013, returning the Socialists to government after eight years. Running alone, the party won the elections of 2017 and 2021 with 74 seats in each, enough to govern by itself, though it has had the outside support of the Social Democratic Party in parliament.

The party is described as social-democratic. Its platform of 2013 pledged to replace the flat tax with a progressive tax and supported universal health care. It is pro-European, supports Albania's accession to the European Union and its membership of NATO, and regards Kosovo as the country's main strategic partner and ally. It is an associate of the Party of European Socialists. Its emblem is based on the fist and rose designed by José María Cruz Novillo for the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party in 1977, used without that party's official consent.
socrates: Socrates left no writings, and what is known of him comes from others: his pupils Plato and Xenophon, the comic dramatist Aristophanes, and Aristotle, who was born after his death. These accounts often contradict one another, a difficulty scholars call the Socratic problem. Xenophon wrote about him in the Memorabilia, the Oeconomicus, the Symposium and the Apology. How far Plato's dialogues portray the historical Socrates is debated, and some scholars distinguish an earlier, more faithful portrait from a later one carrying Plato's own views.

Socrates was born in 470 or 469 BCE in the Athenian deme of Alopece, to Sophroniscus, a stoneworker, and Phaenarete, a midwife. He had the usual education of a well-off Athenian and served in three campaigns of the Peloponnesian War, according to Plato. He married Xanthippe, with whom he had three sons, and also a daughter of the statesman Aristides. He was indifferent to comfort, owned one ragged coat and walked barefoot, and he criticised both the democrats and the oligarchs of Athens.

The method named for him, the elenchus, is shown mainly in Plato's early dialogues. Socrates asks an apparent expert for a definition, and further questions lead the expert to contradict it. A new definition is then tested in the same way. The discussion usually ends in an impasse, with the interlocutor unable to define what he thought he understood. Socrates frequently proclaimed his ignorance, saying he was sure only that he did not know.

Scholars dispute what the method achieves. In 1982 Gregory Vlastos argued that it could show only that an interlocutor's beliefs were inconsistent. Because Socrates taught no fixed doctrine, later schools drew different conclusions.

In 399 BCE Socrates was accused of impiety and of corrupting the youth. The accusation was brought by a poet, Meletus, with Anytus and Lycon. The trial came after the defeat of Athens by Sparta at the Battle of Aegospotami in 404 BCE and the rule of the Thirty Tyrants, and it probably lasted most of a day. A jury of hundreds of citizens found him guilty. He proposed free meals from the state, or alternatively a fine of one mina of silver, and the jurors ordered his death. Plato relates that he was put to death with hemlock after refusing offers to help him escape.

Almost every philosophical current after Socrates traced its roots to him, among them Plato's Academy, Aristotle's Lyceum, the Cynics and the Stoics, except the Epicureans and the Pyrrhonists. He was considered to have shifted philosophy from the natural world to human affairs.
sofia: Sofia lies in western Bulgaria in the Sofia Valley, at the northern foot of the Vitosha mountain, on an average altitude of 550 metres. It is surrounded by mountains: Vitosha to the south, Lyulin to the west and the Balkan Mountains to the north. It is built west of the Iskar. Its development as a settlement owes much to its central position in the Balkans: three mountain passes lead to the city and have been key roads since antiquity, and Vitosha is the watershed between the Black and Aegean seas. Hot water springs still flow abundantly in the centre.

The area has a history of nearly 7,000 years. A Neolithic village at Slatina is documented. The earliest tribes were the Thracian Tilataei, and in the 500s BCE the area joined the Odrysian kingdom. In 339 BCE Philip II of Macedon destroyed and ravaged the town for the first time. The Celtic tribe Serdi gave the city its name, Serdica; the earliest mention is an Athenian inscription of the 1st century BCE, and according to Dio Cassius the Roman general Crassus subdued the Serdi. The emperor Marcus Ulpius Traianus gave it the name Ulpia Serdica.

During the decline of the Roman Empire the city was raided by Huns, Visigoths, Avars and Slavs. In 809 Khan Krum incorporated it into the First Bulgarian Empire, and it became known as Sredets. In 1018 the Byzantines ended Bulgarian rule until 1194, when the Second Bulgarian Empire took it back. Sredets was a major administrative, economic, cultural and literary hub until the Ottoman conquest in 1382. From 1530 to 1836 Sofia was the regional capital of Rumelia Eyalet, the Ottoman Empire's largest and most important province.

Its population fell from 70,000 in the late 18th century to 19,000 in 1870 and 11,649 in 1878. Bulgarian rule was restored in 1878, and Sofia was selected as the capital of the Third Bulgarian State the next year, beginning a period of intense demographic and economic growth. After the Liberation War, knyaz Alexander Battenberg invited architects from Austria-Hungary to shape the new capital.

Sofia is the capital and largest city of Bulgaria. Ancient Roman, Byzantine and medieval Bulgarian buildings survive in the centre, among them the 4th-century Rotunda of St. George, the walls of the Serdica fortress and part of the Amphitheatre of Serdica. The Boyana Church was included on the World Heritage List in 1979.
solomon: Solomon was born in Jerusalem, the second child of David and his wife Bathsheba, the widow of Uriah the Hittite. The first child of the union, a son conceived while Uriah was alive, died seven days after birth, which the Hebrew Bible suggests was a judgment from God. Solomon had three named full brothers and six known older half-brothers. His two names, Solomon and Jedidiah, are traditionally taken to mean peaceful and friend of God. The conventional dates of his reign, about 970 to 931 BCE, derive from biblical chronology.

According to the Hebrew Bible, God appeared to Solomon in a dream and asked what he wanted. Solomon asked for wisdom in order to rule his people, and God, pleased that he had not asked for long life or the death of his enemies, promised it. The account describes a reign of forty years in which Israel reached a height of splendour and wealth. He allied himself with Hiram I, king of Tyre, who sent materials and an architect for the Temple that David had gathered materials to build. The account also gives him 700 wives and 300 concubines, many of them foreign princesses, and disapproves of his building temples to their gods. It tells of a visit by the Queen of Sheba.

Solomon died of natural causes at around 55 years of age. His son Rehoboam succeeded him, but ten of the tribes refused him and followed Jeroboam, splitting the monarchy into the northern Kingdom of Israel and the smaller southern Kingdom of Judah. The historicity of Solomon is much debated. Current scholarship generally allows that a historical Solomon is possible, but regards the biblical picture of his opulence as almost surely an anachronistic exaggeration. Tradition ascribes to him the books of Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and Song of Songs. He is revered in Islam as the prophet Sulaiman ibn Dawud, and the Solomon Islands were named for him by Álvaro de Mendaña in 1568.
solon: Solon's family belonged to a noble Eupatrid clan of Attica. His father was probably Execestides, which would trace his lineage back to Codrus, the last king of Athens. According to Plutarch he was related to the later tyrant Pisistratus. When Athens and Megara contested possession of Salamis, Solon led the Athenian forces after repeated disasters and raised their morale with a patriotic poem. With the support of Pisistratus he defeated the Megarians around 595 BCE, and the Spartans, asked to settle the dispute, awarded the island to Athens.

According to Diogenes Laërtius, Solon was chosen archon in 594 BCE and repealed all of Draco's laws except those on homicide. His debt relief, later called the seisachtheia, the shaking off of burdens, addressed a system in which farmers who could not honour their obligations, and their families, could be sold into slavery. Aristotle's Athenian Constitution calls him the first people's champion, and says he admitted all citizens to the Ekklesia and formed a court, the Heliaia, from all citizens. His laws were inscribed on wooden axones kept in the Prytaneion.

Modern knowledge is limited. His laws survive only in fragments quoted by Plutarch and others, and fourth-century orators such as Aeschines tended to attribute to him every law of their own day. His poems also survive only in fragments.

After completing his reforms Solon surrendered his extraordinary authority and travelled abroad for ten years so that the Athenians could not press him to repeal any law. Within four years of his departure the old social rifts returned, and Pisistratus ended the factionalism by force and established a tyranny. Solon opposed him and died shortly after, around the age of 70. Pausanias lists him among the Seven Sages of Greece, and Demosthenes credited his reforms with starting a golden age.
somalia: Somalia is the easternmost country in continental Africa. It borders Ethiopia, Djibouti and Kenya, and has the longest coastline on the mainland, more than 3,333 kilometres, along the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. Its land area is 637,657 square kilometres of plateaus, plains and highlands. In the north a semi-desert plain, the Guban, runs parallel to the Gulf of Aden coast, and the Cal Madow range contains the highest peak, Shimbiris, at about 2,416 metres. The country sits at the mouth of the Bab el Mandeb gateway to the Red Sea.

The oldest evidence of burial customs in the Horn of Africa comes from cemeteries in Somalia dating to the 4th millennium BCE. The Laas Geel rock art near Hargeisa is approximately 5,000 years old. Ancient stone ruins have been taken as evidence of a civilisation that traded with Egypt and Mycenaean Greece from the second millennium BCE, supporting the hypothesis that Somalia or adjacent regions were the Land of Punt. An Egyptian expedition to Punt sent by Queen Hatshepsut is recorded on the reliefs at Deir el-Bahari. Puntites traded myrrh, spices, gold, ebony, ivory and frankincense.

In the Middle Ages the Ajuran Sultanate, Adal Sultanate and Sultanate of the Geledi dominated regional trade. The Italian and British empires colonised the sultanates in the late 19th century, forming Italian Somaliland and British Somaliland, which united in 1960 as the Somali Republic. Siad Barre seized power in 1969, launched a failed invasion of Ethiopia and brutally attempted to quash the Somaliland War of Independence.

Barre's regime collapsed in 1991 with the onset of the Somali Civil War. A provisional constitution adopted on 1 August 2012 made Somalia a federation. About 85 per cent of residents are ethnic Somalis. Somali is the official language, Arabic is recognised as a second, and the overwhelming majority are Sunni Muslims. About 80 per cent of the population are nomadic or semi-nomadic pastoralists.
sonderbund-war: In the early 1840s the radical Free Democratic Party of Switzerland, strong in the largely Protestant cantons and among the urban bourgeoisie, won a majority in the Federal Diet, the Tagsatzung, and proposed a new constitution that would draw the cantons closer together. The Diet had also acted against the Catholic Church, closing the monasteries and convents of Aargau in 1841 and seizing their property. When Lucerne recalled the Jesuits to head its education, bands of armed radicals known as Freischärler invaded the canton.

In 1845 Lucerne, Fribourg, Valais, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden and Zug, all predominantly Catholic and under conservative governments, formed the Sonderbund, or separate alliance. Ticino and Solothurn, Catholic but liberal, stayed out. On 21 October 1847 the Diet ordered the league dissolved as a breach of the Federal Treaty of 1815, which forbade such alliances. Austria sent the Sonderbund some money and munitions, but the great powers could not agree on intervention, which Lord Palmerston of Britain refused to support.

The Sonderbund's commander was Jean-Ulrich de Salis-Soglio of Grisons, himself a Protestant. The Diet's choice, Guillaume Henri Dufour of Geneva, was sworn in on 25 October after first declining the office. Neuchâtel and Appenzell Innerrhoden declared themselves neutral and sent no troops. The Sonderbund moved first: troops from Uri seized the St. Gotthard Pass in early November, and the first deaths came on 4 November.

Dufour turned first on isolated Fribourg, which surrendered on 14 November; its act of surrender became the template for the other cantons. Zug's parliament voted to give up on 21 November. On 23 November the federal divisions converged on Lucerne. At Gisikon a third assault, led in person by Colonel Eduard Ziegler, carried the Sonderbund position after two hours; thirty-seven men were killed and about 100 wounded. Federal troops entered Lucerne unopposed the next morning. Unterwalden, Schwyz and Uri yielded between 25 and 27 November, and Valais on 29 November.

The federal army reported 78 killed and 260 wounded; later research arrived at 60 dead and 386 wounded on the federal side and 33 killed and 124 wounded among the Sonderbund. Dufour had ordered his troops to care for the injured and declined to use Congreve rockets, so as not to give the war a violent character. The Sonderbund governments were forced to resign, and Liberals took power in Fribourg, Lucerne and Valais. Federal troops left the occupied cantons by February 1848. The constitution of that year banished the Jesuits from Switzerland, a provision lifted by a vote on 20 May 1973.
song-of-songs: The Song of Songs, in Hebrew Shir ha-Shirim, is one of the five megillot, or scrolls, in the Ketuvim, the last section of the Tanakh. Unlike other books of the Hebrew Bible it is erotic poetry, in which lovers express desire, exchange compliments and invite one another to enjoy. It tells a love story between a woman and her lover through dialogues, dreams and metaphors, and the woman warns the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken love before its time.

Its title follows an idiom of biblical Hebrew that marks the supreme member of a class, as in Holy of Holies, and the name Song of Solomon means a song of, by, for or dedicated to Solomon. It has no plot, but links between its beginning and end form a framework, and scholars have not agreed how to divide it.

The text gives no explicit reference to its author, or to when, where or how it was composed. Its superscription calls it Solomon's, but modern scholarship argues that it may contain ancient material while there is no evidence that Solomon wrote it. Since the 1800s most scholars have dated it to the 3rd century BCE, chiefly on its language, whose vocabulary, morphology and syntax point to a date centuries after Solomon.

It has parallels with Mesopotamian and Egyptian love poetry and with the pastoral poems of Theocritus, and proposals range from the 10th to the 2nd century BCE; some scholars doubt that its language demands a date after the Babylonian exile. Scholars also debate whether it is a single poem or an anthology, and some connect it with the sacred marriage of Ishtar and Tammuz.

Most scholars now read the Song as erotic poetry celebrating human love, not as a divine metaphor. Judaism accepted it into the canon and long read it as an allegory of the love between God and Israel; canonicity was tied to its attribution to Solomon, and Rabbi Akiva is reported to have forbidden singing it in taverns while defending its place in scripture. Kabbalah later gave it a mystical reading.

Many Jews read it during Passover, a custom first recorded in the 8th century. In Christianity it is viewed as an allegory of Christ and his bride, the Church. It has inspired works by Marc Chagall, Carl Theodor Dreyer, Toni Morrison and John Steinbeck.
sophocles: Sophocles was the son of Sophillus, a wealthy member of the rural deme of Hippeius Colonus in Attica, which later became the setting of his play Oedipus at Colonus. He was probably born there a few years before the Battle of Marathon in 490 BCE, and 496 or 497 BCE is the most likely year. His father manufactured armour, and he was highly educated.

In 480 BCE he was chosen to lead the paean, a choral chant to a god, for the Greek victory over the Persians at the Battle of Salamis. He lived through both the Persian Wars and the Peloponnesian War, and died at the age of 90 or 91 in the winter of 406/5 BCE.

His first artistic triumph came in 468 BCE, when he took first prize at the Dionysia and beat Aeschylus, the reigning master of Athenian drama. According to Plutarch, the archon departed from the custom of choosing judges by lot and asked Cimon and the other generals present to decide. His first production was probably in 470 BCE. For almost 50 years he was the most successful playwright in the dramatic competitions at the festivals of the Lenaea and the Dionysia. He competed 30 times and won 24, and was never placed lower than second. Aeschylus won 13 competitions and Euripides four.

He also served Athens in public office. In 443/2 BCE he was one of the Hellenotamiai, the treasurers of Athena, and in 441 BCE, according to the Vita Sophoclis, he was elected one of the ten generals as a junior colleague of Pericles and served in the campaign against Samos. In 411 BCE he was chosen as one of the commissioners, the probouloi, who responded to the destruction of the Athenian expedition in Sicily. Foreign rulers invited him to their courts, but he never accepted.

Sophocles wrote more than 120 plays, of which seven survive complete: Ajax, Antigone, Women of Trachis, Oedipus Rex, Electra, Philoctetes and Oedipus at Colonus. Only Philoctetes, of 409 BCE, and Oedipus at Colonus, staged in 401 BCE after his death by his grandson, can be dated securely. The three Theban plays, Oedipus Rex, Oedipus at Colonus and Antigone, were written for separate competitions many years apart, and they are not a trilogy, which explains some inconsistencies among them.

He is known for innovations in dramatic structure and a deeper development of character than earlier playwrights. Aristotle credits him with adding a third actor, which reduced the role of the chorus, though Themistius attributes this to Aeschylus. Aristotle also used Oedipus Rex in his Poetics as an example of the highest achievement in tragedy. Fragments of the satyr play Ichneutae were discovered in Egypt in 1907, and fragments of the Epigoni in 2005.
soren-kierkegaard: Søren Aabye Kierkegaard was born on 5 May 1813 in Copenhagen, the youngest of seven children of an affluent family. His father, Michael Pedersen Kierkegaard, was a devoutly Christian wool merchant from Jutland who was devoted to the rationalist philosophy of Christian Wolff. The figure of Socrates, whom Kierkegaard met in Plato's dialogues, later shaped his interest in irony and indirect communication.

He met Regine Olsen on 8 May 1837 and proposed to her on 8 September 1840, after passing his theological examinations. He broke off the engagement on 11 August 1841, and after she pleaded with him he ended it verbally on 11 October 1841. His journals blame his melancholy, but his precise motive remains unclear, and the broken engagement is generally considered to have had a major influence on his work.

Kierkegaard published some works under pseudonyms, each presenting a distinct viewpoint, as a way of indirect communication. Either/Or, considered his magnum opus, and Fear and Trembling, his central writing on religion, both appeared in 1843. Critics have accused him of playing with viewpoints without committing to one, though he said all his work came from a service to Christianity.

His key ideas include subjective and objective truth, the knight of faith, anxiety, faith as a passion and the three stages on life's way. He wrote, "Christianity teaches that the way is to become subjective, to become a subject." He attacked Hegelianism by parody, though he admired Hegel personally. A dispute that began with an article by Peder Ludvig Møller in December 1845 led him to ask the satirical paper The Corsair to satirise him. His journals run to over 7,000 pages.

In his last years Kierkegaard attacked the Church of Denmark in newspaper articles and in a series of self-published pamphlets, The Moment. The attack began after Hans Lassen Martensen called the dead Bishop Jacob Peter Mynster a truth-witness, which Kierkegaard strongly objected to. He later said his earlier writing had been preparation for it. He collapsed in the street, spent over a month in Frederiks Hospital, refused communion, and died on 11 November 1855. His nephew Henrik Lund protested at the funeral against burial by the official church.

His work was written in Danish and was at first read mainly in Scandinavia, but was translated into French, German and other languages around the turn of the 20th century. Georg Brandes published the first book on his life and philosophy in 1879. His fame grew greatly in the 1930s, when the existentialist movement named him a precursor, and philosophers both theistic and atheistic drew from him the notions of angst, despair and the importance of the individual.
south-africa: South Africa covers 1,221,037 square kilometres at the southern tip of Africa, with 2,798 kilometres of coastline along the South Atlantic and Indian oceans, and it encloses Lesotho. The interior is a large, almost flat plateau between 1,000 and 2,100 metres high, surrounded by the Great Escarpment, whose eastern stretch is the Drakensberg; Mafadi, at 3,450 metres, is the highest peak. The south-western plateau is the sparsely populated Great Karoo, and the well-watered Highveld holds a great proportion of the commercial farmland and the largest conurbation, Gauteng. The country has three capitals: Pretoria, Cape Town and Bloemfontein.

South Africa holds some of the oldest archaeological and human-fossil sites in the world, among them the caves of the Cradle of Humankind in Gauteng, and modern humans have inhabited Southern Africa for at least 170,000 years. The indigenous San and Khoikhoi were predominantly hunter-gatherers, and the Khoikhoi also practised pastoralism; they were largely displaced or absorbed by the Bantu expansion between 1,500 and 2,000 years ago.

The Kingdom of Mapungubwe formed in the north in the 13th century, and the Venda Kingdom in the 17th. The Dutch established the first European settlement at Table Bay in 1652, the Cape Colony. Its invasion in 1795 and the Battle of Blaauwberg in 1806 led to British occupation, and the Mfecane, a period of upheaval, led to the formation of kingdoms including the Zulu Kingdom.

The Mineral Revolution brought industrialisation and urbanisation. After the Second Boer War the Union of South Africa was created in 1910 by the amalgamation of the Cape, Natal, Transvaal and Orange River colonies, and it became a republic after the 1961 referendum. The multi-racial Cape Qualified Franchise was gradually eroded, and the vast majority of black South Africans were not enfranchised until 1994. The National Party imposed apartheid in 1948, institutionalising earlier racial segregation, and after a struggle by the African National Congress and others the repeal of discriminatory laws began in the mid-1980s.

Universal elections took place in 1994, and since then all racial groups have held political representation in a parliamentary republic of nine provinces, in which the president is both head of state and head of government. The 2022 census counted Black African South Africans at 81%, Coloured at 8.2%, White at 7.3% and Indian or Asian at 2.7%. The country has 12 official languages and has been called the rainbow nation.
south-america: South America lies entirely in the Western Hemisphere and mostly in the Southern Hemisphere. It is bordered on the west by the Pacific Ocean, on the north and east by the Atlantic Ocean, and on the south by the Drake Passage, and it has an area of 17,840,000 square kilometres. The geography of the west is dominated by the Andes, the longest mountain range in the world, whose highest mountain is Aconcagua at 6,962 metres. The east contains highlands and vast lowlands where the Amazon, Orinoco and Paraná flow.

The continent holds several superlatives: Angel Falls in Venezuela is the world's highest uninterrupted waterfall, the Amazon is the largest river by volume, and the Atacama Desert is the driest non-polar place on earth. Lake Titicaca is the highest commercially navigable lake. Most of the population lives near the western or eastern coasts, forming what is called a hollow continent.

South America is thought to have been first inhabited by people who crossed the Bering Land Bridge at least 15,000 years ago and moved south through North America. The Monte Verde II site in Chile, suggested to date to around 14,500 years ago, is among the oldest evidence of human presence. Ancient DNA evidence shows that the peopling was more complex than a single migration, with at least three major dispersals. Llamas and alpacas were domesticated in the Andean highlands circa 3500 BCE.

Caral-Supe on the central Peruvian coast, generally dated to around 3500 BCE, was a pre-ceramic culture whose monumental architecture created one of the first cities of the world. Chavín followed by 900 BCE according to some estimates, and its civilisation spanned 900 to 300 BCE, with artefacts found at Chavín de Huántar in Peru. Irrigation systems and widespread fishing helped establish agrarian societies by 2000 BCE.

The continent includes twelve sovereign countries, two dependent territories and one internal territory, French Guiana. Brazil covers a little less than half of its land area and holds around half of its population. Most countries are presidential republics, and Guyana and Suriname are parliamentary republics.
