A payroll register of 1526 lists 40 societies with more than 600 members. The poets Fuzûlî and Bâki worked under him. In 1534 he broke with tradition by marrying Hürrem, a former concubine.

Suleiman died on 6 September 1566, aged 71, on campaign in Hungary, before an Ottoman victory at the siege of Szigetvár. His Grand Vizier Sokollu Mehmed Pasha kept the death secret during the retreat so that Selim II could be enthroned. His body was taken to Istanbul, while his heart and some organs were buried at Turbék, where a mausoleum became a pilgrimage site.

His image as an ideal ruler was built in his own reign, notably by the chancellor Celalzade Mustafa. Later Ottoman writers of advice literature held his reign up as a model and presented departures from it as decline. Western historians long accepted that account, but since the 1980s scholars have overwhelmingly rejected the idea of decline after his death, seeing instead a period of crisis and adaptation.
sumatra: Sumatra is one of the Sunda Islands and the largest island entirely within Indonesia, about 482,286 square kilometres including adjacent islands. It stretches about 1,790 kilometres along a northwest-southeast axis, with the equator crossing its centre. The Bukit Barisan mountains, with several active volcanoes, form its backbone, while the northeast has large plains of swamps, mangrove forest and river systems. The narrow Strait of Malacca separates it from the Malay Peninsula, and the Sunda Strait, with the Krakatoa archipelago, separates it from Java. The Great Sumatran fault and the Sunda megathrust run along its west coast, so earthquakes and tsunamis are common.

Sumatra has been inhabited since prehistoric times. Its ancient Sanskrit names, Svarṇadvīpa and Svarṇabhūmi, meant the Island of Gold and the Land of Gold, after gold deposits in its highlands. The earliest known mention of the form Sumatra is from 1017, when a local king, Haji Sumatrabhumi, sent an envoy to China. By 692 the Melayu Kingdom had been absorbed by Srivijaya, whose influence declined in the 11th century after a defeat by the Chola Empire of southern India in 1025. By the end of the 12th century Srivijaya had shrunk to a kingdom, and the Palembang area later declined as Srivijaya's heritage was superseded by the economic policy of the Singhasari and Majapahit.

Because it lies close to the Strait of Malacca, Sumatra was the first area of the archipelago to receive Islam, which spread through trade and the formation of kingdoms; in the 13th century the king of the Samudra kingdom converted. Aceh became known in the 16th century as a trading centre for pepper, with trade routes to the Mediterranean via the Red Sea to rival the Portuguese. Under Iskandar Muda, whose reign is called the golden age of Sumatra, it extended its cultural influence to Padang and Johor.

The Dutch Empire gradually took over the princely states. Aceh posed a major obstacle, and the Dutch fought the long and costly Aceh War from 1873 to 1903. Japan invaded Sumatra in 1942, and in 1945 it was one of the eight original provinces of Indonesia.

Sumatra is divided into ten Indonesian provinces and has about 62 million people, with more than 52 spoken languages. Its largest indigenous peoples are the Malays, Minangkabau, Bataks, Acehnese and Lampungs, and its largest city is Medan. Most Sumatrans are Muslims. Three national parks form the Tropical Rainforest Heritage of Sumatra World Heritage Site, and the island is home to the Sumatran tiger, elephant, rhinoceros and orangutan.
sumer: Most historians have suggested that Sumer was first permanently settled between about 5500 and 3300 BCE by a West Asian people who spoke Sumerian, a language isolate that is neither Semitic nor Indo-European. Other suggestions, that the Sumerians came from the Green Sahara or the Caucasus, are not generally accepted. In their own inscriptions the Sumerians called their land Kengir, the country of the noble lords. The Sumerians were unknown in the early period of modern archaeology. Jules Oppert first published the word Sumer, in a lecture of 17 January 1869, and the first major excavation of a Sumerian city was at Girsu in 1877.

In the late 4th millennium BCE Sumer was divided into many independent city-states, each centred on a temple to its patron deity and ruled by a priestly governor, the ensi, or by a king, the lugal. The first war recorded in any detail, between Lagash and Umma about 2450 BCE, is shown on the Stele of the Vultures. The Akkadian Empire, founded by Sargon of Akkad about 2334 BCE, was the first state to unite larger parts of Mesopotamia. The Third Dynasty of Ur under Ur-Nammu and Shulgi, about 2112 to 2004 BCE, did so again. By then Amorites were founding competing powers in the south, and Babylon united Mesopotamia about 1700 BCE.

Sumerian farmers on the Tigris and Euphrates grew a surplus of grain, which allowed urban life, and the need to manage temple accounts led to writing. The earliest known texts come from Uruk and Jemdet Nasr. Sumerian cuneiform is the oldest deciphered script, or the second oldest after Egyptian hieroglyphs. The Sumerian language continued as a sacred and school language in Babylonia and Assyria for as long as cuneiform was used, as Latin did in medieval Europe. Sumerian mathematics used a sexagesimal place-value system, and the Sumerians were among the first to map the stars into constellations.
sun-tzu: Sun Tzu means Master Sun and is an honorific. His birth name is said to have been Sun Wu. The earliest account of his life is a short biography in the Shiji, the Records of the Grand Historian, written around 97 BCE by Sima Qian. It says he was born in Qi, in present-day Shandong, near the end of the Spring and Autumn period. The scholar Victor Mair considers the biography essentially fictional.

According to the Shiji, King Helü of Wu heard of Sun Wu's Art of War, summoned him and asked him to show how he trained soldiers, using the king's harem of 180 concubines. Sun Tzu appointed the two concubines the king favoured most as commanders and gave orders, which they ignored, laughing. Over the king's protests he had the two commanders executed, after which the rest obeyed at once, and the king made Sun Wu a general. He is said to have led Wu to victory over the much larger state of Chu at the Battle of Boju in 506 BCE.

Beginning in the 12th century scholars began to doubt that he existed. Ye Shi noticed that the Zuo Zhuan, which describes the Battle of Boju in far more detail and was written centuries before the Shiji, never mentions Sun Tzu, and the name Sun Wu appears in no text earlier than the Shiji.

The Art of War is a Classical Chinese text in 13 chapters, each devoted to a different set of skills related to warfare, strategy and tactics. It also advocates diplomacy and the cultivation of relations with other states. The earliest parts probably date from at least a century after Sun Tzu, and since the 12th century most scholars have placed the text at the beginning of the Warring States period. Bamboo slips found at Yinque Shan in Shandong in 1972 hold about a third of the chapters of the modern text, with closely matching wording.

The earliest known commentary was written by the warlord Cao Cao in the early 3rd century CE. Emperor Shenzong of Song formalized the Seven Military Classics in 1080, and the Art of War led that anthology for almost 1,500 years. Lionel Giles completed the first annotated English translation in 1910.
sun-yat-sen: Sun Yat-sen was born on 12 November 1866 in the village of Cuiheng, Xiangshan County, in Guangdong, to Sun Dacheng and Madame Yang. His father owned little land and worked as a tailor in Macau and as a journeyman and porter. At 13 he went to live in Hawaii with his elder brother Sun Mei, who paid for his schooling at the ʻIolani School, where he studied English, mathematics, science and Christianity. His brother, alarmed at his interest in Christianity, sent him back to China in 1883. He graduated from the Hong Kong College of Medicine for Chinese in 1892.

In 1894 Sun wrote a petition on modernising China and travelled to Tianjin to present it to the viceroy Li Hongzhang, who did not receive him. He turned to revolution and founded the Revive China Society in Hawaii. Its First Guangzhou Uprising of 26 October 1895 failed after the plan leaked. In London in 1896 he was detained for 12 days at the Chinese Legation, which planned to smuggle him to China, and was freed through the efforts of James Cantlie, the press and the Foreign Office. Further uprisings also failed, and he raised money among overseas Chinese. His Three Principles of the People were nationalism, democracy and welfare.

After the 1911 revolution representatives meeting in Nanjing elected him provisional president on 29 December 1911. When the Qing emperor abdicated on 12 February 1912, Sun stepped down and Yuan Shikai became provisional president. The Kuomintang was formed on 25 August 1912, and its leader Song Jiaoren was assassinated on 20 March 1913, almost certainly on Yuan's secret order. Sun's Second Revolution failed in July 1913 and he fled to Japan. In 1921 he began a military government in Guangzhou, and he later cooperated with the Chinese Communist Party.

In January 1925 an operation at Peking Union Medical College Hospital found extensive cancer of the liver. Sun died on 12 March 1925, aged 58, and an autopsy gave the primary cancer as that of the gall bladder. After his death the Nationalist government split into rival factions led by Chiang Kai-shek, Wang Jingwei and the Western Hills Group. The Republic of China calls Sun the Father of the Nation, while the People's Republic of China honours him as the Forerunner of the Revolution, and his home county of Xiangshan was renamed Zhongshan in his honour.
suniti-devi: Suniti Devi was born on 30 September 1864, a daughter of Keshub Chandra Sen of Calcutta and Jagonmohini Sen. She was fourteen when she married. For two years afterwards she stayed in her father's house, since her husband left for London for higher studies immediately after the wedding. She had four sons and three daughters. Two of her sons, Rajendra Narayan and Jitendra Narayan, later became Maharajas of Cooch Behar. Her daughters Sudhira and Pratibha married the brothers Alan and Miles Mander of Wightwick Manor in England, and Sukriti married Jyotsna Nath Ghoshal, a nephew of Rabindranath Tagore.

In 1887, when she attended the Golden Jubilee of Queen Victoria with her husband, she was made a Companion of the Order of the Crown of India, the first Indian woman to receive the honour. She was also present at the Delhi Durbar of 1911.

The girls' school that her husband set up in her name in 1881, later called Suniti Academy, was her idea. She gave it annual grants, exempted the pupils from tuition fees and rewarded those who did well. She arranged for palace cars to carry the girls between home and school and, to avoid controversy, ordered the car windows to be curtained. With her sister Sucharu Devi, Maharani of Mayurbhanj, she financed the foundation of the Maharani Girls' High School in Darjeeling in 1908. She was President of the State Council and in 1932 the first President of the All Bengal Women's Union.

She was also an author. Bengal Dacoits and Tigers, a collection of short stories, was published in Calcutta in 1916. The Beautiful Mogul Princesses, published in London in 1918, tells the lives of Mumtaz Mahal, Zebunissa, Nur Jahan and another princess. The Autobiography of an Indian Princess appeared in London in 1921, and her last book, The Life of Princess Yashodara: Wife and Disciple of the Lord Buddha, in 1929. She died suddenly at Ranchi on 10 November 1932. In Cooch Behar the school, Sunity Road and a tank known as the Sunity Tank or Bairagi Dighi are named after her.
suriname: Suriname lies on the Guiana Shield on the northern coast of South America, bordered by the Atlantic Ocean to the north, French Guiana to the east, Brazil to the south and Guyana to the west. It is the smallest sovereign country in South America. The northern lowland coast has been cultivated, and most of the people live there. The south is tropical rainforest and sparsely inhabited savanna, covering about 80% of the land. The name may come from an Indigenous people called the Surinen, who lived there at the time of European contact. British settlers wrote it Surinam, which long remained the standard English spelling until the official change to Suriname in January 1978.

Indigenous settlement dates back to about 3,000 BCE. The Lokono were a nomadic coastal people who lived by hunting, foraging and fishing, and the Carib, using superior sailing ships, conquered them. British settlers founded the first European colony at Marshall's Creek on the Suriname River in 1630. Jews, expelled from Spain and Portugal, began to settle from the early 17th century and were granted freedom of religion in 1665. In 1667, in the negotiations leading to the Treaty of Breda, the Dutch kept the plantation colony they had gained from the English, and the English kept New Amsterdam, which they renamed New York.

Under Dutch rule Suriname was a lucrative plantation colony, mostly of sugar, driven by African slave labour. About 300,000 enslaved Africans were taken there from the mid-1600s to the early 1800s. After slavery was abolished in 1863, indentured servants were recruited mostly from British India and the Dutch East Indies. Suriname became a constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in 1954 and independent on 25 November 1975.

Suriname is a representative democratic republic under the Constitution of 1987. Paramaribo is the capital and largest city, home to nearly half the population. Dutch is the official language, and Sranan Tongo, an English-based creole, is widely used. No ethnic group forms a majority. The population includes descendants of indentured workers from India, Java and China and of enslaved Africans, among them the Maroons, whose ancestors escaped to the interior. The Central Suriname Nature Reserve, established in 1998, became a World Heritage Site in 2000.
suva: Suva lies around a harbour on a hilly peninsula in the south-east corner of Viti Levu, between Laucala Bay and Suva Harbour, in Rewa Province. The mountains to the north and west catch the south-east trade winds, so conditions are moist all year. The city has a tropical rainforest climate and averages about 3,000 millimetres of rain a year, with no true dry season. Fiji's second governor, Sir Arthur Gordon, is said to have remarked that he had never seen it rain anywhere as it rains in Suva. Although the city is almost surrounded by sea, its coast is lined with mangroves, and a significant part of the centre, including the Parliament buildings, stands on reclaimed mangrove swamp.

In 1868, when Suva was still a small village, the Bauan chieftain Seru Epenisa Cakobau granted 5,000 square kilometres of land to the Australian-based Polynesia Company in exchange for its promise to pay off debts owed to the United States. More than a tenth of that land, 575 square kilometres, was near Suva. The company meant to develop cotton farming, but the land and climate proved unsuitable. Control of the Fiji Islands was ceded to the United Kingdom in 1874.

The colonial authorities moved the capital to Suva from Levuka, on Ovalau, because Levuka's position between a steep mountain and the sea made expansion impractical. Colonel F. E. Pratt of the Royal Engineers, appointed Surveyor-General in 1875, designed the new capital, assisted by W. Stephens and Colonel R. W. Stewart. Suva became a municipality in 1910 under the Municipal Constitution Ordinance of 1909, and its area stayed at one square mile until 1952, when it annexed the Muanikau and Samabula wards. In October of that year it was designated a city, Fiji's first. Later it took in Tamavua and the Cunningham area.

Among its colonial-period landmarks are the Suva City Carnegie Library, built in 1909, and Government House, built in 1882, destroyed by a lightning fire in 1921 and rebuilt in 1928. The government building complex stands on a drained creek bed, with foundations of reinforced concrete pilings driven in from 1935, and was completed in 1939. The Fiji Museum was founded in 1904 and moved to Thurston Gardens in 1954.

Suva is the capital and most populous settlement of Fiji, with 93,874 people at the 2017 census and a metropolitan population of 268,423. Indigenous Fijians and Indo-Fijians form the bulk of its population, alongside Rotumans, Lauans, Europeans, part-Europeans and Chinese. English is the most widely spoken language, with Fijian, Fiji Hindi and others also used. It is the site of the main campus of the University of the South Pacific, and Kings Wharf handles much of Fiji's international shipping. Suva hosted the Pacific Games in 1963, 1979 and 2003.
swami-vivekananda: Vivekananda was born as Narendranath Datta on 12 January 1863 in Calcutta, in an aristocratic Bengali Kayastha family. His father, Vishwanath Datta, was an attorney at the Calcutta High Court, and his mother, Bhubaneswari Devi, was devout. In 1879 he was the only student to receive first-division marks in the Presidency College entrance examination. He read widely in Western philosophy and in Hindu scriptures, corresponded with Herbert Spencer, and completed a Bachelor of Arts in 1884. He first met Ramakrishna probably in November 1881, and after his father died in 1884 Ramakrishna became his primary spiritual focus. On Christmas Eve 1886, at Antpur, he and eight other disciples took formal monastic vows.

In 1888 Narendra left the monastery as a wandering monk, with a water pot, a staff and two books, the Bhagavad Gita and The Imitation of Christ. For five years he travelled on foot and by railway, living on alms and meeting people of every religion and station. On the suggestion of Raja Ajit Singh of Khetri he took the name Vivekananda. He left Bombay for Chicago on 31 May 1893. At the Parliament of the World's Religions, opened on 11 September 1893, he began his short speech with the words Sisters and brothers of America and received a two-minute standing ovation. He then lectured across the United States and founded the Vedanta Societies of New York and San Francisco.

Vivekananda synthesised classical yoga and Advaita Vedanta. Influenced by Ramakrishna, he saw Vedanta as the basis for serving human beings as manifestations of the divine. He taught that each soul is potentially divine and that all religions are different paths to the same goal. Most of his published works, among them Raja Yoga, were based on lectures. He founded the Ramakrishna Math as a monastic order and the Ramakrishna Mission for social service and education. He died on 4 July 1902 at Belur Math after meditating. His birthday, 12 January, is observed in India as National Youth Day.
sweden: Sweden lies on the eastern part of the Scandinavian Peninsula, west of the Baltic Sea and Gulf of Bothnia, and covers 450,295 square kilometres, making it the largest Nordic country. The Scandinavian mountain chain separates it from Norway, and Kebnekaise, at 2,096.8 metres, is the highest point. About 15% of the country lies north of the Arctic Circle, and around 65% of the land is forested. The north, Norrland, takes up almost 60% of the territory and is sparsely populated, while the highest density is in the Mälaren valley and around Stockholm. Vänern is the third largest lake in Europe.

Sweden's prehistory begins around 12,000 BCE, with reindeer-hunting camps of the Bromme culture in Scania. The Roman historian Tacitus first described the Swedes, as the Suiones, in his Germania of 98 CE, noting ships with a prow at each end. The runic script was in use among the south Scandinavian elite by at least the second century CE.

In the sixth century the Byzantine historian Jordanes named two tribes in Scandza now taken to be Swedes, the Suetidi and Suehans, who supplied black fox skins to the Roman world. The inhabitants emerged as the Geats and Swedes, part of the sea-faring Norsemen, and a unified Swedish state was established during the late 10th century.

In 1397 Sweden joined Norway and Denmark in the Kalmar Union, which it left in 1523. When Sweden entered the Thirty Years' War on the Protestant side its territories expanded, forming the Swedish Empire, which controlled much of the Baltic Sea and remained one of the great powers of Europe until the early 18th century. Most conquered territories outside the peninsula were lost in the 18th and 19th centuries, and the eastern half of Sweden, present-day Finland, passed to Imperial Russia in 1809. In 1814 Sweden forced Norway into a personal union by military means, the last war in which it was directly involved; the union lasted until 1905.

Sweden is a constitutional monarchy and a parliamentary democracy, with a 349-member unicameral Riksdag. Under the 1974 Instrument of Government the king has no formal political power. The country is divided into 21 counties and 290 municipalities, and its Nordic welfare system provides universal health care. Its population is about 10.6 million, and five minority groups are officially recognised: Jews, Romani, Sámi, Sweden Finns and Tornedalians. Sweden joined the European Union in 1995 and NATO in 2024.
sweet-potato: The sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) originated in the warm tropical regions of South America, in what is now Ecuador, and was domesticated in either Central or South America. In Central America domesticated sweet potatoes were present at least 5,000 years ago, and local peoples most likely spread them to the Caribbean and South America by 2500 BCE. The oldest radiocarbon-dated remains known, from caves in the Chilca Canyon in Peru, are about 8080 BCE old. Ceramics modelled after sweet potatoes are often found in the Moche culture.

Before Europeans reached the Americas, the sweet potato was grown in Polynesia and has been radiocarbon-dated in the Cook Islands to 1210-1400 CE. A common hypothesis is that Polynesians who had travelled to South America and back brought a cutting to central Polynesia. Genetic similarities with indigenous Americans such as the Zenú, and the likeness of the Polynesian word kumala, as in Māori kūmara, to Quechua k'umara, point the same way, and the present scholarly consensus favours pre-Columbian contact.

The plant is a herbaceous perennial vine whose stems crawl on the ground and root at the nodes. Its large, starchy, sweet-tasting tuberous roots are eaten as a root vegetable, and the young shoots and leaves as greens. It belongs to the morning glory family and is only distantly related to the potato, and the darker sweet potatoes called yams in parts of North America are even more distant from true yams. The plant does not tolerate frost and grows best at an average temperature of 24 °C. It is propagated by cuttings or by shoots called slips, and the roots mature in two to nine months.

The first Europeans to taste sweet potatoes were members of Christopher Columbus's expedition in 1492. The name that stayed was the Taíno batata, which the Spanish combined with the Quechua word for potato, papa, to make patata for the common potato. In some tropical areas the roots are a staple food, usually cooked, though the American colonists of the Southeast ate them raw. In northeastern Uganda sun-dried slices, amukeke, are a staple, and in West Africa the leaves and vine tips are widely eaten as a vegetable. In South America the juice of red sweet potatoes mixed with lime juice dyes cloth in shades from pink to black.
switzerland: Switzerland covers 41,291 square kilometres between the Alps, the Swiss Plateau and the Jura Mountains. The Alps make up about 60% of the area, while most of the population lives on the plateau, where cities such as Zurich, Geneva, Basel and Bern stand. Glaciers cover 1,063 square kilometres, and the headwaters of the Rhine, Inn, Ticino and Rhône rise there; the springs of the Rhône and the Rhine are only about 22 kilometres apart, although one river reaches the Mediterranean Sea and the other the North Sea. The country has more than 1500 lakes, among them Lake Geneva, Lake Constance and Lake Maggiore.

The oldest traces of hominids in Switzerland date to about 150,000 years ago, and the oldest known farming settlements, at Gächlingen, to around 5300 BCE. The La Tène culture developed from around 450 BCE, and the Helvetii, one of its most prominent tribes, held the Swiss Plateau.

In 58 BCE they left it, under the influence of the aristocrat Orgetorix, and were defeated by Julius Caesar at the Battle of Bibracte, after which Caesar forced them back to their lands. In 15 BCE Tiberius and his brother Drusus conquered the Alps for the Roman Empire. Towns such as Aventicum and Augusta Raurica reached a considerable size in the first and second centuries CE.

The Old Swiss Confederacy arose in the Late Middle Ages as a defensive and commercial alliance, and the Federal Charter of 1291 is regarded as its founding document. Its independence from the Holy Roman Empire was formally recognised in the Peace of Westphalia in 1648. Revolutionary France invaded in 1798 and imposed the centralist Helvetic Republic, which Napoleon abolished in 1803, reinstating a confederation. After 1830 liberal and conservative movements came into conflict, and the constitution of 1848 created the present federal system.

Switzerland is a federal republic of 26 cantons, with Bern as the federal city. The Federal Assembly has two houses, the Council of States with 46 members and the National Council with 200, and the executive is the seven-member Federal Council. Citizens may challenge laws passed by parliament through optional referendums. The country has four principal linguistic regions, German, French, Italian and Romansh, and about 9 million people. It has followed a policy of armed neutrality since the 16th century, joined the United Nations in 2002 and hosts many international institutions.
sydney: Sydney is a coastal basin, with the Tasman Sea to the east, the Blue Mountains to the west, the Hawkesbury River to the north and the Woronora Plateau to the south. The urban area surrounds Sydney Harbour and extends about 60 kilometres from the Pacific Ocean to the escarpment of the Blue Mountains. The Cumberland Plain, relatively flat, lies to the south and west of the harbour, and the Hornsby Plateau, cut by steep valleys, lies to the north. The flat southern areas were developed first, and the northern reaches became more heavily populated only after the Sydney Harbour Bridge was built. About seventy surf beaches lie along the coast.

The first people in the area were Aboriginal Australians. Flaked pebbles in Western Sydney's gravel might indicate human presence 45,000 to 50,000 years ago, and radiocarbon dating shows human activity from around 30,000 years ago. Before the British arrived there were 4,000 to 8,000 Aboriginal people in the region, living by fishing, hunting and gathering plants and shellfish. Greater Sydney covers the traditional lands of 28 known clans, among them the Gadigal, whose territory along the southern shore of Port Jackson includes the site of the first British settlement.

In 1788 Captain Arthur Phillip, the first governor of New South Wales, named the cove Sydney Cove after Home Secretary Thomas Townshend, 1st Viscount Sydney; its Aboriginal name was Warrane. The population was under 1,000 in 1788 and almost tripled in ten years to 2,953 with convict transportation. The first five governors had near autocratic power. Governor Macquarie set ambitious standards for building, and the convict Francis Greenway, pardoned in 1818, designed the Hyde Park Barracks in 1819. Sydney was declared a city in 1842, when an elected municipal council was set up. New South Wales achieved responsible government in 1856, and in 1901, with the federation of the Australian colonies, Sydney became the capital of the state.

Greater Sydney consists of 658 suburbs spread across 33 local government areas, and the 2021 census recorded a population of 5,231,150. The Australian Museum, opened in 1827, remains Australia's oldest natural history museum, and the Museum of Sydney stands on the site of the first Government House. The Sydney Opera House is World Heritage listed. Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park holds around 1,500 pieces of Aboriginal rock art, the largest cluster of Indigenous sites in Australia.
syria: The modern state of Syria covers 185,180 km2 in the Eastern Mediterranean and the Levant. Its land runs from the Mediterranean coastal plains to the mountains of the west, where Mount Hermon, at 2,814 metres, is the highest point, and much of the centre and east is arid plateau and desert. The valleys of the Euphrates, Orontes and Khabur rivers support agriculture and settlement. Commercial petroleum was first discovered in the northeast in 1956.

The name Syria is borrowed from Ancient Greek, which took it from Luwian sura/i-, attested in the 8th century BCE, and mainstream scholarship relates it to Assyria. From the Seleucid Empire the Greeks applied it to the Levant without distinguishing the Assyrians of Mesopotamia from the Arameans of the Levant. Under the Roman Empire the larger Syria was divided into provinces such as Judaea, renamed Palaestina in 135 CE, and Phoenice, established in 194.

The Natufian culture became sedentary around the 11th millennium BCE, and the site of Tell Qaramel has round stone towers dated to 10650 BCE. The earliest recorded indigenous civilization was the Kingdom of Ebla, near present-day Idlib, which appears to have been founded around 3500 BCE and grew rich through trade with Sumer, Assyria and Akkad and contact with Egypt.

One of its early texts, the Treaty between Ebla and Abarsal of about 2300 BCE, is a trading agreement. Ebla was weakened by a long war with Mari, and in the first half of the 23rd century BCE the conquests of Sargon of Akkad and Naram-Sin ended its domination of Syria.

The modern state emerged from a French Mandate. It gained de jure independence in 1945 as a founding member of the United Nations, and French troops withdrew in April 1946. Coups and coup attempts followed between 1949 and 1971, and a union with Egypt lasted from 1958 to 1961. The Ba'ath Party took power in 1963. Hafez al-Assad came to power in 1970 and was succeeded on his death in 2000 by his son Bashar. A civil war began in 2011, and the Assad government fell in December 2024.
szczecin: Szczecin lies on the Oder, south of the Szczecin Lagoon and the Bay of Pomerania, near the Baltic Sea and the German border. It is situated along the southwestern shore of Dąbie Lake, on both sides of the Oder and on several large islands between the river's two branches, and is surrounded by forests and heaths. The name, Stettin in German, is of Proto-Slavic origin, and Maria Malec lists eleven theories about it, among them an Old Slavic word for a hill peak and the personal name Szczota.

The recorded history of Szczecin began in the 8th century, when Vikings and West Slavs settled in Pomerania. The West Slavs erected a stronghold on the site of the later castle. Mieszko I of Poland took control of Pomerania in the Early Middle Ages and it became part of Poland in the 10th century, but Mieszko II Lambert effectively lost control and had to accept German suzerainty. The city was later the capital of the Duchy of Pomerania, ruled by the House of Griffin, which was at various times under the suzerainty of Poland, the Duchy of Saxony, the Holy Roman Empire and Denmark.

From the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 Stettin was the capital of Swedish Pomerania, and it was turned into a major Swedish fortress. After the downfall of the Swedish Empire under Charles XII it passed to Prussia in 1720. In October 1806 the Prussian commander Friedrich von Romberg surrendered the city to the French under General Lasalle, who had only 800 men against Romberg's 5,300; Romberg was sentenced to life imprisonment in 1809. The city grew from 6,081 inhabitants in 1720 to 224,119 in 1905.

After the Second World War the city became part of Poland again under the Potsdam Agreement, which resulted in a nearly complete exchange of population. In 1980 the first agreement between protesters and the communist regime was signed in Szczecin, paving the way for the creation of Solidarity.

Szczecin is the capital and largest city of the West Pomeranian Voivodeship and the seventh-largest city in Poland, and a major seaport. Its architecture reflects the late 19th century and early 20th, historicist Gründerzeit and Art Nouveau, with social realism prevalent in areas rebuilt after the Allied bombing. Its landmarks include the Szczecin Cathedral, the Ducal Castle and the National Museum.
szeged: Szeged lies near the southern border of Hungary on both banks of the Tisza River, just south of the mouth of the Maros, almost in the centre of the Carpathian Basin. The name may be a shortened form of Partiscum, a Roman colony of the 2nd century, or it may come from the Hungarian szeg, 'corner', for the bend of the Tisza.

The name Szeged first appears in 1183, in a document of King Béla III. The Mongol invasion destroyed the town, but its people returned from the swamps and rebuilt it. In the 14th century, under Louis the Great, it became the most important town of southern Hungary, and King Sigismund of Luxembourg had a wall built. It became a free royal town in 1498.

The Ottoman army pillaged Szeged on 28 September 1526 and occupied it in 1543, when it became a sanjak centre. It was taken from Ottoman rule on 23 October 1686 and regained free royal status in 1715. Charles III gave it the coat of arms still in use in 1719, and Piarist monks opened a grammar school in 1721. Witch trials were frequent between 1728 and 1744. In July 1849 the town was the last seat of the revolutionary government of the Hungarian Revolution.

The flood of 1879 swept away the town: only 265 of 5,723 houses remained and 165 people died. Emperor Franz Joseph promised that Szeged would be more beautiful than before, and a new city with palaces and wide streets rose from the ruins. The University of Kolozsvár moved to Szeged in 1921 after Hungary lost Transylvania. In the Second World War 6,000 inhabitants were killed, and the ghetto holding the Jews of the city and nearby villages was liquidated in June 1944.

Szeged is the largest city and regional centre of the Southern Great Plain and the seat of Csongrád-Csanád county. The University of Szeged was established in 1581. The city is known for paprika, for the Pick Szeged salami factory, which began as Mark Pick's shop in 1869, and for its fish soup, halászlé.
